name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana will offer death row inmate Todd Wessinger lethal injection option
text:
Louisiana officials, including Gov. Jeff Landry, say they will agree to execute Todd Wessinger through lethal injection if he agrees to the use of pentobarbital. Wessinger, convicted of the 1995 murder of two Baton Rouge restaurant employees, is challenging the state's use of nitrogen hypoxia to carry out the death penalty. (Photo courtesy of Louisiana Office of Attorney General)Louisiana leaders will offer a man who’s been on death row nearly 30 years the option to die by lethal injection in response to his legal challenge of nitrogen gas executions, the method the state has used most recently.
Attorney General Liz Murrill formally extended the offer Monday in a federal court filing to Todd Wessinger, who was convicted in the 1995 murders of his former two co-workers, David Breakwell and Stephanie Guzzardo, at a Baton Rouge restaurant. Wessinger, who had recently been fired from his job, was sentenced to death two years later.
Wessinger’s attorneys filed a lawsuit Sept. 4 to avert Louisiana’s use of nitrogen hypoxia for his execution, during which the gas is administered to deprive the condemned person of oxygen until their vital organs fail. The method violates the Eighth Amendment ban on cruel and unusual punishment, his lawyers argue. 
They also objected to the use of a two-drug regimen for lethal injection using midazolam and hydromorphone, which Louisiana lists under its approved execution protocols. That option “presents a substantial risk of serious harm to a condemned prisoner” who could remain conscious and in distress during the procedure, the lawyers wrote. 
Wessinger’s legal team also noted in their federal court complaint that Louisiana can also carry out executions with a single drug, pentobarbital, the same one used in the botched execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike in Tennessee on Sept. 30.
“(P)entobarbital is a feasible and readily implemented alternative that would significantly reduce the substantial risk of severe harm presented by execution through nitrogen hypoxia or the two-drug midazolam and hydromorphone series,” Wessinger’s lawsuit reads. 
His attorneys, with the MacArthur Justice Center, did not respond to a request for comment. In the lawsuit, they said the state could obtain pentobarbital from a pharmacist without putting at risk its contracts with pharmaceutical companies that supply medications for people at state prisons. Major drugmakers have declined to provide components for lethal injections since 2016 following pressure from death penalty opponents.     
A spokesperson for the Louisiana Department of Public Safety and Corrections declined to answer a question about whether it has a supply of pentobarbital, citing the ongoing lawsuit.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Murrill’s filing on Monday asks U.S. District Judge John deGravelles, an appointee of President Barack Obama to Louisiana’s Middle District Court, to dismiss Wessinger’s lawsuit if he declines pentobarbital. She also noted that Wessinger’s attorneys acknowledge no state has carried out executions with midazolam and hydromorphone since 2014, and she rejected suggestions from Wessinger’s attorneys that nitrogen hypoxia is unconstitutional.
State Corrections Secretary Gary Wescott provided a declaration to the federal court, saying that will use pentobarbital if Wessinger chooses that method of lethal injection.
State corrections officials have not set a date to put Wessinger to death, though deGravelles agreed earlier this month with a federal appellate court ruling that essentially clears the way for the state to carry out his execution. Murrill has described Wessinger’s latest lawsuit as another delaying tactic.  
Louisiana carried out its first and only nitrogen gas execution March 18, 2025, ending the life of Jessie Hoffman for the 1996 kidnapping of Mary “Molly” Elliott in New Orleans and her murder in St. Tammany Parish. U.S. District Judge Shelly Dick in the Middle District Court, also an Obama appointee, had blocked Hoffman’s execution, but the U.S. Supreme Court overrode her stay in a 5-4 vote. 
Hoffman would have likely been the second man in the state put to death with nitrogen gas, but Christopher Sepulvado, 81, died Feb. 22, 2025, at Louisiana State Penitentiary from an infection that followed a leg amputation less than a month before his execution was scheduled. Sepulvado was convicted in DeSoto Parish for the 1992 murder of his 6-year-old stepson Wesley Allen Mercer.  
Murrill pledged to carry out as many as four executions last year, but district attorneys in Caddo and Rapides parishes who obtained death warrants had their efforts blocked when judges determined the defendants in question had not pursued all of their appeals options.
Louisiana hasn’t administered a lethal injection since 2010 when Gerald Bordelon was put to death for the 2002 kidnapping and murder of his 12-year-old stepdaughter, Courtney LeBlanc, in Livingston Parish. Officials used a three-drug combination for Bordelon’s execution — sodium thiopental, pancuronium bromide and potassium chloride — which would be the last in Louisiana for 15 years until the legislature approved the use of nitrogen hypoxia in 2024. 
Since pharmaceutical companies stopped providing drugs for lethal injections, states with capital punishment have struggled to obtain the medications and turned to other execution methods.
Alabama was the first state to use nitrogen hypoxia to carry out the death penalty in January 2024 and has since put seven people to death using the method.
The very first nitrogen gas execution at Holman Correctional Center in Atmore, Alabama, took place days after Gov. Jeff Landry took office in Louisiana. He called state lawmakers into a special session the following month to focus on criminal justice measures. The laws they approved included adding nitrogen hypoxia to the state’s approved methods of capital punishment.     
Louisiana also allows execution by electric chair but hasn’t used the method since 2011. Though its use hasn’t been outlawed, several states moved away from the electric chair once lethal injection became available and because some courts have raised Eighth Amendment concerns. Tennessee conducted the most recent electric chair execution in 2020.
In a social media post Monday, Landry said the state will execute Wessinger if he opts for lethal injection with pentobarbital. 
“Three decades without justice is three decades too long,” the governor wrote.
There are currently more than 50 people on death row at Louisiana State Penitentiary.

name: WyoFile
title: Private property condemnation for proposed Alkali Dam on hold for water board election
text:
Directors of a water district at Hyattville have put off condemnation of private property until after a Nov. 3 district election that could end the eminent domain efforts.
The board of the Nowood Watershed Improvement District agreed Saturday to postpone condemnation until voters elect three board members, a majority of the district’s leadership. The condemnation of easements would enable construction of a controversial dam that’s been estimated to cost up to $113 million.
Incumbent directors John Joyce, Martin Mercer and Mitch Vigil face challengers Tom Shirran, Todd Jones and Doug Hamilton. Should all the incumbents lose, the new leadership might not choose to condemn the private property.

Martin Mercer on Radar. (Courtesy photo)

“If they vote John, Mitch, and myself off …I don’t know what that [new] board will do with it,” Mercer said of the condemnation plan. “In other words, the eminent domain’s not going to be put on the table until after the election.”
The board notified the owners of five properties in September that the district was making a final offer to buy options for permanent and temporary easements on their properties. If the offers weren’t accepted, the district “will reluctantly initiate eminent domain proceedings,” the letters read.
The offers were addressed to Paul and Kathy Hughes, Keith Hamilton of the Hamilton Ranch, Tom Shirran, Thomas Searfoss and Gene and Kris Robertson of the Diamond S Ranch, according to letters WyoFile obtained through a public records request.
None of the landowners had signed the options by the time of Saturday’s meeting, according to those attending the gathering.
Water developers estimated the dam and reservoir would cost $20 million in the early stages of the project, which was conceived in 2007. Since then, estimates have ranged as high as $113 million.
The 100-foot high earthen embankment dam would be almost a half-mile long and impound a reservoir of between 132 and 312 acres. The reservoir would deliver a little more than 5,000 acre-feet of water in eight out of 10 years, earmarked for late-season irrigation for about 33 irrigators.
“The eminent domain’s not going to be put on the table until after the election.”Martin Mercer
Water developers face an end-of-year deadline imposed by Cheyenne lawmakers, some of whom are skeptical about the project’s worthiness and frustrated by the planning process. The Wyoming Water Development Office and commission have come under criticism for spending money — more than $5 million — without first securing options for the necessary private property easements.
“It is the intent of the legislature that no further time extensions shall be authorized for this project,” a bill passed earlier this year reads. “Beginning January 1, 2027, funds from the appropriation made in this paragraph shall not be expended or used to exercise eminent domain for the purposes of this project.”




A map of the Nowood Watershed Improvement District shows where irrigators would benefit from the proposed Alkali Creek Dam and reservoir. (Wyoming Water Development Office)
Critical landowners have objected to impacts to their ranch land for a project that is downstream from their property. Dam backers say upstream lands can benefit through an exchange.
Saturday’s meeting of the irrigation district lasted about an hour and a half during which landowners raised numerous questions, including how many members of the district are eligible to vote.
Landowner Tim Gardiner has accused district directors of a conflict of interest, charges they reject.
“This project is of marginal benefit to the state as a whole,” he said Saturday. “From its inception, this proposed dam has been tarnished by massive conflicts of interest. The project’s promoters stand to gain financially should the dam become a reality.”
Mercer disagrees. “We followed all the rules,” he has said. “Everything was voted on by our peers. It’s been transparent. It’s been democratic. I don’t know there’s any conflict of interest.”
The project is beneficial, Mercer said Saturday.
“The only reason [we’re] talking about this is they’re about to take their money and leave,” he said of the state and its funding. “We have an opportunity, and the state’s willing to invest money in helping everybody in this room.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Free school meals debated as a win for families or wrong for North Dakota’s constitution
text:
Measure 2 opponent Bob Harms gestures while debating Measure 2 proponent Zac Ista on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota voters will decide this fall whether to approve free school meals for K-12 students in a ballot measure proponents see as a way to ease costs for families while opponents view it as a wrong addition to the state constitution.
Measure 2 would provide free breakfast and lunch for North Dakota’s roughly 125,000 K-12 students, costing as much as $134 million every two years. Supporter Zac Ista, the Democratic House minority leader from Grand Forks, and opponent Bob Harms, a former state GOP chair and legal adviser to two past governors, debated the measure on the Plain Talk Podcast hosted by Rob Port and Chad Oban. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Ista said the measure will ensure every student receives a nutritious breakfast and lunch and take as much as $1,000 per student off of families per school year. The economy is top of mind for voters, and the state government has few levers it can pull to quickly respond, “and here’s one that we can pull,” he said.
The measure also weds the state constitution’s requirement of a uniform system of free public education with a state law mandating no student be turned away from lunch because he or she can’t pay, he added.
“We know if our kids are well fed, they’re going to learn better and they’re going to be able to meet their God-given abilities in the classroom,” Ista said. 



Harms criticized the measure as a constitutional amendment, requiring a vote for potential future changes, and the wrong policy at a time when Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong is calling for budget cuts as high as 10% for some agencies.
The measure is “wasteful spending” in applying to all schoolchildren regardless of their family’s income, Harms said. The state already is spending $40 million a year to feed needy kids, nearly all of that in federal money, he said.
The measure also mandates the meals be covered by earnings of the state’s $15 billion oil tax savings fund if the Legislature can’t find the money in addition to required federal reimbursement. Harms said that backstop impedes on the purpose of the Legacy Fund to ensure the state’s financial future when oil tax revenue dries up.
“If we want to meet that value that Zac’s talking about, that we should have kids study in school and not go hungry, we’re doing that today, and we should modify that policy, adjust that policy in the Legislature, not mandate it in the constitution,” Harms said.
Measure 2 proponent Zac Ista, who is the North Dakota Democratic House minority leader, listens to Measure 2 opponent Bob Harms during a debate on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
Voters have shown a willingness to make technical changes to the state constitution as recently as 2024 on a Legacy Fund measure, Ista said. Voters also have seen the Legislature defeat past bills to pass free school meals in state law, leading many to feel fed up, he said. 
“The Legislature has shown this is not a top priority for it, and the constitution provides a protection for that,” Ista said.
The Legislature also would have flexibility on its own terms for how to fund the meals under the measure, he said. The funding amount is a tiny fraction of the state’s overall $20 billion two-year budget, he added.
North Dakota’s constitution represents fundamental principles that manage state government, not day-to-day policies to adjust from time to time, Harms said.
Complexity around potentially losing federal funds is another reason the measure shouldn’t go into the constitution, he added. The measure does require school districts to “maximize federal reimbursement” for meals.
60% threshold for changing North Dakota’s constitution debated as a protection or a barrier

Oban, one of the moderators, wondered why school meals are treated differently than textbooks, classroom devices and transportation. Harms said that’s a question for the Legislature to address. Meals follow the same principle as those other services schools already provide, Ista said.
“Why not shoes and clothes as well? What’s the difference?” Harms responded.
Oban is executive director for North Dakota United, a public employees and teachers union that has given at least $210,000 to Together for School Meals, the group that brought Measure 2.
The measure group has raised more than $1.4 million in monetary donations, including $760,000 from the Fairness Project, a D.C.-based organization that has supported ballot measures in other states on topics such as reproductive rights and redistricting. The group also has spent more than $1.1 million to oppose Measure 1, which would require at least 60% voter support to amend the constitution.
Harms wondered why the Fairness Project is “trying to manipulate the people of North Dakota,” saying voters have been “duped” before by out-of-state groups on past constitutional amendments. Ista said voters vote for what they want, and called Measure 2 a genuine grassroots issue for North Dakotans, not just national donors.
Measure 2 needs a simple majority to pass.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia utility commission’s balance of power at stake in midterm election
text:
Early voting is underway across Georgia, including for two down-ballot races that could decide which party controls a little known state regulatory board that influences how much Georgians pay for their utilities. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderThis coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Two seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission are on the ballot in this year’s election, and the outcome could see Democrats controlling the powerful commission for the first time in decades.
The commission regulates utilities, including Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. It has received increased scrutiny in recent years due to a series of rate hikes and the scramble to make enough energy for a massive spike in demand Georgia Power is predicting from the data center boom. 
Last year, frustration over rising power bills helped two Democrats win seats on the commission in a landslide. One of those seats, the District 3 post now held by commissioner Peter Hubbard, is back on the ballot this year. If the party can hold onto it and win the District 5 seat that’s currently up for grabs, Democrats would hold a majority.
Hubbard stressed that point in the Atlanta Press Club’s debate.
“In this election, you can vote for Peter Hubbard and Shelia Edwards to flip the commission to a Democratic majority who will lower your bills and hold Georgia Power and data centers accountable,” he said.
District 3: Hubbard vs. Johnson
Peter Hubbard, a Democrat who is currently representing Public Service Commission District 3, participates solo at the Atlanta Press Club debate this month after Fitz Johnson declined. Photo by J Glenn Photography
Hubbard worked as an advocate and a solar consultant before he won his seat on the commission. He puts a big emphasis on clean energy as a way to lower power bills.
His opponent, Fitz Johnson, didn’t participate in the debate. Johnson served four years on the commission before losing his seat to Hubbard last year. During that time, he voted to approve the six rate hikes that became the major focus of last year’s election, as well as a temporary rate freeze that began last year. He also voted to approve Georgia Power’s ongoing expansion, which relies heavily on fossil fuels.
At a campaign event in the spring, Johnson told WABE he has unfinished business on the commission.
“To get to dig a little deeper and to make sure that we are on track to take care of our ratepayers,” he said of his plans if he regains the seat. “Also, to promote the economic development.”
District 5: Tolbert vs. Edwards
Republican Josh Tolbert is running against Democrat Shelia Edwards for the District 5 seat on the Georgia Public Service Commission. Tricia Pridemore previously held the post, but decided to run for Congress this year instead of seeking reelection. She lost, then stepped down early for a job at a corporation that builds data centers. Gov. Brian Kemp appointed former Commissioner Stan Wise to the seat until the term ends in January.
Atlanta Press Club General Election Debates: Candidates for Public Service Commission District 5, Sheila Edwards (D) and Josh Tolbert (R). Debates held at GPB. Photo by J Glenn Photography
Tolbert has leaned into his background as an engineer working on power plants.
“Ratepayers need a voice and representative on the commission,” he said during the debate. “When it comes to utility decisions and power bills, that voice needs to know something about energy.”
Edwards argues the commission already has engineers and energy experts on its advisory staff.
“You don’t need another nuclear engineer,” she said during the debate. “You need a commissioner who will stand up for families, seniors and veterans. And that’s me.”
Edwards worked with Lockheed and NASA in the wake of the Challenger shuttle disaster, and she points to that experience as proof she can work with engineers and wade through technical material.
What’s at stake
Though the candidates have to live in specific districts, the elections are statewide, meaning all registered voters in Georgia can cast a ballot for both seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission.
The winners of these two races will oversee several issues with substantial implications for power bills and Georgia’s climate future, since burning fossil fuels to make electricity is a leading producer of greenhouse gas emissions.
Georgia Power’s next long-term plan for making and delivering energy is due in 2028 — an opportunity for the commission and interest groups to weigh in on power plants, transmission lines and other key issues. A rate case, in which the utility, the commission and many of those same interest groups hash out exactly what customers will pay for electricity, is due to follow — the first since 2022.
Current commissioners have said they also expect Georgia Power to file another update to its long-term plan next year, much as the utility did in 2023, as part of the ongoing effort to supply energy to data centers.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Amid criminal investigation, Iowa chiropractor surrenders his license
text:
Camanche Chiropractic Center in Clinton County. (Photo via Google Earth)An eastern Iowa chiropractor accused of initiating “nonconsensual” sexual contact with patients has agreed to voluntarily surrender his license.
The agreement, dated Oct. 14 and published by the state Tuesday, comes 15 weeks after police executed a search warrant at the chiropractor’s clinic in Camanche.
The Iowa Board of Chiropractic recently charged Gary Parsons, an Iowa-licensed chiropractor since January 1974, with engaging in professional incompetence and engaging in improper sexual contact with a patient.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the board, Parsons provided chiropractic services for a particular female patient sometime in 2023 and 2024, and the patient now asserts Parsons, during their initial appointment, initiated what the board describes as “nonconsensual, inappropriate sexual contact.”
Specifically, the board alleges, the patient claims Parsons massaged her uncovered breasts and that he made what the board describes as “inappropriate comments.” According to the board, the patient also alleges that during one appointment, Parsons took a photo of her uncovered backside without her consent and later shared the photo with her.
Board records indicate the patient also alleged that her son was seen by Parsons and that Parsons engaged in “nonconsensual, inappropriate contact” with her son. The board has disclosed no information as to the age of the son or whether the “contact” was sexual in nature.
The female patient also claims Parsons sent her text messages about “non-chiropractic care matters,” the board alleges.
In September 2025, the board alleges, Parsons provided chiropractic services to another patient who claims Parsons made inappropriate, nonconsensual sexual contact with him or her.
According to the board, Parsons has admitted no wrongdoing or guilt but has not contested the disciplinary charges against him. While affirming that no criminal charges have been imposed in the case, Parsons has entered into a settlement with the board, agreeing to voluntarily surrender his license with the understanding that he can apply for reinstatement after one year.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Parsons for comment. State records indicate he has worked at the Camanche Chiropractic Center since 1974. His son, Mark, who continues to work at the clinic as a chiropractor, declined on behalf of the clinic and his father to comment Tuesday on the licensing board’s actions.
In late June, the Camanche Police Department posted a press release to Facebook indicating that its officers, along with representatives of the Clinton Police Department, Clinton County Sheriff’s Office, Iowa Department of Public Safety, and the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing, had served a search warrant at the Camanche Chiropractic Center.
“Because the investigation is active and ongoing,” the news release stated, “specific information regarding the details of the investigation cannot be released at this time.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Cooke, Van Orden meet for debate in toss-up 3rd CD race
text:
U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden and Rebecca Cooke met Oct. 20, 2026 for a debate in the race for Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden and his Democratic opponent Rebecca Cooke met Tuesday at Chippewa Valley Technical College in Eau Claire for a debate in which Van Orden continued his ardent defense of President Donald Trump and Cooke worked to establish her moderate bonafides. 
The debate Tuesday morning was the first that Van Orden has appeared in since he first ran for Congress, losing in 2020 against former U.S. Rep. Ron Kind. In his two successful campaigns since then against state Sen. Brad Pfaff (D-Onalaska) in 2022 and Cooke in 2024, he refused to participate in any debates. 
The two candidates met two weeks before the election on the day that early voting opens across the state. Democrats are hoping the president’s record low approval ratings and voters’ concerns about the direction of the economy and war in Iran will spur a sweep in competitive districts across the country. On Tuesday morning, the election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball changed its rating of the race from a toss-up to leaning Democratic. 
Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District stretches across the Driftless Region from the state’s southwest corner up to Eau Claire, with an extension into central Wisconsin and Stevens Point. One of the most closely contested districts in the country, the seat has frequently been a top target for both parties. 
Millions of dollars in spending have flooded into the area from both campaigns and outside groups in a race that observers have seen get increasingly negative — with Democrats attacking Van Orden’s often aggressive temperament and vociferous support of Trump while Republicans take jabs at Cooke’s authenticity and history of work as a political consultant for Democratic groups. 
During the hourlong debate hosted by the Eau Claire Area Chamber of Commerce and WEAU 13 News, Van Orden defended his votes to pass Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, sustain his trade wars on countries around the world, send masked federal immigration agents into communities across Wisconsin and continue his war in Iran. He also repeatedly plugged a website created by his campaign that accuses Cooke of being a “commie” who supports defunding the police, giving sex change surgeries to transgender youth and letting undocumented immigrants vote. 
Cooke argued that Van Orden’s support of Trump has hurt working class people, farmers and families across the district while at the same time trying to establish that she disagrees with her party’s left wing. During the debate, she said that she’s actually the candidate in the race who is “putting America first and that we’re investing in our communities, putting Wisconsin first.” Van Orden responded that he’d get her a MAGA hat.  
Cooke also said she doesn’t support sanctuary cities, banning assault rifles, estate taxes or forgiving student loan debt. 
“I think that voters on the trail feel like this administration has been a disaster, and that their policies have made their lives harder and not easier,” Cooke said in a post-debate news conference. “I’m hearing from a lot of working families and retirees who are just really hanging on by a thread.” 
Moderated by WEAU’s John Frank and Kim Leadholm, the debate covered  the economy, government spending, immigration, healthcare, housing, childcare, energy, higher education, infrastructure and foreign policy. 
Economy
On the economy, Van Orden argued that the struggles people are currently facing began during the Biden administration. He named several home staples that are cheaper now than under Joe Biden. He also touted the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act as offering support to working people. 
“I’m so glad you said that out loud. You would have voted against what you called the One Big Beautiful Bill. That’s the Working Families Tax Cuts and Jobs Act,” he told Cooke. “This is the largest tax cut in the history of our country, and Rebecca Cook is now again officially on record saying that she would not vote for it.”
Polling shows that the law is broadly unpopular, with a July survey from Politico finding that about one in three Americans believe it has hurt their personal finances. 
Cooke countered by saying that the only permanent tax cuts in the bill are the ones that went to the wealthiest Americans while the provisions that Van Orden touted, most notably cutting taxes on tips and overtime, expire after two years. She also argued that the war in Iran and Trump’s tariffs have done nothing but squeeze people in the 3rd CD. 
“I’m focused on an America-first agenda and making sure that we’re putting more resources back into the pockets of American taxpayers,” she said. “I want to make sure that you can afford your healthcare. I want to make sure that our public schools are not having to vote on a referendum every year, and I want to make sure that you can go to the grocery store, to the gas pump, pay your rent or mortgage and have a little left over.” 
Immigration
In January, when federal agents flooded into Minnesota’s Twin Cities as part of Operation Metro Surge, immigration enforcement actions also stretched into Wisconsin, going as far as Eau Claire and affecting the manufacturing plants and dairy farms in the 3rd CD that rely on immigrant labor. 
Van Orden brought up a 2024 incident in which a 26-year-old Venezuelan man attacked a woman and her teenaged child in Prairie du Chien — saying Cooke has refused to condemn violence by immigrants — while touting the endorsements he’s received from law enforcement organizations in the state. 
He also touted his proposed legislation through which currently undocumented farm workers will obtain legal status by going back to their home country, paying a fine and waiting in line to be given a visa — a policy proposal that some farmers see as unworkable. 
“Rebecca Cooke is saying that she wants these secure borders. There was up to 200,000 illegal aliens entering into the country every single month under Joe Biden’s presidency, and she said nothing,” Van Orden said. “Rebecca is right. Cows aren’t going to stop milking because of foreign immigration policy. A hog’s not going to stop growing because of foreign immigration policy. So as opposed to saying one thing and doing another, I’ve actually been working on this within the three years that I’ve been in Congress.”
Cooke said she supported some of the visa reforms that Van Orden has been working on while also arguing for a pathway to citizenship for the district’s immigrant workers, which she said hasn’t been achieved because both parties have used immigration as a political wedge. 
“It’s very, very important that we make sure that our border remains secure, right? And I want to make sure that our communities remain safe places to live and work and play, but I also want to recognize what a big part immigrant labor is to our workforce here in west central Wisconsin,” she said. “You look at the contributions from the manufacturing sector to our dairy farmers, and I think that we’ve got to have a clear pathway to citizenship and one that puts people that are playing by the rules that don’t have criminal backgrounds on that track. And I think for too long people have been playing partisan politics when it comes to immigration and playing partisan football. And we’ve got to focus on getting something done.”
Healthcare
On healthcare, Van Orden blamed rising costs on Democrats’ 2010 passage of the Affordable Care Act and took credit for protecting local healthcare providers by working to get hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding into the state. 
“Those programs exist for a reason. They’re critically important,” he said. “I’ve done everything I can to fully fund them into the future, so that babies don’t have to worry about whether they’re getting pre-natal care or whether we’re delivering the babies. Or if we’re breaking arms, we can afford to get a cast.”
But that funding, Cooke pointed out, is a “backfill” that amounts to only a “drop in the bucket” when compared to the billions that will be lost because of the cuts to Medicaid included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
“I think everybody knows about the hospital closures here in the Chippewa Valley, and that was out of Derrick Van Orden’s watch,” she said. “We saw Sacred Heart close. We saw St. Joe’s and Chippewa Falls close. We’ve seen labor and delivery close in neighboring Menomonie. This was during his term as a congressman, and then you look at the vote that he took for the One Big Beautiful Bill, they cut healthcare for millions of Americans.” 
Tariffs and Iran 
Two of the Trump administration’s most unpopular policies have been the president’s tariffs and the war in Iran. Van Orden backed both on Tuesday. 
He argued that in Trump’s trade wars with Canada, Mexico, the European Union and China, those other countries are “not the good guy,” that the tariffs are helping the district’s farmers and that they’re an important tool for fair trade. 
“Tariffs are a tool to make sure that we have fair trade throughout the United States, and Canada is not the good guy of the story. China is not the good guy of the story. Mexico is not the good guy in the story. The European Union is not the good guy in the story. What you’re about to hear is a candidate for federal office take Canada, Mexico, China and the European Union over Wisconsin farmers,” Van Orden said. “So, do I like tariffs for everything? Absolutely not. But they’re a tool.” 
Cooke said the tariffs are unpopular for a reason and that the district’s farmers don’t want “handouts” from the federal government to make up for the harms of federal policymaking. 
“I grew up on a dairy farm, like two miles down the road from here. I have lived a lot of failed policies from many different administrations,” she said. “People that have put partisanship or D.C. politics over the livelihoods of farmers across the state and across this country, and these tariffs, I’ve talked to people all across the 3rd Congressional District, at dairy breakfasts, county fairs, I’ve convened roundtables to talk to farmers explicitly about tariffs. Nobody likes them, right?” 
On Iran, Van Orden mentioned his military record as a former U.S. Navy SEAL while arguing the United States had to fight the “radical Muslim world” and prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
“So if people can rape, murder, torture, hold us economically hostage, and Rebecca Cooke is unwilling to fight that conflict, then I’d say that it’s disqualifying to be a member of Congress because we have to make decisions we don’t want to make, oftentimes,” he said. “And this is one: Do I want to be in a war with Iran right now? No, I don’t want to be in a war with anybody right now. Is it making it exponentially harder for Republicans to hold the House and the Senate? Yes, it is. But we have to think about our children and grandchildren. We’ve been fighting the war that the radical Muslim world has declared on us for 50 years, and I don’t want my grandchildren fighting the same war that I do. I think it’s time for this to stop. We must finish this.” 
Cooke said American foreign policy should lead with diplomacy — a tactic that Van Orden said amounted to a “strongly worded email” to Iran — while standing up to bullies around the world but that Congress should be more focused on the everyday needs of Americans right now.  
“We’ve seen so much spending — billions of taxpayer dollars go overseas when they could be invested in things here to put Wisconsin first, to put our communities first,” she said. “We’re looking at hospital closures here. We’re looking at our public schools flailing. We’re looking at so many difficult things for our Main Street businesses to be able to keep their doors open. So I’d like to end the war in Iran, which no one voted for. Even if they voted for Derrick Van Orden or for President Trump, they voted for no more foreign forever wars.” 
Energy
With energy prices rising across the country, both candidates said they opposed the controversial proposed transmission line that will cross through the region and attempted to tag the other with support for data centers. 
But Van Orden denounced the “war on fossil fuels” that he says Democrats have been waging while Cooke called for an “all of the above” energy strategy. 
Van Orden said Wisconsin should get its power from natural gas, “clean burning coal” and nuclear power. 
“It’s going to get 20 degrees below zero in the state of Wisconsin. Whether or not you want to have a windmill or a solar panel, we have to have base load power, nuclear, cleaner coal, gas,” he said. “That’s what we need to turn to. We need to stick with it. And then guess what? When it’s locally generated, you don’t need these monstrosities that they’re going to wreck the driftless with. It’s physics.” 
Cooke accused Van Orden of being “in the pocket of big tech” because of financial support from people including Elon Musk while saying she supported building renewables and maintaining other energy sources like nuclear. 
“I believe in mixing renewables while keeping our grid reliable. I also support advancements in small modular nuclear, which weans us away from our reliance on fossil fuels,” she said. 
Higher Education 
Colleges and universities across Wisconsin have been financially struggling due to decreasing enrollment, rising costs and federal cuts to both student aid and grants for universities. In the 3rd Congressional District, the University of Wisconsin campus in Richland Center closed in 2024. 
Cooke said she wants to better support the area’s students and higher education institutions through better grant programs for students in traditional colleges and the trades. 
“I was able to go to college with the help of Pell grants. I think that we need to have more federal funding to be invested into Pell grants, so more low-income and middle-income young people have the opportunity to go into whatever school they’d like to,” she said. “I also believe strongly in work-study programs, and also thinking about how that builds pipelines into our workforce within our communities.”
Van Orden said that his “trade happened to be war” and argued that government support should go to education in the trades or STEM programs. He also proposed that federal student loans should be offered interest free. 
“These lights are not on because someone has a degree in 13th century French poetry, they’re not,” he said, indicating the lighting on the debate stage. “They’re on because someone did get a STEM degree, then they got a master’s degree in electrical engineering. They wrote those plans and handed them to someone that went to trade school. That’s why the plumbing works. That’s why the road is flat. That’s why this glass is in place. That’s why we’re not freezing right now because we have heat here, which is an HVAC tech. So we have to invest money in younger people because that is an actual investment in the United States of America.”
In the debate room, the dozens of invited attendees — mostly the invited guests of the campaigns and local leaders — strictly followed the rules against vocal responses to the candidate’s remarks and after it ended, both candidates claimed victory. 
With Election Day two weeks away, voting has already begun. Locations for voting early absentee and in-person on Nov. 3 can by found at MyVote.WI.gov

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Second lady Usha Vance visits Arkansas to promote childhood literacy efforts
text:
Second lady Usha Vance speaks to Glenview Elementary School students in North Little Rock on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Second lady Usha Vance visited Glenview Elementary School in North Little Rock Tuesday to promote childhood literacy by reading to students and discussing Arkansas’ literacy efforts with state officials.
The wife of Vice President JD Vance and mother of four read the picture book “Chrysanthemum,” which she said is her daughter’s favorite book, to the Glenview student body.
“I came all the way from Washington, D.C. because I heard what amazing work all of you guys out there do every day in the classroom, and I wanted to see it for myself,” Vance told the students.
Vance’s work encouraging children to enjoy reading included a summer reading challenge for the past two years.
Earlier, Vance took part in a roundtable discussion about Arkansas’ efforts to boost childhood literacy, a core tenet of the LEARNS Act. The wide-ranging 2023 law required literacy screenings for K-3 students and provided literacy coaches for every K-3 teacher in schools graded “D” or “F.”

Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, second lady Usha Vance and Arkansas Education Secretary Jacob Oliva meet for a childhood literacy roundtable discussion at Glenview Elementary School in North Little Rock on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

The Arkansas Department of Education’s Division of Elementary and Secondary Education grades public schools based on how well students do on state assessment tests and how much they improve in core subjects from year to year, among other things.
State Education Secretary Jacob Oliva noted that the North Little Rock School District was graded “F” last year and rose to a “C” this year.
“What we know matters is if we build the right systems and invest in high-quality teachers, get them great leaders, provide the right robust support, and get the systems aligned, we’re going to see great results,” Oliva said.
The roundtable participants also included Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, First Gentleman Bryan Sanders, several State Board of Education members, North Little Rock School District Superintendent Gregory Pilewski and Republican state Rep. Keith Brooks of Little Rock. 
Brooks chairs the House Education Committee and was a lead sponsor of the LEARNS Act, which was signed by Sanders.
Most of the roundtable was closed to the press.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Free community college helping to shore up state university enrollment
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
text:
STATE UNIVERSITIES ARE SEEING a surge in transfer students this fall, plus their first overall enrollment boost in more than a decade, according to new estimates from higher education officials that point to persistent struggles around degree completion. 
Across the state’s public higher education system, enrollment is up by 2.2 percent compared to last fall. Enrollment is up by 3.9 percent at community colleges — marking the fourth consecutive year of growth — and up by 2.2 percent at state universities, which is the first increase since 2013, according to data presented to the Board of Higher Education Tuesday. Enrollment is “level” for the University of Massachusetts system.
Department of Higher Education staff zeroed in on transfer student trends, with their enrollment increasing by 16.6 percent at state universities and by 3.8 percent at UMass.
“We are encouraged that students continue to find opportunities in Massachusetts’s public higher education system,” Interim Higher Education Commissioner José Luis Santos said in a statement. “But getting students through the door is only the beginning. The gains we see in on-time credit accumulation are promising, and we remain focused on closing equity gaps and making sure every student has the support they need to complete their degree.”
Community colleges, with their enrollment buoyed by tuition-free policies in recent years, “remain the largest source of new transfers at the state universities,” said Mario Delci, associate commissioner for research and planning.
“In our informal polling of the state university research directors, they’ve attributed these increases to more community college transfers, which is what we thought would happen,” Delci said. “They also called out students transferring from recently closed institutions, which is a really important finding on its own, in the sense that we are providing opportunities to students who have lost that opportunity through the closure of some of the independent institutions in recent years.”
Anna Maria College in Paxton shuttered at the end of the spring semester and Hampshire College plans to close after the fall semester, part of a wave of small liberal arts colleges struggling to adapt to shifting demographics and economic pressures.
Eight out of nine state universities saw “notable gains” in transfer student enrollment, Delci said. More data should be available in December to help education officials make better sense of the trend, including where exactly students are transferring from and their course enrollments, Delci said.
The latest data also underscore challenges for students to complete their degrees and equity gaps for students of color.
For the state’s public higher education system, the completion rate has “flattened out” at about 56 percent, which is below the department’s 60 percent target for 2033, said Sarah Mealey, assistant commissioner for analytics and digital services. The metric tracks the percentage of new students entering Massachusetts public institutions and successfully completing a degree or certificate anywhere in the U.S. within six years.
Francesca Purcell, a board member and senior lecturer at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, urged her colleagues and education officials to keep a “laser focus” on completion rates.
“Because at the end of the day, some college with no degree…is, sure, a little bit helpful, but really we want our students leaving our system with a credential in hand,” Purcell said.
On the community college front, Mealey pointed to “good news” for a metric that gauges the percentage of full-time students completing at least 24 credits or part-time students earning at least 12 credits in their first year. The rate was 40.3 percent for the fall 2025 cohort, an increase of about 18 percentage points compared to the fall 2012 cohort. The latest rate exceeds the department’s 2033 target of 40 percent. 
There’s been “substantial improvement” for on-time credit accumulation across Black, Hispanic/Latino and white students at community colleges, Mealey said.
“Nonetheless, gaps persist,” she said. “Outcomes for white students currently meet or exceed the target across the board here, and outcomes for Black and and Hispanic students remain below the targets for the most part.”
At state universities, on-time credit accumulation climbed to 70.6 percent for the fall 2025 cohort after dropping during the COVID-19 pandemic. The state target is 80 percent target for 2033. The volume of students enrolling for a second year is also climbing after a pandemic-induced decline.
The completion rate for transfer students in 2025, measuring the percentage of individuals who graduated from a state university or UMass within four years of transferring from a community college, climbed to 64.6 percent. That’s just just below the 2033 target of 65 percent. Mealey described the trend as a “success story.”
While Gov. Maura Healey applauded the enrollment growth Tuesday and touted her administration’s investments in higher education, Delci noted the “initial boom” from free community college appears to be “moderating.” The dynamic is unfolding as Massachusetts also faces an enrollment “cliff” as the population of college-age students declines, Delci said.
“Everyone’s going to have to look together for new strategies, new ways to continue to grow enrollments at the community colleges,” he said.

name: Delaware
title: NBA Foundation grant boosts YMCA of Delaware youth workforce program
text:
Image created on 10/20 using AI.
WILMINGTON, Del. — The YMCA of Delaware has received a $25,000 grant from the NBA Foundation to expand a workforce development program that has helped hundreds of Delaware teens and young adults prepare for jobs and careers.
The YMCA’s Workforce Development program serves people ages 16 to 24 through career training, paid internships, mentoring, financial literacy education and industry-recognized credentials.
Since the program began, the YMCA says it has trained 651 young people and helped place 562 participants in paid internships. The program reports an 86% internship placement rate.
“Young people across Delaware have the talent and determination to succeed. What they need are opportunities, practical skills, and caring adults who show up for them,” YMCA of Delaware President and CEO Jarrett Royster said.
“Through this investment in our Workforce Development program, the NBA Foundation is helping more young people build confidence, gain experience, and take the next step toward a brighter future.”
Participants receive training in communication, professionalism, workplace expectations, résumé development and interviewing before many move into paid internships.
The internships are intended to give participants hands-on experience while allowing them to develop relationships with professional mentors and potential employers.
YMCA officials said every graduate from the first year of the organization’s EVOLVE program secured either a new job or a raise.
EVOLVE serves as the YMCA’s credentialing and career advancement track. Through Delaware Technical Community College and other training partners, participants can pursue credentials in areas including certified nursing, early childhood education, forklift operation, fitness training and artificial intelligence.
The YMCA also cited an independent evaluation of its 2025 participants that found 94% demonstrated growth in self-management and 94% reported increased confidence in their schoolwork. Every participant showed growth in at least one core social and emotional skill area, according to the organization.
Blue Coats partnership expands beyond basketball
The grant also builds on an existing relationship between the YMCA and the Delaware Blue Coats, the Philadelphia 76ers’ NBA G League affiliate.
The organizations previously developed the YMCA Junior Blue Coats Developmental Basketball League, which serves more than 525 young athletes in five YMCA communities across New Castle County.
“The Delaware Blue Coats and the YMCA of Delaware share a deep commitment to youth opportunity across Delaware,” said Alex Yoh, vice president of business operations for the Delaware Blue Coats.
Yoh said the basketball league gives young people an opportunity to develop as athletes and leaders, while the YMCA’s workforce programs extend that work into career preparation.
“The Y’s Workforce Development and EVOLVE programs extend that same commitment into career readiness, equipping teens and young adults with the skills and resources they need to succeed,” Yoh said.
The NBA Foundation supports nonprofit organizations in NBA markets that focus on education, employment, career advancement and economic opportunity for young people from underserved communities.
The YMCA said the new funding will help it continue providing training, mentorship, work experience and career support to young Delawareans moving from school into the workforce.

What it offers: Career training, paid internships, mentorship, financial literacy education and industry-recognized credentials
Career pathways: Programs include certified nursing, early childhood education, forklift operation, fitness training and artificial intelligence

name: Source New Mexico
title: Alcohol-related deaths in New Mexico on the rise, new state health data shows
text:
The New Mexico Department of Health released data on Oct. 20, 2026, that showed a 2.6% increase in alcohol-related deaths in the state between 2024 and 2025. (Source NM file photo)New data released Tuesday by the state health department shows a 2.6% rise in alcohol-related deaths in New Mexico between 2024 and 2025 after a three-year decline. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Between 2021 to 2024, alcohol-related deaths dropped by 21%, the New Mexico Department of Health said in a news release. New Mexico ranks first in the nation for alcohol mortality, and had 1,756 alcohol-related deaths in 2024, the latest data available from the health department. 
Additionally, alcohol accounted for 9% of all hospitalizations statewide during the same time period, according to a January news release from NMDOH.
“Though the decreasing trend in alcohol-related deaths since 2021 is good news, the recent uptick is a reminder alcohol use remains a health concern,” Rebecca Neudecker, section manager for the NMDOH’s Office of Alcohol Misuse Prevention, said in a statement. Studies show alcohol use can be tied to heart disease, cancer and liver malfunction. 
Chronic conditions, such as alcohol-related liver disease, cancer and hypertension, cause most alcohol-related deaths. Acute causes of alcohol-related deaths include motor vehicle accidents and drownings.
In the news release, NMDOH expressed support for New Mexicans committing in Sober October, an alcohol abstinence initiative to “reset habits, strengthen wellness and rethink their relationship with drinking.” 
A reduction in alcohol consumption can reduce the risk of cancer, improve sleep quality, improve liver function and digestion, NMDOH added. 
NMDOH noted it works with local communities and Tribal entities to increase culturally-based education and prevention efforts. The health department launched the Drink Less, Live More initiative in January that highlights the benefits of reducing alcohol consumption through self-check guides, daily drink trackers and community support materials.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont taxpayers can’t compare school budgets. The state could fix that.
text:
This commentary is by Matt Rkiouak, founder of Hunger Mountain Intelligence, a growth and automation consultancy for small and mid-sized businesses.
Every March, Vermonters vote on school budgets they cannot compare with the district next door. Each district lays out its budget differently. What one district calls “special education shared services” is three separate lines in the next. When a budget goes up, the explanation is a list of pressures: health insurance, special education, enrollment. Voters have no way to tell whether those pressures are bigger here than next door.
The state’s reports should settle this. Instead, they contradict each other. The Agency of Education’s staff survey is the only place every district’s positions and pay are coded the same way. Yet for one district, it lists 7.2 teaching positions costing $4.9 million. For the same district, it shows $18 million in salaries and no benefits, while federal census figures show $6.9 million in benefits. 
To compare districts, the state divides each one’s spending by a weighted pupil count, known as LTWADM. The count starts with resident students and adds extra weight for those who cost more to educate, including students from low-income families, older students, English learners, and students in small schools or sparsely populated areas. The state published the breakdown of that count for 2025-26 in January 2025. It hasn’t done so for 2026-27.
I wanted to see how my own district, Washington Central, compares with four nearby districts. Washington Central runs six schools. Measured per weighted pupil, and leaving out debt payments and building projects, it spends about $2.3 million a year more than it would at the average rate of Harwood, Montpelier Roxbury, Mount Abraham and Barre. 
Most of the gap is pay. Washington Central’s average teacher salary on the staff survey, $79,827, is the highest of the five. Higher pay rates, not more teachers, explain most of the difference. Its superintendent is the lowest paid of the five. But its special education director and curriculum director are the highest paid in their roles, and its administrative costs are second only to Mount Abraham’s. 
Building costs rose by a third over three years while consumer prices rose about 13%. Special education and student support spending grew 36%, nearly half the district’s total increase. Yet its cost per child with an individualized education program is at the neighbors’ average.
The district’s annual report includes an enrollment table where the school columns don’t add up to the totals in any of the seven years. This year’s budget comes in two versions, one for three elementary schools and one for five. They have the same total but different line items, and nothing shows how money moved between them. 
The district estimated that closing two schools would save $881,920 in 2024 and $1,088,508 in 2025. In January 2026, it said neither figure “is accurate data as of our current budget scenario.” It has not published the model behind them. Calais and Worcester voters rejected the closure of their elementary schools in February, but in August district voters gave all five towns a say in future closures. My own math, using the district’s salary roster and enrollment projections, puts the savings at $1.5 million to $1.9 million a year. I may be wrong, but there’s no published figure to check it against.
None of this is unique to Washington Central. It is what the rules allow. 
Vermont requires districts to file budgets on the state’s form and report staff to its survey. It then compares them using a pupil count it hasn’t fully published this year. Under Act 73, passed in 2025, the state would pay each district a set amount per weighted pupil, starting in 2029 if certain conditions are met. A formula that pays per pupil makes one question central: What does it cost to run a school here, compared with there? Right now, the state cannot answer it.
Three things would fix that. The Legislature and the Agency of Education can make all three.
First, require every district to publish its general ledger by purpose and type of expense, in a spreadsheet, on the state’s chart of accounts, with its position roster by year. Not a budget book. The ledger.
Second, have the state publish its own calculations every year, once they’re final: the weighted pupil count broken down for every district, as it did for 2025-26; special education cost reports for every year; and the per-pupil spending measured the same way from year to year. 
Third, reconcile the three sets of numbers that describe each district: the district’s budget, the state’s surveys, and federal census and education reports. Where they disagree, say which is right and why. That takes staff and money, and the Legislature should fund it.
Vermont’s new education law puts pressure on small schools, and state spending limits tighten every year from 2028. Voters will be asked to approve whatever comes next. They should be able to see, in numbers that mean the same thing in every town, what their district spends and what the alternatives would cost.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont taxpayers can’t compare school budgets. The state could fix that..

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Senate ad targeting Hertel family denounced by former Republican officials
text:
Sen. Kevin Hertel (D-St. Clair Shores). March 4, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceA series of ads released in Michigan’s 12th Senate District have targeted Democratic state Sen. Kevin Hertel, including one aimed at his family, which includes current Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr. and their father, former Michigan House Speaker Curtis Hertel Sr. At least two former Republican officials have said the ad crossed a line.
Kevin Hertel, of St. Clair Shores, is seeking reelection to the 12th District, which spans the shoreline of Lake St. Clair, from northern Macomb County to the Grosse Pointe communities of Wayne County. He is being challenged by Republican John Goldwater. 
The most recent ad, titled “Silver Spoon,” was released by the Michigan Senate Republican Campaign Committee on Monday and claims that the Hertel “political dynasty,” cashed in “$4 million in government paychecks,” with the on-screen text indicating that it references government salaries from 2000 to 2025. 
When questioned by Michigan Advance about the $4 million claim, the SRCC said it included the government salaries of not only Hertel, but also his brother and father, as well as his sister-in-law, Elizabeth Hertel, wife of Curtis Hertel Jr. and the former director of the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
Hertel’s office called the ad “gutter politics.” Hertel also said he was proud of “what I’ve accomplished for our lakeshore community, and I’m proud of my family’s work serving our state.“
Sen. Kevin Hertel (D-St. Clair Shores) discusses a slate of proposed regulations on data centers at a press conference. June 18, 2025 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceMichigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel at the party's 2026 nominating convention in Lansing on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Elizabeth Hertel, the former director of the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services, speaks at a press conference urging state legislators to fully fill gaps in Medicaid funding left by federal cuts. April 28, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.Curtis Hertel Sr.
Former Republican Speaker of the House Paul Hillegonds, who served alongside Hertel Sr. as co-speaker of the House during a period of divided government in 1993-1994, also came to bat for Kevin Hertel and the Hertel family.
“Curtis saw the House as a place to sit down, learn from the other side, work through our differences, and problem solve. His son has continued that legacy as a legislator who’s respected on both sides of the aisle for setting aside differences and getting problems solved for his community,” Hillegonds said in a statement. “The latest ad from Republicans and Sen. Hertel’s opponent is deeply disappointing. Campaigns should be about presenting a strong vision to voters, not attacking your opponent and his family’s dedication to serving our state.”
Also denouncing the ad is former Republican state Rep. Edward Gaffney, who said that Kevin Hertel was someone who has shown that “ he’s willing to put people above politics, just like his father did.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“My party should be ashamed of itself for attacking the Senator’s family. This is especially true because of the Hertel family’s outstanding and long record of bipartisan public service,” Gaffney said in a statement.
In response to Hillegonds and Gaffney’s criticism, state Sen. Roger Hauck (R-Mount Pleasant), who heads up the Michigan Senate Republican Campaign Committee, told Michigan Advance that “the last thing Southeast Michigan needs is another creature of Lansing.”
“Kevin Hertel is a career politician who has voted to raise taxes and fees more than 50 times while putting special interests ahead of the families he’s supposed to represent,” Hauck said in a statement. “If you’re happy with Michigan being a bottom 10 state in education, jobs and public safety, then by all means, stick with the status quo. But if you believe Michigan can do better, John Goldwater represents the change you’re looking for.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Early voting turnout so far shows enthusiasm among unaffiliated voters in NC
text:
Unaffiliated voters are casting ballots in surprisingly large numbers in the first days of early voting  for the 2026 midterm in North Carolina. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)Early voting stats don’t predict Election Day winners, but the first few days of voting in North Carolina have produced a surprise – the eagerness among unaffiliated voters in North Carolina to cast ballots in a midterm election. 
In the first five days of early voting, Thursday through Monday, unaffiliated voters cast 34% of ballots. In 2022, unaffiliated voters cast 29% of ballots over the same time.
The number of unaffiliated voters in North Carolina is growing by both raw numbers and share of the electorate. There are about 20% more voters registered as unaffiliated today than there were in 2022, and they now outnumber both registered Democrats and Republicans. 
In 2022, voter registration was split about evenly between Democrats, Republicans, and unaffiliated voters, with Republican registration holding a slight edge over Democrats. This year, unaffiliated voters account for 40% of registrants, with Democrats and Republicans each hovering around 30%.
However, turnout among unaffiliated voters in these first few days of early voting has risen even faster than their share of the electorate.  In raw numbers, their votes increased 88%, from 133,683 in the first five days of 2022 early voting to 251,891 this year, according to the Center for NC Politics substack run by Catawba College political science professor Michael Bitzer.  
In the 2022 midterm elections, unaffiliated voters had cast fewer ballots than Democrats or Republicans at this point in early voting. This year, they are ahead of Republicans. 
“Historicaly, unaffiliated voter turnout is 10% below partisans,” David McLennan, a retired political science professor, said in an interview Monday.  The increase in early voting thus far is a sign of enthusiasm, he said. “Put that against the backdrop of Democrats up and Republicans down, that makes it interesting.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Only 40% of independent voters said in an Elon Poll University released Tuesday that they were “very”” or “extremely” excited to vote, compared to 55% of Republicans. However, early voting turnout among unaffiliated voters is stronger. Democrats were the most enthusiastic about voting, according to the Elon University Poll, with 65% saying they were extremely or very excited. 
Through Monday, nearly 670,000 people had voted in person. 
Democrats have cast nearly 45% of early ballots this year, with their numbers also way ahead of 2022. Unaffiliated voters have cast about 34% of early votes, Republicans have cast nearly 21%, at numbers slightly below 2022. 
Bitzer attributed the jump in unaffiliated voters’ early vote turnout to enthusiasm and the fact that some people are registered unaffiliated but are partisan. 
“Energy and enthusiasm is on the center-left,” Bitzer said in an interview Monday. 
The John Locke Foundation vote tracker and the Carolina Forward Turnout Tracker also follow early voting turnout and absentee ballot returns. 
High unaffiliated turnout in toss-up legislative races
It’s become a commonplace observation that independent voters decide statewide races in North Carolina. This may be the year that the impact of unaffiliated voters becomes obvious in toss-up legislative districts as well.
In House District 37, for example, where incumbent Rep. Erin Pare, R-Wake, is running against Democrat Winn Decker in a district considered a toss-up, unaffiliated voters have cast more ballots than Democrats or Republicans. The same is true in House District 105, where incumbent Rep. Tricia Cotham (R-Mecklenburg) is running against Democrat Ken McCool in what’s expected to be a close race. 
Republican turnout spikes on Election Day
It’s not unusual for Democrats to outpace Republicans in early voting, while Republicans more than make up for it on Election Day. It’s the Election Day Republican surge that helps lift many statewide GOP candidates to victory. 
That doesn’t always happen, however.
Republican early voting lagged so far behind Democrats’ in 2008 that the GOP’s Election Day push fell short. Then-Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama, running for his first term, created an early-voting advantage Republicans could not overcome. Obama won the state by 0.5%. 
This year’s midterm is far from over. 
Vance touts $858M in Helene relief funding for Western North Carolina

Vice President JD Vance campaigned in North Carolina on Monday and President Donald Trump is in North Carolina today as part of the GOP voter turnout effort. 
At campaign stops, Trump often tells supporters to pretend he’s on the ballot.
That Trump refrain is a double-edged sword, Bitzer said. He motivates his base, and he also motivates voters who oppose him. 
“By the end of this week and into next weekend, things will get firmed up in terms of the pattern,” Bitzer said. “This week will be a critical week if Republicans are going to get out the vote for early voting or take their chances on Election Day.“
Early voting ends Oct. 31.
Elon University Poll shows Cooper maintaining lead in US Senate race
In the Senate race, the Elon University Poll has Democrat Roy Cooper, a former governor, ahead of Republican Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, by 52% to 39% among likely voters. 
Cooper led among voters the poll identified as independents who don’t lean Democrat or Republican, 43% to 12%. 
“Roy Cooper’s sustained lead over Michael Whatley in North Carolina is being driven in large part by strong support among moderates, true independents and women,” Jason Husser, director of the Elon University Poll, said in a statement. “We also are seeing signs of a potential turnout gap, with Cooper voters expressing higher levels of excitement about voting in the election and placing more importance on the election for real-world outcomes in their lives.”
The race can still tighten, Husser wrote. When pressed, undecided voters give Whatley a slight advantage, and Whatley’s supporters appear motivated to vote.
The poll was conducted between Sept. 9 and Oct. 10 and had 800 participants. The poll has a margin of error for all respondents of 4.03 percentage points and 4.9 percentage points for likely voters.

name: National
title: Nine states shed jobs in the past year
text:
Scout Motors assembly line workers working earlier this year inside the electric vehicle maker’s new on-site training facility in Blythewood, South Carolina. South Carolina had the largest percentage growth in jobs among states. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)  Nine states and the District of Columbia lost jobs in the year ending in September, according to a report released Tuesday by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Hit hard by the Trump administration’s cuts to the federal workforce, the District of Columbia suffered the largest percentage job loss, down 3.5% or 25,800 jobs. Montana, which lost jobs for the first time since 2020, shed 1% of its total workforce, or 5,300 jobs. Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Virginia all experienced declines of less than 1%.
The state that gained the most jobs was South Carolina, up 2.3% or 55,200 jobs, followed by Louisiana (up 1.8% or 36,000), and Nevada (up or 1.6% or 25,300).
South Carolina’s job growth was concentrated in construction, health care, and leisure and hospitality, said William Floyd, the state’s employment and workforce executive director, in a statement.
In addition, car parts manufacturers in the state have been ramping up to supply a planned Scout Motors factory, which has already begun training workers. Hiring also has begun for a new BMW battery factory.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota specialty courts cost thousands less than incarceration, report says
text:
An equal justice statue stands outside the doors of the Minnehaha County Courthouse in Sioux Falls. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota specialty courts are saving taxpayers money on prison costs, according to an annual report presented to the state’s Drug Court Advisory Council.
The council oversees the state’s 17 specialty courts, which include drug courts, mental health courts and DUI courts. 
Each court is an intensive program with weekly check-ins that take place in courtrooms but function more like mental health group therapy sessions led by a judge, who checks in with participants one by one to ask about their jobs, families, addiction treatment sessions and other life stressors. The judge can issue sanctions for poor behavior, like failing a drug test or quitting a job, or rewards for good behavior, like finishing outpatient drug treatment.
Pretrial monitoring could reduce missed court appearances and improve outcomes, court officials say

Each participant pleads guilty to a felony charge up front, avoiding prison time through a promise to stay sober and move through the program, which typically lasts around 18 months. Those who leave or fail typically go to prison.
The Drug Court Advisory Council includes judges, prosecutors, defense lawyers and treatment providers. The council oversees the specialty courts and makes recommendations on policy adjustments for the courts.
The group met virtually on Tuesday and discussed the South Dakota Treatment Courts Annual Report for fiscal year 2026, which ended June 30.
The courts had 707 participants in that timeframe, said Noreen Plumage, the treatment court director for the state’s Unified Judicial System. That’s a drop from the 759 people participating in the previous fiscal year, she said, but “our new admissions are on the rise,” Plumage said, with 304 people starting in treatment court.
There were 167 graduations, Plumage said. The price to the state to move each of those graduates through the program is $8,137. The average annual price of a year in prison in South Dakota is $34,000, the report said.
The courts had a 60% graduation rate last year, and 71% of graduates did not commit any new crimes within five years of their graduation.
Terry Dosch is a member of the advisory council, and is director of the South Dakota Council of Mental Health Centers. Dosch asked Plumage to make sure the report is shared “with our legislative friends.”
“I think the data are very compelling, especially the cost contrast between drug court and incarceration,” Dosch said
