That same month, BLM officials asked the federal appeals board to dismiss the agency’s approval of the data center in order “to allow the agency to conduct additional review of the application.” 
Townsite Solar 2 LLC, the data center developer, did not oppose the motion and Center for Biological Diversity and Sierra Club took no position. Boulder City opposed the motion, requesting a ruling on whether BLM’s decision was lawful under environmental law. 
Boulder City welcomed the appeals board decision to revoke approval for the data center and supports a comprehensive environmental review, said Lisa LaPlante, the communications manager for the city.
“It remains the City’s position that the BLM must follow federal law in approving of such a use and provide the City and the public with meaningful opportunity to be involved in if, how, when, where and why these facilities are authorized,” LaPlante said.
Townsite Solar 2 LLC did not respond to a request for comment. 
Patrick Donnelly, the Great Basin Director for the Center for Biological Diversity, said they are now waiting on the BLM’s next move.
 “We got the approval thrown out, so we feel pretty good about that,” Donnelly said. “We’re kind of waiting for next steps or what’s going to be happening from BLM or the developer, but we know they’re starting from ground zero.” 
Donnelly said there’s no precedent for a data center on federal land, raising questions on how the federal government will analyze enviromental impacts, including noise, wildlife habitat, air quality, and socioeconomic issues. 
“These are all pressing questions that we raised in our appeal that they’re going to have to answer if they expect to permit one of these projects,” Donnelly said. 
As more local governments push back against data centers, public land will become more attractive to developers, said Donnelly. The Townsite Data Center could influence how future projects are permitted on public lands, he added. 
“It’s actually getting kind of difficult to put data centers on private land because county commissions are getting swayed by their angry constituents. But meanwhile, this administration is taking a battering ram to all of our federal environmental statutes, paving the way for seemingly very easy development of data centers on public land,” Donnelly said.
President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order directs federal agencies to accelerate the construction of large data centers and supporting energy infrastructure on federal land.
BLM invoked the policy in its initial approval of Townsite, saying the development “supports federal efforts to accelerate permitting for data center infrastructure.”
If implemented on BLM lands, the plan could have major implications for public lands throughout the West, and especially in Nevada where about 80% of the land is managed by the federal government.

name: Nevada Current
title: A midwife solution to Nevada’s maternity care problem
authors: Lorraine M. Garcia, PhD, WHNP-BC, CNM
text:
(Photo: Catherine Delahaye/Getty Images)Nevada recently received an overall failing grade on the March of Dimes 2025 Report Card for key indicators of maternal and infant health. March of Dimes is a leading U.S. nonprofit organization that works to improve the health of moms and babies with a focus on ending preventable morbidity and mortality and correcting inequitable outcomes. The report card for Nevada shows poor grades for preterm birth rates, adequacy of prenatal care, the low-risk cesarean birth rate, infant death rates, and the maternal death rate. Notably, Carson City and Las Vegas are called out for their F grades on preterm birth rates.
Nevada state lawmakers have rightly made improving maternal and infant outcomes a priority as they prepare for the upcoming legislative session, with maternal health provisions proposed in a state “momnibus” bill. But for these efforts to be effective, our legislative and policy leaders need to expand and strengthen two underused and previously overlooked solutions: accredited freestanding birth centers and integrated access to licensed midwives.
Birth centers are freestanding health care facilities focused on providing midwifery-led maternity care services. Birth centers offer highly personalized attention, holistic support programs and comprehensive midwifery care, while coordinating consultations with physicians and hospital transfers as needed.
Research consistently shows that low-risk women who receive care at accredited, freestanding birth centers have better outcomes when compared with similar women who receive hospital-based maternity care. That’s why leading organizations like The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society of Maternal-Fetal Medicine recognize accredited birth centers as an integral part of the health care system in the U.S.
Midwifery care through birth centers also lowers costs. Most savings come from lower cesarean rates for low-risk women, lower preterm birth rates, and lower rates of neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions, all of which can be costly for families and society. For example, in Nevada it is estimated that the annual cost associated with each preterm birth is around $65,000. According to the think tank Heartland Forward, the total workplace productivity lost due to preterm births cost the state $6,648,863 each year between 2014-2020.
Midwifery care—whether in homes, hospitals, or birth centers—has also been shown to provide better experiences for mothers, with lower rates of reported mistreatment, disrespect, and abuse. This is particularly true for Black women and other minoritized groups who experience harm at higher rates during pregnancy, birth, and postpartum.
Better access to midwives and birth centers isn’t a solution by itself. To work safely, midwives must consult with physicians and make coordinated transfers to obstetricians and hospitals for medically complex pregnancies and births, and in cases of rare obstetric or newborn emergencies.
That’s why it’s important for Nevada to improve its integration of midwives across all birth settings, meaning that women have routine access to midwifery care for home births, birth center births, and hospital births without discrimination. While Nevada is a strong parental rights state where the right to home birth with any chosen birth attendant has been defended in previous legislative sessions, our ranking for midwifery integration is the lowest among the Western states.
In addition to low midwifery integration, Nevada has one of the smallest midwifery workforces in the country. Nevada continues to be the only state in our region with no pathway to licensure for Certified Professional Midwives who focus on births in homes and birth centers. Meanwhile, Certified Nurse Midwives, who mostly attend childbirth in hospitals, do have an autonomous licensure pathway, but often face restricted hospital privileges, are excluded by insurance payers, and receive unsustainable reimbursement rates.
This matters because where midwives have greater integration in a healthcare system, mothers and newborns have better outcomes on a host of quality measures, including many of the ones for which Nevada is graded so poorly. Our fellow Western states of Washington and Oregon, for example, have seen great successes with high midwifery integration and the resulting association with better perinatal outcomes.
Expanding access to midwifery and freestanding birth centers can also address the lack of childbirth providers across the large rural and frontier areas of Nevada. A March of Dimes report shows that 47.1% of counties in Nevada are maternity care deserts, which means they lack a hospital or birth center offering childbirth services by a licensed midwife, obstetrician, or family physician.
Nevada has the capacity to scale up its midwifery workforce and the capability to support freestanding birth centers in areas of need. The UNLV School of Nursing has had a Master of Science Nurse-Midwifery program since the fall of 2023. State-directed funds that support the ability of UNLV to continue to educate and retain Certified Nurse Midwives to work in Nevada are vitally important. Nevada also has the opportunity in the upcoming legislative session to pass an optional licensure bill for community-based Certified Professional Midwives, who are already popular and practicing throughout Nevada, but who currently remain without a pathway to licensure which limits their ability to work with more families and be a recognized part of the healthcare system.
There are promising developments already happening in our state that demonstrate solutions for how we can improve the health and happiness of our moms and babies. For one, Nevada already has an existing facility model for how to provide excellent maternal and newborn outcomes in the community: Serenity Birth Center in Las Vegas, the only freestanding birth center in the state. Serenity is also where I am a co-medical director and work as a midwife. Midwives at Serenity have attended over 1,200 births since the center opened five years ago and the performance outcomes for the moms and babies at Serenity earn an A-grade by the same March of Dimes indicators for which Nevada is failing.
Additional encouraging news is that the Nevada Health Authority is working to support access to birth center care for women and their newborns who rely on Medicaid. Currently, state Medicaid programs must cover licensed freestanding birth centers, but without reasonable contract rates for essential services, birth centers are forced to deny services to Medicaid-covered clients due to an inadequate payment structure that does not cover the costs of care.
The evidence is clear. Nevada needs to increase midwifery integration through updated regulatory and payment structures that recognize licensed midwives and community-based birth options as essential parts of the solution to our state’s maternity care crisis. If we continue to neglect these proven solutions, we will continue to be an outlier among the Western states with more money spent while Nevada moms and babies continue to suffer from avoidable pregnancy and childbirth-related harms.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: ICE in the crosshairs as NJ Democrats fight to win back control of Congress
text:
New Jersey Democrats say more hearings probing immigration enforcement and less money for ICE are in the cards if their party wins control of Congress. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]New Jersey Democrats who have spent more than a year clashing with the Trump administration over the president’s mass deportation effort say winning the House in November could give them real power to probe what they call the administration’s immigration enforcement abuses.
They have protested outside Newark migrant jail Delaney Hall, fought the feds’ plan to build a detention center in Morris County, and held a shadow hearing to reveal what they say is the human cost of immigration enforcement and detention.
“Part of the reason you do those is to clearly demonstrate what you would do if you had the gavels and what type of hearings you would have,” said Rep. Rob Menendez (D-08), who is running for his third term in November with no Republican opponent.
The Nov. 3 midterm elections will decide whether Republicans retain control of Congress or whether President Donald Trump’s plunging approval ratings will allow Democrats to flip the House of Representatives, the U.S. Senate, or both. Here in New Jersey, Sen. Cory Booker (D) is on the ballot, as are all 12 House seats.
A Democratic victory could force more Trump administration officials to testify in front of Congress at hearings controlled by Democrats, and it could give the party a stronger hand in deciding how much money U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement receives in the future.
New Jersey has made national news for being on the front lines of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, with Delaney Hall becoming a flashpoint in the debate earlier this year when protests erupted outside the facility. Morris County residents, too, saw themselves at the center of the debate when the administration said it would open an immigrant processing center in Roxbury, a plan that quickly became the target of a lawsuit by the Sherrill administration and Roxbury’s GOP leadership. And Rep. LaMonica McIver (D) is set to stand trial on federal assault charges related to one of her oversight visits to Delaney Hall last year, a trial she said is part of the president’s crusade against his administration’s critics.
New Jersey Democrats have touted the work they’ve already done as the party in the minority, including regular oversight visits to Delaney and Elizabeth Detention Center. Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-11) said she found a constituent in detention during one of those visits, a Morristown small business owner with a work permit who paid taxes and who had been detained and “given a quarter of her diabetes medication.” Mejia won a special election in April to represent the 11th District in the House and is running next month to remain in the seat for the 120th Congress, which begins its term in January.
“As we prepare for the 120th, we need to ensure that we’re creating a roadmap, a pathway to citizenship, to as many law-abiding people that actually build and support our economy, our nation, our democracy,” she said.
Her Republican opponent, Joe Hathaway, said he worries a Democratic majority would lead to a rise in power for the party’s left-leaning faction. Hathaway, a councilman in Randolph, said those Democrats want “no jails, no Supreme Court, no borders.”
“That group will have now an outsized influence when it comes to legislation,” he warned.
At a recent town hall in Bloomfield, Mejia told voters she does indeed believe the nation should have borders.
“It is important for us to realize, however, that our immigration system, one, it has evolved,” she said. “Part of the problem that we are seeing is that people stay in limbo for over a decade, even if you’re following the law. And so what I have advocated for is we should invest in a system — if you can fill out a credit card application and in 15 seconds you are determined credit-worthy, that means that it shouldn’t take a decade to investigate someone’s background to make sure we understand who they are and whether or not we want to absorb them, welcome them into the fabric of the United States.”
Much of the conversation about New Jersey’s role in the national debate on immigration has focused on Delaney Hall. But it has reverberated statewide, even down to the 2nd Congressional District.
Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock (D), left, is running to unseat Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District. (Mullock photo courtesy of his campaign/Van Drew photo by Anne-Marie Caruso)
Rep. Jeff Van Drew flipped that district to Democratic control in 2018 before he changed parties and became a Republican. Van Drew visited Delaney Hall back in June and said critics of conditions inside the jail are lying about what they’ve seen. Democrats “continue to choose the side of illegal immigrants over the American people,” he said during a congressional hearing in July.
This week, Van Drew said an alleged drunk driver who struck and seriously injured a Middle Township police officer on Friday has an active ICE detainer. He called the incident another in a line of “preventable tragedies.”
“Just weeks ago, a baby was killed in a New Jersey parking lot by an unlicensed driver who was in this country illegally. Then a six-year-old girl was kidnapped and sexually assaulted by a man who should have been deported. Now we have a young South Jersey police officer fighting to recover from devastating injuries. When is enough enough?” Van Drew said in a statement.
Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock, the Democrat challenging Van Drew, in an interview blasted the Trump administration’s mass deportation effort and Van Drew’s support of expanded enforcement.
“He represents an area where we need immigrants. We need them in our restaurants. We need them on our farms. They are out there right now farming in South Jersey, and he would like you to ignore that,” he said.
Mullock said he supports a strong border but said he would return “decency and respect” to immigration enforcement efforts. He also would ban private prisons in New Jersey, expand transparency around immigrant detention, and work to expand pathways to citizenship.
“We should decide who and who isn’t invited into our country. There’s no doubt about that. Full stop. Period. Strong border. However, we were supposed to be going after the worst of the worst, and that is not what’s happening,” Mullock said. “People who are washing dishes or working on a home on my own street are being arrested by ICE with basically no criminal history. That is insane.”
Rachel Peace, a Democrat hoping to unseat Rep. Chris Smith, the Republican incumbent in the 4th District, said she’s heard from voters that immigrants need to come to the U.S. “the right way,” but she thinks that misunderstands American immigration rules, which have become overly complicated.
“It used to be very simple: You come to Ellis Island, you provide them with your name and information, and you’re allowed entry,” Peace said.
But people emigrating here now face varying caps on who can come from what countries and other restrictions where missteps can result in reentry bans or worse, she said.
“Instead of making it so hard for people to ‘do things the right way,’ can we not modernize our process?” Peace said.
Making immigrants gain citizenship “the right way” is a campaign talking point for Michael McGuire, a Republican hoping to unseat Rep. Herb Conaway (D) in the 3rd District. McGuire released a video this week calling for a strong border and a path to citizenship for “people who follow our laws.”
“This is about being smart and fair, securing our border while giving people who do it the right way a real chance to become citizens,” McGuire said in a statement.
Ryan Michael Kelly, an independent also running in the 3rd District, said this message means little “when the system itself is broken.”
“When Congress begins its new term in January, I want to see real immigration reform. That means fixing processing delays, improving legal pathways, protecting asylum seekers and families, and restoring strong civil rights oversight” at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Kelly said. “I also support abolishing ICE and replacing it with an accountable enforcement system that focuses on real public safety while respecting the Constitution.”
Hathaway has also called for immigration reform. He said he supports a path to green cards for long-term residents who contribute to the economy, raise their families here, and do not have a criminal background. People who commit crimes, he said, should be deported.
“People who are trying to achieve the American dream, they shouldn’t have to look over their shoulder all the time, wondering when the other shoe is going to drop,” he said. “I think we need to be creating a system that gives folks like that a real pathway toward recognition.
Adam Hamawy speaks during the 12th Congressional District candidate forum at First Baptist Church of Lincoln Gardens in Somerset on April 11, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Adam Hamawy, the Democratic nominee in the 12th District, said he’s not confident that Republicans and Democrats could agree on meaningful immigration reform. The most immediate change if Democrats are in the majority would be increased oversight, he said.
“We need to have some subpoenas. We need to have some hearings,” he said. “We need to charge the criminals that are shooting our neighbors in the street and kidnapping them while they’re dropping their kids off to school.”
Hamawy said immigrants in his district, including naturalized citizens who now carry their passports with them, have been made to feel “second class,” whether they are here legally or not.
“If there’s a normal legal process, people will go through it,” Hamawy said. “We just are lacking that.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Will $1 billion for the Great Salt Lake materialize? Sen. Curtis says he’s working on it
text:
At right, Tim Davis, Utah Department of Environmental Quality commissioner, briefs U.S. Sen. John Curtis and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin during a tour of the Great Salt Lake at Farmington Bay on Saturday, May 23, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune) During a discussion focused on water and saving the shrinking Great Salt Lake, U.S. Sen. John Curtis said on Monday he’s trying to drum up the political will in Congress to help President Donald Trump’s $1 billion proposal for the lake materialize. 
The president’s budget request is just that — a request, which needs approval from Congress. 



This article is published through the Great Salt Lake Collaborative, a solutions journalism initiative that partners news, education and media organizations to help inform people about the plight of the Great Salt Lake — and what can be done to make a difference before it is too late.


“Now we, as legislators, have to figure out where that money’s going to come from,” the Utah Republican said at the University of Utah’s Hinkley Institute of Politics in Salt Lake City during a speaking event hosted by the Sutherland Institute, a conservative think tank. 
Utah’s federal delegation is now working to convince their colleagues the effort “is worth $1 billion.” 
“So that’s the mode that I’m in right now, is working with my colleagues to help them understand why a $1 billion investment in the lake is a good investment,” he said. “To do that, I’m physically inviting them here to Utah, talking to them, trying to educate them.” 
He said it’s also Utah leaders’ jobs, in order to help convince Congress to bring that money to fruition, to answer the question: “What would you do with $1 billion?” 
Curtis warned, however, that it may take multiple years to bring that $1 billion to the state. 
“In a perfect world, we’d get a $1 billion in this year’s budget. In reality, we may work for a couple of years,” he said. “But I do actually think, ultimately, the federal government’s investment may exceed $1 billion, and it probably should.”
He argued the shrinking Great Salt Lake is a “regional issue,” with ecological and economic threats that could hurt not just Utah, but the West. He also said it could have global implications, if state and federal leaders figure out a way to save the saline lake — which hasn’t been done before, ever. 
“There is no track record of success of ever saving a lake like the Great Salt Lake. We have never done it in the world’s history. Every place has failed in actually doing it,” he said. “So doing it here, figuring it out, it’s important for the world, not just Utah. It’s important for the region. And that’s why I think it’s important to make a case federally for some assistance.” 



 
Curtis’ comments came during a livestreamed interview with Sen. Todd Weiler, a Republican legislator who also works as president and CEO of the Sutherland Institute. 
Weiler said there have been “some pretty far-fetched ideas” to solve the problem, including building a canal or a river from the ocean to Utah or from Mississippi, or a pipeline from southern Idaho. 
“Do you put much stock into those ideas?” Weiler asked. 
In August, Curtis convened a panel of experts and policymakers, challenging them to come up with “bold and audacious” ideas for saving the Great Salt Lake, KSL reported. He has also called for “pioneer-scale ambition” to do so.
Curtis pointed to Utah pioneers building a 28-mile canal only equipped with picks, shovels and horse-drawn equipment as an example of what Utahns’ ancestors accomplished during their time — and he called for ideas that may seem wild for our time. 
Visiting EPA administrator throws support behind Great Salt Lake, punts on controversial data center

“I think we should take some of these constraints off and say for a minute, just dream. Like, what would happen if we piped water from Idaho?” Curtis said, adding he’s also heard ideas to bring water from Louisiana. “What would happen if we worked with California folks and said, ‘Look, let’s put in desalination in California. We’ll help you pay for it and then you pull less water out of the Colorado River.” 
Curtis added that “I guarantee you, if we did any of those things and we sat in a room 50 years from now, we would go, ‘Wow, man, that was cheap.’”
Weiler said he thinks the desalination partnership with California “actually has merit” and will “probably happen.” 
Curtis said what’s been “missing in the conversation” around saving the Great Salt Lake is, in addition to encouraging Utahns to conserve water, “we’ve got to be more bold and more audacious and think of the things right now that seem impossible.” 
“We have to change the math. There is not enough water, even with conservation,” he said. “Well, how do you change the math? You do something dramatic like that.” 
Weiler asked what Curtis’ message is to young Utahns “who worry they won’t have a reliable water source for a healthy Great Salt Lake to raise their own children here” 30 years from now.
“Well, the evil part of me wants to say, ‘Yes, you should move away, right? Because I’d like less people here,” Curtis said. “But in reality, this is an amazing place to live. And if you look at every place where you would consider living, they’re going to have issues. … So the reality of it is, you have to make your home better, no matter where you decide to live. … I’d also say roll up the sleeves and be part of the solution. Like, let’s figure this out.” 
When Weiler asked if state or federal government “mandates” are the solution to saving the Great Salt Lake, Curtis said mandates have problems.
Farmers want to help the Great Salt Lake, but feel like ‘scapegoats’ for a more complex problem

“I would question the efficacy of mandates and exactly what would we mandate?” he said. “How do you mandate a shower time? How do you mandate water — everybody’s lawns are different sizes. … I cannot personally think of a lot of situations where mandates have actually been that effective.” 
Weiler said “the most effective mandate” would be to require water metering statewide. Curtis agreed, saying, “I like that one.” 
Weiler said alfalfa farmers in recent years have become “the boogeyman” when it comes to the lake, but he noted the crop is often “grown in areas that are outside the watershed for the Great Salt Lake.”
“So if we banned alfalfa hay growing tomorrow, it wouldn’t necessarily help the Great Salt Lake nearly as much as people think it would,” Weiler said. “And other things would be grown in place of those crops.”
While encouraging big ideas to find solutions, Curtis also warned against placing the blame for Utah’s water problems on one actor.
“If you’re coming up with boogeymen, you’re going to come up with enemies,” Curtis said. 
He urged that the conversation not be focused on “good versus bad” but rather on how everyone involved can do their part. 
“We’re all part of this, right? If you single out any group, you’re just going to make them an enemy … We need everybody on the team,” Curtis said. “So I would advocate for, ‘Look, nobody’s at fault here. It is what it is. It’s developed over time. Now let’s come together, put our best minds together, and make good decisions.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Elbows up in Washington state over Canada’s proposed oil tanker terminal on border
text:
Medium-sized tankers, like this one anchored near Anacortes, could be joined in the Salish Sea by much larger crude oil supertankers if Alberta, Canada succeeds in building a new pipeline and export terminal to the southern British Columbia coast. (Photo by Tom Banse)Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and comedian Mike Myers made the phrase “elbows up” a national rallying cry in the midst of a trade war incited by the Trump administration. 
Canada’s economic pivot away from the U.S. includes fast-tracking a new oil pipeline from Alberta to a proposed marine terminal in British Columbia, practically on the border with Washington state.
The proposed Pacific Link crude export project entails a 775-mile pipeline from Alberta’s northern oilsands region to a new tanker loading terminal on the Strait of Georgia in the Vancouver suburb of Delta. As proposed, the pipeline will be capable of delivering up to 1 million barrels per day to a pair of supertanker berths located less than two miles from the maritime border with Washington.
The massive undertaking has environmentalists, tribes and Democratic politicians in the Evergreen State sharpening their own elbows. They are deeply concerned about increased tanker traffic and oil spill risk in the shared Salish Sea and are working to coordinate their opposition efforts with like-minded British Columbians. 
But how can this Washington state-styled “elbows up” influence a project to be built entirely on Canadian soil?  
 “We recognize that there are conflicts between our countries that are much greater than us. We are not going to be able to solve those issues. But on this issue, we can coalesce for the good of the environment and for the good of our communities,” said San Juan County Council Chair Justin Paulsen about the council’s collaboration with counterparts in the Canadian Gulf Islands.  
Paulsen said the San Juan council has coordinated with councilors in the Islands Trust government to raise concerns about increased vessel traffic. If the new pipeline becomes operational in the early 2030s as planned, many more oil-laden tankers would travel through the narrow passageways between the Gulf Islands and San Juan Islands, then down Haro Strait and out to sea past Victoria and Port Angeles.
“The U.S.-Canada border is not going to stop a spill, right?” said Lovel Pratt, marine policy director for the group, Friends of the San Juans.
Pratt found common ground with environmental groups on the other side of the border, including the Georgia Strait Alliance and Raincoast Conservation Foundation. Together they are sounding alarms about the risk to endangered orcas, the danger of rampant underwater noise and the potential damage of a catastrophic oil spill.
Friends of the San Juans is collecting signatures on an online petition to Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson and Ecology Department Director Casey Sixkiller. It asks those two leaders to use “every available regulatory, diplomatic, technical, and legal avenue to oppose the Pacific Link pipeline.”
 “Governor Ferguson was our attorney general for many years. I would hope that if there were any legal challenges that could be made to oppose the project that he would find the options to pursue,” Pratt said. “I don’t know what those are.”
Ferguson met last month in Seattle with the Canadian ambassador to the U.S., but the governor’s office won’t say what they talked about. Ferguson and Sixkiller subsequently issued a statement in which they called on the Canadian government to fill anticipated gaps in oil spill response capabilities.
Ferguson’s joint statement and a separate Friends of the San Juans post with qualms about the Canadian oil project drew a high proportion of negative responses on social media from Washingtonians more concerned about high gas prices. “Drill baby drill” and “What Canada does is Canada’s business” were common refrains.
Alberta responds
The government of Alberta is taking the lead in promoting and defending the new pipeline and supertanker terminal project. Provincial leaders have made a two-pronged case to address the potential of a tanker accident and oil spill.
A YouTube video produced by the government opens by noting the exemplary safety record of the oil tankers serving the existing crude export terminal in suburban Burnaby, B.C. 
“In B.C. waters, there hasn’t been an oil spill in more than 50 years. That strong track record has continued even with increased tanker traffic,” the narrator intones.
Preliminary documents submitted by the province for federal review said the Pacific Link project would build upon major upgrades in spill prevention and response capabilities that accompanied a recent Trans Mountain Pipeline expansion. All of the tankers departing the proposed new export terminal would be double-hulled and have extended tug escorts.
The new energy infrastructure will be built with tens of billions of Canadian taxpayer dollars – 45% from the government of Alberta, 45% from the federal government and the remaining 10% from private investor Pembina Pipeline Corporation. The partners have been clear that a prime objective is to lessen Canada’s dependence on the United States by increasing capacity to ship crude to customers in East Asia and as far away as India.
The federal and Albertan governments are pushing to finalize the pipeline route and complete the regulatory review by Sept. 1, 2027. Construction could start as soon as next autumn with oil flowing in 2032 or 2033.
“Canada has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to become a global energy superpower,” Carney said in Alberta at the beginning of this month. “We have to do this.”
Tribal opposition spills across border
Though the Pacific Link pipeline has undeniable political momentum, it could have an Achilles heel due to misgivings among Indigenous groups along the route to the West Coast. South of the border, there is outright opposition.
Delegates to the annual convention last month of the Affiliated Tribes of Northwest Indians passed a resolution enumerating more than four pages worth of perceived transboundary threats.
“ATNI stands in solidarity with Tribal Nations and Indigenous peoples working to protect their territories, waters, salmon, cultural resources and future generations from the impacts of the proposed West Coast Oil Pipeline and associated tanker traffic,” the resolution said.
The Swinomish Indian Tribal Community in Skagit County portrayed the stakes in starker terms in a statement provided to the Standard. Tribal Chairman Steve Edwards noted the Swinomish exercise treaty fishing rights in the San Juan Islands.
“Shipping such a huge new amount of oil in these narrow internal waterways represents an existential threat to Swinomish’s Treaty fishing rights, our salmon and shellfish, our cultural lifeways and our friends the Southern Resident killer whales,” Edwards wrote. 
“A single spill of this highly toxic tar sands oil would poison the Salish Sea for generations because there is no technology in existence to recover tar sands oil once it hits the water,” he wrote.”
One northern Washington tribe, the Lummi Nation, may try to demand a seat at the table in British Columbia for consultation and project review. Lummi leaders assert that the project proponents have a legal duty to consult and accommodate their concerns because the tribe’s traditional territory extended to the Fraser River estuary prior to the establishment of the international border. 
The transboundary rights of American tribes along the border are an evolving area of Canadian law. The Lummi Nation has recent experience with it through dueling in Canadian court with the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority. The Lummis express grave concern about the cumulative impact of big infrastructure projects around the Fraser River estuary – not just the proposed supertanker terminal, but also an adjacent container terminal expansion and a liquefied natural gas project.
The proposed Pacific Link pipeline would be buried alongside the existing Trans Mountain pipeline for most of its route, until a divergence in the suburbs of Vancouver, British Columbia, where it would branch off to a new deepwater export terminal close to the U.S. border. (Source: Government of Alberta)
Supertankers might be a leverage point
Plans to build a deepwater terminal capable of serving supertankers could provide another point of leverage for opponents. They don’t fit in Vancouver’s Inner Harbour where Alberta crude is currently loaded for export in medium-sized tankers. Supertankers have been banned from Washington’s inland waters for nearly 50 years. 
The appearance of supertankers greater than three football fields in length in the Salish Sea would be unprecedented. A selling point for what are known in the industry as Very Large Crude Carriers is that they can move more oil with fewer trips. The flip side is that the worst-case grounding or collision can result in a bigger oil spill.
Fred Felleman is a longtime marine protection advocate and elected Port of Seattle commissioner. He said the prospect of an even more catastrophic spill motivated him to research in his private time what strategies the U.S. government could pursue to keep supertankers out of the shared border waters.
“All the king’s horses and the king’s men will not put Humpty Dumpty back together again if a supertanker spills here,” Felleman said. Maritime law could be used to force Canada to the bargaining table, he said.
Felleman is preparing a white paper that would explain how the U.S. could declare a breach of a 1979 vessel traffic agreement if Canada allows passage of supertankers through the border waters. Another move could be to threaten to block free passage of Canadian-bound tankers that routinely use the shipping lanes on the U.S. side of the maritime border, he said.
“This is like State Department level stuff. It’s international treaties,” Felleman said.
Getting the U.S. Department of State and Coast Guard on board with such a pressure strategy could be difficult. However, if Democrats hold majorities in both chambers of   Congress next year, U.S. Rep. Rick Larsen and U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, both Democrats, will be in position to chair the respective committees with oversight over the Coast Guard.
“The people I represent have serious concerns about this new pipeline and how it could harm the Salish Sea,” Larsen said in early October. “They deserve answers to their questions and updated spill response plans that account for more oil tanker traffic, and I will keep fighting to get them both.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Trump’s attack on Rep. Ilhan Omar is an attack on Congress itself
text:
U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)Republished with permission from The UnPopulist. 
Before dawn last Monday, agents from Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, entered the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., with a search warrant. They left with her phone, computers, notebooks and passport. Only she and her husband were in the house. The Justice Department confirmed a court-authorized search in connection with an ongoing criminal investigation and said nothing more. Omar is up for reelection in two weeks.
Search warrants have been served on members of Congress before, usually in corruption cases. Those inclined to minimize what happened to Omar will point to them. But the comparison is a false one. Search warrants involving elected lawmakers can be, and often are, part of the regular, lawful process for investigating felonies such as bribery. This instance is fundamentally different because it represents a dangerous attempt to manipulate the legislature’s qualification rules to oust a congresswoman whom President Donald Trump dislikes.
A pretext for denaturalization
To start with, the investigation exists because the president has singled out a member of Congress as part of a broader and explicitly racist campaign against Americans of a particular ethnic origin. There is no other way to put it. Last November, Trump announced on Truth Social that he was ending Temporary Protected Status for Somalis in Minnesota, declared that Somali gangs were “roving the streets looking for ‘prey,’” and vowed to send Somalis “back to where they came from.”
In December, he told a Cabinet meeting that Somali immigrants were “garbage,” that Somalia was “barely a country,” and that “Ilhan Omar is garbage. She’s garbage. Her friends are garbage.” He has posted that she “should be in jail” and “sent back to Somalia.” At the same time, Haitians, whom the president himself accused of eating pets during his campaign, are being stripped of TPS and deported.
Jeanine Pirro, the former Fox News host Trump appointed as U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, where the raid was conducted, once mused whether Omar’s hijab showed fealty to Sharia law over the Constitution. The remark was so egregious that Fox disavowed it and publicly reprimanded her.
The great majority of Minnesota’s Somali community immigrated legally and have become American citizens, or else were born here as citizens.
Trump’s hateful screeds against Somali Americans are not a matter of dog whistles or subtly implied bigotry. This is overt, explicit, virulent racism, without any attempt to pretend otherwise. His obsession with attacking Omar is inseparable from that context.
In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told an audience that Omar had “married her brother” and that if the government could prove it, “we’ll deport you.” Border czar Tom Homan confirmed days later that HSI had opened a criminal investigation. Grand jury subpoenas went out to her relatives, including her sister — meaning the administration is targeting not only her but her extended family. The raid followed. That same evening, when Trump brought her up at a rally in Ohio, the crowd chanted “Deport!” The hostility came long before the investigation, and an investigation was found to fit it.
The investigation’s guiding theory seems to be that Omar’s late father lied that she was 17 instead of 18 when he filed her naturalization papers in 2000 so that she could obtain her citizenship without having to apply separately as an adult. Children under 18 become citizens automatically when a parent naturalizes; adults have to apply on their own. HSI looked at the same allegation under the Biden administration and dropped it for want of any evidence of fraud. DOJ also looked into Omar during Trump’s first term and declined to pursue a full investigation because of insufficient evidence.
Even granting the suspicion some factual basis — and there is none — no evidence of a long-ago paperwork discrepancy was going to turn up in a congresswoman’s townhouse a quarter century later. The government already holds every form she or her father ever submitted.
DOJ claims that its warrant was for a criminal investigation. But the statute of limitations for naturalization fraud is 10 years from the date citizenship was obtained, which in Omar’s case ran out in 2010. And her father, who actually filed the forms in question, is dead. A criminal charge would therefore have to rest on something Omar herself did more recently, such as a false statement on a later passport application or other form, and prosecutors have not said what that would be.
But the purpose of the criminal investigation may not be to pursue criminal charges against her. Rather, it may be a way to advance a civil lawsuit under the denaturalization statute to revoke citizenship. It’s a rarely used law, most famously applied to eject war criminals who had lied about their past. A civil denaturalization suit has no statute of limitations, no jury, and no requirement of a prior conviction. The government still has to prove the original fraud, but it gets to do so in a civil suit, under a lower standard of proof, decades after the fact.
The Wall Street Journal reported, citing administration officials and others familiar with the investigation, that the aim is to build a case to strip Omar of her citizenship and then deport her. She would become the most prominent target of a denaturalization drive that has already produced more than 200 lawsuits since Trump returned to office. The criminal investigation is the pretext that gets a search warrant signed; denaturalization and removal are the goal.
The predawn entry by armed agents into a family’s home may or may not yield evidence of a crime allegedly committed decades ago, but it is a show of force. The administration went out of its way to do it this way, and the only purpose that serves is to intimidate a political opponent.
The raid also sets aside a norm DOJ has maintained for decades. The department’s longstanding practice has been to avoid overt investigative steps against candidates in the roughly 60 days before an election, especially when waiting would not jeopardize the investigation. Searching a candidate’s home three weeks before she stands for reelection is about the clearest example of what the practice exists to prevent. Trump and his lawyers, several of whom now run the department, loudly invoked the same rule in 2024 against the prosecution of Trump himself.
What the House alone may judge
All of that would be bad enough if Omar were a private citizen. That she is a member of Congress matters, and it matters in a specific constitutional way that has so far gone mostly unremarked.
Article I, Section 5 provides that each house “shall be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members.” The qualifications themselves are fixed earlier in Article I: a representative must be at least 25, must have been a citizen for seven years, and must inhabit the state she represents. Whether a seated member meets those three qualifications is for the House to decide, and not for the president, DOJ, or a district court hearing a civil suit the executive branch has brought.
The administration has not disputed that only the House can make this determination, and for now it does not need to. Its strategy is to change the facts the House would be judging rather than to contest who gets to judge them: make her a non-citizen first, then hand the House the result and demand it comply.
The Framers embraced this rule for structural reasons. A legislature exists to check the other branches, and it cannot do so if one of those branches gets to decide who sits in it. An executive able to remove his critics from the chamber, or to decide which of them were ever entitled to be there, would not face a legislature at all, only a body whose membership he had selected.
The same section of the Constitution gives each house control over its own rules, its own discipline, and expulsion of its own members, and the next section shields members from being questioned anywhere else for what they say in debate. The judgment of qualifications sits among those provisions because it serves the same end. The members answer to their constituents and to their colleagues, and to nobody else.
The House’s control over its own membership does not put members beyond the reach of the ordinary law. A representative who takes a bribe can be investigated, indicted and convicted like anyone else, and nothing in Article I stands in the way. A conviction is not among the qualifications and does not by itself cost anyone a seat. What is different about the Omar investigation is its purpose. It is not aimed at punishing a crime but at taking away one of the three constitutional qualifications for the office she already holds, her citizenship.
The courts have treated the judging of qualifications as the House’s power to exercise, not theirs to review. When a house decides a contested election or a member’s qualifications, that decision is final, one of the few places where the Constitution makes a branch other than the judiciary the last word on a legal question. Both the House and Senate have considered and decided such disputes, including citizenship qualifications.
A denaturalization campaign against a sitting member is an attempt to get around that power first, and to contest it once the House has been presented with a result. The administration cannot expel Omar from Congress; that takes a two-thirds vote of the House. It cannot refuse to seat her; the House also has the sole power over that. What it can attempt is to go to court, obtain a judgment that her citizenship was procured by fraud, and then declare that she no longer satisfies the citizenship qualification and has to go. Every step in that sequence takes place outside the House. The chamber the Constitution makes the sole judge of its members’ qualifications would be handed a result and told the matter had already been settled elsewhere.
That assumption is already being made on the administration’s behalf. Ilya Shapiro of the right-wing Manhattan Institute told the Daily Caller that if Omar were denaturalized she “wouldn’t be able to serve in Congress and would likely have to leave the country.” He skips the step that matters. A court can rule on her naturalization. It cannot say whether she sits in the House. A civil judgment revoking naturalization is a judgment about immigration status, and nothing in it binds the House on the separate question the Constitution reserves to it, whether she is qualified to keep her seat. The House could examine a denaturalization order obtained by this process, for this purpose, and judge that its duly elected and already seated member remains qualified to serve. That she remains a member is the status quo unless and until the House says otherwise.
The House may have ultimate control over its membership, but the attempt to short-circuit that authority by abusing other processes does real damage. The House would keep its power on paper while being dared to assert it, and to assert her privileges as a member in full standing. That power would not be taken away so much as made beside the point, because the administration would already have decided the question the House is supposed to answer: whether she is a citizen. If the House declined to go along, there is every reason to expect the administration would insist and try to deport her anyway, and the indirect route would become a direct confrontation.
None of this turns on the technicality that the House could decline to go along. Suppose a member really had lied about a disqualifying past on her naturalization papers, a war criminal, say, who had concealed it to get in. That is the charitable hypothetical. DOJ should still follow proper process, free from political interference and partisan bias, including overt racial and religious animus. A more normal DOJ would proceed cautiously, observing the traditional norms to avoid the appearance of interfering in an ongoing election or challenging the House’s own constitutional powers in this area. The DOJ also knows how to work with Congress when the two are potentially running parallel investigations, or when they have overlapping responsibilities for a topic. This is an expected level of inter-branch comity and cooperation completely absent here.
The actual case is an investigation that began with the president’s public contempt for a member and for the ethnic community she belongs to, built on a claim two earlier reviews found baseless, and pursued with the reported aim of having a court declare a sitting member of Congress a non-citizen and potentially putting her out of the country while she still holds her seat. There is no version of that which avoids a constitutional crisis.
Nor could the administration simply arrest her without violating the Constitution. Until the House says otherwise, she remains a member, and Article I, Section 6 protects members from arrest while Congress is in session and while going to and returning from it, in all cases except treason, felony and breach of the peace. Normally those exceptions are so broad the protection has little practical effect. But immigration detention and removal are civil proceedings, not criminal ones, and fall under none of the exceptions. An ICE officer who arrested a sitting congresswoman on her way to the Capitol would be doing precisely what that clause was written to prevent.
Reaching past Congress
There is no reason to suppose Omar will be the last. An executive that can manufacture a disqualification for one member can do it for others, and she is far from the only naturalized citizen in Congress (currently there are 17 in the House and two in the Senate). A president willing to do this three weeks before an election is not going to stop at one.
The pattern is familiar from elsewhere. In Nicaragua, Daniel Ortega first had his electoral council remove 28 deputies from the National Assembly, then in 2023 had a court strip the citizenship of more than 300 opponents, many of them put on a plane and declared traitors.
In Russia, the Duma expelled the opposition deputy Gennady Gudkov in 2012 on a pretext about his business dealings.
In Hong Kong, Beijing reread the territory’s constitution, the Basic Law, to find that six elected legislators had taken their oaths improperly and so forfeited their seats, then in 2020 disqualified four more by decree. It’s a familiar authoritarian playbook.
What separates the campaign against Omar from the ordinary run of abuses is that it is aimed at the one body with the constitutional means to hold the president to account. Congress can investigate him, subpoena his officials, cut off his funding, and impeach and remove him. An executive that can threaten individual legislators with the loss of their citizenship and their country has found a way to reach past Congress as an institution and into the personal security of the people who make it up.
What one thinks of Omar’s politics has no bearing on any of this. The objection would be identical if the target were a member of the other party.
Our republic has been in an accelerating state of constitutional collapse for some time. But manufacturing grounds to unseat a member of Congress is still a serious escalation and shouldn’t be set aside as merely another Trump effort to punish his critics. It is an attack on the core load-bearing constitutional structure.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Republicans pour $300,000 into defense of GOP-leaning Senate seat in northwest Missouri
text:
The Missouri Senate at the end of the 2023 legislative session (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).Donald Trump carried Missouri’s 34th Senate District by 11 percentage points in 2024. The incumbent Republican state senator won re-election two years earlier by 18 points.
Yet with Election Day approaching, Republicans have spent more than $300,000 on television advertising to keep the northwest Missouri seat in GOP hands.
The spending comes as Democrats hope an increasingly unpopular president, energized voters and a slate of contentious ballot measures could put a traditionally Republican district in play.
Republican state Rep. Mike Jones of Kansas City faces Democrat Shereka Barnes, a member of the Park Hill Board of Education, in the race to replace term-limited state Sen. Tony Luetkemeyer in the 34th District.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Luetkemeyer won the seat with 52.5% of the vote in 2018, then won re-election with 59% in 2022. But the district’s boundaries changed in between, with Platte County becoming a larger share of the electorate after Buchanan County was split during redistricting.
A poll from August suggests that Republicans are doing more than using up accumulated cash. Between February and August, the St. Louis University YouGov poll of the generic congressional ballot moved 41 points against Republicans in northwest Missouri, generally Boonville to Maryville moving to the northwest and St. Joseph to Mercer County going from the southwest corner. From 56 points ahead, the survey put Republicans 11 points behind.
The results come with a significant caveat: The regional samples included just over 50 voters in each poll, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about the size or significance of the shift. But the survey suggests a serious shift in sentiment toward Republicans, said Ed Taylor, a professor of political science at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph.
“The poll’s broader findings fit a tougher environment for Republicans than a year ago,” Taylor said in an email. “(President Donald) Trump’s approval among Missouri likely voters slipped underwater for the first time in that poll, and approval of Gov. (Mike) Kehoe and the legislature hit new lows.”
Despite the shift in polling, Democrats face a steep climb in the 34th District.
“The district leans Republican, roughly R+11 based on the 2024 presidential vote,” Taylor said. “Republicans outnumber Democrats considerably among Missouri voters. Even with a better environment for Democrats, they’d need to overperform that baseline substantially.”
If Barnes defeats Jones, it won’t be by outspending him. Barnes has raised $39,877 since starting her campaign, spent $29,168 and had $3,831 on hand on Sept. 30. 
Jones raised $124,204 from late August to the end of September and had about $220,000 on hand on Sept. 30. Beverly PAC, a committee backing Jones, raised $166,827 and had just over $245,000 available. 
Beverly PAC reported another $122,000, mainly from PACs associated with other Republican senators, in the past week.
Jones’ campaign spent $190,000 on Kansas City broadcast ads, while Beverly PAC purchased more than $50,000 worth time on St. Joseph television stations. Another $73,000 in television buys came in the St. Joseph market from the Missouri Senate Campaign Committee, the PAC that backs GOP Senate candidates generally.
The main factor working against Republicans in northwest Missouri is Trump, said Jessica Gracey, an associate professor of political science at Northwest Missouri State University.
Gracey was the treasurer for a Democratic Missouri House campaign that spent nearly a quarter of a million dollars in 2022 and got a quarter of the total vote.
Polling nationally shows voter discontent with inflation and the war. Northwest Missouri farmers are buying diesel at record prices to harvest crops and making contracts for fertilizer that has also gotten expensive as the price of oil has increased.
“Democrats here have gotten a lot more energized than they would have before in a lot of ways, and a lot of that is being angry at President Trump,” Gracey said. “That is a big motivator for a lot of people.”
In northwest Missouri Senate primary, two GOP lawmakers who vote alike differ on styles

The political tide may be running toward Democrats, but Gracey said she doubts it is strong enough to overcome party identity in far northwest Missouri.
“It is hard for a Democrat to convince Republicans, and vice versa,” she said. “There’s just a whole lot more Republicans here than there are Democrats, and so while a lot of Democrats here feel very hopeful and are a lot more energized, I don’t know that that necessarily changes the outcome of the election.”
That leaves turnout as a potentially decisive factor, both Gracey and Taylor said.
Statewide, the focus this year is on three ballot measures: Amendment 3 to ban abortions; Amendment 6 to limit legislative power to change measures passed by initiative; and Proposition A, on the 2025 Republican effort to gerrymander congressional districts.
Through Saturday, campaigns had spent $12.3 million on broadcast ads for ballot measures on the Nov. 3 ballot. The only statewide candidate election, for state auditor, has not seen any broadcast ad spending by candidates.
Political research shows each ballot measure, Gracey said, can increase turnout by 1% to 2%. That would translate to 3% to 6% more voters than would otherwise come to the polls.
But how many people would otherwise vote is more uncertain this year than in many others. 
In the six off-presidential elections in Missouri this century, turnout has averaged about 2 million votes. The lowest was 2014, when, like this year, state auditor was the only statewide race. That year, Democrats did not field a candidate and a ballot measure on teacher tenure received the highest total vote of 1.44 million cast. 
The highest was in 2018, when 2.4 million people voted in the U.S. Senate race between Josh Hawley and Claire McCaskill.
The questions on the ballot, Gracey said, are likely to increase the effect seen by research.
“Having so many ballot measures, especially ones about abortion, something really big for voters, really salient for voters, probably will increase voter turnout quite a bit,” Gracey said.
Ballot measures definitely drove statewide turnout in August, when 1.4 million people cast ballots statewide. 
Much of the increase in this year’s primary was among voters who took Democratic ballots. Democratic primary turnout was almost 50% higher than average of primaries this century, while Republican turnout was only slightly above average.
“The best hard evidence of Democratic energy that I’ve seen is statewide primary turnout,” Taylor said.
Whether that Democratic enthusiasm carries into November — and whether dissatisfied Republicans stay home — could help determine the outcome in the 34th District.
The portion of Buchanan County remaining in the district has been represented by a Democrat on the county commission for five terms, though his most recent victory was narrow. 
Ron Hook, Western District county commissioner, won re-election in 2024 by just 23 votes. He  did not raise or spend more than $1,000 for his campaign and has not in any election. He counted on his experience in office to carry him through but told KFEQ/St. Joseph Post after the election that many voters are choosing a party rather than a person.
“There’s a lot of people that just want the courthouse to be completely Republican and red and whether you do a good job, I guess, or not in this community it doesn’t make any difference,” Hook said.
Both Buchanan and Platte counties supported abortion rights in the 2024 election, with Platte voting 62.3% in favor. Both counties supported Proposition A that year, which increased the minimum wage and set minimum standards for employee paid sick leave.
Republicans subsequently repealed the sick leave provision and a long-standing law requiring annual inflation adjustments in the minimum wage.
Democrats are making a big push for Missouri House seats in Platte County and see it as one of their most likely places to make gains.
 “What would most likely make the race more competitive is depressed Republican turnout,” Taylor said, “whether from dissatisfaction with national leadership, the economy, or other issues.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri task force drafts new child safety rules for courts, caseworkers
text:
Members of the child welfare task force consider draft legislation on Oct. 19 in Jefferson City. Pictured from left are Missouri Children's Division legislative liaison Haylee Musso, attorney and guardian ad litem Tamara Veit, Missouri Network Against Child Abuse Executive Director Jessica Seitz and Children's Division Director Sara Smith (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).Missouri child welfare workers and courts would be required to use the same standards to determine when children are unsafe and what must change before they can return home under draft legislation being developed by a state task force.
The proposal, discussed Monday by the 18-member task force appointed by Gov. Mike Kehoe, aims to make decisions about children’s safety more consistent across the state, give parents clearer expectations and help move cases more quickly through an overwhelmed child welfare system.
The draft bill would amend state law to establish common definitions and practices for division workers, juvenile officers, judges and guardians ad litem to use when assessing children’s safety and determining next steps. Courts would be required to use the same framework in protective custody and permanency hearings.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The proposed legislation would also require the Missouri Department of Social Services and the Office of the State Courts Administrator to develop standard forms for the division’s court reports and social service plans that outline what parents and the division must do to address safety concerns.
The task force was created to propose a statewide definition of child safety, identify gaps and contradictions in existing laws and policies, and establish processes to put the new definitions into practice.
The executive order establishing the task force came less than 24 hours before a bipartisan legislative hearing examining foster care deaths, staff turnover and rising investigation backlogs in the Missouri Children’s Division. It set a Nov. 15 deadline for the task force to recommend legislation.
 Establishing statewide safety standards

Walking the task force through the draft bill, Teri Armistead, director of the department’s Division of Legal Services, emphasized the importance of identifying and clearly describing safety threats early in a case. She said it provides clarity to parents about the expectations of the division and courts and, if a child is removed from their home, can provide a blueprint for the division, juvenile office and courts to address those threats.
“If we on the front end can articulate well what the safety threat is for that child, and if that child does have to be removed from the home, that through line carries throughout the entirety of the case,” Armistead said.
The draft says a child is unsafe when parents or adult caregivers are unable or unwilling to protect them from “present or imminent” safety threats. A safety threat must be “specific” and “articulable” and could include a “situation, behavior, motive, emotion, perception, capacity or lack thereof in a child’s home” or household.
The goal is to ensure that the reasons a child is considered unsafe — and what must change before that child can return home — remain consistent as the case moves through the child welfare system.
The proposed legislation would require the use of a “safety framework” to identify threats and decide how to respond. The division currently uses a safety assessment tool called Structured Decision Making, or SDM. During the last task force meeting on Oct. 5, members discussed the SDM and a child safety guide from the American Bar Association as models for Missouri legislation.
Armistead said the division would consider putting safety threats from the American Bar Association safety guide into its regulations. That guide lists fifteen types of safety threats, including living arrangements that endanger a child’s health and caregivers who lack the knowledge, skills and motivation to meet a child’s basic needs.
The draft bill would require courts to use the same definitions and practices as the division during hearings after children enter the division’s custody. During permanency hearings, when courts assess whether it’s in a child’s best interests to stay in foster care, return home or be adopted, courts would have to consider “whether safety threats persist, the protective capacities of caregivers and potential caregivers, the child’s vulnerabilities and whether less intrusive means are available….”
Children’s Division Director Sara Smith said standardized statewide forms and practices will help streamline the work of frontline staff and reduce caseloads by moving children’s cases through the system more quickly.
“I think it’ll directly impact our caseloads to be able to move children into more sustainable care and permanency in a more timely way because those standards and what we’re looking for are clearly articulated to families about how to have their kids back,” Smith said. 
Armistead said standardized forms would prevent frontline workers from having to duplicate their work. Currently workers must complete the division’s paperwork as well as separate court forms that vary among judicial circuits, she said.
In addition to developing new forms, the division would design a training program on child safety and the safety framework for all division employees and contractors who work with children. 
Republican state Rep. Melissa Schmidt of Eldridge, the chair of the task force, said the proposed changes could bring relief to overwhelmed division workers.
 “A standardized process — knowing that we’re all speaking the same language, that definitions are the same across the board — takes some of that frustration out and also takes out that burden of having to figure it all out by yourself,” Schmidt said.
 Concerns about temporary placements

The discussion of new safety standards came as Children’s Division officials shared findings from a year-long review of the agency’s existing practices, including concerns about how workers use temporary arrangements to place children with relatives.
Kara Wilcox, the department’s head of safety policy, said some staff were over-using temporary alternative placement agreements, or TAPAs.
TAPAs, which were put into state law in 2020, place children in a relative’s home for a maximum of 90 days, subject to renewal, while parents work with the division to address safety threats.
Wilcox said the division should ensure that parents are willing and able to make the changes needed to keep their children safe before initiating a TAPA.
“What we’ve seen is we don’t necessarily take into a lot of consideration whether the parent is truly ready for change,” Wilcox said.
Significant substance use issues often can’t be addressed within the timeframe of a TAPA, Wilcox said.
“So we should probably be considering all of our other resources and be recommending removal,” Wilcox said.
Part of the 2020 law requires TAPAs to identify “behaviorally specific changes” needed before the child can return home.
Marcia Hazelhorst, the division’s deputy director of safety, said workers have sometimes focused too heavily on providing services rather than determining whether parents have actually changed the behavior that put their children at risk.
“We should be building in services, but not relying on them, and getting a lot more concrete about what behavior it’s going to take (to move a case forward),” Hazelhorst said.
Haylee Musso, deputy legislative liaison for the division, said that while offering services can “help us get that behavior change,” it “doesn’t generate immediate safety.” 
Musso also emphasized that the goal of safety planning is to do everything possible to prevent children from being removed from their home.
Emily van Schenkhof, executive director of the Children’s Trust Fund of Missouri, said the state needs to do more to link families to behavioral health services.
“I’ve been perennially disappointed in our ability to truly make these connections happen,” van Schenkhof said. “So much of the risk that children and families that children face are when a parent or caregiver has a substance abuse disorder or mental health disorder.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska auditor presses state retirement agency for answers on outgoing director’s pay
text:
Nebraska Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley testifies before the Legislature's Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee. Feb. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — With no clear answers from the Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Board on the continued pay for its seemingly absent executive director, State Auditor Mike Foley said he is growing frustrated.
“The board is completely abdicating their fiduciary responsibility to the state, to the employees, to retirees,” Foley told the Examiner. “I’m very upset about this.”
NPERS current executive director Thomas Pfeifle submitted his resignation to the board on Sept. 21 after roughly three months leading the agency, saying he wanted to be closer to his children in Colorado. His resignation letter set his last day as Oct. 31, which the board approved at a special meeting Sept. 30.
NPERS staff have said Pfeifle has not worked in the NPERS office since Sept. 21. According to an Oct. 6 report from Foley, Pfeifle turned in his state cellphone, keys, laptop and identification, and ceased “all further interactions with the agency that day.”
Foley’s report estimated that NPERS would be paying Pfeifle roughly $23,000 in salary and benefits for roughly five weeks of unperformed work. Emails Foley sent to the Examiner show Pfeifle has already been paid roughly $7,800 — before deductions — for one payroll period since then, with several paychecks still to come.
To Foley’s knowledge, Pfeifle has put in zero hours of work since Sept. 21, and his pay has been distributed across his multiple pension plans.
“It’s just truly an assault on the taxpayers of Nebraska,” Foley said.
Pfeifle started working for NPERS in mid-June, earning an annual salary of $205,000, equivalent to about $98 per hour, according to Foley. His employment ended an 18-month stretch of NPERS being without an executive director after the resignation of John Murante in December 2024.
Foley said paying Pfeifle for unperformed work also implicates the Department of Administrative Services in what he alleges was an illegal payroll. Foley said NPERS officials had to coordinate with DAS to approve the payroll without Pfeifle logging any hours.
“An agency that reports directly to the governor has now approved a payroll for this man knowing full well he did not work those hours,” Foley said.
DAS Director Lee Will did not respond to a request for comment.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Foley recommended the board reconsider their decision to continue paying Pfeifle. At its latest meeting on Monday, it’s unclear whether the board took any action on Foley’s recommendation because most of their discussion about leadership happened behind closed doors.
The retirement board did not discuss Pfeifle during its public meeting, but it did address personnel matters, pending legal matters and “protection of public interest” among other items during a nearly two-hour executive session.
After the executive session, the board authorized NPERS legal counsel Tag Herbek to hire a consultant to aid in the search for a new executive director. Herbek said in an email that he will serve as interim director until further notice.
When asked if the board planned to make any changes in response to Foley’s concerns, Herbek said: “The board is always open to reevaluating agency operations when it will improve service and efficiency.”
Foley said he asked Herbek directly about Pfeifle’s pay, and he simply replied “no comment.” He said the board ultimately did comment by approving Pfeifle’s pay.
Foley said NPERS officials have also refused to share a document they received from the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office expressing an opinion on Pfeifle’s payment plan. He said he still intends to access that document, as it’s within his purview as auditor.
“Our statutes are very, very strong regarding access to all records,” Foley said. “It doesn’t say ‘some of the records’ or ‘most records.’ It says ‘all records,’ and I will see all the records of what really happened here.”
