name: Missouri Independent
title: Pain from the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ is coming after the midterms. Missouri isn’t ready.
text:
(Getty Images).The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the legislation President Donald Trump called the “One Big Beautiful Bill” would increase the federal deficit by $3.4 trillion over a decade, despite its massive cuts to healthcare and food assistance. It was designed so that its worst impacts wouldn’t be felt until after the midterm elections. 
Now the midterms are nigh, and Missouri has done too little to mitigate the coming pain.
Cuts to Medicaid are not popular. That’s why congressional Republicans denied they were cutting Medicaid in the legislation. And yet, Republicans looking for offsets to renew tax cuts passed in the first Trump administration found what the CBO estimates will be a $911 billion reduction in federal Medicaid spending over a decade. The law is expected to leave 10 million more Americans uninsured.
Health policy organization KFF estimates $326 billion of the Medicaid spending reductions will come from the legislation’s imposition of “work requirements” on people who are eligible for Medicaid through the Affordable Care Act expansion. Numerous studies show that people on Medicaid who can work are already working. Work requirements do not increase employment, just paperwork.
The savings will come from working poor people and people too disabled to work losing their health insurance, despite remaining eligible, because of administrative burdens that they can’t handle — or their states can’t handle. 
Missouri is terrible at administering benefits generally and particularly unprepared for this.
From January 2025 through February 2026, 333,265 Missourians lost Medicaid coverage, 91.9% of them not because the Missouri Department of Social Services found them ineligible, but for paperwork reasons. 
People lose coverage when they don’t receive their renewal letters, when the letters are confusing, when their work hours vary, when they can’t get ahold of the department after hours on hold, when the agency loses their documents or when the agency receives their documents but doesn’t process them before the computer automatically terminates their coverage. 
That’s without the federal work requirements that take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. It’s also without the new federal requirement that Medicaid expansion enrollees renew every 6 months.  Imposing that hurdle is expected to “save” another $63 billion when eligible people lose their insurance.
Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy is tracking states’ readiness to implement the law’s Medicaid requirements across eight metrics: call center wait times, call abandonment rates, application processing times, renewal rate, ex parte renewals (when the state uses data it already has to determine eligibility), disenrollments at renewal, disenrollments for procedural reasons and pending renewals. Missouri was one of three states to earn a red flag for 7 of the 8 metrics.
Cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or “SNAP,” formerly known as food stamps, will bring additional hardship. The law delays one major change until after the midterms: Beginning in October 2027, states with sufficiently high payment error rates will have to pay a portion of SNAP benefit costs for the first time. How much they pay will depend on their error rates, which measure overpayments and underpayments, often resulting from minor mistakes. 
Missouri has a history of failing to administer SNAP in compliance with the law. A federal lawsuit documented disabled people waiting on hold with the department’s call center for many hours only to have their calls dropped and their applications terminated. 
On Oct. 1, Missouri began requiring applicants and people renewing their SNAP benefits to provide additional documentation of their eligibility, in an apparent attempt to lower the error rate that will determine how much Missouri must pay for SNAP. 
Missouri’s error rate dropped from 9.42% in 2024 to 8.26% in 2025. But in the eight months after Missouri’s more stringent documentation requirements went into effect, 46,630 fewer Missourians received benefits.  
If Missouri’s error rate stays in the same range, the state will need to pay an estimated $150 million previously covered by the federal government.
The “One Big Beautiful Bill” has been a freight train headed toward us for a long time. Our representatives did nothing to stop it and little to prepare for it. U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley did so much talking about his opposition to Medicaid cuts, some of us thought he was serious. Instead he voted for the legislation despite it having $340 billion more cuts on top of the work requirements. Those cuts put an estimated 446 hospitals at risk of closing, nine of them in Missouri. Hawley said he’d work to restore the funding just after he voted to cut it. That entailed introducing a messaging bill that has no chance of going anywhere.
U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt and all of our Republican Congressional representatives voted for it as well.  
With the freight train approaching, our Republican state lawmakers put their all into an attempt to eliminate the income tax that voters rejected in August. A plan for filling our coming $1.7 billion budget hole has not been forthcoming.
The math ain’t mathin’. Republicans knew it was never going to, but they were clever enough to evade accountability by pushing the pain past the midterms.

name: WyoFile
title: Elections, data centers and court battles: Three secretary of state debate takeaways
text:
The secretary of state race is down to three candidates. At a Thursday debate, the remaining contenders shared their thoughts about elections, data centers, court battles and more. 
Republican Robert Short, a Converse County commissioner who sported a Jerry Garcia-inspired necktie at the debate, beat out three Republican candidates in the primary election, including Rep. Rachel Williams. Tamara Trujillo, a former Republican state representative, entered the general race as a Constitution Party candidate. Worland Democrat Bryan McCarty was unopposed in the primary election. 
Wyoming’s secretary of state post has risen in prominence in recent years as concerns about elections and shady corporations have intensified. The executive official’s responsibilities include overseeing elections and registering and authorizing businesses in the state. The secretary also serves on various boards. 
Here are three takeaways from the debate hosted by Wyoming PBS, Wyoming Public Media and Cowboy State Daily. 
Trujillo defends election monitors, giving voter data to feds
During the state’s primary elections, two U.S. Department of Justice attorneys were dispatched to Laramie County to monitor polling places. Gov. Mark Gordon described the monitors’ conduct as “aggressive” and “irregular.” 
In 2025, current Secretary of State Chuck Gray gave the department the driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers of every registered Wyoming voter. The move prompted a legal complaint, but Attorney General Keith Kautz declined to bring charges. 
Tamara Trujillo fields a question from the panel during the Wyoming PBS secretary of state debate on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
Asked about federal election monitors, Trujillo said she believes Wyoming is capable of running elections, but doesn’t see “anything wrong with a little bit of oversight.” “There’s nothing wrong with being a witness to something as long as you’re not overstepping and getting into the wrong lane,” she said. 
And while she doesn’t “really believe in helping the federal government more than it needs to be,” Trujillo defended Gray’s decision to hand over voter data to feds. “I’m not exactly sure what law he broke or what he did wrong if the courts didn’t find nothing to bring forth.”
Meanwhile, Short and McCarty said that elections should be in state hands. And they both criticized handing over voter records. 
Short says data ‘has to go somewhere’
As data centers flood Wyoming, the public has raised increased concern about these facilities’ environmental and economic impact. 
“There’s been a lot of disinformation spread about data centers,” Short said. 
Republican candidate Robert Short makes his opening remarks on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, during the Wyoming PBS secretary of state debate hosted at Riverton High School. (Carl Cote/County 10)
“If somebody wants to build something on their private property, it’s very difficult to tell them no. However, if they’re going to do something that takes away your right to water or electricity, that’s another conversation.”  
He added, “in the next five years, we will double all of the data ever created in the history of the world.” 
“It has to go somewhere,” he said. 
Candidates diverged on fighting out-of-state court cases
In 2024, Gray and two other Republican secretaries of state filed an amicus brief advocating to overturn a Colorado court’s decision to remove Donald Trump from that state’s ballot because of his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, riots at the U.S. Capitol. (The U.S. Supreme Court restored him to the ballot.)
Short and McCarty opposed using Wyoming tax dollars to fight such court cases. 
“I think it’s imperative that the secretary of state stay focused on the great state of Wyoming and what we do in Wyoming to help benefit the people of Wyoming,” Short said. 
Democrat Bryan McCarty takes his turn answering a question on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, during the Wyoming PBS secretary of state debate in Riverton. (Carl Cote/County 10)
McCarty put his thoughts in harsher terms, asking the audience how it feels about the secretary of state using tax money to “carry water for … a puppet of our most capable and consistent adversary on a global scale?” 
Meanwhile, Trujillo said that this is “a really tough decision.” 
“At the end of the day, I believe that in order to have a successful federal government, you have to have states unite.”
The post Elections, data centers and court battles: Three secretary of state debate takeaways appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: Some Wyoming voters have no clue who they’re voting for
text:
I did an informal exit poll outside Storey Gym in Cheyenne on Aug. 18, Wyoming’s primary election day. I’ve conducted similar polls to spot voting trends for various media outlets, usually in presidential election years, but what I found this time genuinely surprised me.

Opinion

About half of the 30 people who I asked to participate declined, which is comparable to what I’ve experienced in other elections. Several said their vote was sacred and they didn’t want to discuss it with anyone. I backed off immediately because privacy is their right.
I thanked everyone for voting as they walked away. That’s probably not something most media poll takers do, but it seemed like the right thing to say to people who showed up to vote.
But of the 50% who willingly participated in my exercise, about one-third couldn’t remember who they voted for in the two major primary races for governor and the U.S. House. This was just minutes after they cast their ballots!
Several asked who their choices were in the Republican primary, which both had contested races for those positions — four candidates for governor and nine for the U.S. House seat. I read their list of options, and while some remembered their choices right away, others were clearly guessing.
A few explained that they entered the polling place with a list of who to vote for, but they couldn’t find it. It sounded like they asked someone to tell them who to vote for and they dutifully checked those names on the ballot.
My results weren’t published, and I purposely didn’t get any voters’ names because it was a voluntary poll and I didn’t want to discourage anyone from participating. But I came away with two conclusions: Exit polls aren’t worth the time and effort it takes to do them, and I vow never to do one again.
But I don’t know what to think about voters who didn’t even know who they just voted for. That was a new one for me, and the sample size was so small I don’t know if it was a trend or I simply ran into a batch of random voters who were clueless about the candidates despite nonstop campaign advertising.
I’ve voted in every election I could since I became eligible in 1974, when I was 19. I know there are many people who have done the same thing once they could register to vote.
But Wyoming needs more voters. The state ranked 37th in 2024 for its 63.8% of registered voters who cast ballots. Washington, D.C. was first with 79.5% participation. We can do better.
Every year as it comes closer to the general election, political columnists and others write about the importance of voting. That should particularly resonate for Wyomingites, whose lack of participation in the 2024 primary changed the course of the state’s history for the worse.
Only 27% of the state’s eligible voters cast a ballot. As a result, the Freedom Caucus was able to win enough House primary races to enable it to take control of the chamber — even though only a total of 9% of the eligible voters in the primary cast a ballot for Freedom Caucus candidates.
The percentage of eligible voters who went to the polls in the 2026 primary jumped to 33%. When a party is internally split, as the GOP is between the far-right Freedom Caucus and traditional Republicans, elections are decided by which faction’s supporters show up.
In this year’s primary, after two years of watching the Freedom Caucus try to dismantle parts of state government, like the Department of Health, Wyoming Business Council and University of Wyoming, no more than 10 caucus members and their allies stand a chance of being elected to the House next year.
I suspect that the Freedom Caucus, which was cocky enough to predict it would also take over the Senate, decided it didn’t need to work any harder. Its leadership didn’t understand the depth of displeasure many voters had with cutting budgets just for the sake of cutting, nor did they grasp the loyalty people have to an institution like UW.
I think it’s the Fourth Estate’s job to encourage people to do their civic duty by doing a better job explaining how the results may affect them. Here’s a sample of what I see in Wyoming:

Proposition One is a ballot initiative that would cut residential property taxes by 50%. It presents a clear choice for voters — if approved, wealthy owners of the most expensive homes will get huge property tax cuts, while local governments and special districts will have to cut essential services like law enforcement, fire protection, road and bridge construction and many more.


Wyoming’s Republican Party was so worried that Democrats would choose who won their primaries that they changed the law so voters must declare what party they belong to before any candidates officially file for office.There weren’t enough Democrats who changed to Republicans in the August primary to pick the party’s U.S. House nominee, Secretary of State Chuck Gray. Though the GOP had a hissy fit over Mark Gordon knocking off two conservatives and winning only one-third of the vote in the 2018 gubernatorial primary, Gray only won 25% of primary votes.It will be interesting to see Gray’s percentage in the general election. He’s one of the state’s most polarizing candidates, he skipped the only televised statewide debate and none of his eight opponents endorsed him. Is that bright red “R” behind his name all he or any other candidate needs?


Many legislative races are close, and only a few votes can make the difference. In the 2024 Republican primary, veteran Sen. Jim Anderson of Casper had his hands full trying to ward off challenger Bryce Reece of Casper, a Freedom Caucus supporter. Anderson won by 30 votes, which changed the course of the Senate for two years. He represented the traditional wing of the GOP, and held the 16th seat in the chamber against 15 far-right senators.


The downballot races are where county and city officers, school board and community college board trustees and other officials are elected. Local contests have much more of a day-to-day impact on Wyomingites than who is elected governor or to Congress.In many communities, party membership doesn’t make as big of a difference for voters as it does in the main contests that dominate the headlines. Many local offices are also nonpartisan.

I’d like to see more voters know the issues and decide who would best represent them. It’s the news media’s responsibility to provide accurate news coverage, but it’s up to individuals to register to vote, do their homework, learn about the issues and get to know what candidates stand for.
I’m not counting it as a win for society if Wyoming keeps adding people who just fill in their ballots based on party loyalty or a list someone gave them. 
In the U.S. it’s “one person, one vote;” not one person and innumerable votes depending on how many cousins and friends are willing to turn their suffrage over to them.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Stream, riparian restoration could protect Idaho’s Kackley Ranch Preserve for generations to come
text:
At an educational media event on Oct. 8, 2026, leaders from the Sagebrush Steppe Land Trust and its co-project leader, Trout Unlimited, share their vision for riparian restoration projects on the Kackley Ranch Preserve in Idaho's Caribou County with project partners, funders and members of the press. (Photo by Liz Cartwright for the Idaho Capital Sun)Kackley Ranch Preserve is a 920-acre piece of land that has been set aside for permanent preservation in rural southeast Idaho. It is also a working ranch, and it will remain that way for future generations to enjoy.
Hannah Murphy, southeast Idaho project manager for Trout Unlimited, speaks on Oct. 8, 2026, at the Kackley Ranch Preserve. (Photo by Liz Cartwright for the Idaho Capital Sun)
At an educational media event on Oct. 8, leaders from the Sagebrush Steppe Land Trust and its co-project leader, Trout Unlimited, shared their vision for riparian restoration with project partners, funders and members of the press. 
The bright yellow aspen mixed with the conifer forests on the hills that surround the preserve, which is located 40 miles north of Soda Springs with Chippy Creek running through it, made for a backdrop that looked like it hadn’t changed in a hundred years. This is a truly beautiful part of rural Idaho. 
The land trust has pulled together a diverse working coalition of conservation groups, local ranchers, mining companies, government and nonprofit agencies to work toward the common goal of preserving and restoring the Kackley ranch in Caribou County, near Wayan, Idaho. 
Sagebrush Steppe Land Trust Executive Director Heath Mann speaks at the Kackley Ranch Preserve on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Liz Cartwright/Idaho Capital Sun)
“The Sagebrush Land Trust was tasked with permanently protected this working cattle ranch,” said Executive Director Heath Mann. “We continue to maintain and improve the Kackley ranch as a profitable operation. We maintain the value of the property, and the values and traditions that have made Idaho what it is today. 
“Through this project, with the helping guidance of our partners and our neighbors, we believe we will increase grass production for the cattle, diversify and improve our native plant life, encourage wildlife habitat and passage, and enhance the upper Blackfoot watershed. We hope that together we can make a tangible difference, improving the health of our ranch and the viability of ranching here within southeast Idaho while improving the habitat for our native creatures.”
Phase 1 of the work includes “restoring riparian vegetation, creating off-site water infrastructure for cattle, fencing the riparian areas to limit livestock access to sensitive areas, replacing damaged culverts under roads and installing wildlife-friendly ‘let-down’ fences to facilitate wildlife movement through the area,” according to Carly Flandro, communications coordinator for the Sagebrush Steppe Land Trust.
Kackley Ranch provides migration corridors for elk, mule deer, moose, and habitat for black bears, birds and native fish like the Yellowstone cutthroat trout. Cattle graze on the land, too. The land trust creates partnerships with local ranching families to work together to make for healthy cattle and healthy streams. 
Idaho Fish and Game’s Becky Johnson and Sagebrush Steppe Land Trust’s Carly Flandro speak on Oct. 8, 2026, at a media availability to talk about upcoming projects on the Kackley Ranch Preserve in Idaho’s Caribou County. (Photo by Liz Cartwright for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Like many of our Western lands, this area has been impacted by roads, reservoirs and ranching; additionally, the region is deep in a drought brought on by very low snowfall during the winter of 2025-26. Snowpack feeds the streams, creeks and underground aquifers. Local ranchers stated that an average snowfall this coming winter is crucial for the survival of their cattle and their communities. 
Faced with these challenges, the next couple of years are important ones for completing these initial projects and solidifying community partnerships and collaborations.  
The leaders said educating the next generation of conservation-minded citizens is a key component in preservation and active restoration of Idaho lands. The Sagebrush Steppe Land Trust and its partners envision the Kackley Ranch Preserve becoming a hub of science education learning for students of all ages.
Phase 2 of the Kackley Ranch Preserve projects include upgrading the ranch buildings to be used for educational facilities, enhancing the habitat for beavers and providing shelters for multiple species of bats to safely roost at night. (Photo by Liz Cartwright for Idaho Capital Sun)
Ongoing and future projects for Phase 2 include upgrading the ranch buildings to be used for educational facilities, enhancing the habitat for beavers and providing shelters for multiple species of bats to safely roost at night.
Ultimately, leaders said, restoration projects like this one are most effective and sustainable when they incorporate socially equitable goals that respect both the local communities and the natural environment. 
Project partners and funders include Upper Blackfoot Confluence members Trout Unlimited, Idaho Conservation League, Itafos, Nutrien, Ruveon and Simplot. Additional funders include U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Natural Resources Conservation Services, Sagebrush Steppe Land Trust, Clint Gilbert/Gilbert Farms, neighboring ranchers, Idaho Foundation for Parks and Lands and the Kackley Family/Alvin and Yvonne Kackley Family Trust.
Horses from a neighboring property look out at the Kackley Ranch Preserve, which a working ranch that has been set aside for permanent preservation in rural southeast Idaho. (Photo by Liz Cartwright for the Idaho Capital Sun)

title: Idaho DEQ awards Island Park $1.4 million for drinking water project
text:
The eastern Idaho town of Island Park is located in Fremont County, a short drive from Yellowstone National Park. (Courtesy of City of Island Park)The Idaho Department of Environmental Quality awarded a $1.4 million low-interest drinking water service line loan to the eastern Idaho city of Island Park, department officials announced Monday.

City officials in Island Park will use the funding to inventory and replace lead service lines in the drinking water system, the Idaho Department of Environmental Quality said. 
According to the U.S Environmental Protection Agency, lead service lines that connect a home to the water main are typically the most significant source of lead in drinking water. Replacing lead service lines can reduce lead exposure, the agency said. 
The loan includes favorable terms that will save the city of Island Park and its taxpayers about $2.4 million compared to the average costs for municipal general obligation debt issuances, state officials said. 
The loan carries a 2.5% interest rate, a 30-year term and features principal forgiveness in the amount of $1,072,702. 
Funding for the loan comes from the federal Infrastructure, Investment and Jobs Act that Congress passed and former President Joe Biden signed into law in 2021.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Jacksonville State University Board of Trustees to vote on alternate faculty senate board
text:
Members of the Jacksonville State University Board of Trustees as seen during its meeting on October 19, 2026. The Board is expected to vote on an alternate to the now-dissolved faculty senate on Tuesday. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Jacksonvile State University Board of Trustees is expected to vote Tuesday on creating a replacement for the university’s now-dissolved faculty senate as public universities continue to wrestle with the application of a new state law.
Christie Shelton, provost and executive vice president of academic affairs, said after the board of trustees meeting Monday the board will vote on the Presidential Faculty Academic Roundtable at Tuesday’s meeting. The newly established roundtable is expected to meet Wednesday afternoon.
“And the president and I are really eager to meet with them first thing Wednesday afternoon,” Shelton said. “We do feel like there may be better opportunities for problem solving because we’re all in the room. We weren’t that way before. We were infrequently in the room together, but never all at the same time. So we feel like this may be a tremendous opportunity for problem solving, just in a new way.”
The JSU Board of Trustees dissolved the school’s faculty senate in August, citing HB 580, sponsored by Rep. Troy Stubbs, R-Wetumpka, and signed by Gov. Kay Ivey in April. 
The bill, which went into effect Oct. 1, limits faculty senate bodies to advisory roles; requires periodic reviews for tenured professors and gives boards of trustees at colleges and universities the final say in developing curricula.
Higher education institutions across the state have been interpreting the law differently. Auburn University also dissolved its faculty senate in June, but other universities, including Troy University and the University of Alabama, opted to keep their faculty senates to varying degrees.
According to the Chanticleer, JSU’s student newspaper, the new JSU board will be composed of six elected and seven appointed faculty members. Shelton said all of the faculty members who will be a part of the Presidential Faculty Academic Roundtable were notified. She did not say which faculty members were on the new board.
Lance Ingwersen, a history professor at JSU, said in an interview Monday afternoon that details about what the alternative board will be doing are still hazy to faculty members.
“There are a lot of things under the academic affairs committee-wise that the state of which are … just kind of unknown right now,” he said. “ I would say there’s a lot that we really just don’t know. That is very clear.”
Ingwersen also said in a text message Monday evening while he understands Shelton’s perspective “the reality is, as a faculty member, the PFAR (Presidential Faculty Academic Roundtable) is less representative” and called it a “step backward for Jax State faculty and for decision-making at the university.”
“The PFAR has 13 members from a handful of departments, and more than half (7) are appointed directly by the president,” he said. “The PFAR will meet half as much as the Faculty Senate did. And PFAR members likely won’t be able to deliberate as openly and candidly as they did in Senate about issues of importance since administrators will share the room with them and because they can be removed at any time per the new law.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Lawsuit: Tennessee to impose immigration checks in HIV/AIDS safety-net program
text:
A Nurse performs a rapid test for AIDS, syphilis and hepatitis. Nashville CARES has filed suit against the Department of Health over new requirements to verify immigration status of patients with HIV/AIDS enrolled in the federal Ryan White program (Photo: Getty Images)In August, Tennessee organizations that aid low-income individuals living with HIV received a surprise memo from the state’s health department:
“Effective immediately,” the memo said, “no patients without documentation of citizenship or legal residency may be newly enrolled” in many of the services provided through the federal Ryan White HIV/AIDS program or a companion program known as HOPWA, or Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS.
The federal government does not require immigration status checks as a condition of receiving services through HOPWA or Ryan White, a program that has served as the cornerstone of the U.S. government’s response to HIV/AIDS for more than 30 years. Even as the Trump administration has sought to exclude immigrants from an array of public benefits, federal law explicitly exempts immigration status checks in federal programs for the treatment of communicable disease.
Attorneys for Nashville CARES, one of the state’s largest providers of Ryan White services, immediately filed an administrative challenge to the new rules laid out in the memo, and the Department of Health rescinded it days later. 
But, in its place, the Department of Health has imposed an even broader immigration verification mandate on agencies serving low-income Tennesseans living with HIV/AIDS.
In a memo dated Oct. 1, the department is now requiring all agencies that serve patients via the Ryan White program to amend their existing contracts to require “eligibility verification for each potential beneficiary/recipient.” The memo cites Tennessee law that requires verifying anyone seeking federal, state or local benefits is lawfully present in the United States; an amendment to the law this year imposes criminal penalties on healthcare and other public benefit providers who fail to report immigrants without legal status to the Tennessee Department of Safety.
Updated RWPB Eligibility Memo 10.1.26 secured
On Monday, Nashville CARES filed suit in Davidson County Chancery Court seeking to declare the contract changes invalid. Ryan White covers the cost of medical care, drug assistance, home health care, case management, financial assistance for health insurance premiums and hospice care for low-income individuals living with HIV.
Nashville CARES argues the state rules violate federal law and is seeking an immediate injunction barring the new contract language from taking effect while its legal challenge is ongoing. 
The new contract language “threatens access to medically necessary HIV-related services for otherwise eligible low-income individuals, frustrates (Nashville CARES) organizational mission, disrupts continuity of HIV treatment and support services, and places burdensome verification” requirements that have never before been required and are not supported by federal or state law, the lawsuit said.  
“Individuals who lose access to those services face increased risk of worsening HIV disease, transmission of HIV, progression to AIDS and other serious health consequences,” it said. 
The contract amendment could directly impact hundreds of Nashville CARES’ patients and clients. Among then are at least 129 patients with HIV who receive financial help to cover health insurance costs, 150-160 individuals whose mental health and medication management care is paid for by Nashville CARES and 80-100 individuals who receive healthcare at Nashville CARES clinics, according to figures cited in the lawsuit. Additionally, patients who are U.S. citizens but unable to provide documentation could also be impacted, the lawsuit said.
Lawyers for the nonprofit have sought further clarity from the department about the new contract requirements, but received none, the legal petition said. In legal filings, the lawyers noted that the new contract language may or may not extend to  core Ryan White services, including medical treatment and medications;  the Tennessee law cited by the department references federal exclusions for these services. But, the lawyers noted, even if that is the case, a critical component of Ryan White funding is financial assistance that enables individuals to purchase private insurance that gives them to access healthcare, a benefit the amended contract language puts at risk for those who cannot provide proof of citizenship or legal immigration status. 
A spokesperson for the Department of Health did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit on Monday. The department, earlier this month, provided the Lookout copies of the memos sent to Ryan White providers, but has not responded to a subsequent request for details about impacted recipients of the contract changes.
Monday’s lawsuit is the second this year to challenge efforts by the health department to impose immigration status verification requirements in public safety-net health programs for low-income patients. 
In July, the department agreed to temporarily halt a new policy requiring the reporting of sick and disabled children to a state immigration enforcement office while a legal challenge brought by three doctors to the policy remains ongoing. About 400 children with chronic and, in some instances terminal illnesses, have remained enrolled in the state’s Children’s Special Services program as a result.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Child abuse case involving Hope Scholarship students illuminates oversight challenges in WV
text:
The West Virginia state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)A Kanawha County child abuse case involving students using the Hope Scholarship poses questions about how public schools can follow up on thousands of students using the program, including children missing school and in potentially dangerous situations.
Public schools like Kanawha County Schools are currently tasked with handling records and reporting for Hope Scholarship students learning elsewhere. More than 25,000 students are using the program this school year. 
A malnourished 12-year-old girl was found alone Oct. 15 at a doughnut shop in Charleston, West Virginia, more than a mile away from her home and wandering the neighborhood for several hours.
A criminal complaint said the girl weighed 40 pounds. The average weight for a 12-year-old girl is 92 pounds. 
WCHS reported that her parents, Nuwna Overton and Clarence Spotsville, both 33, were charged with child neglect creating risk of bodily injury.
Five children found in the couple’s home were enrolled in the Hope Scholarship program, Kanawha County Schools confirmed. The Hope Scholarship is the state’s education voucher program that provides around $5,400 per student for private school tuition, homeschooling and more. 
The State Treasurer’s Office, which runs the Hope Scholarship program, couldn’t confirm or disclose whether the students utilized the Hope Scholarship under current law. 
“Under current law, information regarding an individual student’s participation in the Hope Scholarship Program is protected,” said Carrie Smith, assistant communications director for the Treasurer’s Office. 
The 12-year-old girl was found by law enforcement on Thursday, a school day. 
“Questions regarding school attendance monitoring and student check-ins fall outside the scope of our office’s responsibilities and would be more appropriately directed to the West Virginia Department of Education or the applicable county school district,” Smith said.
An email conversation with Kanawha County Schools Communications Director Chris Williams revealed a loophole in attendance monitoring of Hope Scholarship students. 
A Notice Of Intent form, which parents fill out to notify Kanawha County Schools that they’re withdrawing their child for the Hope Scholarship, only requires the parent to list “participating school” for where the child will attend. 
“The only thing they are required to put down is ‘participating school,’” Chris Williams said. 
In Kanawha County, officials review attendance at the end of the year.
“At the end of the school year, all participating schools (those that accept the Hope Scholarship) send KCS progress reports for students who attended using the scholarship. Our attendance office reviews those lists and records each student’s progress in the Hope Scholarship Portal,” Chris Williams said. “If a student does not appear on any of those lists, our attendance office records ‘no progress report’ in the Hope Scholarship Portal.”
Del. Kathie Hess Crouse, R-Putnam, speaks on the House floor about House Bill 2777, which would change some requirements for homeschooling in West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Kathie Hess Crouse, R-Putnam, is one of the Legislature’s leading school choice advocates. She said the Kanawha County situation showed there could be more work to do on communication between those involved with the program.
“I think we need to look where there are gaps somewhere — it seems like there may be some gaps — and fill those in,” Hess Crouse said on Monday. “I will be speaking to the Treasurer’s Office to see what gaps they’re seeing and the West Virginia Department of Education.”
Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. John Williams, D-Monongalia, questioned if changes to the Hope Scholarship regarding children’s safety would get traction after his and other lawmakers’ proposed financial guardrails to the program didn’t move forward this year. Those proposals came from both Republican and Democratic House members. 
“It would make common sense to improve the communication between public schools and Hope to know what’s going on, but I’ve heard a lot of commonsense guardrails that would help kids with the Hope Scholarship, so I don’t know if this would have any success or not … In the Legislature, common sense is rarely seen,” John Williams said. 
“I think that we have to do better than what we’re doing at keeping track of where these kids are,” he continued. “Obviously it’s a safety issue. It just makes you wonder how many kids are out there like this.”
The Hope Scholarship has its own checks and balances for students and education providers participating in the program this school year. 
Participation in the program has surged this year since program eligibility expanded to all West Virginia students for the first time since its launch in 2021.
“We do monitor when students select a school or IIP in our system to help us indicate where the student is being educated,” Smith said. “We also work closely with our participating providers to make sure that Hope Scholarship funds are being used for services rendered, so if a student was not actually attending the school, we would be working with the school on the refund process.”
Smith said that the Education Service Provider agreement holds schools and providers accountable for only charging services rendered.
“While this is not an academic progress ‘check-in,’ this is a way that we work with parents, schools and providers to help ensure attendance,” Smith explained. 
Hope Scholarship not notified of parents’ criminal charges 
Hess Crouse is in the process of setting up a school choice portal for homeschoolers through the state education department that will track forms, progress and more. Adding Hope Scholarship students to the portal in the future could help alleviate some oversight challenges, she said. 
She has also proposed a School Choice Office, potentially run through the Governor’s Office, to handle attendance and monitoring rather than public schools. 
“Child safety is paramount. Bad actors are everywhere, but by numbers alone there are more bad actors in public schools than in homeschooling, charter schools, private schools and microschools,” Hess Crouse said. “I’m not saying there aren’t ever abusers in home (schooling), private and charter … There are more in public. We need to make sure there is follow through no matter where the child is placed.”
Under current state law, the Hope Scholarship Program is not notified when a participant or account holder faces criminal charges, nor is there a statutory requirement for an account holder to report such charges, according to Smith. 
If a parent or guardian becomes unable to be the account holder due to incarceration or loss of temporary or permanent custody, the program allows another individual who is not the student’s parent to serve as the account holder. 
“Such determinations are made on a case-by-case basis and are subject to legal review,” Smith said.
“If lawmakers believe additional notification requirements are necessary to strengthen student protections and accountability, it is incumbent upon the Legislature to address those gaps in the law. The Treasurer’s Office must operate within the authority granted to it under current legislation,” she added.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Denver to close Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy, a tiny HBCU-style high school, after 6 years
text:
Denver Public Schools will close Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy, an HBCU-style high school, at the end of this school year. (Karen Pulfer Focht for Chalkbeat)This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
The vision for Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy was to provide as many as 500 Denver students with an education modeled after historically Black colleges. But five years after opening, the school has just 24 students and is set to close at the end of this school year.
Denver Public Schools Superintendent Alex Marrero is recommending an operational closure, according to letters sent to families and staff last week. Denver schools are funded per student, and an operational closure is when a school’s enrollment is so low that it’s financially unsustainable. Unlike most school closures, operational closures do not require approval from the elected school board, a district spokesperson said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Chelsey Moore’s son is a senior at Robert F. Smith. He enrolled there after the school board voted to close his previous school, the Denver School of Innovation and Sustainable Design, because of low enrollment. Moore said her son, who is not a student of color, found a “magical … standalone safe space” at Robert F. Smith.
Even though her son will graduate before the school closes, Moore is mourning the loss.
“They’re not just closing schools. They’re not just making economic choices,” Moore said. “They’re changing the trajectory and futures for students.”
In some ways, what happened at Robert F. Smith is emblematic of a bigger pattern. The number of small Denver schools is increasing as enrollment decreases. In line with a statewide trend, DPS’ student count dropped by 1,780 this fall, which was more than the district was expecting. Marrero has warned that more school closures are likely coming.
But Robert F. Smith also faced unique challenges.
The idea for the school came from a group of Black parents and sports coaches in far northeast Denver who were advocating for better schools in that region. Their advocacy followed a damning district-commissioned report that detailed the ways in which DPS was underserving Black students and led the school board to pass a resolution pledging to do better.
In 2019, the board took the rare step of ordering the district to help the parent group strengthen an application it submitted to start a school modeled after historically Black colleges and universities, or HBCUs. A few months later, the board greenlit the school to open, despite some members’ worries that district enrollment could soon decline.
Named for a DPS alumnus, Robert F. Smith struggled to enroll students. The school doesn’t have a boundary, so all of its students must proactively choose it. Before Robert F. Smith opened in the fall of 2021, DPS incorrectly listed its address on the district’s school choice website. Despite aiming to enroll 125 students that year, the school’s final count was 78, according to district data.
Enrollment increased to 135 students in 2022 but fell to just 44 in 2023 after the school moved to a new building 10 miles away. The school’s first location was a former office building that it shared with another school. That building didn’t have a kitchen, an auditorium, or sports fields — all of which students and the school’s founders said they’d been promised.
“The ninth grade biology classes have to come into the 10th grade chemistry room to do experiments because the biology class is the size of a prison cell,” former student Jessie Matthews told the school board in 2022.
But Robert F. Smith’s new location, a former elementary school, wasn’t ideal either, in part because it relocated the school out of far northeast Denver. The move was meant to give Robert F. Smith room to grow, but enrollment never got higher than about 90 students.
This year, the district cut ninth grade from Robert F. Smith after fewer than 20 freshmen applied, a district spokesperson said.
The school also endured a leadership change and friction between its founders and DPS. In 2022, the district banned founder Brandon Pryor, a parent and vocal district critic, from the grounds of Robert F. Smith and nearly all other DPS schools, citing Pryor’s treatment of district staff. Pryor sued DPS, and a judge ordered the district to lift the ban.
Pryor did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story.
In letters this week to Robert F. Smith families and staff, district officials promised to help students find new schools and teachers find new jobs. But Moore said she’s disappointed in how families found out about the closure. After receiving a vague message Tuesday about a meeting on Thursday to “discuss the future of the school” at which only a few parents showed up, families got another message Thursday announcing the operational closure.
“Most parents didn’t know until last night that the school was closing,” Moore said. “Our question was, ‘Why weren’t we informed?’ Why didn’t the district give us the opportunity to speak out for the school and help recruit? It’s a tight community and we would have stepped in to help.”
Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Republicans out gun Dems by 200,000 voters, West Virginia Secretary of State’s office says
text:
A sign telling people to register to vote sits outside of West Virginia Secretary of State Kris Warner's office on Feb. 10, 2026, in the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)The Republican Party has a little more than 200,000 registered voters as it heads into the 2026 general election, according to the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office. 
The Democratic Party, which ruled the state for nearly a century, has been seeing steady, declining numbers over the years, dropping from 572,000 in 2016 to 326,000 today. Meanwhile, Republican membership has risen to 527,000. 
Only Monongalia County has more registered Democrats than Republicans, and that’s just by 155 registrations. 
West Virginia Republican Party Co-Chairman Tony Hodge said while the numerical advantage bodes well for his party, GOP candidates aren’t resting on their laurels. 
“All of our candidates are out working hard. A lot of them are hitting the pavement. They’re out talking to voters,” he said. “Just because we have a voter advantage does not mean that we take any election for granted.” 
However, West Virginia Democrat Party Chairman Mike Pushkin said he thinks the state’s 307,000 independents could help flip seats come Nov. 3, especially on issues like data centers, water quality and healthcare. 
“On the issues that voters care about, they overwhelmingly trust Democrats,” Pushkin said. “What’s important is who comes out to vote and how they vote on Election Day. And we feel pretty good about that.” 
Pointing to the last primary, which saw only 21% of the electorate casting a ballot, Pushkin said he believes there’s more enthusiasm among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents to come to the ballots. 
Republicans saw a 22% decrease in the number of ballots cast in the primary compared to the 2022 mid-term primary, as a result of closing its primary to independent voters. On the other hand, Democrats saw a 4% increase. 
The number of non-partisan ballots accepted in the primary skyrocketed by nearly 75% when compared to the 2022 primary. 
Hodges said his party will be studying results closely to see if independents are shifting registration into the Republican Party by looking at results from the upcoming election. The Republican Executive Committee will revisit the issue in summer 2027.  
Since the spring, just a few hundred shy of 18,000 new voters have registered, according to a Secretary of State news release. In addition to major party and independent registrations, the West Virginia Secretary of State’s Office also said around 48,000 voters are registered to third parties, such as the Mountain, Libertarian and Constitution parties. 
Early voting starts Oct. 21 and ends on Oct. 31.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Democrats outraise opponents in NC’s most contentious congressional races
text:
When it comes to fundraising for North Carolina's US Senate race, former RNC and NCGOP Chair Michael Whatley (left) is far behind his Democratic rival, former Gov. Roy Cooper. (Photos by Brandon Kingdollar and Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)Democrats in North Carolina’s most competitive congressional races are significantly ahead of their Republican opponents in fundraising, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission.
Former Gov. Roy Cooper reported bringing in more funding and has more cash on hand than his GOP rival. The same is true for U.S. Rep. Don Davis and Jamie Ager in their U.S. House races. Democrats have poured money into the campaigns, seeing them as critical to the control of Congress. 
Campaign finance reports covering fundraising and spending during the third quarter, spanning from July 1 to Sept. 30, were due last week with the FEC. Election Day is Nov. 3. 
Cooper reports nearly 14 times more cash on hand than Whatley
Two weeks before Election Day, North Carolina’s marquee U.S. Senate race has shifted into a lower gear after an active late summer and early fall. 
GOP U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis’ retirement left an open seat drawing plenty of attention and money. With 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independents in the Senate, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip control of the chamber. 
Cooper, a Democrat, broke records when he raised $3.4 million during the first 24 hours of his campaign. Democrats saw the seat as one of their best pick-up opportunities this election cycle, and political observers expected it to be among the most expensive. 
Democrats see opening in NC as Whatley campaign pauses ads

But now, both national parties have pulled ads from the airwaves as they rethink their campaign strategies. They’re funneling their money into states like Georgia and Maine, and unlikely battlegrounds like Texas, Iowa, and Kansas.
The Cook Political Report, an elections forecaster, rates the race as “likely Democratic.”
Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee and North Carolina Republican Party, has consistently trailed Cooper in the polls. He’s doubled down on his allegiance to President Donald Trump despite the president’s dwindling approval numbers in the state. 
Cooper raised about $4.4 million during the third quarter. He spent about $20 million, and has about $12.5 million left in cash on hand. 
On the GOP side, Whatley reported receiving about $1.6 million, spending about $4.6 million, and having about $916,000 remaining in the bank. 
Over the course of the race, Cooper has more than tripled Whatley in fundraising. Cooper has raised a total of $47 million since 2025, compared to $13 million for Whatley.
WinSenate, a Democratic super PAC, removed $1.1 million from the North Carolina Senate race, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact, but still has $18.8 million in future reservations through Election Day. 
Outside groups reported spending almost $9.3 million during the third quarter on Cooper’s behalf, while other political action committees spent nearly $7.4 million to back Whatley before cutting their spending earlier in October. 
Ager is millions of dollars ahead of Balkcom
Following incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards’ withdrawal from the campaign after being censured by the U.S. House, two farmers are competing to appeal to Western North Carolinians. 
The 11th District has supported Republicans for most of the past 35 years. But with the vacancy and current political climate, Democrats are optimistic about their chances. Cook Political Report rates the seat as “toss up.”
At the moment, Republicans hold a 218-212 majority in the House, with four vacancies and one independent.
A tale of two farmers: Ager, Balkcom compete for NC-11 seat

Democrat Jamie Ager is a fourth-generation farmer from a political family. He owns Hickory Nut Gap Farms, which supplies products to restaurants, grocery stores and individual customers. 
Ager reported a $2 million haul in the third quarter. After spending $2.8 million, he has $1.6 million in his campaign coffers. 
The NCGOP selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, a mortgage loan officer who grew up on her family’s apple farm in Henderson County, to replace Edwards on the ballot in August. The timing left her with roughly three months to campaign.
Balkcom entered the race with approximately eight weeks remaining in the third quarter. She raised about $307,000, spent about $54,000, and reported about $295,000 left in the bank. 
Edwards reported receiving about $58,000, spending about $153,000, and keeping about $415,000 in cash on hand. 
Political action committees reported spending about $272,000 in support of Ager, and about $693,000 to oppose Edwards before he dropped out. 
Vice President JD Vance held a rally in Hendersonville on Monday to encourage turnout for Balkcom, Whatley, and other Republicans on the ballot. 
Davis leads Buckhout in a rematch of 2024
North Carolina’s 1st District had the state’s most expensive congressional race of the 2024 cycle. 
Now, the same candidates are vying for the seat again: GOP Army veteran Laurie Buckhout is challenging incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Don Davis. Ahead of the primary election in March, millions of dollars poured into the contest. 
However, Republican state lawmakers redrew the district last year, moving some Democratic leaning cities out and more Republican-voting areas in. Cook Political Report rates the seat as “toss up.”
Davis reported raising about $1.3 million, compared to about $628,000 for Buckhout. 
His spending also dwarfed his opponent — Davis spent about $2.8 million during the filing period, while Buckhout spent about $476,000. 
Still, the pair has similar amounts of cash on hand. Davis has about $2 million left in the bank, and Buckhout sits on about $1.9 million. 
Those numbers don’t include independent expenditures, which have heavily favored the Republican this quarter. PACs reported spending about $949,000 to back Buckhout, and about $190,000 to support Davis. 
Trump will head to Greenville on Tuesday to stump for Buckhout.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennesseans should oppose displays of the Ten Commandments in public schools
text:
At least five public school districts have approved the display of the Ten Commandments since a GOP-backed law allowing them to do so took effect July 1.  (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)



Photograph by John Partipilo/My parents homeschooled me through 11th grade to ensure religion would play an essential role in my upbringing. 
Then they sent me to public school for 12th grade and a public college to ensure I had a well-rounded education and a fulsome understanding of how civil, secular America worked.
What would my education, or yours, have looked like if our parents didn’t have the choice to bring religion into, or keep it out of, our schooling?
When government-run institutions such as Tennessee public schools recognize a specific faith, even in something as seemingly anodyne as a depiction of the Judeo-Christian Ten Commandments, it sets a precedent for sidelining all other faiths and establishing a state-recognized religion, an act anathema to what the Founding Fathers intended.
Republican legislators want to rewind Tennessee into the pre-Enlightenment era when religious power and state power were one and the same
Following a Republican-led bill that became law on July 1, at least five Tennessee public school districts have voted to display a specific, state-approved version of the Ten Commandments in prominent common areas like entryways and cafeterias throughout dozens of schools.
To use public schools to boldly depict Biblical scripture is to interfere with parents’ well-established rights to guide their children’s religious education. Furthermore, it is a significant step in the direction of using state power to recognize the religious laws of one faith.
ACLU queries Tennessee school districts on Ten Commandments

The move is reminiscent of a period in history no one in their right mind would want to return to.
Before and during the 1688-1789 Enlightenment period that gave us sweeping democratic revolutions and the idea that legitimate political power comes only from the consent of the governed, European monarchs ruled their countries and colonies not just with sheer military force, but by so-called divine decree bestowed upon them by a singular, state-recognized religion; be it Roman Catholicism in Spain, France, and Italy, Anglicanism in England, or Lutheranism and Protestantism in Prussia and much of northern Europe.
The irony, of course, is that Tennessee’s Republican leaders, many of whom claim to be constitutional conservatives and admirers of the Founding Fathers, are attempting to create in Tennessee the very pre-Enlightenment conditions that the founders boldly repudiated.
What the Founding Fathers actually said about religion and the government
Christian nationalists who seek to remove the barrier between church and state often trot out the line that, because many of the Founding Fathers were vocal about their Christian and Deist beliefs, that must make the nation Christian.
They never make the next obvious logical step.
The Constitution is one of humanity’s greatest creations because it was created by deeply faithful men who knew our founding document had to be secular, not in spite of it.
The Founding Fathers did not err when they wrote “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion” into the First Amendment. And they did not make a mistake when they explicitly banned religious tests for public office under Article VI (both instances of which are the only times the Constitution ever mentions the word “religion”).
If you do not believe me, just hear it from them.
In 1802, then-president Thomas Jefferson came to the aid of the Danbury Baptists who were being forced to pay taxes to Connecticut’s then-official Congregationalist ministers and buildings. Jefferson said the First Amendment’s establishment clause built “…a wall of separation between Church & State.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
James Madison argued that only by preventing the government from recognizing a state religion could America truly promote religious freedom. “The number, the industry and the morality of the priesthood, and the devotion of the people have been manifestly increased by the total separation of the church and state,” he wrote. He also penned Memorial and Remonstrance against Religious Assessments in 1785 to protest a bill that would have used public tax money to pay Christian teachers.
George Washington opposed establishing a state religion and rejected infusing Christian language into government. “You will permit me to observe that the path of true piety is so plain as to require but little political direction,” Washington wrote in 1789. “To this consideration, we ought to ascribe the absence of any regulation, respecting religion, from the Magna-Charta of our country.”
In 1787 John Adams wrote, “The United States of America have exhibited, perhaps, the first example of governments erected on the simple principles of nature. In the formation of the American [state] governments, it will never be pretended that any persons employed in that service had interviews with the gods, or were in any degree under the influence of heaven. These governments were contrived merely by the use of reason and the senses.”
Contrast those founding principles with Tennessee’s Republican lawmakers’ efforts to legislate a single religious doctrine into public schools, and you can see how far we have fallen from what the founders intended.
Demanding the separation of church and state isn’t an attack on religion; it is a means of protecting all faiths
At the time of this writing, the ACLU of Tennessee, ACLU, Americans United for Separation of Church and State and the Freedom From Religion Foundation have sent letters requesting public records from school districts planning to put the Ten Commandments in school buildings, but no lawsuits have been filed yet.
Tennesseans need to make their voices heard. Even, and especially, the most religious among us should demand a government that does not play favorites with faith. 
The Founding Fathers rebelled against totalitarian alliances between churches and kings. The fruits of that rebellion are borne in the freedoms we enjoy today. 
We would be fools to surrender them.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A bluer NC could be in the offing
text:
Early in-person voting runs Oct. 15-31, 2026 in North Carolina. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)The association of modern American Republicans with the color red and Democrats with the color blue has always left me a tad perplexed and amused. For those of us old enough to remember significant chunks of the 20th Century, red was always the color of world communism and the far left. 
In the 1920s and 1950s, the term “red scare” was applied to the anti-communist paranoia that gripped the U.S. in the periods after both World Wars I and II. After communists prevailed in the Chinese civil war that ended in 1949, their country was commonly referred to in the western press as “Red China.” And during the Vietnam War, it was common for U.S. newspapers to feature weekly casualty counts (figures that we later learned had frequently been doctored by American officials) that specified the number of U.S. service personnel killed or wounded juxtaposed with the numbers of “reds” who had met a similar fate.
Meanwhile, blue, while not always understood to be associated with particular causes or political persuasions in the U.S., is in Great Britain, the color – or “colour” as Brits would say – of the monarchy. Even today, many an English football (soccer) team sports a blue “kit” as a sign of this historical connection.
Today in the U.S., however, as with so many aspects of our culture, the nation’s political hue associations have been altered by a force that long ago surpassed the influence of communists and monarchists in the national and global political dialogue – the all-powerful electronic media. 
For years, television networks and other news outlets colored their U.S. maps during national elections blue and red to show which way states had voted. It wasn’t until the never-ending 2000 presidential election between George W. Bush and Al Gore, however, that, for no particular reason that anyone can pinpoint or recall, Bush states got painted red and Gore’s blue. And since then, the associations have stuck.
Today, Democrats raise millions of dollars for their candidates through websites like “Act Blue,” while Republican President Donald Trump is known for sporting trademark red ties and palling around with former longtime communist and current Russian dictator Vladimir Putin. 
Of course, the transient nature of these color associations coincides well with the fact that few parts of the U.S. political quilt seem to be permanently stitched in place. Many states that once reliably voted one way or the other have done a 180 in recent decades. Meanwhile, battleground states like North Carolina that swing both ways in their partisan preferences are commonly referred to as “purple.”  
And with the 2026 election now upon us and in full swing, it appears increasingly possible that North Carolina will take on an even bluer tint in the coming weeks. Boosted by Trump’s plummeting approval numbers in the polls – a trend that most observers attribute to the war against Iran, its impact on the U.S. economy and the general chaos in Washington – Democrats appear well-positioned to win races up and down the ballot.
Among the contests generating the most optimism for Democrats:

The race to succeed retiring Republican U.S. Senator Thom Tillis – Barring some kind of remarkable last-minute comeback, GOP nominee Michael Whatley appears likely to lose to Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper by a significant margin. At last check, national Republicans had all but written off the race.
The state Supreme Court contest between incumbent Anita Earls and GOP state lawmaker Sarah Stevens. If Earls prevails as many expect, Democrats would be poised to take back control of the seven-member high court in 2028 when three GOP-held seats will be on the ballot – something that would bode well for lawsuits seeking to revisit the state’s egregiously gerrymandered congressional and legislative maps. 
The 11th District U.S. House race – After having elected three successive Republicans ultimately tarred by scandal (Mark Meadows, Madison Cawthorn and Chuck Edwards) voters in the state’s far west could elect a folksy and centrist farmer, Democrat Jamie Ager, over GOP state lawmaker Jennifer Balkcom. Despite the district being badly gerrymandered to favor Republican candidates, most analysts rate the race as a tossup.
The partisan makeup of the General Assembly – While it would take a true political tidal wave for Democrats to win control of the state legislature after 16 years of Republican dominance and district map gerrymandering – the GOP currently controls the Senate 30-20 and the House 71-47 with two unaffiliated reps – the chances for narrowing the margins and thereby forcing more genuine negotiations with Gov. Josh Stein by ending the prospect of partisan veto overrides seem high.

Very little is certain in modern politics. With billionaire plutocrats capable of flooding races with vast sums of dark money, rogue actors spreading lies on social media, and even the nation’s chief executive issuing repeated and false claims about the validity of our elections, last-minute “October surprises” (and even November and December surprises) remain a possibility. For now, however, with the 2026 election already underway and early voting numbers up over the last midterms in 2022, the chances for North Carolina emerging with a slightly bluer shade of purple look to be high.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: 2 major coastal projects get go-ahead from BP oil spill settlement trustees
text:
A satellite map shows the locations of coastal restoration projects the BP oil settlement trustees have approved. (Image courtesy of CPRA)Two major coastal restoration projects got the final go-ahead to begin construction in Louisiana, together restoring up to 1,700 acres of coastal shoreline and wetland habitat at a total cost of $265 million.
The East Orleans Landbridge and Raccoon Island restoration projects have been given final approval by Trustees of the BP Deepwater Horizon oil spill settlement dollars. 
The East Orleans project will create and restore marsh habitat along the landbridge separating Lake Pontchartrain from Lake Borgne and the Gulf of Mexico.
This narrow strip of marsh serves as an “important protective and hydrologic feature,” according to the trustees, providing habitat for fish, birds and other Louisiana wildlife as well as reducing the intensity of waves and storm surge that can threaten people and homes during hurricanes and flood events.
“It’s protecting over a million people who live around the lake,” Amanda Moore, senior director with the National Wildlife Federation’s Gulf program, said. The organization advocates for science-backed coastal restoration efforts in Louisiana as part of the Restore the Mississippi River Delta Coalition.  
The restoration project will dredge and place 5 million cubic yards of sediment to restore up to 1,320 acres of wetlands and provide almost 3 miles of shoreline protection at a cost of $109 million dollars. 
Moore said the “steadfast” public support for this project, part of the overall Louisiana Coastal Master Plan, played a key role in moving it forward. 
“It matters when you speak up and when you show support for these projects, and it helps decision makers understand where to direct funds,” she said. 
The Trustee Implementation Group also granted final approval for a restoration plan on Raccoon Island, one of Louisiana’s outermost barrier islands off the coast of Terrebonne Parish. 
The approved plan will dredge 2.9 million cubic yards of sand from offshore to restore up to 410 acres of barrier island habitat. It also includes construction of nine living shoreline structures, four new breakwater structures near the bayside and maintenance of existing breakwaters. In all, the Raccoon Island plan is expected to cost $156.3 million. 
The state Coastal Restoration and Protection Authority’s 2027 annual plan lists the projects’ construction timeline beginning at the end of next year.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘A huge need’: Free healthcare day event draws hundreds to Charleston clinic
text:
West Virginia Health Right hosted #WeCareWV Day Saturday, Oct. 1, 2026. During the one-day event, clinic volunteers provided free vision, dental and medical care to people with no income requirements. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)More than 400 people got medical, dental or vision care at a one-day free health care event in Charleston, West Virginia on Saturday. 
West Virginia Health Right, a free and charitable clinic on Charleston’s East End, typically requires its patients to meet income restrictions, but on #WeCareWV Day there are no income questions asked. 
Health Right CEO Angie Settle said she’s glad the clinic hosts the event, but seeing the need in the community makes her sad. 
“It makes me sad because I think we’re doing such a good job at West Virginia Health Right but there’s still a huge need,” she said. “And that’s why we do the event.”
Sen. Tom Takubo, R-Kanawha, is a physician who has volunteered with the annual free healthcare day most years since it started in 2016. Takubo said the need for free healthcare efforts like #WeCareWV Day will only increase in West Virginia in the coming month.
Beginning in January, many Medicaid recipients will have new work requirements under the One Big Beautiful Act. 
An analysis by the state Department of Human Services earlier this year found that about 33,000 West Virginia residents would be affected by the changes. Policy analysts say eligible people will lose their health coverage because of the increased paperwork requirements.
Fewer people enrolled in plans this year under the Affordable Care Act as well, as costs for the program spiked.
“The hope is we bring in more high-paying jobs and things where people can have health coverage, but until then, this type of stuff is filling the gap,” Takubo said. 
Takubo said he tries to convey to other lawmakers the need and what happens to people who don’t get regular healthcare. 
“These are people with real needs that are trying to do better with what they have,” he said. “…That’s why what (Settle) does and what the whole team here does is important. There’s a lot of hurting West Virginians, and (Health Right) fills a huge gap.”
Richard Jaye, of Charleston, came to the #WeCareWV clinic to have a dental provider pull his teeth, he said.
“They’ve been hurting for years,” he said. Jaye’s health care coverage, Medicaid, limits the amount of dental work recipients can have to $2,000 per 2-year period. 
Jaye works for his landlord and also does Doordash and other side jobs. He said he understands the principle behind the new work requirements, but he has concerns about the new rules.
His wife has medical problems that make it extremely difficult to work, he said. The couple is working on getting her disability benefits, but the state is “dragging their feet,” Jaye said. Until her disability is approved, his wife will be required to either work, train or volunteer for 80 hours a month in order to stay on Medicaid, he said. 
She’s still considered “able-bodied” until the government sends her an official letter saying she’s disabled, he said. 
“Even her doctors have sent them letters, and nobody cares that much enough,” he said. 
Takubo said there is “absolutely” a role for the West Virginia Legislature to offer more help to people once Medicaid enrollment declines, but lawmakers may not be convinced. 
“What they believe the reality is versus what the reality actually is are two different things,” Takubo said. 
Takubo said more lawmakers should visit Health Right to see the need for healthcare firsthand.
“A lot of legislators say, ‘Well, these people should just go get a job.’ Well, that’s really easily said,” Takubo said. “There’s a lot of these people here that would love to have a job with health insurance. 
“A lot of these people work really hard, they’re just not in jobs that offer health insurance,” he said. “That’s the part that I constantly stress: These are some of the hardest working people I’ve ever met, but they just don’t have jobs that offer health insurance, and so they go without.”
Brian Singleton, of Charleston, got new glasses at the clinic. Singleton had been on Medicaid but at his restaurant job he now earns too much money for Medicaid and not enough to be able to afford healthcare on his own, he said. 
“I’m in the middle of having too much and not enough,” he said. 
Bridget Nesselrotte, of Charleston, came to the clinic for a dental exam and flu shot. She’s in a drug recovery program, and just recently got a job after leaving a domestic violence situation, she said. The new job will offer health insurance, she said, but that will take time to get established. 
“If you don’t have health, you don’t have nothing,” she said. “Because that’s the most important thing. To even recover or anything, you’ve got to have your health. Without your health, you can’t have any of the things you love.”
