name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho’s Sen. Risch could lead the effort to stop Trump’s Russian diesel policies. But will he?
text:
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, meets with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in June 2022 in Kyiv. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Sen. Jim Risch)After President Donald Trump issued an executive order on Thursday lifting new stiff sanctions on Russia, one of Vladimir Putin’s closest advisers issued a glowing statement praising the president.
“The suspension of some provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and historic moment,” Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s economic adviser, said. Dmitriev probably does not realize how right he is. Trump’s executive order is historic, but for all the wrong reasons.
Trump’s decision to buy diesel fuel from Russia and now his decision to lift the Lindsey Graham Act sanctions that were just approved by Congress in September, makes the United States a Russian ally in its unlawful invasion and war against Ukraine.
The Wall Street Journal editorial board, which no one can accuse of being liberal, called Trump’s decision to buy diesel from Putin both a “moral and strategic mistake” that will “directly finance Mr. Putin’s bloody war.” Meanwhile, the Journal concluded that the deal with Russia will do nothing to reduce the price of diesel for Americans.
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who wrote the sanctions bill that honors GOP U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham who worked on sanctions for a year before dying in July, said lifting the sanctions shows that Trump “stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug and enablers of Russia’s war machine” against the wishes of the American people, Congress and our European allies.
Lindsey Graham’s sister, U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace her brother and now faces her own election campaign, issued a mild rebuke of the president’s executive order. “Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down,” she said. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
The sanctions, which passed the U.S. Senate and U.S. House with overwhelming bipartisan support, were intended to target Russian officials and oligarchs and institutions doing business with Russia, all to put pressure on Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
In effect, these twin executive orders by Trump reverses 80 years of American history in which presidents of both parties – including Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Reagan – did all they could to stop Russia’s expansionist ambitions and its authoritarian leaders.
It is the first time in history that an American president has parted from America’s closest democratic allies to support a Russian dictator and his unlawful war against a sovereign nation. A war which is killing hundreds of Ukraine civilians every single day.
By now Idahoans must realize the direct connection between their daily lives and events thousands of miles away. Thanks to Trump’s unnecessary war with Iran prices are soaring for the American people. Last week it was announced that Consumer Price Index is up 3.7 percent from last September. The cost of fuel oil for homes is up 74 percent, gas for cars 34 percent, airline fares 22 percent, and fruits and vegetables nearly 4 percent.
The average price of diesel in the United States was $6.32 per gallon last weekend, according to the AAA. Trump has tried to blame the soaring diesel prices on the war in Ukraine, but that is just a smokescreen to cover his own mistake in launching a war of choice against Iran.
“The main issue is still the Strait of Hormuz – that there is not enough diesel coming out of the Strait of Hormuz,” Sarah Raffoul, an oil product analyst for Argus Media, told The New York Times.
As Idahoans suffer this economic malaise, they may not realize that their own United States senator, Jim Risch, has the power to help end their suffering. As chair of the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which helps set policies for our country’s foreign affairs, Risch is one of the most powerful figures in Washington.
Risch could lead the effort in the Senate to stop Trump from buying Russian diesel and from lifting the Lindsey Graham sanctions if he had the courage and will to do so.
So far Risch has not whispered a word on Trump acting to shift the country’s support from the democratic Ukraine to the authoritarian Russia. He has not criticized Trump’s decision to buy Russian diesel which will only help finance Putin’s war, and he has not issued a statement condemning Trump’s lifting of the Lindsey Graham sanctions, even though he was one of 86 senators who voted for the bill on Aug. 7.
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, tours cities in Ukraine that have been most affected by the Russian invasion, including Kyiv. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Sen. Jim Risch)
Risch’s silence is shameful, but not surprising. In March 2025, Risch did not criticize Trump’s decision to suspend military aid to Ukraine, even though on a trip to Ukraine in June 2022, Risch said the most important thing the U.S. could do is give Ukraine all the military resources it needs to win the war. Of course, in June 2022 a Democrat, Joe Biden, was in the White House.
If Ukraine loses this war because Trump is not stopped in his quest to support Putin, this betrayal by the United States will go down in history right along with Neville Chamberlain’s Munich Agreement which allowed Hitler to annex part of Czechoslovakia in September 1938 – an appeasement which emboldened Hitler and led to World War II a year later.
Trump has finally shown his real colors. He is demonstrating that his allegiance is with the authoritarian Putin. He has finally tipped the scales against democratic Ukraine. There is no longer room for Republicans who love democracy, freedom, and peace to hide or remain silent.
It is time for them to show the same courage that Winston Churchill displayed when he told Chamberlain after he signed the Munich Agreement: “You had the choice between war and dishonor. You chose dishonor, yet you will have war.”
It is time for Jim Risch, as chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, to speak up, become the leader that this dangerous period in history demands, and stop Trump’s betrayal of the Ukrainians, our closest allies, Congress, and the American people who are paying the price for Trump’s moral and strategic mistakes.
If Risch cannot do this, if he cannot be the statesman we need at this dangerous hour, then one wonders why he even wants to serve another six-year term in the Senate.
Rod Gramer is an Idaho native, a longtime journalist, and co-author of “Fighting the Odds, The Life of Senator Frank Church,” the last Idahoan before Risch to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Memphis schools state takeover paused again
text:
Control of Memphis-Shelby County Schools returns to the local school board as the state takeover faces another court-ordered pause. (Andrea Morales / For Chalkbeat)This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters
Did you know search engines like Google are changing the way you see news? Keep Chalkbeat’s valuable education coverage at the top of your feeds by clicking here and checking the box next to our name.
The state takeover of Memphis-Shelby County Schools has once again been temporarily blocked, this time by a local judge on Monday.
That decision came minutes before the state-appointed oversight board was set to meet for the second time this month, oversight board Chair Billy Orgel said. The ruling throws control of the district back into uncertainty, returning full authority to the local school board only days after a federal judge reinstated the oversight board’s authority.
The federal case over whether the takeover is constitutional remains ongoing. But MSCS and Shelby County leaders filed a separate lawsuit against the takeover law in chancery court on Oct. 7.
As of Monday afternoon, the court order was not available on the Shelby County Chancery Court website. But in a request for a temporary block filed Sunday, district leaders amended their complaint to remove allegations that the state takeover law violates the Tennessee Constitution, a key argument in their federal case.
Instead, the plaintiffs argue that the takeover was ordered without evidence that the district qualified for it and that the takeover will irreparably harm district operations.
Orgel said Monday’s meeting had been canceled around 12:50 p.m., 10 minutes before it was scheduled to begin virtually.
“Hopefully this will be resolved soon so all of us can get together and improve our school system,” Orgel said in a statement to Chalkbeat.
At its first meeting in months earlier this month, the nine-member oversight board fast-tracked approval of key policies and processes to prove it was ready to begin its work. That included a draft approval process for contracts over $50,000.
The draft plan, along with job descriptions for an executive director and oversight board procedures, came from Florida-based consulting group MGT. The firm, which had also advised the state takeover of Houston schools in 2023, was hired by local philanthropists including longtime state takeover supporter Seeding Success.
Editor’s note: This is an ongoing story and will be updated as it develops. 
Bri Hatch covers Memphis-Shelby County Schools for Chalkbeat Tennessee. Reach Bri at bhatch@chalkbeat.org.
Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: In 7th Congressional District race, candidates focus on affordability, quality of life
text:
In Alabama's 7th Congressional District, U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham (left), who has held the seat since 2011, faces Republican nominee Ammie Akin (right), a first-time candidate. (Left: William J. Ford/Maryland Matters; Right: Courtesy Ammie Akin; photo illustration by Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)The two candidates for Alabama’s 7th Congressional District agree affordability is the defining issue of the race, but they disagree on what caused it and how it should be fixed.
First-time political candidate Ammie Akin won the Republican nomination for the district against David Perry in the August 11 Republican special primary. She is challenging U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham, who has held the seat since 2011. 
The 7th District spans key portions of Jefferson and Tuscaloosa counties, alongside Black Belt counties like Dallas, Wilcox, Lowndes and Sumter. The district saw some alteration after Republican lawmakers implemented its controversial and previously contested 2023 congressional maps earlier this year. However, the Cook Political Report rates it a D+10, solid Democratic district in November.   
The candidates
Akin, a long-time educator, school administrator and non-profit operator said two of her campaign priorities—crime and education— come back to that core issue of affordability.
“I think we need to start asking quality of life issues and affordability-type issues because what is driving people to crime? Well, crime is when people are desperate,” Akin said. “Are they desperate for food? Are they desperate to feed their family? Can they make money? Do they have a job? We have to look across the district, and we have to consider the communities and the quality of life in these communities, and what we need to do to improve that quality of life if we’re going to stop crime.”
Like Democratic candidates across the country, Sewell has made affordability a focal point of her re-election bid.
“When people talk about affordability in my district, they’re talking about the cost of gas, the cost of housing, the cost of groceries—people are concerned with, you know, everyday kitchen table issues, and they want to see change in Washington to address those concerns,” Sewell said. 
Sewell cited legislation she has sponsored to stop President Donald Trump’s tariffs as a member of the U.S. House’s Trade subcommittee, part of the Ways and Means Committee. 
“And hopefully—God willing—with the election of the Democrats, I’d get the gavel and be the chair of the subcommittee on trade, so we can work on trying to bring down the prices of everything,” she said.
Trump’s tariff war is projected to cost households an average $820 in 2026; executive tariffs have cost Alabama $5.4 billion, at a per-household equivalent of $2,365. Trump’s  war on Iran, which began February of this year, has further exacerbated inflationary pressures on everyday commodities like gas and food. 
After federal cuts to the program, Affordable Care Act enrollment in Alabama has also dropped by 23%—roughly 95,000 people, statewide—and some 21,000 of those are in the 7th District.
In the 7th Congressional District, roughly 15.7% to 21.3% of the general population lives below the poverty line, with child poverty reaching 25% to 28% in recent estimates. Approximately 26.7% to 28.1% of adults hold a bachelor’s degree or higher, trailing state and national averages. According to Sewell’s annual report, the district received more than $398 million in federal grant money during 2025.
Akin argued the challenges facing the district—which suffers from the highest poverty rates and lowest-performing schools—originate from within, the misallocation of federal funds, and said “the answer isn’t always another government program.”
“You know people are going to say: ‘Well, Alabama is a ruby red state; it must be the fault of the Republicans.’ Oh no!’ Akin said. “You look at who’s run District Seven for the last sixteen years, and it’s not a Republican. It’s a solid blue, woke Democrat who campaigns with Stacey Abrams and Alexandria Cortez, and [Sewell] is a woke liberal who is spending her time traveling the country with people that do not represent her district.”
Sewell said she was “very much aware that our district was the poorest district of the state of Alabama when I inherited that district, and we’ve worked very hard to try to address those concerns.” 
“Our district didn’t get into this shape overnight,” she said. “It has been decades, generations of disinvestment in Alabama’s 7th Congressional District. And since I’ve been elected, we’ve done nothing but try to address that by investing heavily in our district.”
Akin said she was “not applying for a job with either party.”
“I’m applying for a job with the constituents of Congressional District Seven and what is most important to me is what helps the people in Congressional District Seven, and so I am not digging my heels in on a party line,” she said. “I’m digging my heels in on what’s right for people.”
Akin did not indicate whether or not she is prepared to vote against Republican leadership if they propose new cuts to Medicare or Social Security, or with Democrats, if there are efforts to restore or extend access to Medicaid. 
Sewell emphasized her commitment to bipartisan work on housing affordability, highlighting the July passage of the 21st Century Road to Housing bill to fund affordable home construction. She plans to reintroduce the John Lewis Voting Rights Amendment Act, which would restore voting protections overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court. Additionally, she pledged that within her first one hundred hours, a Democratic-led House would immediately reverse the Trump administration’s $1 trillion in proposed Medicaid cuts to protect vulnerable families in Alabama. 
Sewell plans to balance the party’s dual stated goals of passing consumer-focused legislation while ramping up aggressive congressional oversight of the current administration, but is not interested in pursuing impeachment proceedings against Trump.
“That didn’t work the first term, right? And so why would we waste our precious power and time doing that?” Sewell said of impeachment. “We’ll be utilizing our power and our time to directly affect the cost of gas and groceries by getting rid of these illegal tariffs by addressing the serious cuts of Medicaid that have come that will be coming down in 2027.”
Fundraising
According to the most recent campaign filings, Akin raised $262,893.67, of which she loaned about 38% ($100,000) at the start of her campaign. She spent $210,806 and had $52,087.67 remaining as of September 30. Akin has not received political action committee (PAC) money.
Sewell raised $2,207,233.12, of which about 19% came from individual donors. The majority of cash contributions, about 81% ($1,795,750.00), came from PACs. Sewell spent $1.6 million and had $281,600 on hand as of July 22.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: When curriculum decisions get taken from educators
text:
A sign for Auburn University seen on March 28, 2026 in Auburn, Alabama. Behind the sign is William J. Samford Hall.  (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Effective October 1, HB580 expanded the authority of Boards of Trustees over curriculum and degree requirements at public universities, reinforcing their role as the ultimate academic decision-makers. At first glance, that may sound like a dry governance issue. It’s not.
Shortly after HB580 took effect, Auburn’s Board of Trustees not only embraced this authority but exercised it. In its new curriculum policy, the Board declares that “no external standard, professional norm, or process can limit the Board’s authority over curriculum.” Students, parents, alumni, and donors should consider these implications. The hubris is astonishing.
Auburn’s trustees are asserting that their authority supersedes not only faculty expertise, but professional norms, disciplinary standards, and even accrediting bodies. That has nothing to do with educational quality or student success. It’s a declaration of raw power.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Imagine the Board deciding that future engineers need a different mix of courses to design and build bridges, so they revise the Civil Engineering curriculum accordingly. And why not? They have the authority.
We know why that would be a terrible idea. Civil engineering faculty, industry experts, and ABET’s Engineering Accreditation Commission determine what future engineers need to know. The program would lose its accreditation, and students would pay the price. Employers and licensing boards care about accredited programs, not trustee-designed curricula.
One would think Auburn’s trustees would know better than to substitute their judgment for that of experts. But that is exactly what they have done. The Board recently intervened in Auburn’s core curriculum by requiring every undergraduate student to complete both a U.S. history and civics course.  Reasonable people can disagree whether that’s a good idea, but the concern is how this unfolded.
Several years ago, Auburn’s history faculty examined this same question from the Board. They considered that U.S. history and civics are already Alabama high school requirements, and students must demonstrate civics knowledge before graduation. After working with the administration to directly assess incoming students’ knowledge, the results showed that students already possessed the knowledge that the proposed requirement was intended to address. Based on both the evidence and faculty expertise, the administration concluded that a change to the core curriculum was not warranted.
Now, all of a sudden, it is. Yet trustees offered no evidence that the previous analysis was wrong. They presented no assessment identifying a deficiency and no rationale for overturning the earlier decision. They simply exercised the Board’s authority. This is how raw power operates. It does not need to persuade, justify, or demonstrate expertise. It simply imposes its will.
Faced with the Board’s directive, Auburn’s history faculty proposed expanding students’ exposure to American history and creating more opportunities for meaningful engagement. Auburn’s Dean Council made the final decision and rejected the faculty’s preferred recommendation. Now every Auburn student will spend time and tuition dollars repeating material they already mastered in high school.
Auburn chose not to follow the recommendation of the people who teach and study history. Instead, it followed the judgment of trustees and administrators with no expertise in the field. Imagine asking them to determine what nursing students must learn to provide patient care or what accounting students must learn to pass the CPA exam. The absurdity is obvious.
This should concern anyone who believes academic decisions should be guided by expertise rather than centralized authority. Universities exist precisely because specialized knowledge matters. The further decisions move from those with the expertise, the more educational quality suffers, and the more students bear the consequences.
The Board has a critical and legitimate role. Trustees decide which programs exist. They allocate resources, approve budgets, and provide oversight. Good leadership is not about exercising every power the Board possesses. It’s about knowing when not to. That is the lesson Auburn’s trustees seem to have forgotten.
It is also a lesson Alabama’s lawmakers should keep in mind. By passing HB580, lawmakers embraced the idea that concentrating authority at the top leads to better decisions. That is a surprising position in a red state where politicians routinely warn about the dangers of centralized power. Conservatives distrust decisions made by distant bureaucracies. History offers ample support for that belief.
Auburn’s Board actions should serve as an early warning about what happens when expertise becomes subordinate to power. If we would never want trustees to meddle in a curriculum that teaches students to design and build bridges, why are we comfortable allowing them to meddle in any curriculum at all?

name: Colorado Newsline
title: State’s inaction leaves Colorado communities vulnerable to data center harms
text:
Construction on a data center expansion at the QTS site in Aurora, Colorado, is pictured on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)For the second year in a row, the Colorado state Legislature has failed to enact policy to regulate data centers. Elected officials in localities across Colorado are rightfully taking matters into their own hands, but priorities of local elected officials vary. Some residents of the state are feeling unheard by those who represent them.
While local governments can and should implement policy to regulate data centers, particularly with regard to industrial zoning and local nuisance ordinances, the state’s inaction leaves communities vulnerable to the negative impacts of data centers that are not as easily regulated at the local level, including climate impacts, water usage, and energy infrastructure concerns.
Coloradans largely are in opposition to uncontrolled, resource-intensive growth of the data center industry, and we need legislators to act in our best interest. As the demand for artificial intelligence and computing power increases, the stress on energy and water resources must be properly assessed to safeguard communities, and the threat of increased climate pollution must be averted.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Evidence of the negative effects of data centers is mounting, not just in Colorado, but across the country and the globe. Residents living near data centers across the country are seeing their electricity rates increase as public utilities invest in expanding energy infrastructure to meet the demand of data centers. Climate initiatives are being compromised, as data center development takes priority over renewable energy development in some regions. Concerns about water use by data centers is particularly resonant for Coloradans as much of the Western U.S. faces severe and worsening drought conditions. And to top things off, data centers are simply a public nuisance — they’re loud, brightly-lit 24 hours a day, and frequently use diesel generators that emit pollutants and contribute to even more noise for nearby communities.
While the negative impacts are being observed and recorded across the country, the true and full scale of rapid data center growth is largely unknown, and so far, current policy has not kept up. Local zoning often does not account for power-hungry industrial sites that operate through all hours of the day and night with minimal staff on site, and it will take time for individual communities to evaluate the impact of specific sites and permits. There are questions about the true values reported for energy demand, job creation, and water usage, prompting elected officials to introduce moratoriums at all levels of government to properly evaluate the issue and associated policy solutions.
Legislators in Colorado have stalled and delayed progress while opposition to the industry is growing at the grassroots level in communities across the state. Several coalitions have formed or shifted their focus to opposing data center development in cities such as Denver and Colorado Springs. In some cases, such as in Longmont and Monument, local elected officials have heard their constituents and acted quickly to permanently or temporarily restrict data center developments.
In others, such as Denver, elected officials imposed a moratorium to evaluate the issue, but only after a massive co-location project was planned and approved for the city’s most polluted ZIP code. Even worse, Colorado Springs commissioners approved Project Taurus and denied five appeals, despite swaths of residents showing up to speak out against the massive project.
Nonetheless, there are Colorado residents who are in support of data centers, particularly pro-business leaders and skilled labor unions, due to the allure of potential economic benefits and job creation. However, the economic benefit is still unknown for Colorado, and estimates in other states were found to be inflated, providing less state revenue and fewer permanent jobs than expected. The vast majority of jobs created by data centers are temporary construction jobs, lasting only 12-24 months, and the handful of permanent roles are often filled by third-party contractors, especially in co-location facilities like Denver’s CoreSite facility.
With so few permanent positions for local workers, large data centers take up space that could be used by industries that provide a greater number of permanent and local jobs. Construction jobs can be provided from a number of industries, including in the development of renewable energy resources. If data centers were required to invest in and be supplied by renewable energy sources, job creation would be far more substantial and longer lasting.
If state legislators and local elected officials fail to come to any kind of compromise to protect Colorado’s constituents, economy and ecosystem, what options are the voters left with? Would they take it to the ballot box? A ballot initiative would be reflective of the will of the people, but it could also be awfully more restrictive than the current concessions communities are requesting from lawmakers.
Take Port Washington, Wisconsin, as an example. These voters passed an initiative to require voter approval before tax incentives are granted for data center development. Monterey Park, California, voters took things even further, passing a permanent and complete ban on data centers in their city. What would the people of Colorado decide, if put to a vote? Do legislators want to risk it?
Given that lawmakers, developers, and some local governments feel data center development is important for economic growth and prosperity, they would be wise to take action now to give the public the protections they want.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Iran, gas, AI: Barr and Booker spar in the only TV debate for Kentucky Senate this year
text:
Charles Booker, right, speaks during a debate at the WKYT studios in  Lexington, Ky., on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Courtesy pool photographer Ryan Hermens)In the race to succeed U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr and former Democratic state Rep. Charles Booker sounded off on a host of issues Monday evening in their only televised debate ahead of Election Day. 
Throughout the debate, which was hosted by WKYT and carried by other Gray Media stations across the state, Barr repeatedly attempted to tie Booker to prominent democratic socialist figures while Booker argued that Barr would continue to be part of the “D.C. swamp” if elected to the Senate. 
Barr criticized Booker for supporting what he called “crazy socialist ideas,” like Medicare for all, which Booker supports, and “defunding police,” which Booker denied. Barr called his opponent “the Mamdani of Kentucky,” referring to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who won election in 2025, has since become a democratic socialist boogeyman for Republicans this election cycle. 
Andy Barr, R-Ky, speaks during a debate at the WKYT studios in Lexington, Ky., on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Courtesy pool photographer Andy Barr)
“Donald Trump seems to like Mamdani way more than he likes you,” Booker said near the end of the hour-long debate, after calling the tactic by Barr an attempt to “sow hate and fearmonger.” Before that, Booker said that he believed in capitalism, but “we simply need to make sure that it works for the people.” 
Barr predicted it would be “very difficult” for Booker to work in a bipartisan manner in Washington as someone “who does embrace the views of socialism” at the end of the debate. 
“Look, if he talks like a socialist, if he embraces views of socialists, if he taxes and spends like a socialist, he wants to pay people to not work like a socialist — he’s a socialist,” Barr said. 
Booker said Barr has become “bought and sold” throughout his time in Congress and pointed to corporate PACs supporting him. 
“I do not apologize for Americans freely supporting my campaign and freely supporting common sense,” Barr said in response. “They don’t want to be compelled to use their tax dollars to fund socialism.” 
The debate was moderated by WKYT’s Bill Bryant and DRB+WAVE’s Lindsay Allen. Here’s a look at some of the other issues discussed during the debate: 
War in Iran 
Trump’s war in Iran has become a theme in the upcoming midterm elections nationwide. Earlier this year, Kentuckians Tech Sgt. Ashley B. Pruitt and Sgt. Benjamin N. Pennington, were killed in the conflict. The candidates were asked about what the exit strategy should look like and if the threat of Iran having a nuclear weapon had been accomplished. 
“We owe it to them to finish the job and win,” Barr said, referring to Pruitt and Pennington. He continued, saying that because of Trump and military sacrifices, blows have been delivered to Iran’s military capabilities. 
“We’ve largely achieved the objective. We have more work to do in the Strait of Hormuz, restoring oil exports,” Barr said. “But at the end of the day, I appreciate the fact that this president has not started a war. He is ending a 47-year war against the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism that has threatened the United States.” 
Booker said “we need to bring our loved ones back home,” and argued that Barr “is in Congress right now signing a blank check to continue this madness.” In September, Barr had voted, along with most other Republicans in the U.S. House, against a war powers resolution to end the war in Iran. 
Charles Booker speaks during a debate at the WKYT studios in Lexington, Ky., on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Courtesy pool photographer Ryan Herrmens)
“None of what he said rings with any sincerity because if he really believed that we need to stand up for our service members, he would do it now,” Booker said. “But no, he has said that the White House, this administration, should be able to do whatever they want in Iran without any checks and balances from Congress. I believe we need a Congress with a backbone to stand up.” 
Affordability
Control of the Strait of Hormuz has frequently been tied to rising prices of fuel in the U.S., which also impacts the price of groceries and other goods. Barr and Booker received a few affordability questions at the start of the debate. 
Asked what they would do to bring down the price of gas if elected, Barr said “we’re working on (lowering costs) and making a lot of progress” and blamed Democrats for rising inflation. Barr said he supported tax cuts to give Kentuckians more money in their pockets and that he would support “American energy dominance” to have more U.S. control over energy and fuel. 
“My opponent supports the radical Green New Deal, which would dismantle fossil energy and skyrocket prices,” Barr said, referring to a policy aimed at transitioning to using clean energy amid global warming. 
Booker questioned what Barr was doing to address the problem as a congressman. 
“Those prices are going up under his watch. The price of groceries is going up under Andy Barr’s watch. The price of gas is going up under Andy Barr’s watch,” Booker said. “So one of the most important things we need to do to bring down costs is get Andy Barr out of office.” 
AI and data centers
As communities across Kentucky and the country grapple with allowing data centers into their towns or not, many are questioning expanding the use of artificial intelligence in their daily lives as well. The candidates were asked if they supported guardrails for using AI while balancing America’s spot in the AI race with other nations. 
“I understand the concerns, and Americans shouldn’t ever have artificial intelligence threaten their job,” Barr said, before adding that he also does not believe Kentuckians should pay higher utility bills if a data center moves into their town. 
“We have to win the AI race because the country that wins the AI race is the country that will set the rules for AI. We are in a strategic competition with China. I believe in local control, American leadership on this, and we need to deter China from their technological ambitions, which do threaten us,” Barr said. 
Booker said Barr was “getting paid by the telecom companies that want to put (data centers) in your backyard.” FEC reports show that a pro-AI superPAC, Leading the Future, has donated to another PAC, American Mission, which has spent money this year in support of Barr independently from his campaign. Booker also said he has called for a moratorium on building data centers. 
“AI should be used as a strategic tool to help working people, not a weapon to exploit and hurt the people. And that’s why I believe Congress must act,” Booker said. “We must put protection in place for our children, for vulnerable communities, for our seniors, and standing up for the people against the way that data centers are being used to bully communities.” 
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Early voting in Kentucky begins Thursday, Oct. 29.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: The hidden billing practices raising healthcare costs
text:
Voters say the cost of healthcare will be a major factor in how they vote in this year's midterm elections. (Getty Images)There is no single explanation for America’s high healthcare costs. But any serious effort to control them must start with hospitals.
Between 2022 and 2024, hospital care accounted for $277 billion, or 40%, of the growth in national health spending, according to a KFF analysis. Those costs reach families through premiums and out-of-pocket expenses, businesses through employee benefits, and taxpayers through Medicaid.
One way bills rise is through “upcoding,” when a medical visit or hospital stay is billed at a higher rate because it is described as more complicated than the record shows. Intent is not the only issue. Even unintentional coding inflation raises costs.
Some AI tools now listen to conversations during patient visits, turn them into medical notes and recommend billing codes. These tools are then marketed to health systems as a way to increase revenue.
Blue Health Intelligence, an independent Blue Cross Blue Shield licensee, analyzed claims from 2022 to 2025. Its analysis found that among the 10% of hospitals with the largest increases in coding intensity, nearly 60% of eligible admissions were classified as complex by March 2025, up from about 47% in 2022. Other hospitals recorded a much smaller increase.
Did patients suddenly become much sicker at a small group of hospitals, or did the billing practice change?
Because health plans see millions of claims, they can spot billing patterns that are invisible on any single bill. They can then compare higher-priced codes to the medical record and correct those the documentation does not support, saving much needed health care dollars.
The stakes are especially high as more hospitals and medical practices become part of large health systems, national corporations or investor-backed networks with sophisticated revenue operations. Data from the Private Equity Stakeholder Project show that Kentucky ranks 11th nationally in the number of private-equity-owned hospitals and eighth in the percentage under private equity control. Its tracker identified 17 Kentucky hospitals owned or operated by private equity firms.
It makes no sense to allow providers to use technology to maximize revenue while restricting health plans from using data to stop unsupported charges.
Kentucky’s sepsis policy shows how outdated billing rules can push costs higher. Sepsis is a life-threatening response to infection that can damage the body’s organs. How it is defined can affect how a hospital claim is classified and how much Medicaid pays.
According to a Kentucky Association of Health Plans review, Kentucky is one of only three states requiring Medicaid health plans to use sepsis criteria rooted in 1991, the year the Soviet Union was collapsing, and the first website went online on the World Wide Web.
International medical experts adopted the more precise Sepsis-3 definition in 2016 after concluding that the older criteria did not reliably distinguish sepsis from other illnesses. Still, in 2024, after the Kentucky Hospital Association and hospital executives pushed to preserve the older criteria, lawmakers wrote that approach into state law.
The old broader definition that Kentucky uses makes it easier for hospitals to classify and bill a patient as having sepsis, even when the patient does not, based on the internationally-recognized modern definition. Because sepsis is paid as a more serious condition than many infections, the label can increase reimbursement without impacting the care a patient receives. This is the definition of waste.
It can also make hospital performance appear better than it is. When less seriously ill patients are counted as sepsis cases, reported outcomes can improve even when the quality of care does not. Researchers have warned that diagnosis and coding can create exactly that misleading impression. That can mean a bigger bill and a distorted scorecard. Ultimately, misreporting sepsis pollutes the sepsis outcomes’ database. Such data is critical for informing appropriate patient care models now and in the future.
Whether a higher charge comes from an AI-assisted billing code or an outdated sepsis definition, the principle is the same: Hospitals should be paid for the care they provide, not for complexity they added on paper.
Kentucky should modernize its sepsis law and ensure health plans can stop unsupported charges before they raise costs for families, employers and taxpayers.
Tom Stephens is Executive Director of the Kentucky Association of Health Plans.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Closing Virginia’s child care affordability gap could cost up to gap  $4.5b a year
text:
Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith and Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway speaking inside the Peake Childhood Center in Newport News during the child care funding summit on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Closing Virginia’s child care affordability gap would require up to $4.5 billion annually over the next decade, according to the Virginia Department of Education — an investment that, under one scenario, would also raise annual pay for 43,000 educators by an average of $17,000. 
Virginia currently lacks at least 140,000 child care slots needed to support working families. Earlier this year, the General Assembly directed the agency to report on parent demand and service needs, calculate funding needs based on current program eligibility, measure historic growth, and account for relevant economic-development projects.
Providers and experts said the additional funding would not only close the gap on child care slots but also support educator recruitment and retention, expand services to meet the diverse needs of students and families, and make care more affordable while helping providers cover costs.
“For us to have a strong economy, we must also have affordable and high-quality childcare options for all Virginians,” said Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith to child care providers. “They go hand in hand.”
Smith spoke at an Oct. 14 summit at the Peake Childhood Center in Newport News, where discussion focused on creating affordable child care.
One takeaway from the summit: Child care costs in every Virginia region exceed three times the historical federal affordability benchmark of 7% of family income, underscoring how far out of reach affordable care remains.
Families and providers are feeling the pinch, with state reimbursements covering 51% of the “cost of quality,” or the estimated amount a provider needs to deliver high-quality early childhood care and education. Raising the minimum wage to $15 without corresponding subsidy increases also poses a challenge for providers, who may have to raise tuition or reduce staff and enrollment.
The agency said 80% of child care providers had to raise tuition for families as a result of the statewide minimum wage increase. Among subsidized providers, one in four cut enrollment and one in five cut staff.

The funding options
Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway said last week the state invests more than $600 million a year in early childhood programs, up from about $75 million in 2018, including funding for child care subsidies and the Virginia Preschool Initiative.
State lawmakers will have access to the agency’s report, which includes long-term projections and three options to expand access and supply.
The Affordability for All plan is the most expensive option, costing $4.5 billion annually over the next 10 years. Families would pay no more than 0%to 10% of their income for child care. The plan would serve an additional 240,000 new children and reach 66% of working families.
The Improving Affordability option costs $3.7 billion annually, caps copays between 2.5% and 20% of household income, serves an additional 190,000 children and increases teacher wages by $14,000 per year. 
The third option, the Sustaining Historic Growth plan, costs $1.6 billion annually, serves 39,000 new children and raises wages by $9,500 per year. Families that qualify would be capped at 5% of the income distribution but would receive no assistance if they make more than $122,000 a year.
Conway said the latter proposal would still leave most families in need without assistance.
The amounts do not account for expected cost increases from inflation and benchmarking over the next 10 years.
Sen. Mamie Locke, D-Hampton, co-sponsored the legislation directing the agency to explore child care demand with Del. Briana Sewell, D-Prince William. Locke said she looks forward to moving the issue toward a “good outcome” after what she called a productive meeting with parent advocates and teachers.
“I think these numbers show that the commonwealth will need to invest in our kids,” Locke said.
Secretary of Education Jeffery Smith and Superintendent of Public Instruction Jenna Conway speaking inside the Peake Childhood Center in Newport News during the child care funding summit on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Child care funding calculations being shared during the child care funding summit on Oct. 14, 2026 in Newport News. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
Advocates now wait
Several child care providers and parents attended the Newport News summit and offered suggestions and feedback.
Jennifer Parish, executive director of Peake Childhood Center, said the funding proposals gave her hope that early childhood providers may receive more support, since the subsidy program covers only about half the true cost of quality care and leaves nonprofits dependent on fundraising.
She said early childhood programs play a key role in preparing children for kindergarten by building early literacy, math, social and self-regulation skills. 
However, low wages are a major reason centers struggle to hire and retain qualified staff. During a tour last week, she showed advocates and providers rooms filled with students and others sitting empty.
“We have empty classrooms at our center right now because we can’t find the staff to open up the room,” Parish said.
Cheryl Morman, a home-based childcare provider in Richmond, said the funding shortfalls make it difficult for her and other providers to pay educators fairly, cover care costs and support inclusive care for children with special needs. 
“There need to be teachers and educators whom we can pay a livable wage so they can provide the care that all children need, especially children with special needs,” Morman said.
Kayla Brewer, a parent representative and member of the Commission on Early Child Care and Education, emphasized that families need affordable, high-quality care with consistent educators, and that public agencies, providers, families, and employers must share responsibility for making childcare accessible.
Addressing the funding challenge, Brewer said, “Educators deserve more, but parents can’t afford to pay it.”
Gov. Abigail Spanberger will present her proposed budget amendments to lawmakers in December, setting up the next step in the debate over child care funding.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: New coalition aims to keep Virginians covered as Medicaid rules tighten
text:
Virginia Health and Human Resources Secretary Marvin Figueroa learns about healthcare workforce training during a tour of Eastern Shore Community College on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Virginia is bringing healthcare and workforce organizations together to help residents keep their health coverage and navigate new federal requirements for Medicaid and other assistance programs.  
Virginia Secretary of Health and Human Resources Marvin Figueroa on Monday announced the Virginia United Coalition, formalizing a partnership that builds on a series of roundtable meetings with him and Gov. Abigail Spanberger throughout the summer, as well as an executive order she signed. 
Streamlining communication and collaboration will be paramount to complying with H.R. 1, a federal reconciliation bill Congress passed last summer that includes current and forthcoming changes to Medicaid, hospital funding mechanisms and other social services, including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
Starting next year, about 300,000 of Virginians are at risk of losing their Medicaid coverage because of additional verification mandates and eligibility requirements. More than 5,000 lawful immigrants lost their eligibility this month alone.
Figueroa noted that some people losing Medicaid coverage may be inevitable under the federal changes, but the state’s role is to help prevent others from falling through cracks. 
“Others may still be eligible but lose coverage because a form was missed, a notice was misunderstood, or the process became too difficult to navigate. That distinction matters,” he said over the summer. “A paperwork failure should not become a healthcare crisis.” 
Building on the coalition’s conversations in recent months, participants are launching public awareness campaigns through digital advertising and adding staff or training to help organizations and agencies make referrals. 
For instance, UnitedHealthcare will send mail, email and text messages, while the Virginia Association of Free and Charitable Clinics will devote part of its statewide advertising budget to targeted ads helping Medicaid patients understand how to maintain their coverage. 
The Virginia Hospital and Healthcare Association will review state-developed notices, forms and other verification procedures to identify potential administrative burdens for patients and help the state streamline the process. 
Goodwill Industries and the Virginia Interfaith Center for Public Policy will draw on their community engagement experience. Goodwill is developing a referral process for people seeking employment who are affected by the new work requirements for Medicaid and SNAP. 
Virginia Interfaith recently hired a faith network community coordinator to help streamline communications among free clinics, food banks, community health centers and other local or regional partners the organization typically works with. 
Along with passing H.R. 1, Congress allowed Affordable Care Act subsidies to expire last year. Those subsidies had helped cash-strapped families without employer-provided insurance who would not otherwise qualify for Medicaid purchase their own health. 
Thousands of Virginians have dropped ACA coverage this year, prompting the state to invest $150 million in subsidies residents can access starting next month. 
Because uninsured people are more likely to put off preventative care, healthcare providers and some politicians have expressed concern that they may flood emergency rooms when crises arise. Hospitals absorb the cost of unpaid care, but those costs can spread to others over time as health systems negotiate with insurers and rates rise. 
Rufus Phillips, president of the state’s free clinics association, said the clinics’ role in the coalition includes  helping people avoid losing coverage and providing preventive care to keep those who do lose it out of emergency departments. 
Western Tidewater Free Clinic director Ashley Greene told The Mercury earlier this year that her clinic has been able to keep about 75% of its patients from visiting a hospital ER by staying on top of their primary care. 
“There’s that much more room for true emergencies,” she said.
Still, Virginia hospitals have documented an 8% spike in ER visits from uninsured patients over the past year. 
“I do applaud the state for pulling all the stakeholders together in this fashion,” Phillips said in an interview Monday.  “It’s good to collaborate where we can to try to ameliorate the effects of H.R.1.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Helena Buonanno Foulkes has always been unflappable. Is she now unbeatable?
text:
Helena Buonanno Foulkes joins a selfie with a supporter at the opening of her campaign office on Broad Street in Providence in July. (Courtesy of Foulkes campaign)Helena Buonanno was 13 years old when the Blizzard of 1978 left her stranded with her toddler sister and their panicked babysitter at the family’s Providence home.
Her three other siblings were snowed in at their elementary school, and her parents were across the country attending a convention in San Francisco, unable to return home for three days.
But her dad, Bernie Buonanno Jr., didn’t worry.
“She was so calm,” Buonanno, now 88, said, recalling hearing his daughter take charge on the other end of the phone, soothing the babysitter who was supposed to be taking care of her.
That unshakable disposition has guided Helena Buonanno Foulkes through many storms, including cancer, a high-powered business career and two runs for governor.
“My husband says that one of my specialties is dealing with complicated men,” Foulkes, 62, said in a recent interview. She and her husband Bill have been married for 37 years.
“He says that as a joke because he’s a complicated man. But I think my whole life I have dealt with complicated men, and I’ve had to be unflappable.”
On every pre-primary debate stage, Gov. Dan McKee hammered Foulkes for profiting off the pain of the opioid crisis during her four years as head of CVS Pharmacy and hurting working families through staffing cuts she oversaw as CEO of Hudson Bay Company. 
Foulkes calmly refuted both claims. In one debate, hosted by WPRO, she pointed out that it was McKee getting “pretty hot” and needing to “settle down” during a tense exchange over the Washington Bridge.
Five weeks later, Foulkes defeated McKee by 24 points, bursting onto a makeshift stage outside Track 15 in Providence to celebrate with her supporters in the cool evening drizzle.
“It’s way more fun to win than to lose,” Foulkes said in an interview.
She lost to McKee by 3 percentage points in her first campaign in 2022. 
“I feel a responsibility when I walk into places where people are genuinely so excited for change, and they recognize me, they’re counting on me,” Foulkes said.
Like the pair of women seated at a nearby table when Foulkes walked into La Casona Restaurant in Central Falls on a sunny October afternoon. They stood, rushing to greet her.
“I’m voting for you,” one declared as Foulkes embraced them.
Helena Foulkes reflects on her 2026 campaign during an interview at La Casona restaurant in Central Falls. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
A friendship forged
Foulkes didn’t spend much time in Central Falls while growing up, despite living a few miles away in Providence. But the tiny city features prominently in her political comeback. 
After her 2022 primary defeat, one of her first calls was to Central Falls Mayor Maria Rivera. The two women had connected during the campaign, even though Rivera made clear from the outset she supported another Democratic contender, then-Secretary of State Nellie Gorbea.
“She used to wear this big Nellie button, so I would go up to her at all the events, and say, ‘Someday, we’re going to work together,’” Foulkes recalled of Rivera.
Rivera acknowledged their instant chemistry and shared experience of being the only woman in a room full of men. Over the next four years, Rivera sought Foulkes’ advice on how to navigate the gender imbalance in her own political career, even calling Foulkes for input before approaching McKee on the topic of returning Central Falls Public Schools to local control.
“It’s been really hard for me, as the only woman leading the city, trying to communicate with so many men,” Rivera said. “With Helena, it was like, ‘Oh my god, I have someone who’s going to pay attention to me, going to listen to me.’”
Foulkes set up an introduction between Rivera and Mike Bloomberg, which led to a $250,000 donation from the New York politician and businessman to Central Falls where one quarter of the city’s population lives below the poverty level, double the statewide average. 



Quotation







I feel a responsibility when I walk into places where people are genuinely so excited for change, and they recognize me, they’re counting on me.


– Helena Buonanno Foulkes


Foulkes graduated from Harvard College and Harvard Business School. Her corporate resume features several C-suite positions. She and her husband, a marketing and strategic planning consultant and a faculty member at the Rhode Island School of Design, own two homes in Rhode Island: an eight-bedroom, six-bath oceanfront summer house in Narragansett, purchased in 2012 for $3.8 million, and a three-bedroom, two-bath home on Providence’s East Side, for which the couple paid $2.3 million in 2023.
Foulkes and her husband reported nearly more than $2.7 million in combined, taxable income (nearly $3 million before deductions) in 2025, according to a copy of her tax return summary shared with Rhode Island Current. More than $1.5 million of that money came from capital gains, along with $450,000 in state earnings, and over $300,000 in dividend payments from stocks, and other investments. 
Her independent opponent Ken Block has refused to release his tax returns, prompting Foulkes’ campaign to criticize her rival for lack of transparency in a statement Monday.
To Rivera, Foulkes’ pedigree and tax bracket don’t matter. The Central Falls mayor said Foulkes has proven she cares about the oft-overlooked city, showing up for meetings, doorknocking and community events throughout the last four years.
“People feel comfortable speaking to her, comfortable approaching her, which is so needed,” Rivera said.
Key to Foulkes’ housing plan is the state millionaire’s tax — something she would have to pay. While the incremental surtax on income over $1 million already took effect as part of the fiscal 2027 budget, Foulkes has proposed designating the revenue for a state-run revolving fund that provides low-interest loans to developers building affordable housing.
“We have millionaires and billionaires who are making more money and richer than anybody at any time since the Gilded Age in our government,” Foulkes said during an Oct. 13 debate on WPRO. She contrasted the rise in wealth with the sudden loss of health insurance coverage under federal Medicaid cuts.
She has overcome her own significant challenges. At 35, with four young children, Foulkes was diagnosed with thyroid cancer. She underwent surgery at Rhode Island Hospital and has remained cancer-free.
Rejected the first time she sought an internal promotion to lead CVS’ retail arm and put into a public affairs position she viewed as a dead-end job, she took it anyway. She was her family’s primary breadwinner at the time, with four kids in private school. She ended up loving the job — and later got the promotion she wanted.
“It wasn’t a straight path to the top,” she said. 
Nor a straight path into politics.
Helena Buonanno Foulkes, left, waves to supporters after Central Falls Mayor Maria Rivera, right, endorsed her in the Democratic primary on July 28. (Courtesy of Helena Foulkes campaign)
Politics in the family
Foulkes has fond childhood memories of attending the campaign events and swearing-in ceremonies for her Uncle Chris. That’s former U.S. Sen. Chris Dodd, Connecticut’s longest serving senator. His dad, and Foulkes’ maternal grandfather, Thomas Dodd, also served in both chambers of Congress after working as executive counsel in the Nuremberg trials. Foulkes’ mom, Martha Buonanno, was former U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s college roommate, and Pelosi visited Rhode Island to raise money for Foulkes in both gubernatorial primary campaigns.
Yet Martha Buonanno dissuaded her children from following in the family’s political footsteps because of the personal sacrifices and public criticism involved.
Her mother died before Foulkes’ political career began but is frequently mentioned in campaign ads and speeches. Bernie Buonanno believes his late wife would be thrilled to see how Foulkes has performed on the campaign trail and the debate stage.
“Once she got going, she was an absolute natural,” Bernie Buonanno said of his daughter. “My god, she was perfect.”
Foulkes’ elementary school adviser at Henry Barnard School in Providence predicted as much, telling her parents she would be president someday, her father recalled.
But beyond several years as class president at the all-girls Lincoln School in Providence —- alongside captaining the tennis, basketball and softball teams her senior year — Foulkes’ career aspirations leaned toward business, not politics.
Foulkes frequently references her “cubicle days” to describe her professional ascent at CVS Health. While she may have worked in a cubicle for the Woonsocket company when she began, it was not in an entry-level role. Recruited directly by the company president, Foulkes was tasked with managing the rollout of a home delivery program for prescriptions. The venture failed, but it launched Foulkes’ 25-year career at CVS, culminating in four years as president of the retail pharmacy.
“I loved retail,” Foulkes said. “It was the merger of my math background, and it’s like, there’s a whole bunch of data coming, but also, what makes people tick.”
Not so different from government, according to Foulkes. 
“Every single day, you know how you’re doing,” she said. “Is it working? It is not? What’s the crisis of the moment.”
Yet a string of local lawsuits and federal investigations allege CVS leaders were complicit in, or even perpetuated, the opioid crisis by improper dispensing, fake prescription filling and record-keeping violations. CVS spent $2 billion on legal settlements and paid more than $70 million in fines to the U.S. Department of Justice while refusing to admit any wrongdoing.
Foulkes is not named in any of the complaints but presided over the retail pharmacy arm during some of the years covered in the lawsuits.
She has denied any role in the crisis, while defending the company’s work to address the opioid epidemic through drug takeback programs, cutting off pill mill doctors and legislative guardrails. A Rhode Island Current analysis of her claims found some of the statistics were exaggerated, while other reforms were driven by market trends and lawmakers, not company executives.
The focus on Foulkes’ alleged connections to the opioid crisis initially faded with McKee’s defeat. Her general election opponents, independent Block and Republican Aaron Guckian, focused more on policy and ideological differences than Foulkes’ professional resume.
Until Oct. 13, one day before early voting, when news broke of a $315 million federal settlement to resolve a 2024 Department of Justice lawsuit alleging that CVS filled unnecessary opioid prescriptions. The company did not admit wrongdoing as part of the agreement, which also does not name Foulkes.
But Guckian’s campaign quickly seized the moment, holding a press conference outside the State House the next morning to call on Foulkes to “answer questions” about her leadership. Block followed suit with his own campaign statement pressing Foulkes to address the public directly.
Angelika Pellegrino, Foulkes’ campaign spokesperson, reiterated previous talking points about Foulkes’ efforts, and the work of the company, to cut off pill mill doctors and launch a drug takeback program.
“It wasn’t so much personal for me as it was wrong about the true work of all the people at CVS,” Foulkes said during an interview at La Casona. 
She dips a chip into a white ramekin of guacamole while reflecting on her ability to not let opponents’ attacks get under her skin.
“They were navigating all this complexity, and to see my opponent attack not just me but really the whole company, yeah, that was stinky,” she added.
Will she smell victory on Nov. 3? If so, Foulkes believes she can make a difference for the people she’s met on the campaign trail: parents unable to afford childcare, seniors struggling to pay their energy bills, immigrants and women who believe their basic protections are under threat by the Trump administration.
“Four years ago, I feel like I was just memorizing a lot of facts,” she said of her first campaign. “This time, the stories are just deep inside me.”
Rhode Island Current published a profile of independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block on Monday. Republican Aaron Guckian was unavailable for a sit-down interview despite multiple requests. The governor’s race has a total of five candidates. Also running are independents Jasjit “Jay” Gotra and C.D. Reynolds.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island voters love history and bond issues. But not always at the same time.
text:
An architectural rendering depicts the proposed Rhode Island State History Center, which would be built across from the State House in Providence if voters approve Question 4 on Nov. 3. The ballot measure would authorize $45 million in borrowing for the project. (Rendering by LLB Architects/courtesy of the Rhode Island Department of State)Rhode Island’s precious historical documents and objects already have a place to stay: the State Archives, which occupies leased space on Providence’s Broad Street. 
What Secretary of State Gregg Amore wants is a place where more of these treasures can be shared and seen. 
This year’s ballot Question 4 will ask voters to decide if they want to authorize $50 million in general obligation bonds, of which up to $45 million would go toward the construction of a new Rhode Island State History Center in Providence. An additional $5 million in grants would preserve historic and cultural properties around the state.
It’s one of five bond questions on the Nov. 3 ballot, which altogether ask voters to authorize $600 million in borrowing — the biggest bond package ever put before Rhode Island voters. 
But unlike the other questions, which focus on higher education, housing, economic development, and green energy, conservation, recreation and environmental cleanup, Question 4 concerns borrowing for something not always embraced by Rhode Island voters, who are otherwise known for being generous at the ballot box.
In the last 18 years, Rhode Islanders have approved every statewide bond issue put on the ballot — a sum of 36 consecutive victories for borrowing proposals. Spiral further back into history, however, and you’d find a less tidy record of voter sentiment, especially when it comes to borrowing for museums, historic preservation and cultural facilities.
“Building a State History Center has been a priority of Secretaries of State for over a decade, and the proposal before voters this fall is the result of a comprehensive study and efforts to constrain the project’s cost,” Amore said in an emailed statement last Thursday.
If approved by voters, Amore said his multiyear effort to find a more publicly accessible home for the state’s most treasured artifacts would dovetail with America’s semiquincentennial.
Question 4 is a modest ask compared to the $102 million proposal Amore floated in 2024 for a combined state archives and history center project. 
Now, plans call for a two-story, 24,600-square-foot history center to be built across from the State House and next to the Department of Administration. Approximately 3,000 square feet of exhibit space would feature both rotating and permanent displays, including the state’s colonial Royal Charter, now exhibited at the State House, and one of Rhode Island’s copies of the Declaration of Independence, currently held by the State Archives.
The Department of State’s executive office would move from the State House to the new building, which would also include space for educational programming and events. State officials expect the History Center could open in fall 2030.
Department of State spokesperson Faith Chybowski said the estimated cost for the History Center is $43.2 million, but the bond allows some leeway and puts the borrowing ceiling at $45 million. The state department’s latest budget request, submitted earlier this month, also requests $4.5 million in Rhode Island Capital Plan funding for the project in fiscal year 2028. That money is separate and subject to legislative approval as part of the annual budget-making process.
The current ask is still too lofty for House Minority Leader Michael Chippendale, a Foster Republican who questioned the pricier proposal in 2024. Chippendale said he plans to vote no on Question 4 even though he said he wants to see state history preserved. 
“Rhode Island’s Democrat-controlled government is running out of other people’s money, and ‘nice to have’ projects like this cannot be piled onto this death spiral of spending and debt,” Chippendale wrote in an email Wednesday.
Question 4’s entire cost would land in the ballpark of $80.2 million, when factoring in a 5% interest rate and 20-year repayment schedule. 
A January analysis by the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council noted that the state ranks sixth nationally in debt service relative to revenue, and ninth in debt relative to personal income. Recent progress on the latter, the policy brief cautioned, could be reversed by the $600 million bond package.
A bust of President John Adams is shown at Fort Adams in Newport. Voters narrowly defeated a $4 million proposal to make improvements at the fort in 2006, the most recent bond measure to fail. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)
Uneven voter awareness
Early voters are already weighing competing priorities when it comes to the state’s bond spending. Retiree Charlotte Tracy said she voted no on Question 4 as she left Bristol’s early voting location at Guiteras School Monday.
“Our economy is, as we all know, in pretty bad shape these days,” Tracy said. “I hadn’t heard anything about it, and I voted to reject because I just feel like we’re spending too much money.”
Stephen Oddo said he knew nothing about the proposed History Center before encountering it at the ballot box. But the human resources director and former history major felt compelled to vote yes.
“I’m a big history buff, and I think that one of the charming points of Rhode Island is history,” Oddo said.
His enthusiasm did not apply to all the proposed bonds. He voted no on Question 5, for instance, which would fund the green economy and clean energy initiatives. 
“I voted based on my own personal interest and what I felt was maybe wasteful versus those I thought would be productive,” he said. “I think you have to prioritize between the different bonds to kind of arrive at what you think is best for the state versus others that are kind of ancillary and not as important.”
Full-time grandmother Molly McCord said she was familiar with Question 4 before voting and also supported it. 
“We are very much into historical preservation,” the self-described New England transplant said, noting that the Ocean State’s rich history serves as a valuable tourist draw.
History doesn’t always repeat
In recent elections, Rhode Island voters have repeatedly been game to borrow money for the arts and culture economy. Voters approved a $35 million package in 2014, a $7 million package in 2021, and a $10 million package in 2024, with each bond’s bundle of recipients comprising theaters, performance venues, museums and historic buildings.
But since 1980, the 17 bond questions that would have benefited standalone museums, cultural facilities or broader preservation have had a 9-8 record.

One notable instance is 1992, when voters rebuffed not one but two preservation initiatives. 
The first was a $2.5 million bond for the Rhode Island Historical Society, which received just 34.8% of voters’ support.
The second was a $4.5 million statewide historic preservation bond that received 39.9% of the vote. Voters had approved the same bond in 1989 with 54.75% support, with the money intended for a preservation revolving fund as well as restoration grants and loans available to projects statewide.
But the 1989 bond didn’t authorize the state of Rhode Island to issue the bonds; it mistakenly gave that power to the Historical Preservation Commission. The Rhode Island Supreme Court ruled in 1991 that the mistake meant voters needed to approve the bond a second time — which they didn’t. 
A similar bond for the same amount failed again in 1994, receiving 44.7% of the vote.
The closest relative to 2026’s Question 4 was in 2000, when voters just barely rejected a $25 million bond for a proposed Heritage Harbor Museum on the Providence waterfront. Its up-to-260,000 square-foot space would have converted the former South Street electric station into a library and history museum. It gathered 49.3% support, less than one percentage point short of approval.
Voters defeated the measure, but a subsequent tranche of $900,000 in federal funding from Congress still flowed toward it. The Rhode Island Historical Society and other historical organizations, including the Smithsonian Institution, continued to back the museum. 
Nine years later, a Providence Journal editorial described the project as a “sinkhole of private donations and public funding” that never came to fruition. 
A $4 million proposal to make improvements at Newport’s Fort Adams in 2006 succumbed to a case of almost enough, securing 49.4% of the vote — just six-tenths of a percentage point separating it from approval. It remains the most recent bond measure to fail.
The campaign supporting Question 4 is looking forward to the future, however. Spokesperson Brad Dufault said the History Center would generate construction employment and also attract tourists, whose spending would help the local economy.
Amore defended the project as “the most cost-effective way to preserve our history and create a permanent destination for Rhode Islanders and tourists alike to see Rhode Island’s treasures on display” in his statement.
He compared it to the state’s effort to commemorate the 1976 bicentennial, when it invested in the construction of the Veterans’ Memorial Cemetery in Exeter.
Indices of birth for the state of Rhode Island on a shelf at the State Archives. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
And what about the archives?
One missing piece from the current State History Center proposal: the fate of the State Archives and its much larger collection of less flashy historical records.
Amore’s 2024 proposal would have combined the State History Center with a new home for the entire archives. He retooled the proposal in 2025, suggesting a partnership with the University of Rhode Island (URI). Amore wanted to relocate some collections in the State Archives to URI’s Carothers Library on its Kingston campus.
Question 4 no longer entertains the idea to combine the History Center and the entirety of the archives under one roof. The proposal would house only a small portion of the archives’ more than 10 million holdings. Currently, these collections are stored at 33 Broad St. in Providence in leased space owned by former Providence Mayor Joseph R. Paolino Jr. 
The state pays approximately $280,300 annually to lease the Paolino space, the state department’s Chybowski confirmed. She said the documents are safely preserved there — the space was outfitted extensively to meet temperature and storage requirements — but that public accessibility is limited. Discussions continue, she said, about where to house archives holdings that wouldn’t fit in the proposed history center.
As for URI, spokesperson Dawn Bergantino confirmed Thursday that the state funded a feasibility study for hosting the archives on campus. It found the Carothers Library would need upgrades to its heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems before it could accommodate irreplaceable documents of historical import.
The school has submitted a capital infrastructure request to the state, Bergantino said, but the library’s deficiencies will need to be addressed first before any further partnership with the State Archives. 
As for the archives’ current landlord, Paolino said he supports the History Center proposal. Yes, more than $1 million was spent to prepare his existing property for the archives, he said. But he’s fond of the idea of a public institution which could accept donations of historical collections — like, say, his own mayoral papers.
Did he think voters would approve the history center? Paolino, the mayor of Providence from 1984 to 1991, admitted he’s now been out of the political game for “so long” that it was hard to gauge voters’ interest. 
“I think the first time people even know there’s something on the ballot is when they go and vote and they start reading the questions,” he offered. 
Paolino, of course, could lose a tenant if the State Archives found a new home. He wasn’t too worried, and mused on the nature of business instead.
“You get tenants, you lose tenants, you get new tenants,” Paolino said.
