name: National
title: Cheaper manufactured homes could be having a moment, if only states can catch up
text:
Swartz Creek Estates in Swartz Creek, Michigan, is the kind of manufactured home community that some experts say can be expanded with a new federal law that allows such homes to be built without a chassis. Some 30 states may need to update their laws, though, and mobile home park operators say the industry still faces major zoning and financial speed bumps. (Photo by Emily Elconin)For decades, manufactured home builders have been working to shed the old image of boxy trailer homes reserved for the outskirts of cities and suburbia. Now, a small change in federal regulations could open the door for architecture welcomed in more neighborhoods.
This summer’s sweeping housing bill, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, removed a 1974 mandate that required every manufactured home to be built on a nonremovable steel frame, known as a chassis. Experts and home producers think the change could help unlock thousands more affordable housing options around the country.
But first, experts say, states have to examine outdated regulations that are blocking the manufactured home industry’s potential. The Pew Charitable Trusts’ housing initiative estimates that 30 states might need to change their regulations to align with the new federal law.
Landmark federal housing law tries new ways to boost local building

Unlocking manufactured homes from chassis will allow manufactured homes to become multi-family developments, said Stephanie Hawke, associate research director of land use and supply at the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at the University of California, Berkeley.
They’ll be cheaper for builders, she noted, and they’ll be easier to stack into two-story and multi-family homes.
“First of all, you were putting a very heavy, expensive thing on the bottom of these homes that is not needed and it is not used, and it’s made out of steel,” Hawke said. “If you’ve got this heavy piece of steel on the bottom of a home, stacking it becomes more difficult.”
Manufactured homes are built entirely in a factory, regulated by U.S. Housing and Urban Development codes, and then trucked to a home site. 
They cost 50% less per square foot than homes built on a site, according to the Manufactured Housing Institute, an industry group. And experts say dropping the chassis could drive down costs by $5,000 to $10,000 per home.
“There’s really the opportunity to stack these manufactured homes to make multi-family developments,” Hawke said. “So it’s unlocking this thing which was primarily used for single-family and it’s making it much more accessible for a multi-family developer, which is great because manufactured housing is far and away the least expensive non-subsidized housing supply in the United States.” 



Quotation







This is a change that's gonna help every manufactured home community out in the country.


– Eugene Landy, founder and chairman of UMH Properties, in an earnings call


In a 2026 earnings call, UMH Properties, a publicly traded real estate company that owns and develops manufactured-home communities, said the chassis rule change will allow it to put two-story manufactured homes on existing lots. The company also is considering designs that could combine two stories with duplex units, allowing for smaller, more affordable apartment rentals. 
“You build 2,000 square feet of homes instead of 1,000 square feet on the same piece of land. It’s a very, very important development,” said Eugene Landy, founder and chairman of UMH Properties, on the earnings call. “This is a change that’s gonna help every manufactured home community out in the country.”
Another benefit to removing the chassis, according to Mark Brunner, president of the Manufactured & Modular Home Association of Minnesota, is that manufactured homes can blend more seamlessly into subdivisions because they won’t look too different from other homes.
Under the new law, states are required to certify before July 11, 2027 — or 2028 if their legislatures meet biennially — that they will treat all manufactured homes the same regardless of whether the homes have a chassis or not. So far, at least three states — North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas — have modernized the definition of a manufactured home to align automatically with code updates from HUD.
“If you are not essentially in compliance with this new regulatory framework, then you’re really limited both in using manufactured homes and making them, which is obviously an economic driver for a state,” Hawke said. “North Carolina did an incorporation by reference, essentially saying, ‘We are just going to define this like HUD defines it. Go see HUD’s definition.’ It’s a lot simpler.” 
From temporary housing to mobile home parks
Rachel Siegel, a researcher and policy expert for Pew’s housing initiative, said her research has found that more than 30 states are going to need to update their definition of manufactured housing to remove language about a required chassis.
HUD certification now requires equal treatment of homes with and without chassis, and changes to state laws may not be as easy as striking a few words, she said. References to permanent chassis can appear throughout state statutes in various manufactured home policies.
“States vary completely across the country on how they treat manufactured housing,” Siegel said. “This requirement of permanent chassis is really pervasive.”
To save affordable housing, states promote resident-owned mobile home parks

A Stateline review found use of the “permanent chassis” language currently written on manufactured housing laws include Virginia, Maine, New York, Missouri, South Carolina, Washington, Nevada and Maryland.
Following World War II, a shift in how mobile homes were being used began forming. No longer reserved as temporary housing, mobile homes were designed to be increasingly more permanent. Mobile home communities sprang up, though many were zoned into rural or suburban areas on a city’s edge.
For decades, manufactured homes — called mobile homes until the early 1970s — have been built in factories and trucked to their new locale. Many were unloaded into mobile home communities, specialized zoning districts where residents own their house but rent the land underneath. 
They are far cheaper than site-built houses: The average sales price of a new manufactured home rose from $81,900 in 2019 to $127,200 in 2025, according to the U.S. Census Bureau’s Manufactured Housing Survey. 
Those factory-built sales have slowed since a late 1990s boom as fewer manufactured home communities have been built since 2000, a trend largely attributed to restrictive zoning and rising land costs. Still, an estimated 20 million people live in one, most of them on acreage owned by a landlord. 
In the past, a home attached to a trailer or visibly hoisted a few feet off the ground were tells of manufactured housing when they first popped up in neighborhoods. But many modern ones are virtually unrecognizable from site-built homes.
“They have the same walls, ceiling, sheetrock, windows and shingles,” said Dustin Brakemeier, who owns and operates manufactured home communities in Minnesota and Wisconsin. “One’s built in a factory, one’s built outside. They’re the same.’” 
Changing zoning, mortgage rules
Pennsylvania Republican state Rep. Dan Moul, who owns a manufactured home park in Oxford Township in Adams County, recalled in an interview that zoning restrictions kept him from expanding the community into an adjoining parcel a few years ago. The township said the land was zoned exclusively for detached single-family residential housing. 
“The bottom line is they look at mobile home communities as that’s where the poor riffraff lives, and we don’t want any more riffraff,” Moul said. 
One of the big domino effects from the removal of the chassis requirement could be state banning or overriding restrictive local zoning policies that targeted manufactured homes. 
In an analysis of over 6,700 zoning districts in Texas, the National Zoning Atlas found 33% of localities have explicit restrictions on manufactured housing and 11% allowed them via special hearing or permit, but not by-right. 
Drive for more housing sparks rare bipartisanship in statehouses

Last year, Kentucky and Texas banned local ordinances that would unreasonably restrict where manufactured homes could be placed. Kentucky also insisted that local governments cannot impose design standards for manufactured homes that are  higher than those for non-manufactured homes. 
Alex Rodino, a real estate agent in Savannah, Georgia, who sells manufactured homes, said the stigma isn’t just among local governments and stodgy neighborhood groups. Some buyers, he said, are confusing modern manufactured housing with the image of older mobile homes.
“I think (that perception) is slowly changing as construction quality improves and traditional housing becomes less affordable,” said Rodino.
Siegel, of Pew, said that because states must align their manufactured housing laws with HUD’s definition by 2027 – there’s an opportunity for states to take a holistic look at their regulations, including whether states can make it easier to define manufactured homes as “real estate.”
Siegel said states also should revisit laws that classify manufactured homes as personal property — like cars. 
“If you own property that’s personal property instead of real estate, you’re not eligible to get a mortgage,” Siegel said. “That’s not about a person’s financial status or financial credibility, and it’s not even about the quality of the home. It’s just this titling component.”
A Pew analysis touting the potential for manufactured homes shows that a typical $100,000 mortgage for a manufactured home would save a borrower roughly $49,000 over the life of the loan when compared with “home-only” or personal property loans, which are the only options now. 
Some states already are taking action: Laws in Georgia, Maine and New York have made it easier for some manufactured homeowners to convert their homes to real property and gain access to mortgage financing.
“If we’re going to title manufactured homes without a chassis the same way as we’re titling manufactured homes with a chassis, let’s make sure that that process is as streamlined and makes the most sense for what these modern homes are today,” Siegel said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Stable jobs support healthier Hoosiers and a more sustainable Medicaid program
text:
CareSource JobConnect pairs participating Medicaid members with life coaches who help them find work, build interview skills, navigate barriers, and access supports such as food, housing, childcare or education assistance. (Getty Images)Indiana’s monthly jobs reports tell an encouraging story: the state’s unemployment rate is the lowest it’s been in years, while the labor force participation rate has outpaced the national average for more than a decade. That is good news for Indiana’s economy, but it also matters for the health and stability of Hoosiers.
In my practice as a physician and experience leading health plans, I have seen how closely employment and health are connected. Losing a job can affect more than income. It can make it harder to afford what it takes to manage chronic health conditions, maintain stable housing and  pay for basic needs.
The effects are not only financial. The stress of unemployment can impact mental and behavioral health, and without the right support, those challenges can lead to more serious concerns.
At first glance, workforce development may not seem like the role of a managed care entity. But at CareSource, our goal is to help people across Indiana achieve long-term health, independence and financial security. Meaningful employment leads to all three.
Connecting people to employment often requires more than pointing them toward an application. CareSource JobConnect pairs participating Medicaid members with life coaches who help them find work, build interview skills, navigate barriers, and access supports such as food, housing, childcare or education assistance.
The program delivers tangible results that support participants, their community and the state. A study of CareSource’s JobConnect program by Health Management Associates, an independent national healthcare research firm, shows that it supports the long-term sustainability of Indiana Medicaid and the state’s economy. JobConnect helps participants earn more, transition off Medicaid when appropriate and generate new tax revenue for the state.
Of the participants who secured jobs in 2024, an estimated 75% transitioned off Medicaid because of increased earnings, creating savings for the Family and Social Services Administration. In total, the program resulted in more than $3.5 million in wages, tax credits and food and housing benefits for Indiana participants that year.
Those earnings also circulated through the local economy. According to the analysis, spending by participants who gained employment supported activity at grocery stores, restaurants, retailers, nonprofit organizations and other local businesses.
The ripple effect created through this spending resulted in an aggregate value of more than $8 million in new revenue for Indiana’s economy in 2024. All told, CareSource JobConnect generated a 12:1 return on investment for participants and communities in Indiana.
Beyond financial and economic effects, the HMA study reveals the health impact of stable employment. From 2021 to 2025, CareSource JobConnect participants experienced a 20% decrease in hospital admissions and an 11% reduction in avoidable emergency department visits. That’s an important shift toward preventative care and away from those more costly outcomes.
The data reinforces what many physicians, health plans and community organizations see every day: health is shaped by the conditions in which people live and work. Stable employment can help people manage their health, support their families and participate more fully in their communities.
By continuing to invest in employment and wraparound supports, managed care entities in Indiana can help more families build the foundation needed to prosper while supporting a stronger, more sustainable Medicaid program.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: State Senate control likely safe for Republicans but Democrats aim to make gains
text:
The Indiana Senate chamber in November 2024. (Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Only a handful of races are truly competitive in this year’s Indiana Senate elections, with most of the money flowing to a northwest Indiana district and a suburban Indianapolis contest.
Democrats are hoping to flip Senate District 1 and Senate District 31 in a national environment working against Republicans who now hold a 40-10 supermajority in the Senate.
“When one party has essentially called all the shots for over 20 years and things are not going well there’s only one group to blame. And I think people are ready for change at the national level, and, of course, at the state level,” said Evan Robbins, executive director of the Indiana Democratic Party.
“I think whether it’s the secretary of state’s office or some of these down ballot state Senate races, people are really just sick and tired of corruption, especially at a time when they’re when they’re hurting and struggling to keep up with bills, and that seems to be the issue we’re hearing about the most.”
(Indiana Senate website)
Senate District 1 is an open seat after Republican Trevor De Vries defeated incumbent Sen. Dan Dernulc in the GOP primary with a boost from President Donald Trump’s endorsement over Dernulc’s vote against congressional redistricting last year. The district covers parts of Lake County, including Highland, Griffith, Schererville, Dyer and St. John.
De Vries, an insurance broker, faces union electrician Scott Houldieson, a Democrat. They have not debated or even met at a candidate forum.

“The conversation at the doors has always been around energy choice for us in northwest Indiana,” De Vries said. “People are really fed up with NIPSCO and the monopoly we have.”

De Vries noted that many people didn’t even see their bills go down even with having their power out for two weeks following devastating August storms.
Overall he said the message from his campaign is about affordability and having government live within its means.
When pressed, De Vries said he would support congressional redistricting in 2027 if Republicans try again but maintained it is not a topic of concern among the district’s voters.
The Senate Democrat Committee — the campaign finance arm of the caucus — has contributed $357,000 to candidates since June 1 and at least $273,000 has gone to Houldieson, who has held leadership roles with his United Auto Workers local.
“I’m a working guy … I know what working families are going through. I’ve lived it myself,” Houldieson said. “I know that our voices are not being heard directly from. That’s the difference I can make. Bring a direct voice of working people to the chamber.
Trevor De Vries, left, and Scott Houldieson, face off in Senate District 1. (Courtesy photos)
The Highland resident has recently focused much of his campaign on recent frustrations with NIPSCO service in Indiana — from reliability to cost.
The Senate Majority Campaign Committee — the Republican campaign group — has given at least $289,000 to De Vries.
De Vries ran heavily on Trump’s endorsement in the primary, but it hasn’t been highlighted in his television ads for the general election in the district where the current Republican senator won with 52% four years ago.
In a recent statewide poll, Trump is underwater with a 54% disapproval rating in Indiana. National polls also show Trump’s approval dropping.
Houldieson said during the primary his opponent had large “Trump-endorsed” signs up that are “nowhere to be found now. He’s definitely running away from Trump now.”
De Vries, 30, said the race has always been about “getting good conservative values back here in Indiana.”
“President Trump’s endorsement has never been the number one reason why I ran, or kind of the number one selling point for a lot of people,” he said. “A lot of people are as excited about having a strong young conservative who’s willing to step up and do the fight at a young age, compared to you know other folks that were on the ballot.”
Another race attracting attention is Senate District 31, which covers northeastern Marion County and parts of Hamilton County including Fishers.
Sen. Kyle Walker, R-Lawrence, opted not to seek reelection after a bitter divide on mid-cycle redistricting.
Republican Juanita Albright faces Democrat Kerry Forestal in what might be the tightest race this cycle.
(Indiana Senate website)
Albright is a doctor at Ascension St. Vincent in Fishers and in 2022 won election to the Hamilton Southeastern School Board. Her campaign messaging has focused on government living within its means. She also promised to tackle rising housing, grocery, prescription and healthcare costs
“I’ve spent my career earning people’s trust by listening before acting,” she said on her campaign site. “As a state senator, I will do the same — hearing out your concerns, your priorities, and everything that matters most to you — because I will always put my community first.”
Forestal has spent his career in law enforcement He is currently in his second term as the elected Marion County sheriff. He previously worked as a deputy for the Marion County Sheriff’s Department and was U.S. marshal for much of Indiana during President Barack Obama’s administration.
He would prioritize lowering healthcare and childcare costs; strengthening penalties for repeat, violent and sex offenders and fully funding public schools.
““The teachers go in there every day. They’re molding the minds of the next generation. They should be getting paid first,” Forestal told Mirror Indy.
The Senate Majority Campaign Committee has given Albright almost $300,000 in recent months. Meanwhile, Forestal is the only other candidate besides Houldieson to receive money from the Indiana Senate Democrat Committee, at $84,000.
Forestal has criticized Albright’s support from a group that works to ban books, Christian conservatives and those who are pushing data centers. Meanwhile Albright has released an ad about problems at the Marion County Jail under Forestal’s leadership.



Other Senate races to watch
Senate District 11 – Republican Brian Schmutzler took out Sen. Linda Rogers in the primary and faces Democrat Gabrianna Gratzol. The district covers portions of Elkhart and St. Joseph counties.
Senate District 22 – Republican incumbent Sen. Ron Alting’s reelection bid against Democrat Natasha Baker has been complicated by allegations that he recently shoplifted. The district covers Carroll and portions of Tippecanoe county.
Senate District 29 – This seat in central Indiana is open because Democratic Sen. J.D. Ford chose to run for Congress. It pits Democrat Kristina Moorhead against Republican John Ruckelshaus, who previously served in the Senate.
Senate District 41 – Republican Rep. Michelle Davis defeated Sen. Greg Walker in the primary and now faces Democrat Ross Thomas in the district covering Bartholomew and part of Johnson counties.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana agencies spent $3.2B with nonprofits over 4 years
text:
Louisiana spent $3.2 billion in state funding with nonprofit organizations between from July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2025. (Photo by Wesley Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana allocated $3.2 billion in state funding to nonprofit groups over a four-year period that straddled Govs. John Bel Edwards and Jeff Landry’s time in office, according to a Louisiana Legislative Auditor report released this month. 
The auditor’s report tracked state government nonprofit spending between July 1, 2021, and June 30, 2025. The period includes the last two and a half years of Edwards’ second term and the first 18 months of Landry’s current term. Each state fiscal year begins on July 1.
Expenditures on “nongovernmental entities,” as nonprofits are referred to in the report, grew over those four budget years from $723.7 million in 2021-22 to $942 million in 2024-25, according to the audit report. 

The Louisiana Department of Education spent the most state funding on nonprofits, with $1.9 billion in allocations. By comparison, the Louisiana Department of Health, state government’s largest agency, spent $266.3 million during the same time period, based on the auditor’s calculations. 

Much of the education department’s nonprofit spending goes toward charter schools, which are often operated by nonprofit boards. Like traditional public schools, charter schools receive funding from the state on a per pupil basis to cover education expenses. 
A large chunk of the education department’s nonprofit money also goes to private schools. They receive funding to help offset the expenses of collecting state data, such as information about truancy and absences, at their campuses. The state also covers a portion of salaries for private school lunchroom staff and transportation expenses at some schools.
Additionally, private schools can receive money to pay for remedial education services and teaching at-risk youth and through a private education voucher program, which Landry has unsuccessfully sought to expand, that covers private school tuition. 
Outside of education, other large areas of state nonprofit spending include: grants to upgrade drinking water systems; law firms that represent people facing the death penalty; horse breeding organizations; domestic violence shelters; and groups that attract major sporting events, such as the Super Bowl, to the state.  
Landry and legislators turned their attention to state spending on nonprofits after President Donald Trump launched the Department of Government Efficiency, an initiative to reduce federal spending. Landry followed with a similar state-focused effort, called LA DOGE, around the same time in late 2024.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Legislative Auditor Michael Waguespack has said he was asked to investigate state nonprofit spending as part of LA DOGE but initially found it challenging. In May 2025, he told the Louisiana Senate Finance Committee there was no easy way for the public to find all of the contracts state agencies have with nonprofits. 

In response, Waguespack and Landry’s staff pushed through a new law state Sen. Heather Cloud, R-Turkey Creek, sponsored. Act 467 requires the state to have a publicly available online database that allows anyone to search state nonprofit spending. 

The information is supposed to be integrated into the existing Louisiana Checkbook website, which provides public access to information about state government contracts and vendors. 

“The truth is, we don’t really know what all and where all we are investing,” Cloud said at a 2025 hearing on her legislation. The public deserves to know “who’s getting the money, how much are they getting, where are they from, what are they using it for and what their measurable outcomes are,” she said. 

This month’s report from Waguespack’s office said the state’s attempt to make its spending on nonprofits more transparent isn’t working as envisioned. 
State law doesn’t define what’s a nongovernmental entity, which means state agencies are using different interpretations of the term. The new law wasn’t specific about what types of spending with nonprofits needed to be included, which has led to different agencies relaying different levels of detail about state expenditures. 
It’s also not clear which state government entities have to comply with transparency requirements, according to the report. The auditor’s office suggested the legislature consider passing an update to the 2025 law to resolve the confusion. 
“State law does not provide key definitions, which impacts the information reported in the NGE database,” Waguespack wrote.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Magaziner leads Mellor in new CD2 poll, but with a narrower gap among independents
text:
Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner, left, and Republican challenger Vic Mellor exchange remarks during their first general election debate at WPRI 12's East Providence studios on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Aaron Aguilar/WPRI 12)A new poll released Tuesday by Salve Regina University’s Pell Center shows incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner holding a 13-point lead over Republican challenger Victor Mellor in the race for Rhode Island’s 2nd Congressional District seat.
Of the voters surveyed, 52% said they support Magaziner, while 39% supported Mellor. Undecided voters comprised 7% of respondents. 
The poll produced similar results to the WPRI/Emerson College poll released Oct. 13. In that poll, Magaziner led Mellor 55% to 39%. The WPRI poll sampled slightly more independent voters than the Salve poll.
The CD2 margin is narrower, however, when compared to Rhode Island’s 1st Congressional District, where Democratic U.S. Rep. Gabe Amo leads Republican Kellie Keenan by 19 points, 52% to 33%.
Katie Sonder, associate director and fellow at the Pell Center, said these results outline a somewhat closer race in the 2nd District than in the 1st, with independent voters playing an important role. 
“I would point to the independents in this race,” Sonder said in a phone interview Monday.
Among independent voters surveyed, Sonder noted the poll showed 44% supported Magaziner and 39% supported Mellor.
“That’s really close,” Sonder said. 
But among likely Democratic voters, Magaziner enjoyed much less ambiguous support. Sonder noted that 90% of Democratic voters said they’re backing the incumbent.
Democratic U.S. Sen. Jack Reed, Rhode Island’s other congressional incumbent, held a 23-point lead over Republican Raymond McKay, 55% to 32%, in the poll.
Embold Research conducted the survey from Oct. 5 to 8, crafting its sample of voters via online recruitment and text messaging. The 815-person sample spanned the entire state and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. 
The margin is larger for certain subsets of respondents, including those involving individual congressional districts. Sonder cautioned against people reading the polling numbers as predictive.
“Surveys like this pre-election give us a snapshot in time,” she said. “We’re doing our best to create a respondent pool that looks like who we think will show up on Election Day, but of course, that’s yet to be seen.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Women see gains, but still struggle to stay in Maryland workforce compared to men
text:
Comptroller Brooke Lierman, right, invited women's advocates and laid-off federal workers Monday to discuss a recent report on how women fare in Maryland's economy. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Ronicsa Chambers did not expect that her job at the Federal Aviation Administration would be one of thousands that would be suddenly cut last year under the second Trump administration’s efforts to reduce federal spending.
But Chambers, who was the FAA’s Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Accessibility manager, was one of almost 30,000 Marylanders who lost federal jobs in the rapid layoffs and project terminations that began in early 2025, cuts that may have disproportionately affected Black women, according to a recent report.
“They said, ‘Don’t show up, and we’ll call you back,’” Chambers said Monday. “And then I got a call later on that said, ‘You are now officially on administrative leave.’ It happened so fast I couldn’t even put out an out-of-office message.”
Chambers told her story to an audience of dozens of state and local leaders, organizers and women’s advocates at the comptroller’s office, where the report was released outlining women’s experience in the Maryland economy.
Among the findings in the Women and the Economy report was that Black women’s overrepresentation in federal jobs compared to their share of the state population may have led to them being hit hardest by the federal layoffs.
Ronicsca Chambers spoke about her experience as a federal worker who was suddently terminated last year. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
“Women, especially Black women, were over-represented in departments that experienced large-scale layoffs, like the Department of Education. National estimates suggest that by August 2025 … cuts had reduced Black women’s federal employment by 25%,” said the report, released earlier this month.
The report also found that women continue to participate in the labor force at lower rates than men; that the participation gap is wider in some parts of the state and for non-English speakers; and that women are more likely to start their own business than men, among other findings.
It’s the latest in a series of  “State of the Economy” reports from the comptroller’s office that have focused on the state’s major industries and the effect of migration trends on the economy, among other topics.
The latest report is the first broad statewide analysis of women’s participation in the Maryland economy, said Comptroller Brooke Lierman, the first woman to hold that office. She said nine roundtables, engaging more than 200 women across the state were convened to learn what barriers keep women from reaching the same economic standing as Maryland men.
Lierman, who is running for reelection, said she hopes that reports like the most recent one will help guide future economic deep-dives under the next comptroller — whether it’s her or someone else.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“I am a working mom, I have two school-age kids … I am the first woman to serve as Maryland’s comptroller. Even if I were not any of those things, I think it is important to recognize the significant contributions that Maryland women make to our economy,” she said Monday. “It should not be contingent on having a woman in office to recognize the opportunities and challenges that are presented to over half of the population through our economy.”
Labor gap and barriers
Much of the “Women and the Economy” report focuses on gap between men’s and women’s participation in the workforce. Overall in Maryland, 68% of people age 16 or older in the civilian, non-institutionalized population are working or actively looking for work, the report said. But the rate for men is 73%, compared to 65% for women.
The reason for the gap is nuanced and varies by population, the report said.
Some counties in Western Maryland and on the Eastern Shore, for example, have a wider gap than more populous areas. Roundtables with residents of those areas attributed the gap to “limited job opportunities, fewer options for higher education and lower educational attainment among residents, inadequate access to public transportation and childcare, and societal expectations placed on women regarding ‘appropriate’ forms of employment and unpaid work – chiefly caregiving.”
Ariana Kelly, a former state senator from  Montgomery County who is now executive director of the Maryland Commission for Women, said a top concern is the caregiving economy, both in terms of the workforce and the pressure for women to take on caregiving duties in their personal lives.
Maryland Commission on Women Executive Director Ariana Kelly. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
“A huge number of women are professional caregivers, which are profoundly underpaid,” Kelly said. “We need to figure out how to treat childcare and elder care as an important part of our economy, of the economic structure we live in, in the same way we treat transportation and public safety and education.”
The report identifies policies that could ease the childcare burden on women to let more of them return to the workforce, including work policies for remote work or hybrid options. It also says paid family leave policies can help keep women in the workforce. Maryland is set to have paid family leave benefits available across the state starting next year.
The labor force divide grows when other elements are factored in.
Men aged 25-64 without a high school diploma have an 81% workforce participation rate, compared to 57% for women in the same group, for example. The largest gap occurs in the working age population who are not proficient in English: Men in that group had a 91% participation rate, compared to 59% for women, the report said.
It also said women are more likely to work part-time occupations that may not offer benefits like health insurance, in industries like hospitality, retail and personal care, contributing to an overall affordability challenge for women.
That said, there are areas where women are making gains. Women were responsible for 58% of new business startups in the state between 2019 and 2023, according to the report.
Comptroller report reveals steep challenges facing Maryland’s healthcare industry

Women also make up the majority of workers in Maryland’s largest industries: They represent 80% of the healthcare workforce and 67% of educational services jobs.  And women make up half of Maryland’s federal government workers.
But even those metrics come with caveats, as women are less represented in the highest-earning positions in those industries.
And the high representation of women in the federal workforce is why they were likely hit hardest by the Trump administration job cuts.
After legal challenges and other efforts, Chambers returned to the FAA in a different position, but she knows that there are thousands of other former federal employees who have not been able to come back to their jobs.
She said that during the 377 days between being laid off and finding an new job, she helped form a community with other women impacted by the federal layoffs.
“Just think about it, you had talented, professional, excited people who just weren’t allowed to come into work, and that’s just a waste in of itself,” she said. “You realize that across this state, and across the country, many women are experiencing this … such needless suffering and trauma for families and communities.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: After Larson’s loss, CT’s 1st District will elect a new representative
text:
This is the first in a series of stories profiling candidates in each congressional race. Credit: ct mirror

Connecticut’s congressional district centered around Hartford has been represented by U.S. Rep. John Larson since 1999. Nearly three decades later, residents will have a new face representing them in Congress after the congressman’s defeat in the Democratic primary in August.
The primary dominated politics in Connecticut for much of the year, but the drama in the state’s 1st Congressional District has reduced to a simmer heading into the general election.
Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin goes into the Nov. 3 election with a major advantage in one of the state’s bluest congressional district, known as the “lobster claw” because it stretches north of Hartford and curves toward Torrington and down past the capital city and stretches toward Bristol. Bronin handily won the four-way Democratic primary on Aug. 11, calling it a “political earthquake.” He premised his primary campaign around calls for generational change.

Luke Bronin celebrates his Democratic primary victory in Hartford on Aug. 11, 2026. Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Bronin will square off against Republican nominee Amy Chai, a physician who previously ran for elected office in a different congressional district. Green Party nominee Mary Sanders is also on the ballot, and Mark Stewart Greenstein is running as a write-in candidate.
In 2022, Chai ran as an independent endorsed by the Libertarian Party against U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro in Connecticut’s 3rd Congressional District, which is centered around New Haven. Chai said she’ll move to the 1st District if she wins the election. She’s also been endorsed by the Independent Party of Connecticut.
Democrats have represented the seat since 1959. And this year, Republicans nationally are confronting a tough political environment in a midterm election seen as a referendum on the party in power. President Donald Trump faces sagging approval numbers.
Chai acknowledges the odds are stacked against Republicans in the 1st Congressional District and in Connecticut more broadly. That hasn’t deterred her from seeking to get her message out to voters. She said her views don’t fit neatly inside a political ideology and she described herself as an “open book.”
Amy Chai, Republican nominee in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District, greets Ann Munger-Chrystal, of Bristol, during a candidate Meet and Greet at the Bristol Senior Center on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
“I don’t really think that liberal and conservative has any relevance in today’s political climate at all. I am a pragmatist, and I have my own ideas, and some of them might be considered a little bit more ‘Democrat’ and some of them more ‘conservative and Republican,'” Chai said. “But I’ve actually been either unaffiliated or Libertarian for my whole life until last year.”
“I’m able to talk to anyone about anything. I’m not afraid to go talk to people. I’m not afraid to listen to people, and my ideas are not my-way-or-the-highway ideas,” Chai said, adding she may be seen as “a little bit ‘eccentric’ because I don’t necessarily think one way or the other way, and a lot of the policy positions that I have that are completely mine.”
Since wining the Democratic primary, Bronin, who served as an intelligence officer in the U.S. Navy Reserve and was deployed to Afghanistan, said he doesn’t take the race for granted and has kept up his campaigning since he won the August primary. He argues that this current moment in politics is about more than the midterm elections.
“I am out there across the district, talking to voters, supporting candidates throughout the district and carrying the message that this is a critical moment when we have to use every minute, every day to build a stronger Democratic Party and to build a movement that is about more than this election,” Bronin said. “It’s about turning the political tide for years to come.”

Luke Bronin, Democratic nominee for Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District,  talks with a supporter during the Riverton Fair on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Connecticut’s entire congressional delegation backed Larson in the August primary. But those lawmakers also had working relationships with Bronin when he served as mayor of Hartford, and they have since unified. Bronin, who attended a recent event with Gov. Ned Lamont and U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy about early voting, said he looks forward to working “hand-in-hand” with the rest of the delegation if he’s elected.
Meanwhile, Republicans running for federal office in Connecticut aren’t getting much financial help or support from their party. Chai said that’s been a major challenge for her campaign. 
Chai is a one-woman shop. She handles all of her campaign operations — with the assistance of bots she programmed to help with emails and other tasks.
“It’s really hard to break through,” she said. “And it’s not just the Democrats, it’s also the Republicans, who are completely not on the side of solving problems for people at all.”
While affordability — whether it’s related to food, gas, housing or utilities — is one of the main issues the candidates hear on the campaign trail, they both have a number of other priority issues.
The debate around regulating artificial intelligence continues to be a top priority for Bronin, something that has been top of mind for him since entering the race.
“I talked about artificial intelligence the first day I launched this campaign a year ago because it was clear that our policymaking is so far behind the pace of change of technology, and there are very real opportunities — and also enormous risks — if we don’t build a regulatory structure that can put some guardrails up,” Bronin said.
As whistleblowers and AI company CEOs themselves sounded the alarm over the technology, Congress seemed more willing to engage in conversations over how to address a growing fear among Americans. But hope for that quickly fizzled as lawmakers left town through Election Day and President Donald Trump propped up AI and the large data centers that power them.
Bronin said the lack of urgency from Congress is “no better demonstration of how broken things are in Washington and how unserious the Republican leadership is in Washington.”
Bronin noted that any potential committee work will focus heavily on oversight of the Trump administration and that his party needs to focus on laying out an agenda on healthcare, housing and electricity. He didn’t name any specific committee he’d look to serve on but noted the ones that have jurisdiction over some of those issues, such as the House Oversight Committee and the House Financial Services Committee.

Amy Chai, Republican nominee in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District, speaks seen during a candidate Meet and Greet at the Bristol Senior Center on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

For Chai, she first got involved in politics because she was concerned “about a lot of what’s going on in medicine.” Mental health and addiction services remain critical issues for her, saying that there’s a “massive tsunami of mental illness in very young people.”
Disability rights are also top of mind — and personal. While working as a doctor, Chai said, she privately lived with chronic pain for decades due to fibrosing mediastinitis. She was hospitalized with a collapsed lung and had part of it removed, which has left her with scarring and inflammation. But she didn’t want to tell her employer because she feared discrimination for disclosing it, particularly in a healthcare setting. But she now wants to be open about her condition.
When it comes to immigration, Chai said she agreed with efforts to secure the southern border. On U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, she said she’s “fully opposed to excessive use of force” and said people deserve due process. Citizens who have been arrested by federal agents need an “apology and quick remediation,” she said.
But she believes politicians in Connecticut and protesters have also been “agitating against ICE.” Chai also argued that the lack of cooperation by the state in immigration matters has exacerbated the issue. Connecticut’s Trust Act, which was expanded in 2025, limits how state and local law enforcement can cooperate with ICE and its requests for detainers of undocumented immigrants.
“That would prevent the vast majority of these problems, but that still doesn’t give license to ICE agents to get upset or frustrated or not be able to handle the job and then do things that are inappropriate or hostile or violent either,” Chai said. “But there are two sides to the story.”
In the wake of the deaths of U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents, Bronin called for abolishing ICE and to “replace or rebuild ICE from the ground up in the longer term.”
Social Security was Larson’s main priority throughout his tenure and continues to be a paramount issue that the next Congress will try to take up. A recent report moved up the estimated timeline for when the retiree trust fund would become insolvent. Those predictions now anticipate benefit cuts by the end of 2032.
Before Congress went on recess prior to the election, there appeared to be some movement on bipartisan legislation to bolster Social Security. A bill from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno would seek to strengthen the program’s solvency by lifting the cap on payroll taxes.
Larson’s own legislation, the Social Security 2100 Act, would increase benefits by 2% for the first time in more than five decades and bolster the program’s solvency by requiring higher earners to contribute more to payroll taxes. 
Bronin said there’s an urgency to fixing the program, adding “the longer we wait to shore up and protect Social Security, the harder it will be.” When asked about Larson’s Social Security 2100 Act or other legislation as a possible vehicle to address the issue, he wouldn’t commit to a specific bill, saying there will be a lot of legislative options to consider and work on in the future.
Chai, meanwhile, said she’s adamantly against raising taxes, even on those in higher tax brackets, as a way of bolstering Social Security. She said funding for it should take precedence over funding for defense or foreign countries. 
“You’re going to fund your obligation to Social Security recipients before you fund anything else,” she said, while adding that addressing insolvency should be dealt with by cracking down on fraud and abuse. “I would love to see Social Security be something that is a welfare for elderly people who need it, but not such a compulsory thing.”

Luke Bronin, Democratic nominee for Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District,  talks with supporters during the Riverton Fair on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Throughout all phases of the campaign, Bronin has maintained a major financial advantage.
Since jumping into the race last summer, he raised a total of nearly $3.7 million and spent about $3.3 million. He has about $350,000 left for the general election. Chai raised about $21,000, spent $16,000 and has a little over $300 left.
Bronin, Chai and Sanders will square off in a debate hosted by the League of Women Voters of Greater Hartford on Oct. 22 at 7:30 p.m. from West Hartford Town Hall.
In-person early voting began Monday, Oct. 19 and runs through Sunday, Nov. 1. The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Kaul, Toney face off in rematch attorney general election
text:
Democratic Attorney General Josh Kaul is facing Republican Fond du Lac County District Attorney Eric Toney in the race for Wisconsin Attorney General. (Official candidate photos)As Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul and Fond du Lac County District Attorney Eric Toney face off again this year in a rematch of their 2022 race, the issues shaping the campaigns are different than they were four years ago. 
Kaul, a Democrat, is running for his third term as attorney general after two years in which he joined other state attorneys general in suing the administration of President Donald Trump more than 70 times. Those lawsuits have included challenges to Trump’s efforts to end birthright citizenship, restrict healthcare access for transgender youth, freeze federal funding and make last-minute changes to federal voting rules. 
“Unfortunately we’re in a place where protecting the freedoms of Wisconsinites, in significant part, means standing up to the federal government,” Kaul told the Cap Times.
In comments on the campaign trail, Kaul has said standing up to overreach from the White House is one of the most important roles he can fill at the moment. 
“We have consistently fought back, and we have won case after case, and what that has meant is that those funds either are not illegally conditioned or they’re not frozen or ultimately cut,” Kaul said of Trump administration changes to federally funded programs. “Instead they can come to our communities and support critical programs in Wisconsin.”
Toney has argued that Kaul has been distracted from his job as top lawyer for the state by federal fights with the president and accuses Kaul of being too partisan for constantly challenging Trump. 
“Unfortunately, what we’ve seen from the attorney general is it depends on who is in the White House, who’s in the governor’s office when he makes those types of decisions,” about joining federal lawsuits, Toney said when the two debated on WISN’s UpFront earlier this month.
Toney has pointed out that when Kaul first came into office, he was critical of former Republican Attorney General Brad Schimel’s lawsuits against the Obama administration. 
“He campaigned against all of the political lawsuits when he first ran, and now that’s effectively what he’s running his entire campaign on is those lawsuits where he’s putting politics over public safety,” Toney said.
But in an election cycle in which Trump’s record low popularity is threatening to kneecap Republican chances, Kaul has countered by saying Toney wouldn’t do anything to protect Wisconsinites from Trump’s actions. 
During the debate, Toney was pressed on what, if any, lawsuits he would have joined. Toney said he would have signed on to a lawsuit against West Virginia’s ban on transgender girls playing sports. 
“One of the federal lawsuits I would have joined was out of West Virginia to protect women and girls sports that the attorney general failed to stand up and protect,” Toney said.
Kaul said Toney was “ducking saying if he’ll stand up to Donald Trump.”
In 2022, the two men ran shortly after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and abortion was a major issue. Kaul had brought a lawsuit seeking to overturn the state’s 1849 abortion ban. In the years since, the Wisconsin Supreme Court sided with Kaul in that lawsuit, restoring abortion access for Wisconsinites. Toney argued in the 2022 race that Kaul’s lawsuit was a “stunt” but has said he wouldn’t try to change the state’s abortion policy if elected. 
Toney has previously said he supports the state’s current 20-week limit on abortions and tied the issue to Republican efforts to restrict access to gender-affirming care for transgender people and limit the ability of trans kids to play sports. In an interview with Wisconsin Watch, he tied his beliefs on abortion to a fight over trans locker room access in the New Richmond school district that has become a frequent GOP campaign reference this year. 
“We have five-month, or 20-week, protections in the law right now,” Toney said. “I’m not advocating for any changes to that, and if there is going to be any change, that needs to be something that’s voted on by the people and not decided on by politicians in Madison. We know how difficult this decision can be for women and girls and their families, and we need to make sure here in Wisconsin that we’re creating a supportive environment for women and girls that I hope life may be the choice that they decide to make. And that support has to extend beyond that as well and making sure that we’re protecting women and girls’ private spaces, bathrooms, locker rooms and sports. And we’ve seen the attorney general has failed to stand up in New Richmond, Wisconsin, where we’ve seen the school district allowing biological boys in the girls bathrooms.”
The 2022 race was also much closer to the racial justice protests of 2020, the pandemic-era increase in crime rates and the subsequent backlash against proposals to reassess police authority. Toney is running with the support of county sheriffs and police unions from across the state, but with crime at its lowest level in more than a decade, and the George Floyd protests six years in the past, the issue is not as much of a flashpoint statewide. 
This year, Toney has criticized Kaul for an increase in homicides since he first took office in 2019.  
“If we want to talk about crime data we’re seeing under this attorney general’s watch since he’s taken over, homicides are up over 30% in Wisconsin. We’ve seen on his watch record drug deaths,” Toney said.
Meanwhile, Kaul has blamed Toney for a recent increase in violent crime in Fond du Lac County. 
“We’ve been making important progress on crime statewide,” Kaul said. “Crime overall is at its lowest number in decades, and violent crime is the lowest number since 2011, but we also have more work to do.
Under the Trump administration, the White House has often focused heavily on allegations of election fraud and aggressively stepping up immigration enforcement — including in Wisconsin where the federal government has sought to obtain the private information of Wisconsin voters and Immigration and Customs Enforcement has made record numbers of arrests. 
Toney has previously supported both efforts. 
In an interview with Wisconsin Watch, he said the state needs to do more to root out non-citizens who are registered to vote — an issue that Republicans have repeatedly raised without much evidence. 
“We need to have a similar process that reviews noncitizens that could be on our voter rolls,” he said. “We have people that are lawfully in the country that are noncitizens, whether it’s for work or school, that may get a driver’s license or an ID card, and we don’t know what that problem could be because there’s no process in place to review it. And that’s where I’d like to see a similar process that we use for felons for that noncitizen process, just to make sure that people have confidence in those results. And if somebody is doing that, that they’re being prosecuted.” 
He has also testified before Congress to argue for stepped up immigration enforcement. 
Toney has focused on delays in testing at the state’s crime laboratories, which the attorney general is responsible for managing. Crime lab backlogs have often been a major issue in Wisconsin’s attorney general races. Kaul was first elected in 2018 after a controversy over a backlog of untested sexual assault kits. 
Toney has pointed to data that shows it’s taking longer for the state labs to test DNA evidence and blamed Kaul for the slowdown, saying he’s “passing the buck” on his responsibilities. 
Kaul has blamed the Republican-led Legislature for failing to provide proper funding to fully staff the labs. In the 2023-25 state budget, Kaul requested 16 additional crime lab positions while the final budget granted him three. In the most recent budget signed into law last summer, Kaul requested 19 additional crime lab staffers and received none.
Throughout the year, the criminal justice issue drawing the most public attention has been the increased scrutiny of law enforcement’s use of Flock license plate reading cameras. The AI-powered cameras are able to track the movement of people and vehicles through communities, drawing complaints that their use is an invasion of privacy and a violation of people’s rights. 
Both Kaul and Toney have said the cameras can be useful, but that there need to be guardrails on their use. 
“It’s clear that we need more action from the Legislature and the governor’s office, and until then local municipalities are the ones that are having to make these decisions with local sheriffs and chiefs that are having to maintain that public trust,” Toney said, pointing to a homicide case he’s working on in which the cameras were used to identify a suspect. 
Kaul said the cameras have been helpful in finding missing persons, but the technology should not be misused. 
“I want to make sure there’s a limit on the disclosure of data, so it’s being limited by law enforcement. I don’t want to see this going to private entities. And then there should be regular auditing in place and punishments if folks are misusing the technology,” Kaul said.
Every four years, the race for attorney general is largely overshadowed by the race for governor. In most cycles, the party that wins the governor’s race also wins the attorney general’s race. 
The last time the two races diverged was in 2006 when Wisconsin elected Democratic Gov. Jim Doyle and Republican Attorney General J.B. Van Hollen. 
In 2022, Toney performed better than Republican gubernatorial candidate Tim Michels, earning about 30,000 more votes, but still losing narrowly. 
“I’m running my own race from when I got into this back in October of 2025,” Toney told PBS Wisconsin. “I talked about the forensic testing failures, the fentanyl epidemic and how partisan our attorney general has become. I mean, we have driven home issues that affect people in all 72 counties. And that’s what I’ve been focused on, is what our Department of Justice can do to help protect everybody in Wisconsin by putting public safety over politics.”
Kaul acknowledges he’s been elected by thin margins in two nail-biter elections, but is confident his record will be enough to carry him to victory again. 
“The results tend to be fairly close, but in Wisconsin we have a lot of close elections, and so sometimes those small differences can make a big difference in the outcome,” Kaul told PBS. “But I’m running based on my record and my time as AG, and the focus can be different. My top priority as attorney general has been public safety, and we’ve made significant progress on really important public safety issues.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: In Kansas and across our nation, people fight daily battles to care for themselves and others
text:
Many Kansas work as caregivers for their family members. Others devote their professional lives to doing good for those in need. (Photo by Lucas Ninno/Getty Images)I recently was listening to that song from the past where the singer proclaims: “Love is a battlefield.”
The song got me thinking about how we fight our own personal battles and then there are much larger battles — in our cities, in our state and in our nation. Then there are battles in our world. It’s just gotten to be too much, hasn’t it? We are fighting, we are drinking our coffee, then we fight some more. We are tired and we feel like giving up.
I think of my friend Haley Kottler of the Kansas Appleseed. I have had the opportunity to get to know Haley over the last several years and her dedication to fighting food insecurity, especially for Kansas children, is commendable. Haley fights a battle every day to help people understand how important it is to keep children fed and cared for.
Sometimes I imagine she feels like she is all alone, praying and hoping that people will show compassion in the face of mounting hunger in our nation. The hunger epidemic is a crisis, and Haley and her team truly care.
I fight my own battle — a battle with mental illness that I have fought every day since I was 18 years old. There were times when I wanted to give up. Then I started a recovery journey where I have given back.
Recently, my younger sister surprised me with the idea of starting a nonprofit organization to help other nonnrofits financially that help people with mental illness. My family is not alone in our battles we face with mental illness, and Laura saw that. She wanted to reach out to help other organizations care for those in need.
One battle I have never really had to face is poverty. However, many Breakthrough House clients and Astra clients in Topeka really experience that battle every day. I see some of them fighting for their life walking downtown, looking tired and hopeless. They are hungry, they are homeless. People like Barry Feaker of Compassion Strategies truly care about the plight of the homeless, and many who experience homelessness also experience a serious mental illness or drug addiction.
Nick Casarona of Mirror Inc. is a fighter for those trying to get their lives back after struggles. I have gotten to know Nick a bit over the past several years, and he is a true champion of helping people in need.
We live in a time when punishment and stigma and hate are rampant. People feel tired and battle weary. Even people like Sondra Knox at Astra — people who are paid to help people in poverty or who experience homelessness or other issues like mental illness and addiction — get tired. They give and give and it seems like no one sees their efforts. Sondra and Kristy Hobbs work to help people find stable housing, and they put in long and draining days.
Caregivers fight a battle every day too, caring for their loved ones with disabilities and perhaps a senior. Caregivers often have no time to care for themselves, and they feel burned out and overwhelmed. To give of oneself every day is a challenge, and women often carry this load. Many mothers are caring for their children and an older parent. The need is great to reach out and offer support to these women.
They navigate systems that have grown more complicated — applying and keeping up with documentation for Medicaid, food assistance, housing and so much more. It seems programs designed to help people have become increasingly more difficult and almost next to impossible. We need to dare to care.
We can help each other with our battles, and we can offer support and hope. Maybe we could purchase a gift card for someone, add an encouraging note, and stick it in them mail. Maybe we could take a hot, home-cooked meal to someone who is just out of the hospital. Maybe we could offer to care for someone’s children so the parents can have a date night. We can come up with all kinds of helpful and creative ideas.
Let’s not give up. Know that the battle won’t last forever. We can find peace in the storm together.
Rebecca Lyn Phillips is a published author, speaker and mental health advocate. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: GOP focuses on fraud, seeking to redirect voters’ ire over healthcare costs
text:
MILWAUKEE, WISCONSIN - JULY 8: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks at the Wisconsin Air National Guard facility at Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport. Vance traveled to Milwaukee to deliver remarks on the Trump administration's anti-fraud initiatives.  (Photo by Mark Schiefelbein-Pool/Getty Images)Heading into the midterm elections, high healthcare costs rank among voters’ biggest concerns. But lately, there’s a twist giving the issue new momentum on campaign agendas: a focus on fraud in government health programs.
The administration of President Donald Trump has used claims of widespread wrongdoing to justify investigations, suspensions of billions of dollars in payments to states, and the cancellation of Affordable Care Act health coverage for hundreds of thousands of people.
The effort has opened a broader political fight over the extent of fraud and the administration’s response to it. Republicans say they’re safeguarding taxpayer dollars by going after bad actors. Democrats contend the administration has relied on insufficient evidence to target blue states and cut programs Republicans have long tried to shrink. Meanwhile, Trump’s pardons of executives convicted of healthcare fraud, administration moves to weaken some protections against abuses, and a high-profile error by Trump regulators stand in contrast with the administration’s proclaimed fraud-fighting goals.
The dispute is becoming a talking point for both parties leading up to the November election.
Republican candidates are trying to win voters’ confidence by emphasizing their efforts to halt what they say is the misuse of taxpayer dollars in federal health programs.
“Going after fraud gives Republicans a healthcare message when they would otherwise just be defending cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act,” said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. The approach, he said, helps “blunt” those attacks.
Democrats, however, traditionally have an advantage on healthcare in general, with polls showing voters are more likely to trust them with such issues. Now Democrats are portraying Republicans’ fraud crackdown as a cover for the GOP’s weakening of safety net programs. But the GOP messaging could resonate at the ballot box.
About 44% of voters — and 54% of Republican voters — say say fraud in government programs is “extremely important” for candidates to talk about, according to a KFF poll conducted in mid-September, suggesting the fraud focus might be connecting with the GOP base. Such fraud is also the top issue rural Republican voters want candidates to talk about, based on a separate survey by KFF and the Associated Press.
It’s an issue that is hardly new, and government watchdogs have repeatedly documented fraud by health providers and brokers, as well as improper enrollment in government health programs. A report by the Government Accountability Office in March warned that the “sheer amount of payments in the Medicare program creates significant fraud risks.” And in a separate probe, GAO investigators were able to get subsidized insurance for fake ACA enrollees.
What has changed is the prominence the issue now occupies in national politics.
Administration’s Fraud Targets
Trump administration authorities have this year charged hundreds of people, including doctors, in alleged billing schemes. It has announced audits of state Medicaid fraud units and increased scrutiny of enrollment in federal programs, withholding billions of dollars in federal Medicaid payments over claims of lax oversight — with what Democrats say is a laser focus on blue states despite a lack of evidence.
The administration’s more expansive claims about fraud — and the actions it has taken in response — have generated fierce political clashes.
Most recently, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services canceled ACA enrollments covering 760,000 people. While Democrats have questioned the methods that found them to be fraudulent, federal officials said they included nonexistent consumers whose applications were submitted by brokers or agents who can earn commissions from insurers.
CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said at a press event that the cancellations included people who had coverage through the ACA but hadn’t used it. He also said some had no Social Security numbers, calling that evidence of problems.
“About 35% of current people on the Obamacare system — 35%, more than a third — had never used the program. They haven’t bought a prescription medication. They haven’t seen a doctor. That just is not possible,” Oz said. “So we know there is fraud.”
Democrats and some health policy analysts challenge that conclusion. They say that younger and healthier people are much less likely to use their insurance and that not using their coverage doesn’t mean they were improperly enrolled. Critics also say the absence of Social Security numbers doesn’t necessarily establish fraud; for example, newborns can be added to their parents’ plans before receiving a number.
“This is yet another attempt by the Trump administration to kick hundreds of thousands of vulnerable Americans off their healthcare,” Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) posted on the social media site X. “Millions are already struggling to access healthcare—and this is their plan?”
There are political risks for the GOP as well. The disenrollment of alleged phantom accounts is likely to ensnare legitimate consumers, say health analysts and ACA advocates, leading to a potential backlash against Republicans if scores of people lose coverage just before the midterm elections.
States that tend to deliver for GOP candidates will be hit especially hard, they say, because ACA enrollees are concentrated in those states. The 4.5 million people in Florida and 4.1 million in Texas who have marketplace coverage account for nearly 40% of the country’s ACA enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.
Conservative health policy advisers say the administration took multiple steps to avoid canceling legitimate coverage, including attempts to contact consumers and requirements that additional criteria be met before coverage was terminated.
“Those criticizing the action either don’t understand it or see some political advantage in mischaracterizing it,” said Brian Blase, president of Paragon Health Institute and a former Trump health policy adviser.
Democrats, meanwhile, highlight inconsistencies in the administration’s broader anti-fraud campaign.
They note that the Department of Health and Human Services last year recertified hundreds of insurance brokers and agents who had been suspended in 2024 by the Biden administration for suspected fraud or abuse. The Trump administration also laid off about 200 employees from a CMS office involved in regional oversight of the ACA marketplace.
On Oct. 3, Trump called on Congress to pass legislation with mandatory prison terms for defrauding Medicare and Medicaid, eliminating probation as an option.
But Trump has also pardoned health industry executives convicted of major fraud schemes, including people who are connected to his political allies or who spent heavily on lobbying on their behalf. The pardons included a nursing home operator sentenced to three years in prison for a nearly $40 million tax scheme and, in Trump’s first term, five executives at a Florida company convicted for Medicaid fraud.
Trump’s pardons in 2021 of executives who profited from massive public healthcare fraud spurred criticism from the National Health Care Anti-Fraud Association. Critics now say the administration is portraying cuts to Medicare and Medicaid as necessary for weeding out waste, fraud, and abuse while exonerating criminals who have engaged in some of the biggest schemes in federal health programs.
Blue State Allegations
HHS has raised concerns about Medicaid fraud and program integrity in several states, and the administration has deferred or threatened to cut federal Medicaid funding while disputes are investigated.
Democrats say the administration is itself engaging in fraud by using unsubstantiated allegations of abuse to politically target blue states.
One of the most striking clashes occurred in New York.
Federal officials launched an investigation of the state’s Medicaid program after claiming that personal care services — including help with bathing, dressing, and meal preparation — had been provided to more than 5 million people, which would have amounted to roughly three-quarters of the state’s Medicaid population — an almost impossibly large proportion.
“It is time for New York to come clean about its Medicaid program,” CMS’ Oz posted in March on X.
CMS later acknowledged its calculations were wrong. The agency said that it had misunderstood the state’s billing codes and that the actual number of beneficiaries who received the services was closer to 450,000. The administration continued its scrutiny of the New York program, however, and later suspended millions of dollars in federal funding for the state’s Medicaid fraud unit, saying the division wasn’t producing enough indictments.
The administration also withheld about $2 billion in Medicaid funding from California, citing concerns about program integrity and oversight of some home medical services. State officials deny the allegations, saying spending on home services has grown because of factors such as higher wages for home health aides and an increase the number of older people receiving care.
The White House announced plans to defer more than $500 million in federal funds from Minnesota, claiming the state had failed to protect its Medicaid program from abuse. State officials have defended their oversight and gone to court to challenge the decision.
Vice President JD Vance, who chairs Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, and other administration officials announced the state deferrals at the White House, giving what traditionally would have been technical disputes between state and federal health officials a much higher political profile. Vance’s office did not respond to KFF Health News questions about the administration’s anti-fraud activities related to healthcare.
“I’ve never seen anything like this,” said Andy Schneider, a Georgetown University research professor and a senior adviser at CMS during the Obama administration. “It’s a deferral, not a finding of fraud. This is being elevated by political decision-makers.”
Republican candidates have pounced on the investigations and allegations. In Minnesota, Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth, who is speaker of the Minnesota House, released a September ad claiming that her Democratic opponent, U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, “has never done anything to stop the fraud here in Minnesota.” Klobuchar has said that as governor she would “launch a top-to-bottom audit of state government to root out fraud.”
In New York, Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat whose office runs the Medicaid fraud unit, criticized the decision to withhold funds and said weakening the operation would benefit criminals. Her Republican challenger in the November election, Saritha Komatireddy, has cited the Trump administration’s claims during her campaign, telling Fox News Digital that James is “totally failing to prosecute Medicaid fraud.”
The administration says its actions are necessary because fraud diverts taxpayer money from people who legitimately qualify for government programs.
“The fraud doesn’t just steal money — it steals our trust,” Oz said in August on CBS’ Face the Nation.
Democrats and healthcare advocates say the White House’s anti-fraud crusade is being used by Republicans to distract from criticisms over its sweeping funding cuts to Medicaid, the ACA, and other federal health programs.
Republican-backed legislation enacted last year is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by hundreds of billions of dollars over a decade.
Congressional Republicans also declined to extend enhanced ACA premium subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, increasing premium costs for many people who buy insurance through the marketplaces. Enrollment has since declined by millions.
Overall, the combined effect of GOP-led changes will result in 16 million more uninsured people by 2034, according to an analysis by the Congressional Budget Office.
Those changes have given Democrats an opening to campaign on protecting healthcare coverage and affordability while Republicans seek to shift some of the debate toward fraud and government spending.
“It’s really a way to distract and reframe the cuts in a different way, to say it’s part of an anti-fraud effort,” said Anthony Wright, executive director of Families USA, an advocacy group focused on expanding health coverage. “Fighting fraud shouldn’t result in people losing coverage.”
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.
