title: Vance touts $858M in Helene relief funding for Western North Carolina
text:
HENDERSONVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 19: U.S. Vice President JD Vance delivers remarks at a campaign rally at Hyder Warehouse on October 19, 2026 in Hendersonville, North Carolina. Vance is headlining a midterm campaign rally organized by the Trump 47 Committee Inc. to support Republican candidates ahead of the upcoming elections. (Photo by Kenny Holston-Pool/Getty Images)Vice President JD Vance promised $858 million in additional disaster relief funding from the U.S. Department of Transportation during a campaign stop in Hendersonville, North Carolina on Monday.
Vance’s event is part of the White House’s push to encourage GOP turnout this election cycle in what polls show is a challenging political environment for Republicans. President Donald Trump will hold a rally in Greenville, N.C. on Tuesday.
The vice president stumped for Michael Whatley, as well as U.S. House candidates Jennifer Balkcom and Laurie Buckhout. 
In the U.S. Senate race, Whatley is running against Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper. With 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independents, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip control of the chamber. Cook Political Report rates the race as “likely Democratic.”
“We are going to rebuild eight major corridors destroyed by Hurricane Helene, including the I-40 and Pigeon River Gorge,” Vance told supporters in Hendersonville.
The U.S. Department of Transportation announced $873 million on Monday in Helene relief funding for North Carolina. 
Last month, Trump jokingly claimed at a campaign rally in Gastonia that he would withhold Helene relief funding unless Whatley won the Senate race. 
Vance joked that U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee and North Carolina Republican Party, “would not shut up” about Helene relief in Western North Carolina. 
Whatley was named Trump’s “recovery czar” in January 2025, but has been accused by his critics, including some in his own party, of doing little to help secure federal resources.  
Trump heads to Greenville as NC Republicans struggle with early voter turnout

Public records show just six text messages and five phone calls totaling 38 minutes between Whatley and a state official helping coordinate recovery efforts over the course of roughly one year, according to Asheville Citizen-Times. 
But at the rally, Whatley said it was Cooper who had failed the region. 
“He was totally unprepared for the disaster and completely failed to respond after the skies had cleared,” Whatley claimed. “Roy Cooper even vetoed a bill that would have delivered key disaster relief to communities who were affected by the storm.”
Whatley was referring to a 131-page bill that, although branded as Helene relief, shifted power away from Democrats elected to office. Cooper referred to the legislation as a “sham” in his veto message. 
“Roy Cooper led North Carolina through several major catastrophic storms, activating emergency resources, keeping families safe and securing significant state and federal funding for recovery,” a Cooper campaign spokesperson told NC Newsline. 
During Vance’s speech, a protester behind him on the stands yelled out, “Release the Epstein files!”
Vance turned around to look at the protester, a man of color. As security dragged the man away, Vance suggested the protestor was an illegal immigrant. “I said that we have had zero illegal border crossings in the United States of America, but one isn’t bad, right?”
The crowd booed the protester and cheered for Vance. 
Balkcom, a state lawmaker representing Henderson County, is facing Democrat Jamie Ager in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. The NCGOP chose her to replace incumbent U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards in August after he dropped out.
Though Hendersonville is her hometown, Balkcom gave a short speech of about three minutes. 
Her primary accomplishment so far in the state legislature, where she’s served since 2023, has been sponsoring a bill banning transgender athletes from competing in women’s and girls’ sports. She and several other speakers at Monday’s rally emphasized that issue.
Last month, Balkcom and Ager both aired ads aiming to appeal to rural voters. Ager’s ad showed him hosting a barn dance at his farm. 
“My opponent, Jamie Ager, likes to have barn dances and drag queen shows,” Balkcom said. “The only thing I know around this area that we like to have in our barn is either crops, hay, tools, or tractors.”
In Balkcom’s ad, she revealed her mom taught her to be strong, and that Balkcom’s mother shot a home intruder. Buckhout and fellow Republican state auditor Dave Boliek referenced the moment during their speeches. 
“She’s as tough as they come,” Boliek said. “When she was growing up, when a guy tried to break into her house, her mom shot the guy. So I know where she gets the resolve from, and she brought that with her to Raleigh.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Nearly 12% of absentee ballots returned, according to Montana Secretary of State’s Office
text:
Montana's new "I voted" sticker. (Secretary of State's Office photo)Montana voters already are turning in their general election ballots — 60,329 as of Monday, according to the Montana Secretary of State’s Office.
That’s 11.6% on average of the 520,035 absentee ballots sent, according to the Secretary of State’s ballot counts tracker. Montana has more than 780,000 registered voters.
People who haven’t registered to vote may still do so, and details are available on the Secretary of State’s website.
In Cascade County, election administrator Terry Thompson encouraged people who need to register to do so sooner rather than later.
“Register early,” Thompson said Monday. “Come down and register so that we don’t have long lines on Election Day.”
Thompson said a steady flow of people have been registering, and her staff are ready to help so voters don’t have to wait at this point.
“It’s all hands on deck with my team,” Thompson said.
As of Friday night, Thompson said her team had processed 5,530 ballots, and the drop boxes had been filling up since then.
“We probably have 2,000 to process tonight,” Thompson said.
As of Monday, Hill County had the highest portion of ballots back so far, 18.47%, or 1,029 out of 5,571. Pondera, Toole and Sweet Grass counties also had an estimated 18% each.
In a couple of the most populous counties, Yellowstone and Missoula, voters have turned in more than 16% of absentee ballots. 
Missoula County Elections Administrator Bradley Seaman said Monday of the 64,000 ballots the county mailed out, voters have turned in more than 10,000.
“We are rocking and rolling on the election,” Seaman said in a voicemail.
He also said county employees are working hard to contact voters who have undeliverable ballots.
One race in particular is heating up in western Montana.
Last week, political analysts shifted the U.S. House race in district No. 1 to a “toss up” between Republican Aaron Flint and Democrat Sam Forstag.
Saturday, Montanans at No Kings rallies said they were motivated to vote to counteract U.S. President Donald Trump’s policies.
They said high gas prices and unaffordable health care were driving their decisions on the ballot.
Trump himself also visited Montana last week to rally his base before the Nov. 3 general election.
Thompson said not everyone has figured out that they don’t have to fill out their birth year on their absentee ballots anymore — a judge found the requirement to be unconstitutional — and ballots won’t be rejected based on that issue.
She also reminded voters that at least in Cascade County, the elections office has extended hours. It’s open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday through Oct. 30, and 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. this Saturday and on Halloween.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ‘Night and day’ difference revealed after restoration in South Dakota Capitol rotunda
text:
A view of the restored rotunda dome in the South Dakota Capitol building on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/101926-Rotunda-Restoration-Done-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
PIERRE — Scaffolding stood in the center of South Dakota’s Capitol building for six months, but now the work is done and the reviews are coming in.
Pierre resident Mary Keeler, who works for the state Bureau of Finance and Management, stood looking up into the dome recently while admiring the restoration work.
“It has always been a beautiful building,” she said. “But this is pretty spectacular.”
Refreshed paint, brighter details and new lighting have made the interior dome more vibrant, she said.
“Just wow,” Keeler said. “And the lighting, it just really makes it even more special than it has been. I think they did a fabulous job.”


Philip Atilano, the project foreman, has years of experience as a professional restorer for Conrad Schmitt Studios in Wisconsin. He told South Dakota Searchlight earlier this year, before completing the restoration, that his team’s focus was restoring the faded wall paint, decorative details and artwork. The lighting had become less visually appealing over time, too, he said.
“It was so dark and dreary in here, initially, for a rotunda. It just didn’t scream ‘state Capitol’ as much as it will now,” Atilano said then. “What we’re doing now, it’s going to blow people’s minds. I think people that were used to it before, now they’re going to see it, and it’s just, I think it’s going to be night and day.”
Restoration artists craft ‘the next phase of history’ in the South Dakota Capitol rotunda

The state paid for the work out of a $3 million pool of money approved last year by state lawmakers for the restoration, maintenance and repair of historic areas and objects within the Capitol.
Since 2019, lawmakers have provided a total of $13 million for various Capitol projects including the dredging of Capitol Lake, plaster and paint restoration work, and to begin saving for a full restoration and renovation that could cost more than $150 million, including updated wiring and utilities. That prediction comes from the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration, which is responsible for maintaining the Capitol.
The next steps toward a full restoration are being evaluated. The last full restoration was conducted ahead of the 1989 state centennial, nearly 40 years ago. Construction of the Capitol was completed 116 years ago in 1910.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Clinic union certified, but Rogers Behavioral declines to say it will start bargaining
text:
A National Labor Relations Board official has certified the National Union of Healthcare Workers as the official representative for employees at the West Allis clinic (above) of Rogers Behavioral Health. The union was previously certified at Rogers' Madison location. (Rogers Behavioral Health media photo)A federal official has affirmed the pro-union vote at a West Allis mental health clinic, rejecting challenges to the outcome lodged by Rogers Behavioral Health.
The decision, issued Oct. 15 by National Labor Relations Board regional director Jennifer Hadsall, certifies the National Union of Healthcare Workers as the official representative for employees at the Rogers West Allis clinic.
Hadsall also rejected a series of challenges that Rogers management made in connection with the election, held April 22, when employees voted 53-4 for union representation.
The union was previously certified to represent employees at Rogers’ Madison clinic, where employees voted 26-4 in favor of the union, also on April 22.
Rogers Behavioral Health, based in Oconomowoc, operates a network of mental health hospitals, residential treatment clinics and outpatient clinics in 10 states. Employees at three clinics in California and one in Pennsylvania organized with the National Union of Healthcare Workers starting a few years ago.
In a statement issued Monday, Rogers acknowledged the union had been certified at both Wisconsin locations but declined to respond to questions about the organization’s next steps, including whether it would begin bargaining with the union.
The organization’s statement said Rogers was “unable to comment further on pending legal proceedings related to these certifications.”
A certification order can be appealed to the full National Labor Relations Board in Washington, D.C. Rogers declined to answer directly when asked if the organization’s management was appealing the certification decisions to the board.
The West Allis certification order rejected a series of objections to the election outcome, including claims that three fired employees trespassed on the day of the vote. An administrative law judge upheld the right of the fired employees to vote and found no evidence of trespass, and the new order upheld those findings.
The certification order follows a finding, also issued by Hadsall, a week earlier that Rogers violated federal labor laws before, during and after the election, including by firing six employees involved in the union organizing campaign. A hearing on the NLRB complaint is scheduled for December.

name: VTDigger
title: ICE looks to boost staffing at intelligence hubs in Vermont
text:
A Department of Homeland Security office off Industrial Avenue in Williston on Tuesday, October 7, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could hire more workers at its offices in Vermont as part of a $100 million plan to boost intelligence-gathering for the branch of the agency that carries out arrests and deportations, federal records show. 
The plan, which is not final, calls for 24 positions evenly split between ICE’s Law Enforcement Support Center and its National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, both of which are in Williston. They’re among 142 total positions proposed for ICE offices around the country, all of which would be staffed by a government contractor. 
The workers would provide “intelligence research and analytical support” for ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division, often abbreviated ERO, according to a contracting document published online last month. That includes “understanding emerging trends, identifying potential threats, recognizing intelligence gaps, assessing relationships and patterns” and a number of other duties.
The contractors would work with a mix of classified and unclassified information, and at least some of them would need “top secret” government security clearance, according to the document. ICE estimates the total cost of the nationwide plan, called ERO Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, would be more than $100 million, according to another federal record published last month.
The government has been “conducting market research” for the plan and issued a request for information to potential contractors, which was due late last month, according to the published records. A final contract could be awarded around February, the magazine The American Prospect reported last week, citing intelligence contracting experts.
One of the Williston centers, the Law Enforcement Support Center, is located on Harvest Lane. It operates a round-the-clock service for police nationwide to get information on a person’s immigration status, as well as a tip line for the public. Workers there also generate leads for immigration enforcement agents and process biometric data for other federal law enforcement agencies including the U.S. Secret Service, according to ICE’s website.
Less than a 10-minute drive away on Industrial Avenue, the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center also develops leads for ICE operations, using an array of digital tools to provide “critical investigative support for daily arrest efforts” according to an agency webpage.
Together, the centers are a major node in ERO’s national intelligence-gathering network. Another key facility, the Pacific Enforcement Response Center, is located in Southern California. That center would get nine contract workers under the plan outlined last month.
The plan marks at least the third time ICE has considered increasing its staffing at Vermont’s facilities since President Donald Trump took office a second time last year, but the agency has disclosed little information publicly about those earlier efforts.
Both Vermont centers have been regular sites for protests in Trump’s second term. Some of those demonstrators have been arrested and are now facing trespassing charges.
The demonstrations in Vermont have been a far cry from the violent clashes that have erupted between protesters and federal agents in other parts of the country. Earlier this month, protesters wrote anti-ICE messages with chalk on the facade of the Law Enforcement Support Center and blocked the road in front of the building using garden beds.
ICE did not immediately respond to a request for more information Monday about its plans for the facilities in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ICE looks to boost staffing at intelligence hubs in Vermont.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: U.S. Department of Agriculture argues it’s not required to enforce Animal Welfare Act
text:
A male Australian shepherd with significant dental health issues was photographed by USDA inspectors in 2021 at Steve Kruse's Stonehenge Kennels in West Point, Iowa. (USDA photo courtesy of Bailing Out Benji)Less than two weeks after the head of the U.S. Department of Agriculture said the agency was stepping up enforcement of the federal Animal Welfare Act, the USDA’s lawyers are arguing in court that it’s not required to enforce that law.
The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals filed a lawsuit against the USDA in September 2024, challenging its past decisions to license three Iowa dog breeders — Steve Kruse, Brian Lichirie and Wuanita Swedlund.
The lawsuit, which is still pending, alleges the USDA has pursued an informal policy of failing to enforce the federal Animal Welfare Act. As evidence, the ASPCA cites the USDA’s decision to repeatedly renew Kruse’s license, despite a history of animal-welfare violations, and by licensing two of his associates, Lichirie and Swedlund.
As a result, the ASPCA claims, hundreds of Kruse’s dogs have cycled through Kruse’s associates as part of a puppy-laundering scheme intended to conceal the role Kruse plays in supplying puppies to out-of-state retailers.
More recently, the ASPCA has noted in court filings that within days of Kruse’s license being canceled in September 2025, the USDA approved a license for another individual, Christine Snakenberg, at 2345 Highway 16 in West Point — the same address as Kruse’s Stonehenge Kennels, which Kruse still owned at the time.
All of that, the ASPCA contends, points to the USDA’s informal policy of refusing to enforce the Animal Welfare Act.
In response to those allegations, the USDA is arguing that the agency is not required to enforce the law — stating that none of the enforcement provisions of the Animal Welfare Act are mandatory, and that decisions on enforcement are entirely at the agency’s own discretion.
The USDA also argues that nothing in the ASPCA’s lawsuit “suggests that this imagined ‘policy’ of non-enforcement even exists.”
Rollins: ‘Those days are over.’
On Oct. 6, 2026, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins appeared at the Animal Rescue League of Iowa and publicly announced the agency was stepping up its enforcement efforts related to inspections — called “surveys” by the agency — and penalties.
“This USDA, over the last year and a half, is very different than prior USDAs,” Rollins said. “We have really stepped up enforcement … The prior USDAs, they would come in, they’d survey, they may fine, and then they would leave. But those days are over. We are now in the active process of shutting down these puppy mills.”
In court, the USDA is arguing that the ASPCA’s lawsuit centers on four Iowa breeders — Kruse, Swedlund, Lichirie and Snakenberg. The first three have voluntarily surrendered their licenses or allowed them to expire, the USDA alleges, and Snakenberg fits the agency’s “regulatory criteria for licensure.” Because of that, the USDA argues, the lawsuit should be dismissed as moot.
The ASPCA’s lawsuit cites the licensing of Snakenberg as evidence that the USDA’s “ongoing policy of non-enforcement persists to this day,” and so the lawsuit should not be dismissed as moot.
Swedlund, whose USDA license expired on July 14, 2026, has since been criminally charged with 34 counts of animal neglect. She has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges. A trial is now scheduled for Dec. 18, 2026.
As the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported in 2024, a USDA inspector visited a dog-breeding kennel in the Van Buren County town of Cantril in late 2023. The business was located on property owned by Kruse but operating under a license held by Swedlund. During the inspection, USDA officials reported six puppies at the facility appeared to have frozen to death.
USDA records showing that in 2025 and 2026, Swedlund repeatedly denied federal inspectors access to her Van Buren County facilities.
On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice obtained a temporary restraining order against Swedlund and then inspected her business, cataloging 20 violations. A few days later, the Van Buren County sheriff seized Swedlund’s 32 dogs, which led to the filing of the criminal charges.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. House advances bills limiting student cellphone use and Flock-like cameras
text:
The Pennsylvania Capitol on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Public and private schools across the commonwealth could soon be required to draft universal bell-to-bell cellphone bans for students. The state House passed a measure, with a handful of exceptions for learning and medical needs. 
The proposal, Senate Bill 1014, mirrors a House version that has sat in a Senate committee since June. 
The backing for a cellphone ban spans party differences and has the support of Gov. Josh Shapiro, but lawmakers haven’t finalized any proposal. 
Rep. Mandy Steele (D-Allegheny) pitched the effort as a way to free children from the “captive” nature of cellphones and big tech, a move she said harms children’s mental health. 
Rep. Mandy Steele (D-Allegheny) introduces House Bill 1814 to restrict cellphone use in Pennsylvania schools. (Screenshot from livestream)
“This is a massive public health crisis, the likes of which we have never seen. An entire generation of Americans rendered captive. We are playing with fire,” continued Steele. “The absolute bare minimum we can do is to get these things out of our schools. Let children have their hearts and minds back for at least six hours a day while they are in school.” 
Rep. Scott Barger (R-Blair) shared a concern about unintended consequences by allowing an exception for students with learning disabilities, saying that the number of children claiming such a need could increase. 
“I would support a version of this bill that prohibits the use of cell phones, period. No exceptions,” said Barger. “If they are as dangerous as you say they are, get them out (of schools) for everybody, all the time.”
The bill moved on a 141-62 vote, getting no votes from 37 Republicans and 25 Democrats and now goes to the Senate.
Last week, parents with PA Unplugged urged legislators to move the bill, noting the limited amount of time left to pass any proposals. 
“Legislators only have a few days remaining to pass this statewide standard so that kids across Pennsylvania can be free from their phones at school and can better focus on learning, both academically and socially,” parents wrote in a release.
There are just four scheduled session days left — two this week and another two in November, after Election Day.
“Pennsylvania has the opportunity to become the 25th state in the country to pass a “bell-to-bell” phone-free school law – the tipping point where half the country will have no phones in schools from the first bell to the last bell of the day,” parents continued.
 Guidelines for Automated License Plate Readers

Following weeks of public outcry, the House also moved a bill that would limit how law enforcement can use Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs), which track and gather information for law enforcement agencies. 
Under House Bill 2771, officers now need to obtain warrants to run searches, with all captured data owned by the local agency — rather than provider Flock Safety or another competitor. 
Earlier this year, the Washington Post reported that at least 50 law enforcement officers nationwide have been charged or accused of misusing similar systems to spy on their spouses or intimate partners, exes and their exes’ new partners.
Pa. lawmakers propose guardrails on automatic license plate cameras as backlash grows

The Post story included an account of a mother from Leechburg, Armstrong County, who said she repeatedly warned police and the district attorney’s office that her police officer husband had used a competitor to Flock to stalk and threaten her. The officer, Michael McSherry, ultimately pleaded guilty to official oppression and served about 11 months in jail, according to the article.
In another case, a Texas officer tracked a woman across state lines when she traveled out of state to obtain an abortion. 
Sponsoring Rep. Jen O’Mara (D-Delaware) described the bill as a rare instance when both supporters and opponents supported restrictions, noting the balance between privacy and crime-solving. 
“We understand that this technology is very useful and very impactful for members of law enforcement in the state,” said O’Mara. “But it was also one of the rare instances when, during a hearing, every presenter … started off with acknowledging that we do need guardrails in place for this technology.”
But Rep. Tim Bonner (R-Mercer) criticized the proposal for allowing camera access for felonies or parking violations, but not for misdemeanors or juvenile offenses. He said misdemeanors could still be serious crimes — such as indecent assault, stalking or drunk driving. 
“I do believe we need to regulate more aggressively,” Bonner added, partially crediting the cameras with falling crime rates. “Yet, we’re going to totally prohibit the use of these cameras to solve very significant cases.” 
Bonner and a dozen other representatives, including one Democrat, voted against the bill, which advanced to the Senate on a 190-13 vote. 
Other lawmakers, from both parties, urged a ‘yes’ vote, saying that specifics could be worked out in the Senate, which is scheduled to meet for two days in mid-November. If a bill isn’t passed this year, O’Mara — who, like all House members, is up for reelection — said she was working to advance another version next year

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: ‘Every single day without them is a struggle’: Mother urges Indiana to uphold death sentence
text:
Alyssa Lynch, 8, and her brother, Caleb, 5, were killed in a 2010 house fire set by Jeffrey Weisheit. Weisheit is seeking clemency ahead of his scheduled Nov. 5 execution. (Courtesy photo)The mother of two children murdered by Jeffrey Weisheit urged Indiana’s parole board Monday to reject his plea for mercy, saying her children deserved the futures he took from them.
Her appeal came hours after Weisheit’s family and attorneys asked the five-member board to recommend sparing his life, citing his history of mental illness and head injuries, his religious conversion and a written request from the murdered children’s father for forgiveness and a sentence of life without parole.
The Indiana Department of Correction also released a $275,000 invoice Monday in response to the Indiana Capital Chronicle’s requests for execution drug purchasing records.
Dated Sept. 25, the invoice does not specify the drug or number of doses, nor does it show if or when the pentobarbital arrived. DOC did not provide an updated drug inventory on Monday.
Weisheit was sentenced to death in 2013 for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a fire at his home near Evansville. Their mother, Lisa Lynch, was working an overnight shift and had left the children in his care.
Monday’s testimony in Indianapolis concluded the public hearings on his clemency request following an interview Friday with Weisheit at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.
His execution is scheduled there before sunrise Nov. 5.
The board did not issue a recommendation Monday afternoon. Chair Gwen Horth said one would not come for several days. Gov. Mike Braun will make the final decision.
Mother asks board to remember her children
Speaking remotely from out of state, Lisa Lynch began her testimony through tears, asking the board to remember the children and not just the case against their killer. At Lynch’s request, only board members could see her video because of privacy concerns.
“I am here today to ensure that my children’s voices are heard, their names are spoken, and their lives are remembered,” she said. “Alyssa and Caleb are not just names on a case file, dates in a record, or photos in an evidence box.”
Alyssa was creative and loved drawing pictures of her family, Lynch recalled. She adored her younger brother. Caleb loved hugs, helping his mother in the kitchen and playing with trucks and trains.
Their deaths robbed her of watching them finish school, build careers and have families of their own, she said.
Retired Vanderburgh County sheriff’s Detective Randy Chapman addresses the Indiana Parole Board on Oct. 19, 2026, in Indianapolis. Chapman, who investigated the murders of Alyssa and Caleb Lynch, challenged death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit’s claims of remorse and urged parole board members to deny clemency. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“Every single day without them is a struggle,” Lynch said. “Every birthday, every holiday, every landmark moment is marked by their agonizing absence. Time passes, but the weight of losing them never fades.”
She described surviving domestic violence and emotional abuse and said efforts to blame her for Weisheit’s actions had continued into the clemency proceedings.
During Friday’s interview, Weisheit repeatedly discussed his anger and suspicions about Lynch while struggling to explain why he directed that anger at her children.
Lynch said that after the murders, she returned to school and built a career that allowed her to support her family and be home every night.
“They will always be my children,” she said. “They will always matter, and I will never stop speaking for them.”
The children’s father, Steven Lynch, took the opposite position in a sworn statement seeking life without parole. He did not attend Monday’s hearing.
“What good does it do the memory of my children to put this man to death?” he wrote. “I seek to save his family the great pain and loss from the taking of his life. I want to prevent another parent from experiencing the loss I have experienced.”
First responders describe lasting trauma
First responders and investigators described the killings and the memories they still carry.
David Bretz, the German Township Fire Department’s assistant chief at the time of the fire, said he arrived first to find flames pushing through every opening.
Firefighters found Caleb’s body on a mattress, with his hands and feet bound behind him. The search for Alyssa continued for hours. Bretz said he ultimately spotted a small hand amid the debris in her bedroom closet.
“Everything from the fire to the investigation, my deposition, testimony at the trial, and now this will be with me forever,” Bretz said. “It weakens me and terrifies me on a regular basis.”
‘I want to live now’: Indiana death row inmate makes clemency plea ahead of execution

At least three firefighters sought counseling, he said. Bretz also read statements from colleagues describing lasting trauma and said Friday’s interview had not persuaded him Weisheit was remorseful.
“Please, I beg of you, carry out the sentence that was placed upon him for the appalling crimes that he committed upon all of us,” Bretz said.
Chad Ferguson, the on-duty patrol supervisor, recalled sheriff’s deputies frantically searching places the children might have been taken. After Caleb was found, he initially could not get the words out to tell their mother.
Forensic dentist Dr. Crunchy Wells described identifying the children using dental records and recent Easter photographs.
“It was the hardest report I ever had to make,” she said. “It was the saddest thing I had ever seen.”
Retired investigators Randy Chapman and Kerri Blessinger challenged the defense’s account of Weisheit’s mental condition and remorse. Blessinger characterized the killings as domestic violence intended to devastate the children’s mother. She said forgiveness did not erase the punishment.
“Let me make one thing very, very clear: forgiveness and punishment are not the same,” Blessinger said. “They do not go hand in hand. One does not equal another.”
Vanderburgh County Prosecutor Diana Moers closed by recalling the children’s personalities and urging officials to uphold the sentence.
“The death penalty was the sentence recommended by the jury, reviewed by our courts, and so is justice,” Moers said. “Each person should be afforded the full protections of the United States Constitution and the due process that it brings.”
State challenges Weisheit’s account
Tyler Banks, chief of capital and habeas litigation for the Indiana attorney general’s office, argued that Weisheit’s sentence had survived extensive review by the courts and that his clemency presentation offered no reason to overturn it.
“A jury of his peers unanimously recommended a death sentence, and that sentence has withstood more than a decade of challenge,” Banks said. “Gov. Braun should not overturn all of those judgments.”
Banks recounted evidence that Weisheit bound and gagged Caleb, placed railroad flares near his body and in his clothing, and left both children in the burning house before fleeing the state.
He disputed Weisheit’s account Friday that he started the fire by placing a phone book on a stove burner. Banks said evidence of an accelerant and the flares contradicted that explanation.
Tyler Banks, chief of capital and habeas litigation for the Indiana attorney general’s office, presents arguments against Jeffrey Weisheit’s clemency request on Oct. 19, 2026, in Indianapolis. Banks urged officials to uphold the death sentence for the murders of Alyssa and Caleb Lynch. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Banks also rejected Weisheit’s unsupported suggestion that police or emergency responders might have placed the flares at the scene.
Horth and board member Jim Shaffer questioned how Weisheit could recall other details while denying responsibility for the flares.
Defense attorney Joseph Perkovich attributed the discrepancy to memory gaps, saying Weisheit sometimes constructs explanations for events he cannot recall. He emphasized that the legal team did not endorse Weisheit’s suggestion that someone else planted the flares.
“I’ve talked with him about it. He has zero recollection of the flares,” Perkovich said. “I don’t think this is guile or artifice on his part.”
Banks said mental health evidence had already been extensively litigated. He argued that Weisheit “used suicide attempts as a mechanism to obtain better housing,” rather than acting because of a psychiatric crisis.
Defense attorneys, however, described those episodes as psychiatric deterioration involving fears that others intended to harm him. Perkovich said Weisheit went on a hunger strike to secure hospitalization because he believed he was unsafe.
Family seeks mercy, treatment and more testing
Several dozen people, including relatives, attorneys and death penalty opponents, crowded into the Indiana Government Center conference room for the morning presentation.
Weisheit’s attorneys opened with a family video. His aunts, sister and parents described childhood behavioral difficulties, suicide attempts and head injuries, followed by years of steady work.
Relatives said they had embraced Alyssa and Caleb as family and struggled to reconcile the killings with the man they knew.

His sister, Carrie Jones, feared his execution would devastate their parents, who have significant health problems.
“I’m going to lose everybody if this goes through,” Jones said, telling the board she fears her parents won’t be able to live through the pain of losing their son.
Jeffrey’s father, Bert Weisheit, a former law enforcement officer, recalled treating the children as grandchildren.
“Alyssa and Caleb were grandchildren,” Bert Weisheit said. “They were a lot of fun to be with. Very smart children.”
Deacon Brian Nosbusch, who has ministered to Weisheit for about 13 years, described his conversion to Catholicism and his efforts to serve other prisoners through his work as a porter and small purchases for those around him.
“I have seen a deep remorse that goes far beyond regret for the consequences that he faced, and I believe it was a true commitment to moral repair and reconciliation,” Nosbusch said. “We pray both for those that he has hurt, and we also pray for his family.”
At a news conference afterward, Perkovich said the defense was asking state officials to consider Weisheit’s moral culpability rather than excuse the killings.
“We don’t contest that he is responsible in the way we understand that,” Perkovich said. “What we’re getting at is a question of blameworthiness.”
Attorney Joseph Perkovich speaks outside the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis on Oct. 19, 2026, after the morning session of death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit’s clemency hearing. He urged officials to consider Weisheit’s mental illness and brain injuries in deciding whether to spare his life. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Board member Mia Kelsaw questioned whether Weisheit would accept treatment and adjust to another prison setting if his sentence were commuted.
“What we would urge, and we would do everything in our power as his counsel, is to work with DOC with regard to its classification and treatment,” Perkovich said.
Even so, he acknowledged the difficulty of treating someone who does not recognize his own illness but said the legal team would help corrections officials pursue care.
“If that were not to succeed, there are other means (allowed) to provide for his care and for the safety of everybody else,” Perkovich said.
Brain scan litigation continues
Weisheit’s attorneys have asked the Indiana Supreme Court to authorize transportation for MRI and PET scans and move his execution date from Nov. 5 to Nov. 19, allowing time for analysis they say could inform Braun’s clemency decision.
U.S. District Judge Sarah Evans Barker approved funding for potential testing but ruled Oct. 7 that she lacked authority to compel state officials to transport Weisheit to gather evidence for a state clemency proceeding.
The attorney general’s office opposed transportation and a delay in a Friday filing, arguing there was no legal basis for the order and further testing might produce no relevant new information. The court received a defense reply Monday, but the clerk noted it exceeded length limits and lacked a request to file an oversized document.
Perkovich said a separate reprieve application would seek a pause in executions to examine Indiana’s procedures and drug procurement following Tennessee’s failed execution attempt of Christa Pike on Sept. 30.
He suggested the states might share a supplier.
“There’s a whole litany of considerations that are shrouded in secrecy under state law, and secrecy laws are typical in capital (punishment) states,” Perkovich said. “But what is atypical and what is extraordinary in Indiana’s is the blanket that they put over any ability to make sense of what the state actually does to carry out the punishment.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Minogue says he’ll govern without a lieutenant governor after Oliver’s arrest
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
text:
REPUBLICAN GUBERNATORIAL NOMINEE Mike Minogue plans to have no lieutenant governor in his administration if he wins the general election, a decision he announced after Republican candidate for the No. 2 job, Shawn Oliver, suspended his campaign Sunday following a drunken driving arrest.
Oliver was arrested in New Bedford late Saturday night on operating under the influence of liquor and negligent operation of a motor vehicle, after Oliver reportedly crashed his SUV into five parked cars and flipped his car. He was sent to the hospital for injuries, and local police confirmed no one else was seriously injured. He pleaded not guilty in New Bedford District Court on Monday morning, according to the New Bedford Light, but suspended his statewide campaign.
Minogue had called for Oliver to suspend his campaign Sunday morning, and at a press availability in his hometown of Hamilton on Monday afternoon, the gubernatorial candidate outlined his plan if he wins in November.
“I am glad he’s safe, but at this point, I called for him to suspend and terminate his campaign, and he will not be my lieutenant governor,” Minogue said. “Maine and New Hampshire don’t have one, and I’m going to move forward without him.”
Ballots are already printed with Oliver’s name next to Minogue’s as a joint ticket, and over 200,000 voters have already cast their ballots through early voting.
Minogue asked his supporters to still “vote for me, knowing that he will not be my lieutenant governor.”
“And please do not mark off or do anything different or write in because it will disqualify the people’s vote,” Minogue said.
He said he will ask Oliver to resign if the pair are elected, then will operate without a second-in-command.
Massachusetts has no process for replacing a lieutenant governor who resigns. The state Constitution doesn’t let the governor appoint a replacement or call a special election, so the office simply stays empty until the next regular election. That was the case for the end of Gov. Deval Patrick’s tenure, after Lt. Gov. Tim Murray resigned a year and a half before the end of his term.
The lieutenant governor’s main constitutional job is to step in for the governor when they are out of the state. With that seat empty, the next person in the line of succession is the secretary of state, followed by the attorney general, the treasurer and the auditor. The lieutenant governor has other duties, such as presiding over the Governor’s Council, and is given other responsibilities based on the administration.
Asked Monday whether he was prepared to take on the roles that the lieutenant governor covers, such as chairing the Governor’s Council, Minogue responded he would “have people around me that are some of the experts.”
“What I’m going to focus on with my staff is to bring in one of the most competent groups that have expertise — many will be like me, in that they won’t be taking a salary, they’ll be volunteering to give back,” he said.
Minogue added, “And I’m very comfortable because, again, Maine, New Hampshire, other states don’t have lieutenant governors, and I think we’re going to be fine. And I’m very focused on just solving problems and putting together an A-plus team.”
Minogue said he had spoken to Oliver, but did not share many details of the conversation.
“I’ve spoken to him. He’s going through the legal process. I’ve expressed my disappointment in the judgement, I’m glad he’s recovering, but he understands that he cannot be and will not be my lieutenant governor,” he said.
Oliver pleaded not guilty to all charges Monday morning: operating under the influence, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, speeding and a marked lanes violation. He was released on the condition that he not drive while the case is pending, ahead of his next court date on Nov. 16.
Asked if Oliver’s not guilty plea impacts his decision, Minogue said, “Whatever he pleads is his process.”
“For what has happened alone, he no longer has the ability to be my lieutenant governor, and he will not be my lieutenant governor,” he said.
Oliver, a New Bedford city councilor, initially launched his campaign as the running mate of gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve. Ahead of the Republican convention in the spring, Minogue endorsed Anne Brensley for lieutenant governor. Despite getting the party’s endorsement at the convention, Brensley failed to qualify for the official ballot when she chose not to submit nomination signatures based on allegations of fraud by her signature collector. Brensley is running instead for secretary of state.
Oliver was the only lieutenant governor candidate on the September primary ballot, and joined Minogue on the ticket after Minogue’s victory over Shortsleeve.
“There was a lot of drama in the convention process. I did not pick an LG during this process. I went in to be the outsider, I said I would follow wherever the path led,” Minogue said Monday. “I did say at the convention that I was going to vote for Anne Brensley. Anne Brensley won first place at the convention, Anne Manning Martin won second place, and Shawn Oliver got 16%, so he made the ballot by 16 percent. And then Anne Manning Martin was eliminated because she was a victim of signature fraud, and by default, Shawn got the LG role.”
“I would have worked with him had this not happened, and I had moved on and was focusing on the campaign, but with this as a distraction, and with this error in judgement, that is not a position that he will be allowed to be,” he said. “He was Brian Shortsleeve’s person, if you just look at the record.”
Minogue used the press availability Monday to cast the situation as his campaign taking accountability, and trying to draw a distinction to Gov. Maura Healey’s handling of a situation in which her former aide was arrested on charges involving alleged cocaine trafficking. Healey says she fired the aide immediately when she heard of his arrest.
“I think it’s important to note that this is what you’re supposed to do as a leader,” Minogue said Monday. “You hold people accountable. You’re tough on the issue. You’re compassionate to the person. You don’t let something bad define you the rest of your life, but there’s an accountability where you basically move forward, and we need to move forward.”
Healey holds a 25-percentage point lead over Minogue, according to the latest UMass Amherst / WCVB poll.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Enrollment-calculation trapdoor will squeeze Iowa’s public schools
text:
Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds was joined by Des Moines Prep students, state legislators and other charter school advocates as she signed into law a measure making changes to charter school and homeschooling regulations May 12, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds signed Senate File 2201, the school funding bill, into law on Feb. 26. The 2% increase in per-pupil funding for the 2026-27 school year works out to $160 more per student. When the decline in public enrollment is taken into account, it’s a statewide increase of $17 million from last year’s allotment.
The law includes a massive change in calculation of enrollment formulas. Instead of a single count of certified enrollment taken Oct. 15, a second count has been added to take place on Jan. 15/the third Monday in January called “adjusted enrollment.” (Because of Martin Luther King Jr. Day, the de facto date can be as late as Jan. 18.) The average of these two numbers will become the “basic enrollment” number used for determining the following school year’s funding.
That means the tally used for calculating state supplemental aid will be an approximation in mid-November and not exact until early February. This will end up in conflict with the law requiring state aid to be set within 30 days of the governor’s budget proposal — a deadline that has repeatedly been blown. But that’s OK, since the Legislature can exempt itself from following the law.



Quotation







“The requirement of section 257.8, subsection 1, regarding the enactment of bills establishing the regular program state percent of growth within thirty days of the submission in the year preceding the base year of the governor’s budget does not apply to this division of this Act.”


– SF 2201, bottom of page 4


This change also runs closer to the deadlines schools are under to submit property tax rates (March 5) and finalize budgets (April 30). A bill that passed the House but stalled in the Senate would have limited schools to using the previous year’s allowable growth rate if state aid is not set by March 5 and enabled updates after the fact.
During debate on SF 2201, Sen. Lynn Evans, R-Aurelia, said the second enrollment count would help in situations where a student moves into a district after Oct. 15. Under the current formulas, that student’s enrollment wouldn’t get counted toward funding until two school years later.
That may sound reasonable, but the overwhelming majority of Iowa districts are losing enrollment, and this only applies to changes in the student body over a three-month period.
The trapdoor with this second count was sprung in a different bill, House File 2754, which mainly concerns charter schools. Rep. Skyler Wheeler, R-Hull, said in opening remarks on the House floor April 16: “This is our One Big Beautiful School Choice Bill, or the one-double-B-S-C-B as we like to call it. This bill is big, and it is beautiful.”
HF 2754 includes a section allowing applications for a student to leave a public school at semester break and take half the value of that year’s state cost per pupil with them as education savings account money. An e-mail from IDOE’s Heather Doe said data updated with the second count “will include certified enrollment counts for public districts and the second ESA student enrollment period.” The exact dollar amount in ESAs overall will depend on it.
On April 27, the same evening that the Senate sent HF 2754 to the governor, the Cedar Rapids Community School District voted to close six schools and reconfigure its entire grade lineup starting in 2027. (Reynolds signed the bill May 12, during National Charter Schools Week, while surrounded by charter school students and advocates.) Another division of HF 2754 puts teacher salary supplement funding in the bundle of money that goes with each student from a public school to a charter school. Based on information from the Legislative Services Agency, that would have cost the Cedar Rapids district an additional $270,000 this past year.
“The continual attacks, generally speaking, against the ESA program I find to be fascinating,” Wheeler said on April 16. “I find it to be fascinating entirely because it has been effective. Parents have been empowered. And so we’re going to get upset, generally speaking, because parents were given the ability to go a different route. There hasn’t been a mass exodus.”
Public school enrollment in Iowa for 2025-26 had the most substantial yearly decreases, in both number and percent, in four decades, while private school enrollment increased 26% in three years to a level not seen in a quarter-century. If that’s not a “mass exodus,” what is?
Who’s not complaining?


Last winter, the Senate wanted a 1.75% increase in state aid, the House wanted 2.25%, and the compromise was 2%. The difference in the one-half percent was $18.9 million statewide, or only $2.1 million more than was spent on ESAs for students in the Davenport school district alone in the 2025-26 school year.


“You know who’s not complaining about a 1.75% increase?” Sen. Jesse Green, R-Harcourt, asked Feb. 10 during floor debate on the original version of SF 2201. “Those private schools. They’re working with a heck of a lot less, and they are happy.”
In 2022, the year before ESAs, Dowling Catholic High School’s tuition was $9,132 for parish families and $12,776 for non-parish families. In 2025, it was $11,076 plus $364 in fees for parish families and $15,498 plus fees for nonparish families. Dowling is also engaged in a $76 million capital campaign that did not require 60% supermajority approval from any public electorate.
Holy Family Catholic Schools in Dubuque raised its tuition from $2,200 in 2022 to $11,500 in 2025.
Siouxland Christian’s tuition went up 18% from 2024 to 2025.
Hull Christian School, which last year received more than $1.25 million in ESA money from students living in the Boyden-Hull school district, broke ground March 27 on a $4.7 million expansion.
Iowa does not require private schools to publish budgets or curriculum information. Iowa does not require them to have public meetings before major construction.
Private schools wouldn’t even have been bound by a bill of Wheeler’s that was approved by the House Education Committee on Feb. 11, but died later in the session, mandating that all students at public schools conform to a statewide dress code.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma health care agency boasts low payment error rate
text:
A Medicaid insurance card is pictured. (Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s Medicaid payment error rate is well below the national average, according to the agency that administers the program. 
Oklahoma’s “improper payment rate” for Medicaid, also known as SoonerCare, was 0.15% in 2025 compared to the national average of 6.12%, according to the Oklahoma Health Care Authority. 
The state’s Children’s Health Insurance Program also has a low payment error rate at 0.88% in comparison to the national average of 7.05%, according to a news release. 
The payment error rates of the two programs are evaluated every three years. Oklahoma was among the states with the lowest rates in both the 2022 and 2025 reviews, according to a news release.
“Oklahomans expect every taxpayer dollar to be spent the right way, and we hold ourselves to that standard,” said Aaron Morris, interim CEO of the Health Care Authority, in a statement. “We are continuously enhancing our tools to ensure Medicaid dollars are preserved and available to fund services for Oklahomans in need.”
In 2022 Oklahoma’s Medicaid program had not yet made the switch to managed care, but overall, the state’s Medicaid error rate was 1.95%, the second lowest rate in the nation. The improper payment rate for the Children’s Health Insurance Program was just over 2%. 
In the three years since the last review, the agency worked on “rigorous staff quality control and enhanced data integrity,” said Rebecca Sheppard, a spokesperson for the Health Care Authority. 
The Health Care Authority is “continually adapting its strategy” to combat fraud through firewalls, automated application screenings and data validation exchanges with partners like Equifax, according to a news release. 
“OHCA’s broader plan to protect program integrity combines strict provider credentialing and revalidations of high-risk providers with targeted post-payment audits that verify medical necessity and proper documentation,” according to a news release. 
Attorney General Gentner Drummond in April requested an audit of the Health Care Authority, specifically how it oversees managed care organizations. 
Oklahoma is also facing a deadline to lower its error rate for SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or face higher costs to the state to administer the program following the passage of President Donald Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill last year. 
The state’s error rate, which is not always a result of fraud, is just over 11% as of July, but must drop below 6% to be compliant with federal requirements. 
The Department of Human Services did not immediately provide an updated error rate.

name: VTDigger
title: Portion of I-91 in northern Vermont named for border agent killed in line of duty
text:
FILE – In this undated and unknown location photo released by the Department of Homeland Security shows Border Patrol Agent David Maland posing with a service dog. (Department of Homeland Security via AP, File)

A state panel has approved a measure to name a northern portion of Interstate 91 in honor of David Maland, a U.S. Border Patrol agent who authorities say was shot and killed while conducting a traffic stop on that roadway more than a year ago.
The Vermont Transportation Board issued a written order last month naming a roughly 11-mile stretch of I-91 north and south between Exit 26 in Barton and Exit 28 in Derby, from mile marker 161.4 to mile marker 172.4, the David Chris Maland Memorial Highway.
“Agent Maland was an active member of the Newport Community. He supported a local church that ran a homeless shelter,” the four-page order stated. “He donated funds, supplies, and time to give meals, clothing, and a safe place for people in need.”
Maland, 44, of Newport, according to the order, was a border agent working out of the Newport Border Patrol Station and had worked for the border patrol for nine years. He previously served in the U.S. Air Force and worked security at the Pentagon during the 9/11 terrorist attacks, the order added.
“Agent Maland was involved in his community near and around the Newport area,” according to the order, “where he indicated he wished to settle permanently, and lived a life of service both in his work and private life.”
According to the Transportation Board’s rules, when considering a naming proposal, the panel may consider “whether the person or family made some significant contribution to the transportation facility or the region where the transportation facility is located.” 
The board can also consider whether the person or family “earned a favorable local, regional, national, or international reputation or whose character and integrity, whether or not accompanied by fame or fortune, warrant remembrance.”
Maland was involved in a fatal traffic stop on the afternoon of Jan. 20, 2025, on Interstate 91 southbound near mile marker 168 in Coventry, according to federal authorities.
The driver of the pulled-over vehicle, Teresa Youngblut of Seattle, Washington, is accused of opening fire and killing Maland during that traffic stop, federal authorities stated in court documents. 

A hearse carrying U.S. Border Patrol Agent David Maland travels in a procession to Ready Funeral and Cremation Services on Shelburne Road in Burlington in Jan. of 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Youngblut, who was also injured in the shootout, was later released from the hospital and charged with crimes in Maland’s killing that carry the possibility of the death penalty.
The case against Youngblut remains pending in federal court in Vermont. A passenger in Youngblut’s vehicle was also killed in the exchange of gunfire with law enforcement, the charging documents stated. 
The American Legion, Newport Post 21, filed a petition to name the entirety of Interstate 91 in Orleans County in Maland’s honor in November 2025, according to the Transportation Board order. The petition had 97 signatures from residents across Orleans County, the order added. 
The board also received letters of support from several people and organizations, including Newport Mayor Rick Ufford-Chase, as well as the Vermont Police Association and the United Federation of Police Officers.
The American Legion of Newport later amended its request to name the south and north sections of I-91 between exits 26 and 28. According to the order, the last four miles of I-91 in Vermont before entering Canada are named the John F. Kennedy Memorial International Highway in honor of the late president.
Following the public hearing earlier this year and notification of towns and villages along the stretches of roadway to be named in honor of Maland, the state Transportation Board issued its order Sept. 28.
Commander Jim Crowe of the American Legion post in Newport spoke at that public hearing. 
“The American Legion wishes to honor our fellow veteran and symbolically commemorate the life of David Maland by renaming a portion of I-91 as a memorial to his life,” Crowe told the panel, adding, “We share the belief that the initiative will provide a meaningful way to honor our fallen comrade who gave his life in service to others.”
Crowe said the plan was to also install signs entering and exiting those sections of the interstate informing people of the designation. A timeline for the installation of those signs was not available Monday.

name: Mississippi Today
title: SPLC president during Jackson visit says organization is ready to fight DOJ prosecution
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Southern Poverty Law Center President Ryan Haygood told Mississippi Today on Monday that his organization is prepared to fight the Trump Justice Department’s indictments in a trial set for April.
Haygood was in Jackson for the start of the organization’s “Truth, Poverty and Democracy Tour” across Mississippi, which will combine community listening sessions to spotlight socioeconomic problems faced by residents. While the Center continues a shift toward anti-poverty advocacy as a central pillar of its work, fighting the lawsuit is of existential importance for civil rights advocacy more broadly, as the lawsuit against SLPC could be a “test case” used against other organizations, Haygood said.
“It’s a vicious irony that the DOJ has been weaponized against the organization that toppled the Klu Klux Klan, even as hateful organizations remain free to operate across the country,” Haygood said. “So it’s a case we intend to win.” 
Without detailing the organization’s legal strategy, Haygood said the trial will shed light on why the SPLC was created and all the ways it serves communities across the South.  
The Justice Department’s probe against against the Alabama-based group has thus far ensnared one of its former political extremism experts, who left the center about six year ago. That former employee, Heidi Beirich, has been charged with wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to submit false statements to a federally insured bank and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering.
Her legal team has said she is innocent of the charges and described the case as politically motivated.
The SPLC is a frequent target of conservative critics who claim the nonprofit is politically biased. Critics argue the organization has used its “Hate Map” to lump ordinary conservative political groups in with militant extremist groups. 
In the wake of the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, anger from Trump and his supporters toward groups such as SPLC intensified.
In the fall of 2025, Trump directed federal law enforcement agencies to investigate what he claimed were wealthy donors and organizations funding left-wing political violence. A week later, Mississippi Today spoke to former SPLC President Bryan Fair, who warned the memo could be used as a pretext to target civil rights organizations perceived to be enemies of the administration and Republican causes in states such as Mississippi.
In April of 2026, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel announced an 11-count federal indictment against the SPLC in the Middle District of Alabama on charges of wire fraud, bank fraud and conspiracy to launder money.
Haygood took over as SPLC’s president in August, at a moment when “civil society organizations face mounting attacks” the Center said.
As the SPLC prepares for a trial this April, Haygood said his organization remains undeterred
“It stands to reason that the kind of work SPLC does, the kind of work to connect people to prosperity and to create a fair criminal legal system, to create a multiracial democracy, and also to identify hateful actors and to topple their organizations,” Haygood said. “It stands the reason that an organization like ours given the work we are doing would be challenged in this moment by this kind of government.”
Haygood, who met earlier on Monday with Democratic state lawmakers, said the center plans to play an active role in pushing for Mississippi to raise its minimum wage, which remains set at the federal minimum of $7.25 per hour. Proposals to do so have repeatedly died in the Legislature.
At the Mississippi Museum of Art, the SPLC convened panels on gaps in the social safety net that impact Mississippi, one of the poorest states in the country. Federal cuts to Medicaid, food assistance, housing, education and childcare have rattled communities across the the state, the center has said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ picks Rutgers to lead social media research center
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Monday that Rutgers University will lead a new youth social media research center. (Photos by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey officials have tapped Rutgers University to lead a new publicly funded social media research center dedicated to protecting children from its addictive features and other risks online.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Monday that Rutgers was selected through a competitive grant process that will provide the state university $500,000 to assess the impact of social media on New Jersey teens, identify specific measures that can be used to mitigate the damage it causes, and promote healthy and responsible use of social media apps.
Findings will be released on a rolling basis, Sherrill said, with more detailed recommendations to follow within a year. The goal is to help policymakers find better ways to keep young people safer, but also to give parents, teachers, and others free tools to guard against the addictive nature of social media, she said.
“We’re trying to generate insights that everyone can trust, not just PR spin, and I want those insights to reach everyone in our state,” Sherrill said Monday.
Studies show nearly half of teens — and 55% of parents — agree social media is harmful to youth mental health.
The announcement is the latest step in Sherrill’s effort to curb the negative impacts of social media on young people.
In her first days in office, Sherrill signed an executive order that created an office of online youth safety within the state Department of Health, and in August she signed a package of bills that prompted additional research and outlined sweeping restrictions designed to limit kids’ access to certain apps, changes that take effect in September 2027.
“If Washington won’t lead on keeping our kids safe from big tech, then New Jersey will,” Sherrill said Monday.
New Jersey Secretary of Higher Education Margo Chaly said Rutgers was selected because it offered a “detailed, clearly defined” proposal.
The social media research team will be led by Rutgers associate psychology professor Jessica Hamilton; Jeffrey Lane, an associate professor of communication; and Vivien Wen Li Anthony, an associate professor at the school of social work and an expert in addiction.
Hamilton said work is already underway with more than two dozen teams of high school students in ten counties responding to questions about their social media use, how it impacts their mental health, and when it makes them feel worse about themselves.
“We want to better understand what specifically are the aspects of social media that are most harmful, when, and what we can do right now to make that better,” Hamilton said.
The center’s work is funded through New Jersey’s $60.7 billion budget for the current year, but the state is also anticipating at least $575 million from a legal settlement announced in August between a group of states and the tech giant Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram. Meta agreed to new limits on daily platform use by teens, among other things, but did not admit to claims that it had intentionally designed addictive systems.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Operator of Alaska North Slope oil field hit by a second fine for gas flaring
text:
An aerial view of the Mustang pad in the Southern Miluveach Unit on the North Slope is seen in a 2024 application from Mustang Holding LLC to the Alaska Division of Oil and Gas for permission to do certain pipeline maintenance and assessment tasks. The Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission has issued a second order finding unit operator Mustang Holding at fault for unauthorized natural gas flaring. (Image provided by Alaska Division of Oil and Gas)A small energy company that was assessed a hefty fine in July for what regulators said was five months of illegal natural gas flaring on the North Slope was cited again for another four months of gas flaring.
The Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission, in an order issued Friday, assessed a $195,214 fine against Mustang Holding LLC, the operator of the Southern Miluveach Unit on the western side of the North Slope. It comes after a $741,520 fine for a similar infraction this summer.
The latest assessed fine equals double the fair market value of natural gas illegally flared at the field from April to July of this year, the AOGCC said in its order. That calculation is in accordance with state law.
In an earlier enforcement action, the AOGCC, which regulates oilfield practices, assessed a fine for gas flaring that occurred at the field from November 2025 to last March.
Gas flaring — the burning of unused gas — is allowed in Alaska for safety reasons and for early development of an oil or gas well, though only with state permission. Outside of those parameters, flaring is considered a waste of state-owned resources.
The commission had granted Mustang Holding permission to flare gas for an initial 180-day well-testing period, then granted extensions that ran through October of 2025. But after that, the AOGCC said, Mustang Holding did not have authorization to flare gas.
Continued flaring after the expiration of an authorization violates state law concerning proper oil field engineering practices and the conservation of natural resources, the AOGCC order said.
“The AOGCC further finds that the continued flaring was knowing and intentional,” the order said.
Mustang Holding’s head of operations, Muammer Alboamemah, said the company contends that it remained in a test period during the entire time covered by the two AOGCC orders and was therefore allowed to flare.
“The facility overall was not in the state of regular production, so all the equipment required for gas injection, such as dehydration units, compressors, processing equipment was not commissioned at that time,” he said.
Since then, the company has put “a lot of capital investment” into the project, installed equipment and, as of late September, has been injecting natural gas rather than flaring it, Alboamemah said.
Additionally, the volume of flared natural gas that is the subject of the two AOGCC enforcement actions is small, he said. It amounts to only about 9% of the total volume that the commission had permitted the company to flare during the designated testing period, he said.
Mustang Holding is contesting the fine assessed in July, Alboamemah said. He declined to say whether the second fine will be contested, but the AOGCC order provides a month-long window for an appeal to be filed.
A hearing to consider Mustang Holding’s defense against the fine assessed in July had been scheduled for Oct. 20. However, that has been postponed, said AOGCC Special Assistant Samantha Coldiron. A new hearing date has yet to be selected, she said.
The Southern Miluveach Unit, located just west of the ConocoPhillips-operated Kuparuk River Unit, has had a troubled history. It has had ownership changes and financial problems that prompted a 2021 foreclosure on the property by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority.
That foreclosure happened after Brooks Range Petroleum, a previous developer, defaulted on an AIDEA loan. The foreclosure made AIDEA the owner of Mustang Holding LLC, the state-approved operator, until a company called Finnex LLC acquired it in 2023. Finnex is owned  by Houston-based Thyssen Petroleum USA.
Mustang Holding was cited by the AOGCC for two other violations prior to the gas-flaring enforcement action, according to commission records.
An Aug. 29, 2024, order said the company violated state law by changing a well-drilling procedure without regulators’ authorization. The proposed fine for that violation was $50,000. Earlier this year, the AOGCC cited Mustang Holding for reporting lapses, and the April 20 order issued by the commission proposed a fine of $30,000.
