name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Floundering North Carolina fisheries agency endangers workers and wildlife
text:
Chloe Dorin is a former North Carolina Division of Marine Fisheries biologist who recently resigned, alleging rampant mismanagement. (Photo: Lisa Sorg/Inside Climate News)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
On a misty and breezy morning last fall, Marc Hamric, a North Carolina Division of Marine Fisheries veteran, and two other technicians were conducting field work in Turnagain Bay, a remote area near Cedar Island.
They had brought their boat ashore, but because the water was so rough, it came loose and floated away.
One DMF technician swam after it and had trouble hoisting himself aboard. Hamric swam to rescue him. Meanwhile, the technician managed to get on the boat and steer back to shore, but didn’t know Hamric had followed him into the bay.
As the two technicians searched the water for Hamric, one was on speaker phone with the team’s supervisors, sobbing as he explained what happened. The technicians eventually found Hamric in the water. They tried to resuscitate him. Shortly after an ambulance arrived, medics pronounced him dead.
Chloe Dorin, then a biologist with DMF and one of the supervisors, was on the call. “I heard the whole thing,” Dorin said in an interview. “It has been a little over a year now, and I still think about him every day.”
The Carteret County sheriff ruled Hamric’s death an accident. Yet current and former employees say DMF routinely requires technicians to work while sleep-deprived and in dangerous conditions: in rain, wind and fog as dense as fresh concrete.
Interviews and government documents depict DMF as a floundering bureaucracy that jeopardizes the safety of its technicians who work on the water. The division has also failed its state-mandated duty to protect aquatic life and coastal habitats, in part because of incomplete and incorrect scientific data, according to court records, state reports and employees.
Some current and former employees who shared their experiences asked not to be named for fear of retaliation. Inside Climate News also relied on internal emails, legislative and federal documents, a confidential whistleblower report filed with the state auditor’s office and a recent superior court ruling against the division.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
DMF, which is housed under the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality, is responsible for the stewardship of the state’s fish, clams, oysters and crabs in all coastal waters up to three miles offshore.
It must comply with federal requirements, legislative mandates and rules passed by the state Marine Fisheries Commission, itself mired in internecine politics between commercial fishermen whose livelihoods depend on their catches and recreational anglers who fish out of tradition or need.
DMF did not answer questions from Inside Climate News about the allegations but provided a statement:
“The Division of Marine Fisheries is aware of claims made by former employees who recently left the agency. An initial review by the Division has found these claims to be unsubstantiated, misinformed or lacking proper context. The Division takes its role to provide science-based guidance to the Marine Fisheries Commission very seriously.
“There are policies in place to maintain a safe working environment for employees and ensure that fisheries data is reliable. DMF is always looking for ways to improve and is evaluating the feedback from these former employees to determine if there are additional steps we can take to improve safety and transparency.”
Shorebirds rest on a sandbar near the Morehead City port. They eat fish, oysters and clams, of which some species are collapsing. (Photo: Lisa Sorg/Inside Climate News)
After two years, Dorin said the workplace culture at DMF eventually became too much to bear. Not only was she concerned about worker safety, but she came to doubt some of the science that underpinned DMF decisions. She said she had uncovered several years’ worth of incorrect data regarding hard clams and poor scientific sampling protocols for bay scallops. She saw technicians break down under pressure.
“There are extraordinarily capable, hardworking people at DMF. In many ways, they are exactly why I feel compelled to write this,” she said in her Sept. 10 resignation letter to DEQ leadership, several state lawmakers and Gov. Josh Stein.
“I have watched good people be ground down by a dysfunctional system,” Dorin wrote. “I believe serious consideration should be given to dissolving the division in its current form and rebuilding it from the ground up.”
Stein’s office did not respond to a request for comment on Dorin’s letter.
In 1997, the state legislature passed the Fisheries Reform Act to address overfishing and plummeting fish stocks. Yet over the past 29 years, DMF has failed to manage fisheries and protect aquatic life and coastal habitats, according to court documents.
Of the 13 species under DMF’s care, seven have collapsed, two are depressed and the status of three others are unknown, court documents show. Only one, red drum, is recovering. None shows signs of long-term viability.
DMF’s challenges—not only politics but also coastal development, degraded water quality and climate change—are legitimate, former and current employees say, but they don’t explain all of its missteps.
“We’re so impressed with short-term economic gain that we don’t take the long-term viability of the resource”—the fish and their habitats—“into consideration,” said Louis Daniel, a marine scientist and a DMF employee for 21 years, including nine as its director. He left the division in 2016, after he was demoted by then-DEQ Secretary Donald van der Vaart, an appointee of Republican Gov. Pat McCrory.
“What’s in the best interest of the resource is in the best interest of everybody, and that’s where we have failed miserably as a state,” Daniel said.
Hamric had been with DMF for 28 years. He was beloved by his colleagues, employees said, and he won a DEQ Distinguished Employee Award in 2024. In her resignation letter, Dorin addressed his death. “There have understandably been many discussions about safety since then,” she wrote. “But there is a question I believe has received far too little attention: Why were staff operating on the water under poor conditions in the ?rst place?”
Questions about safety
On a sunny, breezy day in early October, Dorin boarded a 21-foot skiff in Morehead City to tour parts of the Intracoastal Waterway. Several men in a boat lugged a large mass shrouded in white cloth onto a dock, Dorin said, probably a tuna. Fish bit at bait at the foot of a cargo ship, where half a dozen people tossed their lines in the water.
Dorin is 30, just over 5 feet tall and lithe, with a buzz cut of brown hair, large blue eyes and a luminous smile. On the inside of her left forearm she sports a tattoo of a spotted salamander, the subject of her master’s thesis at Appalachian State University in Boone.
A bridge connects Morehead City, where the Division of Marine Fisheries has an office, to Atlantic Beach, N.C. (Photo: Lisa Sorg/Inside Climate News)
Dorin started at DMF as a temporary technician and within nine months received a promotion to biologist She managed several technicians and conducted gill net surveys herself. It is a critical and risky job, done on open water and often at night.
Technicians unfurl several hundreds yards of net, which stand vertically in the water with the aid of floats and weights. The size of the mesh ranges from 3 to 6 ½ inches, depending on the species the technicians are trying to catch.
The purpose is to catch certain types of fish, then measure and weigh them, and identify their sex to help biologists determine the health of the species.
DMF uses the survey data to publish a stock assessment and to guide species management. The division’s decisions—limiting the number and size of species that commercial and recreational anglers can harvest, the length or cancellation of a fishing season—can make or break livelihoods.
DMF’s federal gill net permit dictates the terms of the surveys. Twice a week from mid-February through mid-December, teams of two gill net technicians ride motorboats into bays and sounds in the late afternoons or early evenings. The nets then “soak” for 12 hours while the targeted species—as well as other aquatic life—are trapped.
The afternoon trip, plus the net-setting, can take six to eight hours. Technicians then go home, sleep a little, and return in the middle of the night or very early morning to do the scientific analysis. They remove the nets and measure, tag and determine the age and sex of the catch, and log the numbers of animals that are dead or alive.
Several current and former employees said some technicians have stayed in hotels on very long trips, but that DMF’s expectations, which include boat maintenance and extensive paperwork, are unrealistic.
Other employees said they’ve not been well-trained on crucial safety measures, such as shooting flares and navigating a boat at night. Sometimes, instead of hands-on instruction, they watch slideshows.
Still others said they had to wait several months to receive personal lifejackets for the first several months of the job, and in the meantime had to borrow them.
Employees said they have seen coworkers fall asleep at the wheel while hauling boats behind state-owned trucks, “or get really tired and are dazed or zoned out.”
Sometimes exhausted technicians have falsified the soak time so they can rest, Dorin said, which can skew the accuracy and quality of the data.
Dorin said she doesn’t blame the technicians, who say their concerns have not been addressed by management.
DMF could ask federal regulators to adjust the soak times, which could have beneficial trade-offs. While potentially reducing the number of captured fish, a shorter soak time could also reduce the catch of unintended species, like sea turtles and sharks, and it would be safer for the technicians. Managers at DMF’s Wilmington office, Dorin said, have instructed technicians to set nets for only four hours because of the high number of sea turtles being caught.
“I have watched what these schedules do to people,” Dorin said. “The extraordinary workload placed on technicians creates incentives to falsify timesheets and field records simply to make an impossible schedule appear possible.”
Systemic mismanagement
River herring, a foot-long fish with shiny teal-and-white scales, is one of the most legendary species in North Carolina. The fish has its own festival. At its peak, commercial fishermen caught 20 million pounds each year. Before DMF enacted a moratorium on river herring in 2007, the annual catch had cratered by 99 percent—to just 110,000 pounds.
The fate of the river herring is one of dozens of examples of DMF’s mismanagement detailed in a court ruling published in August. In 2020, the Coastal Conservation Association, a nonprofit composed of recreational fishermen and conservationists, sued DMF for allegedly mismanaging its fisheries to the point of collapse.
NC failed to protect coastal fisheries, court says

The trial started in January and lasted five weeks.
Over a 190-page decision in August, Wake County Special Superior Court Judge Bryan Collins Jr. eviscerated DMF for its “systemic, decades-long pattern” of management that favored the commercial industry “to the detriment of North Carolina’s coastal fisheries and the general public.”
Although overfishing and habitat destruction has nearly eliminated some species in coastal waters, the state responded that “DMF does not use the term ‘collapsed’ regarding marine fisheries management,” Collins wrote.
“Notably, the State did not contend that it was improper to make such an assessment,” the judge added, “only that it would not engage in such an exercise.”
At trial, DMF witnesses did not rebut any of the plaintiffs’ claims, but rather only confirmed them, court records show. The division’s own witnesses confirmed that it is not managing its fisheries to achieve long-term viability, as legally required, and employees had no documents to guide staff on meeting that standard.
Tina Moore, a bivalve expert at DMF, testified that the hard clam had been overfished, but the division has no rebuilding plan for the species or the bay scallop, whose commercial catches are “essentially zero.”
Dorin did not testify at the trial, but said she encountered several instances of incorrect data. When she began overseeing the bay scallop program, Dorin said she discovered a predecessor had miscalculated data that allowed harvesting seasons to open in 2022 and 2023, in contradiction with the species’ management plan.
Bay scallops are nearly wiped out along the North Carolina coast, Dorin said. “Those seasons should not have opened.”
Dorin also discovered 76,000 rows of hard clam data listing widths and lengths had been transposed and gone uncorrected from 1996 until 2024. These errors affect the reliability of size and growth analyses that guide decisions on managing the species.
DMF published the data in years’ worth of management plan updates. Dorin fixed the error and footnoted it in a 2026 fisheries management report.
Daniel, the former DMF director, said if these accounts are correct, “it is a catastrophic failure of a reliance on data that are meaningless because they’re not being done properly.”
Dorin said when she mentioned the hard clam error to a manager, they responded, “Good thing no one will ever notice but you, Chloe.”
“I have never forgotten that sentence,” Dorin said.
Accidentally ensnared
When the technicians reel in their gill nets to examine the catch, they find targeted species, like blue fish, Southern flounder and spot. But they also capture endangered species.
One DMF employee said they had seen hundreds of baby sharks dead in the nets, a report corroborated by another technician.
“I have witnessed the fatality of multiple scalloped hammerhead sharks,” an endangered species, one employee wrote in an email forwarded to Inside Climate News, “as well as the fatality of over 100 other adult sharks. All of those were a direct result of the gill nets we set.”
Endangered Kemp’s Ridley sea turtles can be inadvertently caught in gill nets. (Photo: NOAA Fisheries)
The nets also entangle sea turtles and Atlantic sturgeon. DMF employees calculated that from July 2021 to September 2026, DMF’s gill net program logged 172 “interactions” with sea turtles, meaning the turtle was caught in the net. Of those, a third of the turtles were found dead; others might have died later from trauma incurred in the net.
Employees say finding even a live sea turtle is “heartbreaking.”
“No one wants to see a sea turtle in a net,” an employee said.
Technicians are trained to identify, measure, log and even resuscitate sea turtles, according to DMF, and tag all live turtles. Dead turtles are sent to the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission for examination.
Employees say tired, time-pressed technicians likely don’t report every protected sea turtle, Atlantic sturgeon or endangered shark caught in DMF gill nets, as required. That means the division could be ensnaring greater numbers than permitted by the federal government under the Endangered Species Act.
A DMF employee told Inside Climate News that technicians generally report dead sea turtles, but not always live ones, as required by the federal permit. “You’re sleep-deprived. You’re going to look at the turtle and say to yourself, ‘I didn’t see it. I’m just going to release it.’”
Atlantic sturgeon are also being killed. Over the past five years, 10 percent of 149 Atlantic sturgeon captured were found dead in the nets, federal data show.
Dorin confirmed that dozens of endangered sea turtles and sharks have been needlessly trapped in gill nets; many of them died.
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which is composed of representatives from East Coast states, concluded that the Atlantic sturgeon remains depleted along the entire seaboard not only because of overfishing but bycatch, habitat loss and ship strikes.
Before becoming DMF director in 2007, Daniel led the congressionally established South Atlantic Fishery Management Council, on which he represented North Carolina. He was an expert witness on behalf of the CCA at the trial.
Daniel told Inside Climate News that the state’s fisheries have been wiped out “because we allow things that no one else allows.”
Crab and oyster dredging kills species on the beds of the sounds. Shrimp trawling and gill netting in estuaries—essentially nurseries for fish—accounts for hundreds of millions of bycatch, fish that have the misfortune to become ensnarled in a net intended for someone else.
Other states, the August court decision noted, prohibit or sharply limit the use of destructive gear in estuaries and fish nurseries.
Trawling and dredging, Daniel said, is the marine equivalent of clear-cutting a forest. The gear has destroyed sea grasses and corals, oyster reefs and sponge communities, Daniel said, “and the interstitial spaces for all these little creatures to live in. Now it’s just a flat, barren bottom.”
Investigating the agency
As part of his August ruling, Collins directed the Coastal Conservation Association and the state to confer and report back to him about possible solutions to the issues raised at trial. Before the 45-day deadline, the state appealed Collins’ decision. It now goes to the N.C. Court of Appeals. No date has yet been set.
The State Auditor’s office announced in April that it is investigating DMF. State Rep. Jake Johnson, chairman of the House Select Committee on Oversight and Reform, recently requested financial and operational information from DMF.
“North Carolina fishery management has shown an inability to keep up with science and a failure to utilize relevant data and reports,” Johnson wrote to the division.
Johnson cited a 1,000-page report released by the North Carolina Collaboratory that found similar problems to those presented at trial. The Collaboratory is a state-funded research agency that includes members of universities and government.
Among its conclusions, the Collaboratory recommended DMF needs an independent scientific oversight committee, binding catch limits, more robust protection of estuaries and greater transparency.
Onboard the skiff, Dorin headed back toward Morehead City. A flock of oystercatchers vogued overhead. A pod of dolphins frolicked in the water. She gazed across the sound.
“Sometimes when I am out in public, I catch sight of a man who looks like him and, for a split second, think I see Marc,” she said. “My mind still does that to me.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: 60% threshold for changing North Dakota’s constitution debated as a protection or a barrier
text:
Measure 1 opponent Dustin Gawrylow gestures while debating Measure 1 proponent James Kerian on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota voters will decide this fall whether to require at least 60% approval of future amendments to the state constitution, a move supporters say would protect the foundational document, but opponents say would make it harder for citizens to enact changes.
Measure 1 opponent Dustin Gawrylow, director of the North Dakota Watchdog Network, debated proponent James Kerian, a Grafton businessman chosen by StrongND, a group backing the measure, on the Plain Talk Podcast hosted by Rob Port and Chad Oban. North Dakota’s Republican-led Legislature put Measure 1 on the ballot.
North Dakota’s constitution provides a stable, firm foundation to the state government, and Measure 1 ensures broad agreement on changes to the document, Kerian said.
“This is where our fundamental, core principles go: limiting the government, recognizing the rights that we have and wielding, of course, tremendous power right there at the foundation of our state government, and voters, of course, should retain the ultimate say, as they will with Measure 1,” Kerian said.



Voters must approve all changes to North Dakota’s constitution, whether from the Legislature or an initiated measure.
Out-of-state organizations with lots of money are targeting North Dakota’s constitution, he said, citing the Fairness Project, a D.C.-based group that supports ballot measures in other states on topics such as reproductive rights and redistricting. The Fairness Project has spent more than $1.6 million to oppose Measure 1, according to online campaign finance filings. Kerian said the group pushes a “left-wing agenda” on red states through ballot measures.
Measure 1’s higher bar would make it harder to fix or reverse anything in the constitution, and effectively hand control to a minority of 40% plus one vote, Gawrylow said.
Out-of-state money is a legitimate issue, and something needs to be done about it, Gawrylow said. He brought up StrongND, which is not required to disclose its donors. The group is aligned with Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong and has spent nearly $1 million to back Measure 1. Fights about who is spending money on either side distracts from the merits of the measure, he said.
Measure 1 proponent James Kerian speaks during a debate with opponent Dustin Gawrylow on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
The Legislature has always tried to chip away at the initiative process, Gawrylow said. He pointed out two camps: people who genuinely believe the constitution is under attack, and those who are vindictive and simply don’t trust voters, he said.
Oban, one of the moderators, wondered whether the 60% threshold is meant to thwart an abortion rights amendment.
North Dakota Right to Life recently cited other states that passed abortion rights measures with less than 60% of the vote, saying, “If North Dakota faces an abortion amendment in the future, the difference between 50% and 60% could determine whether abortion is written into our state Constitution.”
Kerian said, “Abortion is certainly one of the issues where the Fairness Project pushes a very left-wing agenda.” Measure 1 is not about past amendments, but rather a “future threat” coming quickly to North Dakota, he said.
“This just provides some protection so that you do not have an extreme agenda on any subject passed on very narrow margins by an extremely well funded, left-wing organization,” he said.
Behind the measure are state lawmakers, who don’t like “the citizens telling them what to do,” Gawrylow said. 
Sponsor, opponent debate need for North Dakota ballot measure to change constitution

For years, North Dakota lawmakers have bristled about out-of-state groups pouring money into constitutional initiatives on topics such as crime victim rights, state government ethics and term limits – all measures voters approved. The Legislature has submitted measures to voters in past years to try to make it harder to change the constitution, with little success until last June, when voters approved a single-subject rule for constitutional amendments.
The initiative process benefits North Dakota’s dominant Republicans from a partisan standpoint, Gawrylow argued. Without the “pressure relief valve” of the initiative process to check the Republican-run Legislature, citizens might have a better reason to elect Democrats, he said.
Some people might have an axe to grind with Republican lawmakers over past issues, but “the issue before us is Measure 1” and whether wider agreement is necessary to change the constitution, Kerian said.
The vast majority of constitutional amendments voters have approved over the last 20 years have had 60% support or greater, he said. Some of those measures were ones creating the Legacy Fund, crime victim rights, legislative and gubernatorial term limits and a congressional age limit. Some measures mustered support well over 80%.
“This is not some impossible-to-reach threshold that good ideas will not be able to clear,” Kerian said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
The U.S. Constitution has high thresholds for amendments, such as support of at least three-quarters of all 50 states. Measure 1 is a “tried and true method of protecting a constitution” from being changed too easily, Kerian said.
Gawrylow said the question is whether North Dakota should change a century-old process to allow a minority of voters to have power over the majority.
“Why would we hold ourselves to a higher bar just because somebody else is taking advantage of the system?” he said. 
Measure 1, which would set the 60% threshold for future constitutional amendments, needs a simple majority to pass. The measure doesn’t apply to ballot initiatives affecting state law.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

In 2024, 209,516 of the 518,330 Delawareans who voted did so early, about 4 in 10. Sussex County led the state in early voting.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware launches pilot to coordinate inspections for new small businesses
text:
Program aims to give entrepreneurs one pathway for permits, licenses and pre-opening inspections across multiple state agencies
DOVER — Delaware has launched a pilot program designed to make it easier for new small-business owners to navigate state permits, licenses and inspections before opening their doors.
The Small Business Joint Inspection Pilot creates a coordinated process intended to replace what can be a confusing series of applications, agency websites and separately scheduled inspections.
The initiative was ordered by Gov. Matt Meyer under Executive Order 21, signed in May as part of a broader effort to reduce regulatory barriers facing small businesses. The order created the Office of Small Business Access and directed state agencies with inspection authority to develop common checklists and coordinated inspection scheduling.
“Opening a small business takes courage and hard work. Navigating state government should not add to the challenge,” Meyer said. “This pilot means fewer websites, fewer delays, and one clear path from an idea to an ‘open for business’ sign.”
The program does not eliminate permits, licenses, inspections or health and safety requirements. Instead, it seeks to coordinate the process and give business owners a clearer understanding of what they need before opening.
One point of coordination
The Office of Small Business Access, led by Director Anastasia Jackson, will manage the pilot with participating state agencies.
Business owners entering the process through Delaware One Stop will be told about the voluntary program and can choose whether to participate.
Those who opt in will use the state’s ServiceNow system, which identifies the permits, licenses and applications that apply to their type of business and provides links to the appropriate applications.
Agency liaisons also are notified when a participating business enters the system, allowing agencies to identify potential requirements and begin coordinating reviews.
The Office of Small Business Access was established earlier this year to serve as a central point of contact for entrepreneurs dealing with state government, including licensing, permitting and regulatory issues.
Business owners also will be able to arrange meetings with agency representatives and receive contacts for local planning, zoning and business licensing officials based on where the business will operate.
Coordinating inspections
One of the most significant changes involves inspections.
Rather than requiring entrepreneurs to independently schedule inspections with several agencies, the pilot allows the Office of Small Business Access to help coordinate those visits.
Executive Order 21 specifically directs agencies to offer coordinated scheduling so required inspectors can visit during the same general window when requested by the applicant. It also says agencies generally should not require another agency’s approval before scheduling an inspection unless health or safety considerations require it.
The participating agencies are the Delaware Department of Transportation; Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control; Delaware State Fire Marshal; Delaware Department of Health and Social Services’ Division of Public Health; and Office of the Alcoholic Beverage Control Commissioner.
Which businesses qualify?
The pilot covers a variety of relatively small new businesses, including retail stores and markets; art galleries; hair salons, barbershops and spas; independently owned restaurants, bars and taprooms; coffee shops and cafes; childcare facilities; fitness centers; furniture stores; ice cream shops; laundromats; and certain small manufacturing, packaging and distribution operations.
Only businesses that have not yet opened and still need applications or approvals from participating state agencies are eligible.
Participants also must create a my.delaware.gov account.
Not every business will need approval from every participating agency, and applications remain subject to the normal agency review process before inspections are scheduled.
The joint inspection effort is one part of a larger small-business initiative established by Executive Order 21. The order also directs the state to develop plain-language requirements for common business types, examine regulations that may unnecessarily impede small businesses and improve coordination among state agencies.
TO GO



What: Delaware Small Business Joint Inspection Pilot
Who qualifies: New businesses that have not yet opened and require permits, licenses or inspections from participating state agencies
How it works: Eligible owners may opt into a coordinated process through Delaware One Stop and ServiceNow
Participating agencies: DelDOT, DNREC, State Fire Marshal, Division of Public Health and Office of the Alcoholic Beverage Control Commissioner
Requirements: Participants must create a my.delaware.gov account. Existing permit, licensing, health and safety requirements still apply.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Expanded scholarship program ‘a huge relief’ for SC’s college-bound high school seniors
text:
Dutch Fork High School seniors hear from Meeting Street Scholarship Fund representatives in Irmo, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Jazz’e Spencer has played soccer — a center back defender — for 14 years. Now the Dutch Fork High School senior dreams of studying sports medicine, either at the University of South Carolina or College of Charleston, to help her fellow athletes treat injuries early so they can stay in the game.
One look at the cost of college, however, and the prospect is daunting.
Before scholarships and financial aid, her top-choice schools are expected to cost between $31,600 and $35,300 annually on tuition, supplies, meals, housing and other expenses.
With an older sister attending college in another state, she’s seen the numbers and Spencer is left worrying about the expense of her own education.
“It’s like how am I gonna pay for this?,” she said. “It makes it a little nerve-wracking.”
So, when representatives of the nonprofit Meeting Street Scholarship Fund came to her school Monday to talk about a new opportunity for high-achieving, low-income South Carolina students to receive as much as $40,000 toward their college education, it gave her hope.
“It would take a lot of the load off,” Spencer said. “And my mom, I think she would worry a little less.”
Scholarship program expands

 Meeting Street expansion
The following is a county-by-county estimate of new recipients annually of the scholarship funded with lottery profits, based on data from the census and state Commission on Higher Education:

Greenville: 273
Richland: 227
Lexington: 175
York: 153
Horry: 141
Berkeley: 120
Dorchester: 101
Anderson: 97
Beaufort: 75
Pickens: 61
Aiken: 51
Sumter: 44
Lancaster: 40
Orangeburg: 39
Laurens: 38
Kershaw: 38
Georgetown: 38
Oconee: 32

Chester: 23

Cherokee: 19

Chesterfield: 18

Fairfield: 15
Union: 15
Edgefield: 15
Abbeville: 14
Calhoun: 11
McCormick: 8
Saluda: 7
Private and home schools statewide: 151

Source: Beemok Education


Spencer is among thousands of high school seniors across South Carolina newly eligible for scholarships enabling them to earn a college degree with little-to-no debt under a partnership between Meeting Street and the state.
It comes after legislators included $18.7 million in the budget to expand Meeting Street Scholarships statewide.
“We want to make sure we keep our best and brightest in state, and this is a way to do that,” said Republican Rep. Nathan Ballentine, who chairs the House’s higher education budget panel and whose district includes Dutch Fork High School.
The scholarship, available to students who meet income requirements for a federal Pell Grant, fills gaps not covered by other aid — up to $10,000 annually for students who keep at least a B average.
‘A huge relief’
The program also added a work requirement to give recipients on-the-job experience.
Starting this school year, students in their second and third years of college must work 250 hours to keep their scholarship. That can include a part-time job on or off campus, internship, or research.
More than 80% of recipients were doing that anyway, according to Beemok Education, which runs the Meeting Street fund.
Lexington-Richland School District Five Superintendent Akil Ross put that in perspective for the Dutch Fork High School seniors, many of whom work minimum wage jobs when they’re not at school. To earn $10,000 at those jobs, they’d have to work for more than half the year.
“Eight and a half months of real work, full-time work, can be given to you because you did what you had to do in the classroom,” he said.
State lottery profits will pay for an estimated 2,300 scholarships awarded next school year. If applications exceed estimates, Meeting Street founder Ben Navarro previously said his nonprofit will make up the difference.
“It’s a huge relief to see that South Carolina has opportunities,” said Christiana Ross, of Irmo. “As far as staying in state, that’s a huge motivation because it’s easier on our parents and ourselves.”
The Dutch Fork senior hopes to attend Coastal Carolina University to study early childhood education and pass on her love of learning.
“Education is something that’s really important to me,” she said. “I know sometimes in school, it’s a process dealing with teachers who you feel like don’t support you or classes that may feel challenging. Being a teacher that helps children want to learn, I think, will make a difference.”
The Meeting Street fund began as a scholarship for Charleston County high school students, starting with the Class of 2021. It spread to 14 counties with private donations from the Navarros and other philanthropists.
In the 14 “legacy” counties, private donations will continue to fully fund scholarships. The state will cover the 32-county expansion.
More funding needed
Once fully implemented in 2030, when today’s eighth graders become eligible, roughly 10,000 students annually will be attending college with a Meeting Street Scholarship. But meeting that goal will require legislators to approve more dollars. Paying for next year’s freshmen and sophomores in the program will require than $30 million next year.
SC students statewide now eligible for scholarship allowing a debt-free degree

By year four, it will take an estimated $60 million each year.
House Ways and Means Chairman Bruce Bannister said it’s too early to say whether the state will have the money available but expressed support for the effort.
“Giving an opportunity to those kids who are right on that bubble and can’t afford college otherwise, I think that’s a great investment,” the Greenville Republican said.
The scholarship stacks on top of Pell Grants, which can range anywhere from $740 to nearly $7,400, and state lottery-funded LIFE or Palmetto Fellows scholarships, which range from $5,000 to $10,000 annually.
On average, the Meeting Street scholarships fill a $7,900 gap after other aid, according to Beemok Education.
The program also has a history of success.
Of the nearly 2,220 students awarded a scholarship since 2021, 88% of them have either graduated or remain in college. And of the program’s graduates so far, 70% left college with zero debt, and 80% stayed in South Carolina to work.
Applications for the program open Nov. 9.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa revokes the license of fired nursing home worker over drug issues
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Nursing)State regulators have revoked the license of a nurse who allegedly confessed to a drug addiction after leaving a bag full of used needles at the nursing home where she worked.
According to the Iowa Board of Nursing, Ranae Fallis of West Des Moines was working at an unspecified nursing home on Dec. 18, 2025, when she left her personal cosmetic bag on a medication cart at the facility. When a colleague reached into the bag, she was stuck by a needle, and further inspection showed the bag contained multiple uncapped “used syringes with visible blood traces and bent needles,” the board alleges.
The board asserts that when questioned, Fallis indicated that although she was struggling with drug issues and had been using cocaine, she had not been using any drugs while on duty. Fallis was fired four weeks later, according to the board.
State records indicate Fallis told a board investigator she had been using drugs “on and off” since 2021, was addicted to cocaine, and that the cosmetic bag that had been found was hers. “Despite the bag being discovered on the medication cart, (Fallis) denied using drugs before or after a shift,” the Board of Nursing alleges.
In April, the board charged Fallis with habitual intoxication or addiction to a drug, and engaging in behavior contrary to professional decorum. After Fallis failed to appear for a board hearing on the matter, her license was revoked.
Board records show that on July 12, 2022, Fallis tested positive for cocaine use during a drug test administered by the hospital where she worked. As a result of that incident, the Board of Nursing placed Fallis’ license on probation for 18 months beginning in April 2023. During her probation, she was to have been enrolled in a board-approved chemical screening program.
Other Board of Nursing actions
Other Iowa nurses whose board-approved disciplinary charges were recently disclosed by the state include:
Patricia Young of Preston – The board has charged Preston with engaging in behavior contrary to professional decorum, but disclosed no information as to the date, location or circumstances surrounding the alleged conduct that gave rise to the charge.
The charge was approved by the board in January 2026, but was only recently made public by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for Jan. 29, 2027.

The charge was approved by the board in July 2026, but was only recently made public by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for April 15, 2027.

According to the board, Harshbarger was practicing in Macomb, Ill., during the period when the alleged misconduct occurred.
The charges were approved by the board in December 2025, but were only recently made public by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for Jan. 29, 2027.

Hoffman of Hartford – The board has charged Hoffman with committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare and with engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum. According to the board, Hoffman was practicing in West Des Moines during the period when the alleged misconduct occurred.
The charges were approved by the board in January 2026, but were only recently made public by the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. A hearing on the matter is scheduled for Jan. 29, 2027.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Juneau hazmat team intercepts suspicious envelope addressed to state Division of Elections
text:
Capital City Fire/Rescue’s Hazardous Materials Team responds to a suspicious envelope received by the U.S. Postal Service in Juneau on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (Capital City Fire/Rescue photo)
A suspicious envelope addressed to the Alaska Division of Elections in Juneau was intercepted by a hazardous materials response team and turned over to the FBI on Saturday, in what is believed to be part of a large number of mailings to congressional and election officials nationwide, according to Capital City Fire/Rescue Chief Tom Hatley.


The FBI notified CCFR on Friday the envelope was expected to arrive in Juneau on Saturday, and at about 9 a.m. Saturday the fire department was notified by U.S. Postal Service officials at the downtown Juneau facility it had arrived, Hatley said in an interview. CCFR Hazardous Materials Team responded and retrieved the envelope.


“At this time, the contents of the envelope have not been confirmed. Our response is being conducted out of an abundance of caution,” CCFR stated in a post on its Facebook page at 12:30 p.m. Saturday.


Juneau Police Department officials blocked the street outside the delivery entrance to the postal facility at the federal building on Glacier Avenue during the hazmat team’s response.


The Associated Press on Friday reported federal officials are investigating letters with suspicious substances mailed to congressional and election offices nationwide and are urging recipients to treat the mailings as “potentially hazardous.”


“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” a statement by the FBI notes. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.”


A similar threat occurred in 2023 when election offices in six states received mailings that contained a white powder, according to the Associated Press. Another series of mailings, including to Alaska, occurred in 2024.


Saturday morning’s response by CCFR occurred shortly before and a few blocks away from a “No Kings” protest whose organizers were urging people to vote early in the Nov. 3 midterm elections due to concerns that include questions about handling of mailed ballots. Early voting in Alaska begins Monday.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Poll finds a strained relationship between CT electorate and officials
text:
Connecticut’s electorate is approaching the midterm elections with a deep distrust of the federal government, a broader sense their opinions are not valued by officials, and partisan differences over taxation and spending priorities in a state with high costs, unmet needs and wealth disparities.
With questions posed to a sample of more than 1,000 voters, a new Wesleyan SurveyLab CT poll takes a measure of voter attitudes towards their government, sources of news and the tensions inherent in a desire for both lower taxes and selected spending increases in an era of state budget surpluses.
The survey found a majority expressing greater trust in local government yet a significant disconnection from public officials. More than 60% said they strongly or somewhat agreed with this statement: “Public officials don’t care much what people like me think.”
Evidence of that disaffection was highest among voters who called themselves working class, as well as Republicans, whose party holds fewer than one third of the seats in the General Assembly and no statewide or congressional offices in Connecticut.
Slightly more than 70% of Republicans and working class agreed with the statement their opinions were unvalued by public officials, compared to 51.7% of Democrats and 48.5% of those identifying as upper class. Racial and gender differences were slighter.
Officials in both parties said they were not surprised by voters’ dour views toward government and public officials, including the extreme distrust of Washington. 
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said the opinion is the natural consequence of a system in Washington geared to pay to play.
“People have figured out that if you have money, you get listened to in a way that you don’t if you don’t have money. People know that the whole system is corrupt, because very big powerful interests have more and more power,” Murphy said. “So, when people say, ‘If I’m poor, I don’t get listened to like the rich and powerful get listened to,’ they’re right.”
State Rep. Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, the leader of a House Republican minority whose base of support has been shrinking in upscale suburbs and growing in blue collar ones, said he understands why working class voters feel especially unheard.
“I think that working class individuals don’t view government favorably, because they don’t feel it’s doing anything to help them,” Candelora said. “When we think about the services and where government focuses, traditionally we focus on items like the safety net and various healthcare subsidies.”
Gov. Ned Lamont and his Republican challenger, Ryan Fazio, addressed the question of disaffection in the context of their own campaigns, each stressing they work to ensure that voters feel heard.
“I make sure I accept as many invitations as possible, go places every day on the campaign trail, take questions in town halls in an unscripted fashion, because I think the most important part of campaigning is not telling people about yourself, but it’s listening to the public,” Fazio said.
Fazio complained that Lamont is shortchanging voters by not agreeing to more than two televised debates, both of which are taking place after Monday’s start of early voting. The first is Thursday night on WFSB, and the second is Oct. 27 on WTNH.
“I’m looking forward to this debate on Thursday, because voters should have an opportunity to see Democrat and Republican nominees for the office debate each other unscripted and answer the tough questions rather than hide from debates,” Fazio said. “It’s unfortunate that it’s taken until tens of thousands of early votes will already be cast for that debate to happen.”
Lamont said outreach to voters is part of his regular routine, whether he is campaigning or not.
“My job is to get out every time I can, talk to people, answer questions, be in front of folks, and make sure they know that I’m listening,” Lamont said. “And you know, the middle class is getting squeezed, doing everything we can to let you know we hear you, trying to make things better.”
Republican respondents in the poll were more favorably disposed than Democrats or independents towards the national government in Washington, D.C., where the GOP controls the White House and both chambers of Congress. More than 85% of Democrats and independents said they did not trust Washington either “very much” or “at all.”
But even GOP voters were mixed towards the federal government: 9.3% trust it “a lot” and 33.2% “somewhat,” while 40.5% don’t trust it “very much” and 17% not “at all.”
Fazio said he shared their distrust. “I’ve been distrustful of the federal government, whether it’s been Republicans or Democrats, for many, many years.”
The poll was designed by Wesleyan with input from The Connecticut Mirror and The Connecticut Project. It was conducted Sept. 22 to Oct. 7 by YouGov and has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.54 percentage points.
As reported last week, the poll found Lamont with a double-digit lead over Fazio, as have other polls. Fazio, who spoke to reporters Monday afternoon after casting his vote in Greenwich, said his internal polling shows a closer race.
Voters want tax cuts — and more spending
The Wesleyan poll asked voters about Connecticut’s long string of budget surpluses and its fiscal guardrails. Nearly half those polled admitted, before being polled, to knowing “nothing at all” about the caps on spending and a requirement for surpluses over a certain amount to be held in reserve or used to pay down debt.
“If the state were to run a budget surplus this year, which option would you most prefer?” the poll asked.
A tax cut was preferred by 52.3%, while 25.8% opted for increased spending on programs and services and 14.5% favored paying down long-term debt. The rest were unsure.
But a majority of voters also said they wanted increased spending on childcare, K-12 education, healthcare, food assistance, housing, transportation, job training and aid to cities. Those desires varied by political affiliation.
Bare majorities of Republicans supported only increased spending for healthcare (51.4%) and transportation (50.1%). The sharpest partisan difference was on more spending for renewable energy: 65.5% of Democrats favored it, compared to only 15.9% of Republicans.
Majorities of Democrats and Republicans, if to varying degrees, expressed support for tax changes, including a permanent tax credit for low- and middle-class families, a cap on property taxes, elimination of the car tax and increased taxes on millionaires and billionaires. 
More specifically, more than 80% of Democrats favored higher taxes on annual incomes of $250,000 for singles and $500,000 for couples. GOP voters were split, 43% in favor and 46% opposed.
More than 60% of voters favored giving tenants greater protections against rent increases and evictions and requiring communities to build more affordable housing.
And the media?
Connecticut voters were more likely to trust local sources than national.
About 45% trusted national media either somewhat (40.9%) or a lot (4.8%.) Connecticut media was trusted a lot by 12.8% and somewhat by 51%.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Omaha father suing DHHS after records-request estimate of nearly $1M, 2076 deadline
text:
The Safranek family poses for a family photo in Omaha. Back row, from left, Clayton, Tim and Will. Middle row, from left, Linda and Curt. At front is the family dog, Bodie. (Photo courtesy of Curt Safranek)LINCOLN — An Omaha father said he was “dumbfounded” when his request for transparency about a DHHS tool used in determining funding for families with disabilities led to a nearly $1 million estimate to provide records, with expected completion by September 2076.
DHHS now faces a lawsuit over the estimate.
Curt Safranek on Sept. 23 requested copies of communications between Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services employees and the firm Alvarez & Marsal. DHHS in mid-August tapped the firm to independently review Nebraska’s use of its “interRAI” tool in a no-bid contract. The agency reversed and began a competitive bidding process in late August.
Signs urge the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services to protect two Medicaid waivers for aging Nebraskans, those with disabilities and those who need care after a traumatic brain injury. Jan. 14, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Since July 2025, the tool has helped calculate funding for Nebraska families receiving Home and Community-Based Waivers through Medicaid. Twenty-five other states also use the tool.
DHHS estimated the cost of compiling the records requested at $976,263.77 for three employees (at 26,017.5 hours of total work). The expected completion: Sept. 29, 2076. The first eight hours of work on any public records request are free under state law.
In total, DHHS’s estimate breaks down to 650.4 work weeks, if each employee worked 40 hours each week. It would be 12.5 years if the employees worked 24/7 without breaks.
By 2076, Safranek would be 105 years old.
“I actually thought I was reading it wrong,” Safranek said Monday, adding he was “dumbfounded” and parsed out the cost projections to check. “It just didn’t seem real.”
“I mean, ‘What the blank’ was kind of the internal what I said to myself, after I realized, yes, this is actually close to $1 million,” he continued. “It’s just unbelievable.”
DHHS did not respond Monday to a request for comment on Safranek’s lawsuit or an update on the bidding process for the third-party review.
Specifics of the records request
On Sept. 29, Safranek revised his request for records between Jan. 1, 2026, and the date of the revision. Each time, he included 11 search terms seeking to also narrow the records.
The response to the new request estimated it would take about half the first cost and time: $474,383.02 and 12,647.2 working hours. 
The lawsuit states, “little about DHHS’s cost estimate makes sense.”
Tony Green, director of the Division of Disability and Aging in the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, at a meeting of the Nebraska Olmstead Advisory Committee. Dec. 19, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
For example, DHHS says in the initial estimate that an attorney, at $44.54 per hour, for 14,475 hours, would search for, gather, review and, if necessary, redact any responsive records. A paralegal, at a $28.15 rate for 9,650.3 hours, would not search for but would finish similar work.
An “administrative programs officer,” at a pay rate of $31.84 for 1,892.2 hours, would then migrate any responsive records for Safranek’s review.
“DHHS can (and does) run search terms through an automated system that generates responsive documents,” the lawsuit states. “Thus, it is unclear why Curt’s request will take decades to fulfill and cost hundreds of thousands of dollars in fees.”
The lawsuit cites a section of Nebraska’s public records laws to expedite the case “as soon as reasonably possible” and take precedence over all other cases on the court’s trial docket. If Safranek wins, his legal team is also asking that DHHS cover attorney fees and legal costs.
‘What do they have to hide?’
Safranek, a founder of Disability Alliance of Nebraska, is requesting that a Lancaster County District Court judge force DHHS to issue a new public records estimate “reflecting the actual added cost of making the copies available.”
A few hundred Nebraskans came to support a news conference led by Disability Alliance of Nebraska to demand a pause in a funding and services system that launched a year ago. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
Safranek’s son, Will, has an intellectual disability and autism. The family relies on the Medicaid waiver for Will’s daily care, but last year, the interRAI downgraded Will’s funding. But by the time the family got its ruling about Sept. 30, 2025, Safranek said, Will had just been having some behavioral issues, and DHHS’s crisis team had been involved in Will’s case.
“It flew in the face of a reality we didn’t understand, that his funding would go down, them saying, ‘Well, he doesn’t need as much support,’” Safranek said.
Since then, Safranek has sought to get more clarity. He said he found 49 errors that he typed up and included in an appeal. He said it’s been an “uphill battle the whole way.”
Some of his records requests have gone to the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office, led by Attorney General Mike Hilgers. In one case, for the proposed contract between Alvarez & Marsal and DHHS, the agency denied the request because the contract ultimately didn’t move forward. The AG’s Office said DHHS’s denial was “appropriate.”
“I’m obviously fighting for my son, but I’m also fighting for all those others who don’t have a voice or can’t necessarily get in the weeds on these kinds of details to shine a light on what’s going on,” Safranek said. “What do they have to hide? This should not be this hard.”
In the 2027 legislative session, which begins Jan. 6, Safranek said, he will ask for changes in public records laws for all state agencies. For DHHS specifically, he said, that’s so the agency can’t stand behind denials with impunity, at least regarding public records.
DHHS pursuing ‘objective recommendations’
In its Aug. 18 news release announcing the no-bid contract with Alvarez & Marsal Public Sector, DHHS said the goal was for “objective recommendations” to “optimize” the state’s allocation of resources for people receiving Home and Community-Based Waivers.
“The main objectives of the interRAI implementation evaluation are to assess the effectiveness of the implementation process, evaluate the impact on service delivery and outcomes, identify areas for improvement, and ensure the system is meeting program, operational and policy objectives,” DHHS said in the release.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center, holds a newly signed executive order shutting off Medicaid dollars for abortion providers in Nebraska. He is joined by Steve Corsi, CEO of the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, left, and Attorney General Mike Hilgers. Nov. 6, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
DHHS has said the interRAI process has “significantly expanded” access to the Medicaid waivers and that approximately 80% of funding for families has remained steady or increased.
“As we continuously have an increase in the number of Nebraskans receiving waiver services, an independent and in-depth evaluation will allow Nebraska to optimize service delivery and allocation of resources to ensure the needs of all are being met while the program remains sustainable,” Tony Green, director of DHHS’s Division of Disability and Aging, said Aug. 18.
The A&M no-bid partnership faced immediate pushback in part because a former DHHS employee, Kristen Smith, is now a manager with the firm.
By the end of August, DHHS reversed its decision to award the $420,000 contract to A&M outright and said it would enter a competitive bidding process.
‘What’s right for our community’
Safranek said he is concerned about retaliation from the state for speaking out, something he’s heard from others who have been more vocal. He hopes that won’t be the case, “but at the same time, what do we do? Do we just remain quiet? Do we let them do whatever they want?”
He said Nebraskans can continue to push for transparency, demand accountability and vote in the interests of their loved ones. He said he’s gone to Gov. Jim Pillen directly and met with Hilgers’ chief of staff, too.
“We have continued to try to engage with them, and they just won’t do it,” Safranek said. “They’re not listening, and unfortunately, sometimes we have to take these avenues and do what’s right for our community.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Trump heads to Greenville as NC Republicans struggle with early voter turnout
text:
GASTONIA, NORTH CAROLINA - SEPTEMBER 16: U.S. President Donald Trump greets supporters before speaking at a campaign rally with North Carolina Republican Senate candidate, former RNC Chairman Michael Whatley at Gastonia Municipal Airport on September 16, 2026 in Gastonia, North Carolina. Whatley, currently trailing in the polls, will face off against Democratic Senate candidate, former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper in the midterm elections being held on November 3. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)President Donald Trump will hold a campaign rally Tuesday in Greenville, following an appearance Monday by Vice President JD Vance at the other end of the state in Hendersonville. They’re aiming to increase Republican voter turnout in two key Congressional races and North Carolina’s Senate contest.
The high-profile visits come at a challenging time for North Carolina Republicans. Democrats are out to a stronger-than-usual lead in early voting, while Republicans are trailing their 2022 numbers.
Trump and the party are also facing underwater approval ratings in North Carolina and nationally amid higher costs for fuel and groceries and an unpopular war.
A recent Washington Post poll of 2,500 U.S. adults found that 33% approve of Trump’s job performance, while 66% disapprove. The president’s approval rating was the lowest recorded in the poll across his two terms.
The same poll found Democrats leading Republicans by eight percentage points among likely voters in the national generic ballot, a measure of which party voters would like to see control Congress.
The Trump rally will take place at Pitt-Greenville Airport at 7 p.m., two weeks before Election Day. His visit comes as Democrats work to flip the open U.S. Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.
Through Oct. 18, North Carolina voters had cast more than 525,000 ballots, about 36% more than at the same point in the 2022 midterm election, according to the state board of elections.
Registered Democrats accounted for 45% of those ballots, compared with about 19% from registered Republicans. Unaffiliated voters, who make the largest share of North Carolina’s registered voters, cast 34% of the early votes.
Civil rights leader William Barber stops at NCCU to encourage early voters    

Democrats and unaffiliated voters have driven the increase. Democratic ballots were up about 52% from the same point in 2022, while unaffiliated voters’ ballots were up about 60%. Republican ballots were down nearly 9%.
Michael Bitzer, a political scientist at Catawba College who studies North Carolina elections, says the early voting data so far is a strong indicator of voter enthusiasm, although there are many days of early voting still to come.
“The first day of in-person early voting has given us the first clear evidence that the energy surrounding North Carolina’s 2026 midterm election is translating into ballots,” he said.
Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper leads Michael Whatley by 14 percentage points in the U.S. Senate race, according to a recent WRAL/WSOC poll. The poll found 54% of likely voters supporting Cooper and 40% supporting Whatley.
The same poll found that just 37% of likely voters in North Carolina approved of Trump’s job performance, while 60% disapproved.
Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee, has closely aligned his campaign with Trump and his agenda.

name: WyoFile
title: State to grant $48M in ‘Energy Dominance’ funds, asks for public input
text:
Wyoming’s top energy shop wants to grant a total $48 million from the state’s new Energy Dominance Fund to three companies, and it’s asking the public to weigh in on the projects during a comment period that ends Nov. 16.
The Wyoming Energy Authority, which administers the grant and loan program, will forward its recommendations, along with public comments, to Gov. Mark Gordon for his approval.
The three recommended grants include:

$20 million to Nucleon Fuel for its Fort Union Uranium Conversion facility in Campbell County. The Canadian-headquartered company proposes to “convert uranium concentrate into uranium hexafluoride, the feedstock for commercial uranium enrichment,” according to the project summary it submitted to the state.


$15 million to Williams Companies for its Flat Top Compressor Station project in Carbon County. The Tulsa, Oklahoma-based company proposes to build a 15,000-horsepower compressor station and about 8 miles of pipeline “connecting to Williams’ existing Wamsutter gathering system,” according to its project summary.


$13 million to WE Soda for its Westvaco Natural Gas Upgrade project in Sweetwater County. The London-based company wants to build a “high-pressure natural gas supply connection from the Williams’ MountainWest Overthrust Pipeline system,” according to its project summary.

Tata Chemicals’ Director of Governmental Affairs for Wyoming, Jon Conrad checks a bin at the company’s soda ash plant. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
The Wyoming Legislature created the Energy Dominance Fund during the most recent legislative session, authorizing up to $105 million for loans and grants to support energy projects in the state. The awards are to be used as matching funds to leverage money from other government and private entities. The pot of money is filled by severance tax revenue from energy extraction, like coal mining and oil and natural gas development.
The Energy Authority is also recommending a $969,243 grant — from a separate pot of money, the Energy Matching Funds program — to Arcadia Minerals, a Riverton-based company partnered with Canadian firm Meta Critical Minerals. The grant would help support “testing” to characterize “potential saleable rare earth, titanium and zircon products” at the company’s Dugout Creek Project in Washakie County, according to its project summary submitted to the state.
The Energy Dominance projects
Nucleon Fuel is hoping to capitalize on a federal push to expand the nation’s nuclear fuel supply chain, which relies significantly on foreign sources, as well as enrichment facilities outside the U.S.
Domestic uranium production is once again on the rise, and Wyoming is poised to lead the charge with four mines currently in operation, industry leaders say. But once Wyoming mines collect uranium and concentrate it into U-3O8, or yellowcake, it must be shipped out of state for processing. The next step is to convert U-3O8 concentrate into the gas hexafluoride (UF₆). There’s only one facility in the U.S. that does that, and it’s in southern Illinois.
Nucleon’s uranium conversion facility would bring that capability to the Fort Union Industrial Park north of Gillette. The new facility would have the capacity to convert about 15,000 tons annually, adding another link in the nuclear fuel supply chain in the state, according to the company. The plant could be in operation by 2032, it said.
A gas gathering hub near Opal on May 2, 2014. (Ryan Dorgan/Casper Star-Tribune)
Demand for domestic natural gas is also on the rise, and Williams controls one of the largest gas-pipeline matrices in the nation. The company plans to increase gas production in the Wamsutter area, noting that, without expansion, “existing gathering and compression infrastructure is projected to become insufficient, potentially resulting in constrained production, reduced operational efficiency and delayed energy development,” it said.
Not far away, WE Soda is among a handful of trona mining and soda ash producers in southwest Wyoming hoping to expand production. To survive global market headwinds Wyoming operations need to become as efficient as possible, the company recently told WyoFile. Part of WE Soda’s effort is to shift from coal to natural gas to fuel its boilers, which are used to process trona to soda ash. 
“The project will help maintain the competitiveness of Wyoming-produced soda ash by providing a cost-effective and reliable thermal energy source for current operations in time to replace the economical local coal which will be depleted by the end 2027,” the company said. “Conversion to natural gas supports emissions reductions and creates a pathway for future facility expansions that could significantly increase soda ash and specialty products production.”

name: VTDigger
title: Windsor, no longer a prison town, still maintains a connection to people who die in state custody
text:
Two flat granite stones engraved with the names of men who died while incarcerated at Southern State Correctional Facility are set in the grass at the end of a row of white crosses. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger
WINDSOR — Tucked behind a Windsor neighborhood and marked only by a small green-and-white sign sits a nearly 60-acre expanse of the state’s incarceration history going back 150 years.
In the shadow of a forested band of pines at the back of Ascutney Cemetery stand four rows of painted white wooden crosses with small black nameplates. Each bears the name of a person who died while incarcerated in a Vermont prison, and whose body went unclaimed by their family or next of kin.
“There’s a certain sadness to it in a way, that nobody cared and that’s why they wound up here,” Mike Coxon, a former superintendent at Southeast State Correctional Facility, said in a 1993 interview with the Burlington Free Press.
Although Windsor’s last prison closed in 2017, the Department of Corrections continues to own and maintain the burial lot at Ascutney Cemetery, where 42 marked plots hold the remains of people who died in state custody. Now, the department is working to correct errors in burial records and plans to replace the deteriorating wooden crosses with permanent gravestones.
The most recent burial in Ascutney Cemetery took place last year. Gregory Penn had been receiving palliative care at Southern State Correctional Facility and was serving a sentence of 40 years to life when he died at age 68.
His is one of only two newer stone markers in a field of painted crosses, some of which are cracked or rotten in places. 
Many existing markers have errors in dates or misspelled names due to inconsistent record keeping practices, something Joshua Rutherford, deputy director for the facilities division of the Department of Corrections, has been working to correct using the department’s Offender Management System database.
“I’ve arranged the last two burials there, and then I’ve been trying to catch up and correct some of the records,” he said.

A wooden cross at Ascutney Cemetery is reinforced with a stake and screws as a makeshift repair until it can be replaced. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger

The state asks people who are incarcerated about their end-of-life plans, particularly older people serving long sentences and those who may have medical issues. Most deaths occur at Southern State Correctional Facility in nearby Springfield, Rutherford said, which houses the department’s elderly and infirm population.
“(We) have those conversations with them in advance,” Rutherford said. “‘Who do you want us to call? Who might be willing to claim your body? Where would you like it to go?’ Those sorts of things.”
In cases where nobody steps forward, the department needs a process to bury a person in a manner that is “respectful and appropriate,” Rutherford said. The prison plot in Ascutney Cemetery is considered the place of last resort for people who die in Vermont’s prisons.
“It’s been that way for well over 100 years now,” he said.
A final resting place
The lot itself was purchased by the directors of the former maximum security state prison in Windsor in 1875, according to a note published in the Vermont Watchman that year:
“The old graveyard within the walls of the prison being a scandal, having been dug over and over again, they bought a lot in the town cemetery, and the prisoners now have decent burial, much to their satisfaction; for even convicts have some human feelings, and like to think that they will have a Christian burial when they die.”
The cemetery’s relationship with Windsor’s prisons extended well beyond burials. For decades, people serving sentences at Southeast State Correctional Facility, the prison farm in Windsor, maintained the grounds.
Mike Coxon grew up across the street from the former maximum security state prison in Windsor where his father worked and where, in the prison yard surrounded by high walls, the first people who died while incarcerated were buried.
Coxon went on to work at the prison himself until it closed in 1975, and served as superintendent at Southeast State Correctional Facility until he retired from the department in 2002.
“We had a lot of workers. We were literally doing maybe $60,000 worth of work for the town, and for free,” Coxon said. “We did the cemetery. We painted the high school. We built the docks for the swimming area.
“You name it, we did it.”
The Southeast State work crews typically consisted of older people serving long sentences, Coxon said, since they were less likely to cause problems for supervising officers. People could work at their own pace under guard supervision and didn’t have a quota to meet like they would working in the sign shop or printing license plates.

The former Southeast State Correctional Facility in Windsor on October 18, 2026. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger 

Coxon would go out and observe the men as they worked, some of whom hadn’t had a personal visitor in 10 years.
“Often, they said that they were doing something very useful,” Coxon said. “You don’t see the usefulness on the license plates or the road signs or the printing.”
Logging trees, clearing brush and mowing grass at the cemetery gave the men a chance to get outside and offered a change of pace for the older people who were incarcerated.
“It broke it up a lot just being out,” Coxon said, for both the men on the crew and those who guarded them. One longtime work crew supervisor, Dave Bellini, was said to have “done 30 years sitting in the pickup truck.”
Tom Gillam is the cemetery commissioner for the city of Rutland and has some experience with burials of people who died while incarcerated. He worked to revitalize a former House of Corrections burial plot in Rutland from the turn of the last century that was abandoned by the state.Gillam recalled that the grounds in Ascutney Cemetery benefited from Coxon’s attention during his years at Southeast State.
“But Mike Coxon took a lot of pride in the cemetery when he was superintendent. It was maintained very well,” Gillam said.
Coxon also knew several of the people who are now buried in Ascutney Cemetery, and made attempts to contact their families when the men died while in prison. Some families declined to accept responsibility for their remains. Other people who were incarcerated had very little connection to the outside world, with no kin to contact.
“We asked him for a list of people we could contact,” Coxon said of one man, Stanley Bentley, who had been convicted of child molestation and died of cancer in 1992. “It was very strange. He gave us some names. Fictitious,” said Coxon. “We didn’t even have his right social security number.”
Coxon would go through the phone book in search of the deceased’s relatives or post obituaries in the newspaper, sometimes reaching family members who had long since lost contact.
“We did reach a couple of families,” Coxon said. “They said, ‘Oh, that’s my great uncle.’ That’s it. They weren’t ashamed. They just said, ‘We don’t — we don’t have any contact.”
The cemetery also became a place where Windsor schoolchildren encountered the town’s incarceration history.
Michael Quinn taught science at Harford Middle School in the 80s and brought his eighth-grade class to Ascutney Cemetery in October each year. The prison lot was always a draw for them, Quinn said.
“There was a fence around it at the time, so they had a lot of questions about why those graves were made separate from the rest,” he said.
Quinn told the class about the lot’s history, and gave them context for class discussions.

Louis Meeker was the second person buried in the Ascutney Cemetery prison lot. He is also referred to in historical documents as “Almon” and the spelling of his last name is up for some debate. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger

One student, Quinn said, lingered among the crosses with her hood up and her back to the group instead of joining the class on the bus when it was time to leave.
“She’s standing there, and she’s looking down, not moving. It was not like her,” Quinn said. When he approached, the student was in tears.
“She told me then – and later, in her writing – that she was adopted, and she realized that she had something in common with these inmates. They both were abandoned,” Quinn said. “This perfect kid who should have come just like that was held in place by the draw of being among the abandoned. I’ll never forget that.”
Permanent record, etched in stone
The fence that once stood to segregate the burials of people who had been incarcerated from the rest of the dead is now long gone. 
Work crews from Windsor stopped mowing in Ascutney Cemetery when the prison closed in 2017. The department also paused its statewide work programs during the Covid-19 pandemic, leading other cemeteries, such as Montpelier’s 35-acre Green Mount Cemetery, to let grass grow wild.
In 2023, the Department of Corrections fully ended its “community restitution program” across the state. No more work crews come to the cemetery, but the burials continue to connect Windsor to people who die in state custody and whose remains go unclaimed.
“The last time I saw it was wooden crosses,” said Tom Gillam, who is also the president of the Vermont Old Cemetery Association. He sees cemeteries as “cultural geography,” and emphasized the historical importance of a permanent marker. “Even a field stone – something – just to say that these people once existed.”

A man walks his dog through Ascutney Cemetery near the lot owned by the Department of Corrections and used as a burial site for persons who die and whose remains are unclaimed by their next of kin. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger

At Ascutney Cemetery, Rutherford said that as budget and time allow, the wooden crosses will all eventually be replaced with permanent gravestones, which are less prone to decay and information loss.
“1875 and 2026 are very different time frames, and the assumption that, you know, everyone wants or even desires a Christian burial, whatever that may mean, is less current now than it would have been then,” Rutherford said.The replacement markers would also eliminate the religious symbolism that has marked the graves since the state first purchased the lot more than a century ago.
“The opportunity, at the same time, to move to something non-denominational, recognizing that not everyone we bury may be Christian or may be practicing at all, just seems more respectful in this day and age.”
