name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana early voting takes place from Tuesday to Oct. 27 (minus Sunday)
text:
Louisiana’s early voting period runs from Tuesday until Oct. 27 for the Nov. 3 election. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana’s early voting period opens Tuesday and closes a week later on Oct. 27 for the Nov. 3 election. Early voting locations will be open from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. every day except Sunday. 

Every parish has at least one early voting location, which can be found on the Secretary of State’s website. Louisiana residents don’t need to provide a reason for voting early in-person, as is required in some other states.

Voters will be asked to provide photo identification or sign a voter affidavit if they do not have a photo ID. Accepted forms of photo ID  include a Louisiana’s driver’s license, a state ID card, a military ID with name and photo, or another form of photo ID with photo and signature. 

For people voting by mail, the final day to request a ballot from their local registrar of voters is Oct. 30. Mail ballots must be received by Nov. 2, with the exception of those from military members and persons overseas.
The Nov. 3 ballot features races for the U.S. Senate, Louisiana’s six U.S. House seats, 10 state constitutional amendments and several local offices.  
Any runoffs necessary after Nov. 3 will be decided in a Dec. 12 election, for which early voting takes place Nov. 28 through Dec. 5.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: Low Medicaid reimbursement rates stunt pediatric eye care
text:
Physicians in Connecticut have long flagged low Medicaid reimbursement rates as a barrier to providing treatment to low-income people seeking medical care. For specialty care, the issue is exacerbated.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Katy Golvala to discuss her article, “CT kids with Medicaid coverage can face long waits for eye care,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read the story here.
WSHU: Hi, Katy. What prompted you to get into this story?
KG: Hi, Ebong. I’ve covered health at the Capitol for several years, and every year one issue comes up as the most important to address: Medicaid reimbursement rates. And Medicaid reimbursement rates refer to how much the state pays doctors for seeing patients who are on the state’s Medicaid program, which is, you know, the government health insurance program for people with incomes that fall below certain limits. And every year we hear legislators and doctors come to the capital and say the state does not pay us enough. We’re actually, in some cases, losing money every time we see them, and that results in doctors opting out of seeing these patients, which in turn means they have fewer options available for where to receive care, and so I wanted to take a look at this issue through the lens of one specialty, pediatric ophthalmology, where that shortage is, you know, particularly dire.
WSHU: Now, tell us about Cassidy Friedl and her son Luca.
KG: Yeah, so Cassidy, when Luca was about six months old, started noticing that one of his eyes was drifting inwards, and she took him to his pediatrician. And the pediatrician recommended that he go see a pediatric ophthalmologist. And these are specialists who go beyond what optometrists can do. They are M.D.s. They can perform surgery, and you know, if your child is dealing with a particularly acute issue with their eye, these are the doctors that you typically want to see. And Cassidy called around, and she was just hearing that the wait times were very long. And eventually, in March, she got an appointment with a doctor who we also spoke with, Cara DeBenedictis, and she was told that the wait was going to be about nine months because Doctor DeBenedictis only had a certain number of slots available for patients with Medicaid, which is the coverage that Cassidy and Luca have.
WSHU: Now, Cassidy and Luca pretty much fall into a group that is the larger number of children in Connecticut who are on the HUSKY program. Correct?
KG: Yeah. So HUSKY covers about half of kids in the state, which, you know, are overrepresented. So Medicaid HUSKY covers about a quarter of people in the state, but half of children.
WSHU: Three-quarters of them are Black and Hispanic children.
KG: So actually, it’s that three-quarters of Black and Hispanic children in Connecticut are covered by Medicaid.
WSHU: Three-quarters of Black and Hispanic kids are covered. Wow. So we’ve been trying to grapple with this problem; what are the solutions? And when you talked with the Lamont administration, what did they say?
KG: So the Lamont administration first said that this is a national problem, not a Connecticut problem, and this is true. There are shortages of pediatric ophthalmologists all over the country. I believe one study found that 90% of counties do not have a pediatric ophthalmologist. There are states without a pediatric ophthalmologist at all, and so you know Connecticut is lucky in that we do have some providers. The state says that there are 21 ophthalmology groups enrolled in Medicaid in Connecticut. They did not clarify whether those groups see children or whether they’re currently accepting new Medicaid patients, and so the pediatric ophthalmologists I spoke to said that the number of pediatric ophthalmologists is around 10 in the state overall, but only five of those accept Medicaid patients. So basically, the Lamont administration said, you know, this is an issue with a national shortage of pediatric ophthalmologists, and what the doctors said was that yes, that is true, but that problem is worse in Connecticut for people who are covered by Medicaid because, you know, people with private insurance presumably have 10 options for doctors to go see, whereas people with Medicaid only have about five.
WSHU: And also, the Lamont administration seems to want to pressure private industry to cover more of their employees, and say that will make it possible for the state to reimburse more. Could you just explain what the thinking is?
KG: So basically, what the Lamont administration is saying, and this is part of Governor Lamont’s campaign, is that businesses need to offer comprehensive health coverage to their employees so that they don’t have to rely on the state Medicaid program, and so the big businesses need to provide comprehensive health insurance for their employees, so that taxpayers aren’t footing the bill for health coverage for those employees.
WSHU: And advocates are also pointing to the fact that the state brings up the pay for doctors.
KG: Yes, what advocates are saying is the state needs to increase the amount that it pays to doctors to see patients with Medicaid, and then more doctors, they say, will accept Medicaid, and then that will help to address some of the shortage.
WSHU: And now Medicaid itself takes funding from both the federal and the state, and the federal government has been cutting back on how much it’s spending on healthcare.
KG: Yeah, so it does seem like legislators have an appetite to again propose legislation to increase the Medicaid reimbursement rates, but Medicaid is definitely going into the session facing some pretty big hurdles. One is that the program has had massive overruns, so it’s gone over budget every year for the past several years, and legislators are also trying to address that. And while it might be good to pay doctors more, that would mean the state spends more on the program instead of finding areas where it can cut back.
WSHU: In the meantime, Connecticut children on Medicaid will have longer and longer wait times to see a specialist.
KG: I think that is what you would hear from doctors and advocates who say that the rates need to increase. Yes.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: GO-NORTH announces rural EMS program during RFK Jr. visit
text:
U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks to reporters about a new rural EMS program funded by the federal Rural Health Transformation Program at the New Hampshire Fire Academy in Concord on Oct. 16, 2026. At left is GO-NORTH Director Donnalee Lozeau and at right is Mark Wholey, director of the New Hampshire Division of Fire Standards and Training and EMS. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)While U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was visiting New Hampshire last week, GO-NORTH announced a new $11 million project aimed at strengthening the state’s emergency medical services.
The project, officials said at a Concord press conference Friday, will provide rural EMS and ambulance providers new equipment and technology, workforce training and partnership assistance for neighboring communities to share resources. It will also expand mobile integrated health, a style of care delivery that provides healthcare in out-of-hospital environments, such as emergency response contexts or community events. Officials said it will bring five new mobile integrated health programs, including in the Concord area and the North Country.
In Concord visit, RFK Jr. renews attack on hep B vaccine that inspired state anti-vaccine bill

“The amount of impact that that’s going to have is significant,” Mark Wholey, director of the New Hampshire Division of Fire Standards and Training and EMS, said, adding that the biggest goal is to relieve strain on emergency rooms from patients who, because they lack primary care, become repeat patients. “Our hope is that the folks that enter back into the EMS system and end up at our emergency rooms, which plague the emergency rooms and slow down the care with their acute need, can get that need met, as the secretary said, out-of-hospital. That’s our goal.”
The project will be funded by money the federal government has already committed to New Hampshire. In late 2025, New Hampshire received $205 million through the Rural Health Transformation Program, and it expects to receive similar amounts every year through 2030. Over the past year, GO-NORTH — the office established to manage the money in New Hampshire — has been developing plans to distribute it. On Friday, the officials announced they were allocating $11 million of that money to this project. GO-NORTH is partnering with the Foundation for Healthy Communities, one of its five designated hubs, for the project.
Kennedy praised the project, which was developed by New Hampshire officials, saying it “is one of the projects that we think should be a model nationwide.”
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, who also ran for president in 2024 and is the nephew of former President John F. Kennedy, spoke during a press conference in Concord May 29, 2026. He announced new initiatives to fight Lyme disease. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
During his visit, GO-NORTH also received strong signals ahead of federal rescoring. When Congress established the Rural Health Transformation Program, it mandated annual reassessments. If the federal government determines states are making progress in distributing the money effectively, the government will continue providing funding. If not, it’ll cut funding. Donnalee Lozeau, GO-NORTH’s director, told the Bulletin earlier this month she was “cautiously optimistic” about the rescoring. Friday, Kennedy gave an even stronger endorsement.
“New Hampshire has been an extraordinary partner on the Rural Health Transformation Program,” Kennedy said. “It had an exemplary application, which is why it got $204 million, which is disproportionately high compared to most states, and in its execution of the program, it’s also been exemplary.”
Kennedy, the nephew of the late President John F. Kennedy, ran for president in 2024 but dropped out and endorsed now-President Donald Trump, who ultimately appointed him health secretary. The divisive figure has been visiting states with toss-up elections — like New Hampshire’s U.S. Senate race between John Sununu and Chris Pappas — throughout 2026. A senior White House official told Politico earlier this year that Kennedy’s visits were part of a strategy to promote popular pieces of his agenda and strengthen Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections. In recent months, the secretary has also visited Virginia, Iowa and Nebraska. 
This is Kennedy’s second visit to Concord in six months. In late May, he came to announce federal funding for Lyme disease treatment, public awareness and research.
The Rural Health Transformation Program was created through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Critics of the sprawling omnibus legislation argued its cuts to Medicaid and other health programs would decimate the country’s already struggling rural health economy. To remediate that, the Republicans behind the bill created the Rural Health Transformation Program, which is distributing $50 billion to states over five years. Critics point out that this figure is dwarfed by the estimated $991 billion that experts expect (per KFF) the bill to cut from Medicaid over the next 10 years.
EMS workers sit on an ambulance ahead of a ceremonial bill signing in Nashua on July 31, 2025. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Hurricane Isaias leaves $582M in insured damage; states seeks $237M from FEMA
text:
Roofing material lies on the ground after Hurricane Isaias tore it off as it passed through Destin, Florida, on Oct. 10, 2026. The storm made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with Category 2 winds. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)In the week following Hurricane Isaias’ landfall in Destin, initial damage estimates reported by insurers and state officials show that the storm financially walloped northwest Florida.
State insurance officials report that as of Oct. 15, 46,509 claims had been filed with insurance companies for residential, commercial, auto, and other losses worth nearly $582 million in damage.
Hurricane Isaias made landfall Oct. 9 as a Category 2 hurricane and is blamed for at least six deaths in Florida.
DeSantis says Florida Isaias death toll reaches six; thousands still without power

Worries initially focused on the storm surge feared at the Destin landfall but the real damage from the fast-forming hurricane stemmed from its winds, which toppled trees, knocked down power lines, and blew roofs off houses.
The majority of the claims filed with insurers came from the state’s three westernmost counties in the Panhandle.
 Santa Rosa County accounts for 22,894 of those claims, followed by Escambia with 13,677, and Okaloosa County with 4,334.
Florida Office of Insurance Regulation (OIR) data show that about 87% of the residential claims remained open and no payment had been made as of Oct. 15. 
Residential claims include homeowners’, dwelling, mobile homeowners’, and commerical residential policies.
Nearly 12% of the residential claims, or 4,773, filed have been closed. Of those, 712 were closed with payment and 4,061 with no payment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Homeowners
Specifically most of the residential claims (35,014) filed are for homeowners and homeowners policies account for ($558.6 million) of the overall insured damages.
Data show that no payment has been made in 86% of the open homeowners claims that have been filed. Of the homeowner’s claims that were closed with no payment, the majority (3,319) were for “administrative reasons,” a broad category that includes duplicate claims, claims opened in error, incorrectly filed claims, and claims closed for “lack of cooperation/communication by insured.”
The data are derived from reports insurance companies are required to file with the OIR on their estimated and paid losses.
In addition to residential claims data the OIR report also contains data for business interruption claims, private passenger auto claims and commercial auto claims.
 FEMA request

Meanwhile, the administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis requested roughly $237 million in federal disaster aid from FEMA for debris removal, public infrastructure, and emergency protective measures for 15 Florida counties.
The state Department of Emergency Management told the Phoenix Saturday that preliminary assessments have identified nearly 1,000 damaged residences in eight counties that could qualify for individual FEMA assistance.
The request isn’t static and DEM is continuing to work with local, state, and federal agencies to identify any additional needs, she said.
“Damage assessments remain ongoing, and determining the full extent of storm-related damages and housing needs could take several months,”  DEM Director of Communications Stephanie Hartman said in an email to the Phoenix.
The DeSantis administration submitted the request for a major disaster with FEMA Thursday, Oct. 15, the governor said.
The 15 counties that could qualify for public assistance if approved by President Donald Trump are Bay, Calhoun, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gulf, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Liberty, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Wakulla, Walton, and Washington.
People who experienced damage to their homes in the following eight counties could qualify for  individual assistance: Bay, Escambia, Gulf, Holmes, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Walton, and Washington.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Attorney General clears Senatobia police officer who shot, killed Kohen Wiley
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Joseph Cranney is a reporter with the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The New York Times. Mukta Joshi is an investigative reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow examining immigration and criminal justice issues. 
The Mississippi Attorney General’s office cleared the officer who shot and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley at a Walmart in Senatobia in June, according to a news release Monday.Many details of the incident remain unknown, and it wasn’t immediately clear if or when law enforcement would release footage from the incident. The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation initially said police fired at a vehicle that was driving toward officers in the Walmart parking lot, “almost striking” one, after a pair of women were accused of stealing a pack of diapers.Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch “found the use of force was justified,” Monday’s brief statement said. The statement said “one officer” was involved, though it didn’t name the officer or share any more details about what happened. Other records identify the officer as Sgt. Hunter Foster.A lawyer for the toddler’s family in July released a photo showing the car’s front side window shot out, which the lawyer said suggested police weren’t in the vehicle’s direct path.Wiley was in the front passenger seat in his mother’s arms when Foster, who is white, opened fire. Wiley was Black, along with his mother and the vehicle’s driver, who was also injured by gunfire.Vellesiya Wiley, Kohen Wiley’s mother, said in an interview in early October that she was never interviewed by MBI agents. Veronica Roberson, the toddler’s grandmother, said Monday she learned of the attorney general’s decision when she logged onto Facebook, and no state or local law enforcement official has reached out to the family.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Conservative legal organization sues – again — over constitutionality of DFL’s 2024 omnibus
text:
House Minority Leader Lisa Demuth and Senate Minority Leader Mark Johnson spoke at a press conference shortly after the legislative session ended on May 20, 2024. The GOP leaders denounced the 1,400 page omnibus bill, which they displayed on the podium and was passed by the Democratic majority in the closing moments of the 2024 legislative session. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer.)A conservative legal organization is representing homebuilders in a lawsuit aimed at invalidating parts of — if not all of — a 1,400 page mega-bill passed by the DFL-controlled Legislature in the chaotic final minutes of the 2024 legislative session. 
The Minnesota Constitution requires that bills address a single subject, and that the title of the bill reflects that subject. Democratic-Farmer-Labor lawmakers assembled and passed the omnibus in the final shambolic hours of the 2024 legislative session following days of filibustering by Republican lawmakers, who shouted “Shame!” and “Follow the rules!” on the House floor as the DFL voted on the bill. 
The bill contained a wide range of new laws, from minimum pay rates for Uber and Lyft drivers to increased penalties for straw gun purchases and changes to the state’s paid leave law. The bill’s title was more than five pages long.
Previous plaintiffs suing over the same issue have already succeeded in getting parts of the bill overturned, and the continued litigation is a cautionary tale for future legislatures that try to cram all their bills into a mega-bill. Although the 2024 example is the most extreme in memory, legislative majorities of both parties have often loaded bills into mega-bills out of legislative and political expediency. 
Central Minnesota Builders Association and Rochester Area Builders Inc. are the plaintiffs in the lawsuit filed Monday by attorneys with the Upper Midwest Law Center. The lawsuit challenges the construction industry regulations in the bill, including restrictions on the use of independent contractors; new registration rules for construction companies; and, a requirement that the state residential energy code reduce net energy consumption by 70% by 2038.
The lawsuit asks that a state judge invalidate the entirety of the 2024 bill under the Constitution’s single subject clause — or to at least strike down its construction-related laws.
“This mega-omnibus bill creates an earthquake of increased costs and opportunities for fraud in our state,” said Nicholas Nelson, an attorney with the Upper Midwest Law Center. 
The Upper Midwest Law Center, representing the Minnesota Gun Owners Caucus, already successfully overturned one major policy provision in the bill: a ban on binary triggers, which increase the rate of fire of semiautomatic firearms. 
In that case, Ramsey County District Judge Leonardo Castro wrote that “the 2024 Omnibus Bill violates the Single Subject and Title Clause, because, at best, it contains many non-germane parts, and at worst, has no identifiable common theme.”
The ruling set the stage for further lawsuits from conservative organizations challenging other portions of the bill. Nelson said Monday’s lawsuit is the fifth such case.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee GOP senator says ‘no basis’ to expel her from caucus
text:
Sen. Janice Bowling, R-Tullahoma, says her Senate colleagues displeased with her endorsement of independent candidate David Hatley in the governor's race don't have the votes to oust her from the GOP Caucus. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee Republican senator says the Senate GOP caucus has “no basis” to expel her for endorsing an independent gubernatorial candidate as a Senate speakership vote approaches.
Sen. Janice Bowling, a 14-year lawmaker from Tullahoma, told the Lookout that she is not concerned about a potential vote by the Senate Republican Caucus to remove her because she backed independent David Hatley rather than the Republican nominee, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, in the governor’s race.
Even though the endorsement could lead to expulsion from the Tennessee Republican Party, Bowling said the caucus has “no basis” to kick her out and “no legal mechanism” to take action against her for the endorsement of Hatley. 
Bowling, who was re-elected in 2024, is expected to vote for Sen. Paul Bailey over Majority Leader Jack Johnson in the Nov. 10 Senate speaker election, which is tight in the 27-member caucus.

In a Facebook post, Bowling said she became comfortable with Hatley after meeting with him. He casts himself as a “conservative” and said he is running as an independent because he didn’t meet the party’s requirement of voting in the last three Republican primaries. Hatley, who is drawing the attention of the Blackburn campaign through negative ads, had his voting rights reinstated after being convicted of bank fraud some decades ago as he tried to start a business.
Bowling told the Lookout that Senate District 16 voters approve of her decision to endorse Hatley rather than Blackburn.
Yet the Tennessee Republican Party has “sole discretion” to disqualify any person from running as a Republican candidate if it determines the person doesn’t meet standards such as voting in GOP primaries, supporting the party or participating in Republican events. The party’s bylaws don’t address Senate Republican Caucus rules.
But Scott Golden, chair of the Tennessee Republican Party, said in a recent statement that failure to back the party’s nominee “absolutely endangers” any Republican’s good standing. Thus, the endorsement of Hatley also could work against Bowling if she seeks another term in 2028.
Caucus members started discussing the possibility of expelling Bowling immediately after she publicly backed Hatley in early October.
Tennessee Senate leaders predict no move to expel member before speaker vote

Senate Republican Caucus leaders told the Lookout last week they don’t expect to take up a potential vote to expel Bowling before the Nov. 10 caucus elections in which the group, which holds a supermajority in the 33-member chamber, will decide who replaces outgoing Senate Speaker Randy McNally. The Senate speaker also serves as lieutenant governor, first in the line of succession in case the governor is incapacitated or removed from office.
Johnson and Sen. Ken Yager of Kingston, who chairs the Republican caucus, told the Lookout last week they don’t plan to take a vote that would change the caucus membership before the Senate speaker vote. But they didn’t rule out a vote afterward to oust Bowling.
Sen. Ferrell Haile of Gallatin, the Senate speaker pro tem, predicted no vote would be taken to expel Bowling. 
Such a move is likely to anger several caucus members. And when Bowling talked to the Lookout, she said, “I don’t think they have the votes.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Data center Project Jupiter air quality permit hearing set for early December
text:
Residents from across New Mexico protest a pending air quality permit application for the Project Jupiter data center outside the New Mexico Environment Department in Santa Fe on Aug. 21, 2026. A new hearing officer presiding over the case scheduled a hearing on the permit to begin on Dec. 7. (Danielle Prokop for Source NM)After hitting several bumps along the way, a hearing over whether the New Mexico Environment Department should approve an air quality permit for the Project Jupiter data center’s proposed power source is scheduled to begin in early December.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Newly filed documents show that Hearing Officer James Browning, a retired federal judge, scheduled the hearing to begin at 9 a.m. on Dec. 7 and to “continue as necessary.” The hearing will take place at the Sunland Park Multi-Generational Center and the first day will be dedicated exclusively to public comments, according to a supplemental document filed with Browning’s scheduling order.
After that, Browning wrote that he will set aside one hour each day for public comment.
Browning filed the documents to the NMED docket on Friday afternoon after holding a public meeting with attorneys representing Project Jupiter’s developers, community members and environmental organizations.
During the meeting, Browning acknowledged the several detours the proceedings have taken so far. The previous hearing officer presiding over the case, who recused himself in August, had rescheduled the hearing after saying in a meeting that he wouldn’t. The New Mexico Supreme Court later paused the hearing while it reviewed anti-Project Jupiter legal challenges from environmental advocacy groups.
Colin Cox, a New Mexico-based attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity, raised concerns about the timeline during a scheduling meeting last week.
Specifically, he pointed to figures contained in newly released NMED documents that indicate recent modeling showed the potential for Project Jupiter’s proposed power system to emit a much higher concentration of pollutants than previously forecasted. Oracle recently announced plans to cut its proposed emissions and, Cox said, experts who plan to testify at the hearing will need time to review the changes and the thousands of pages of documents in question.
“I’m sensitive to that. I’m also thinking we need to get something on the calendar,” Browning responded. “If everybody agrees that it’s not workable, then I will be receptive.”
Browning also scheduled an Oct. 26 hearing on whether to dismiss the case in light of the new pollutant figures and an Oct. 29 hearing on whether to allow discovery in the upcoming hearing.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Democrat in lieutenant governor’s race hopes to bridge divides, fix Oklahoma’s big problems
text:
From left, lieutenant governor candidates T.W. Shannon and Kelly Forbes are pictured. (Provided photos)OKLAHOMA CITY — The Democratic candidate running for lieutenant governor hopes to reshape the oft-ignored role into one that brings Oklahomans together to create policies that can help solve the biggest issues affecting the state.
Kelly Forbes said he wants to change the perception that the job of lieutenant governor is merely to fill in for the state’s chief executive when they’re out of town or break a tie in the rare event of a deadlock in the Republican-dominated state Senate. 
“People would joke with me sometimes, the role of lieutenant governor feels like you just pick up the phone and you call and you say ‘Hey, is the governor alive today? Yeah, perfect. All right,’ and they hang up and don’t do anything whenever we could be out and about and being a representative of people,” he said.
Forbes, 42, of Oklahoma City, will face Republican T.W. Shannon on the Nov. 3 ballot for lieutenant governor. Matt Pinnell, who has held the role for the past eight years, cannot run again due to term limits. Republicans currently control every statewide elected office and the last Democrat to win election to the lieutenant governor’s office was Jari Askins. Her term ended in 2011.
Shannon, 48, who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump, declined interview requests earlier this month to talk about his priorities.
Shannon, of Oklahoma City, was elected to the state House in 2006. In 2013 became the first Chickasaw and Black legislator to serve as Oklahoma’s House speaker. He held the position for about a year before stepping down as speaker to run for U.S. Senate. He’s launched two unsuccessful bids for U.S. Senate, losing to U.S. Sen. James Lankford and former U.S. Sen. Markwayne Mullin.
A former community bank CEO, Shannon’s campaign website says he serves as a “senior advisor” in Trump’s administration. Shannon plans to focus on “growing Oklahoma’s economy and creating opportunity,” according to his campaign website.
This marks the first run for office for Forbes, 42, of Oklahoma City.
The owner of an education consulting business, Forbes is fluent in Spanish and holds a doctorate degree in education and administrative leadership.
He said his education background will be critical because educators and support staff make up the state’s largest workforce and everyone that enters the workforce first receives an education, he said.
If elected, Forbes said he will continue to travel the state to meet with constituents when not at the Capitol or attending board or commission meetings.
The lieutenant governor chairs the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Commission, a nine-member board that oversees the Tourism and Recreation Department. Tourism is the state’s third largest industry, Forbes said.
The lieutenant governor also serves on the state Board of Equalization which, among other things, determines how much money the Legislature has to appropriate.
They also serve on the Commissioners of the Land governing body, which manages state lands and mineral interests. The board distributes over $100 million each year to public education.
They also chair the Oklahoma Film and Music Advisory Commission, which advises on the state’s film and music incentive programs.
And they serve on the Oklahoma Linked Deposit Review Board, which helps farmers and ranchers and other entrepreneurs connect with local banks to help obtain lower-cost loans.
Forbes said the next lieutenant governor has the opportunity to continue the great work that Pinnell has been doing in tourism as “an ambassador and cheerleader for the state” but also envisions the role as one that ensures that the voices of Oklahomans are being leveraged and represented in the Capitol.
Forbes said as he’s toured the state, he’s discovered officials aren’t doing enough to help communities have access to broadband internet. Community leaders said that federal internet maps that show connectivity rates are inaccurate, which hinders economic development, education, public safety and healthcare outcomes, he said.
He’s also heard complaints that the Legislature has been passing unfunded mandates down on municipal governments, which is something he believes needs to be addressed. He believes the lieutenant governor, whose scope of power extends across the legislative and executive branches, can help bridge that divide.
Forbes said Oklahomans have delivered a consistent message on his trips: They just want people who can work together to solve the “big needs” confronting the state.
“There’s so much division right now, and people are really just tired of that,” Forbes said. “They just need us to be able to do hard, good work to make sure that we’re always asking ourselves: Is this the best decision that we’re making for Oklahomans?”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Max Engling claims defamation over driving allegations in new Beau Bayh ad
text:
Max Engling speaks with reporters after winning the Republican secretary of state nomination on June 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Republican Max Engling is threatening to sue Democrat Beau Bayh over a new television advertisement in their increasingly bitter Indiana secretary of state election campaign.
Engling alleges that references in the ad that he had been convicted of reckless driving is “defamation on its face.”
The Bayh campaign is defending the commercial, which features a uniformed sheriff’s deputy saying Engling “has been convicted and investigated at least eight times for reckless driving and reckless behavior.”
Engling’s campaign acknowledged in a weekend statement that his driving record “includes eight speeding tickets, the most recent from 16 years ago, all traffic infractions, not misdemeanor charges or convictions.”
“Beau Bayh can spend money repeating this claim, but he cannot produce a reckless driving charge against me because there isn’t one,” Engling said in the statement. “If Beau has evidence, release it. Otherwise, pull the ad and tell Hoosiers the truth.”
A search of online Indiana court records show Engling with eight speeding tickets in Hamilton or Marion counties between 2006 and 2010 — when he was 19 to 23 years old — but no other court cases.
The Bayh campaign provided the Capital Chronicle with a timeline supporting its ad that also included an expunged misdemeanor criminal reckless case from 2007 in which Engling threw eggs at passing vehicles from a U.S. 31 overpass in Carmel, along with a 2023 speeding ticket in Arlington, Virginia.
That timeline includes no “reckless driving” criminal charges against Engling.
Who’s a real Hoosier? Secretary of state candidates spar over time in Indiana.

Bayh, meanwhile, was initially charged in 2018 at age 22 in Brunswick County, Virginia, with misdemeanor reckless driving for driving faster than 85 mph. That charge was reduced to an infraction for defective or unsafe equipment and Bayh was fined, according to Virginia online court records.
Engling’s campaign said Bayh should “withdraw his latest attack ad and correct its false claim about Engling’s driving record, or face a lawsuit.”
Bayh’s campaign responded to the Capital Chronicle that it “is reckless for Max to drive 87 in a 60mph zone. It is reckless of Max to throw things from an overpass at moving cars.”
“His driving is reckless. His behavior is reckless. His threats of frivolous lawsuits are reckless,” Bayh campaign manager Jack Tormoehlen said in an email. “This ad is accurate and Max Engling needs to take a deep breath.”
The dispute over Engling’s driving record follows attack ads from Engling over Bayh’s voter registration history.
Bayh first registered to vote in 2014 while still a high school student in Washington, D.C., using the address of an Indianapolis condominium owned by his father, former U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh. 
An Engling ad says Beau Bayh “voted in Indiana elections 14 times. Had his ballot mailed to his parents’ D.C. mansion. Sounds like voter fraud.”
Bayh, who has never been charged with voter fraud, cast ballots regularly in Indiana through his time as a student at Harvard and during services with the Marine Corps — often by mail but sometimes voting early in person. He moved full time to Indiana in 2024 after graduating from Harvard Law School.
Bayh has defended voting in Indiana, saying he always considered the state home despite mostly growing up in the Washington area after his family moved there when he was three with his father’s election to the U.S. Senate.
The Indiana Supreme Court ruled in 1988 — in a case involving Evan Bayh’s residency — that physical presence in a place is only one circumstance in determining domicile, and that a person’s residency hinges on intent.

name: VTDigger
title: What can we do? An answer from Vermont’s premiere theater.
text:
By Leslie Swackhamer, Executive Director, Susan Smith Blackburn Prize, and Jay Wahl, Executive Director, the Flynn
We began with an impossibly large question: What is the current state of democracy in America?
But underneath it was a smaller and much more personal one: What can we do? What should we do?
What can a couple of Vermonters who run a performing arts organization and a playwriting prize do? Some days, hiding under the bed seems like a reasonable option. The world feels frightening. The 2026 midterm elections are approaching. Our country seems increasingly divided not only about politics, but about reality itself.
We’re not politicians or constitutional scholars. But we believe in the power of theater to bring people together, to ask difficult questions, and to help us see the world through someone else’s eyes. That’s what we have to offer.
So we teamed up, leaning into Susan Smith Blackburn’s belief that both our stories and our civic life are richer with women’s voices at the center. And we invited some of the most influential playwrights of our time to take on this question with us.
We thought maybe six or seven playwrights would say yes to an invitation to write short plays or monologues. Instead, our invitation opened a floodgate. Thirty-four plays by award-winning women+ playwrights make up the project. They are funny and furious, intimate and unruly, historical and speculative. They contradict one another. Some make us uncomfortable. Others make us laugh. All ask us to pay attention.

Together, these plays do not argue for a single point of view or prescribe a single course of action. They offer something more interesting: an invitation to consider perspectives we might not otherwise encounter.
That is why we’re producing all of them throughout a full day at the Flynn on October 24.
A play can’t encompass democracy. A conversation won’t allay all our fears. But something can happen between people who gather to listen to a story that would not have happened otherwise. That is a critical beginning.
And we didn’t want that conversation to happen only in Burlington.
We’ve invited theaters, schools, colleges and universities, libraries, museums, community organizations, and independent artists to bring these plays into their own communities across the United States and beyond. More than 100 groups have answered the call, with free performances planned around the country and the globe in the weeks leading up to the midterms. We are approaching our goal of participation in every state and Washington, D.C.
Some will present a single play around a kitchen table. Others will gather hundreds of people in a theater. Each community will decide which stories matter most to them and what conversations they want to have.
There is something particularly meaningful to us about this national conversation beginning in Vermont, a state whose motto, Freedom and Unity, holds two ideas that can be difficult to reconcile. We believe the arts can help us practice both.
The election will pass. The arguments that seemed all-consuming in 2026 will give way to others. And these plays will still be here. They will be available in an anthology, though that collection is not a time capsule containing the correct thoughts about American democracy in 2026. It is a record of artists being brave enough to look directly at their moment and make something.
Democracy requires more than agreement. It asks us to share a public life with people who see the world differently. To listen, to question, to disagree, and to remain in conversation even when it would be easier to walk away.
We can’t promise that 34 plays will change the course of American democracy.
But we can invite people into a room together.
And right now, that feels like something very worth doing.

To learn more and reserve free tickets for the Saturday, October 24 world-premiere of all 34 Women+ on the Edge of Democracy plays at the Flynn in Burlington, VT, visit: https://www.flynnvt.org/see-and-do/democracy/.
To explore the full Women+ on the Edge of Democracy project, visit: https://www.democracy.flynnvt.org/.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Letter with white powder addressed to Utah Lt. Gov. Henderson intercepted, given to FBI
text:
Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks to reporters about the launch of Utah's digital apostille program after a news conference at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City on Sept. 1, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson is among several election officials across the country that have been sent suspicious white powder and threatening letters ahead of the midterm elections. 
Reports of the letters in Arizona, Ohio, Oklahoma and Louisiana began last week, prompting building evacuations and an FBI investigation with just over two weeks to go until the Nov. 3 elections. 
 


View on Threads

 

In Utah, Henderson said in a social media post that on Sunday “our local postal inspector was able to intercept ours and hand it off to the FBI before it could be delivered to my office.” 
“We are grateful for his diligence and service!” Henderson wrote. “Also, nothing is going to disrupt the midterm election. We won’t let it happen.” 
Last week, when reports of the letters began surfacing and Utah News Dispatch asked about whether Henderson’s office had received any, the lieutenant governor’s office said in a prepared statement that U.S. Postal Service staff were keeping an eye out for any suspicious packages. 
“We have been in contact with postal service employees who are actively monitoring our mail for a similar letter so they can intercept it before it reaches our office,” Henderson’s office said Thursday. 
It’s not the first time threatening packages have been sent to Henderson or other election officials across the country. It happened in September 2024, when the FBI found a letter containing white powder addressed to Henderson’s office. It was signed by the “United States Traitor Elimination Army.” 
FBI intercepts ‘suspicious’ envelope containing white powder addressed to Utah Lt. Gov.

“This incident is the latest tactic in a nationwide trend of threats and intimidation toward election officials. But we will not be intimidated,” Henderson said in a statement in 2024. “I am grateful for the swift action of postal workers and law enforcement and the perseverance of election workers who show up and do their jobs every day despite all the rhetoric and risk. We love them. We owe them. They are heroes.”
In her post on Sunday, Henderson’s message was short, saying “nothing is going to disrupt” the election.
She also took the opportunity to point out that early in-person voting starts this week, and that Utahns can sign up for ballot tracking notifications at trackmyballot.utah.gov. 
Henderson has been in a national spotlight this year, including on CBS’ 60 Minutes over the weekend, as she has pushed back against an order from the Trump administration to turn over sensitive information from Utah’s voter rolls including social security numbers, full birth dates and driver’s license numbers. 
Her resistance has elicited both a lawsuit against the state and a personal investigation against her from the U.S. Department of Justice.

name: Delaware
title: Hayrides, Hope and Helping Hands: Building a Foundation for Recovery in Delaware
text:
Annual Friends of Delaware Hayride at Milburn Orchards invites supporters of its healing mission to enjoy family time while strengthening connections centered on recovery.
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
A hayride and a bonfire might seem like simple ingredients for an autumn outing. For Firm Foundation Recovery, they are also opportunities to bring families together around a mission that reaches far beyond a fall evening.
The nonprofit hosts its annual Friends of Delaware Hayride at Milburn Orchards each October, inviting supporters of its healing mission to enjoy family time while strengthening connections centered on recovery.
The gathering is one example of how the organization combines community activities, peer support and service to address substance addiction in Delaware.
Firm Foundation Recovery grew out of what its website describes as an enormous need for a long-term, God-centered recovery resource in the state. Its approach brings people and fellowships together around shared principles for healing, with an emphasis on addressing needs that can leave individuals and families struggling to find support.
“Together we can help to heal our communities one recovery at a time,” the organization states on its website.
That mission includes an ambitious undertaking: building a long-term, God-centered recovery facility with transitional living and a work program. The planned facility reflects the organization’s focus on sustained support and helping people establish a foundation for their lives in recovery.
Its broader vision extends throughout Delaware. Firm Foundation Recovery seeks to develop a recovery culture rooted in principles, service and community involvement, with people in recovery taking active roles in strengthening the communities around them.
Family events are one way it works toward that goal.
The organization reports hosting seven annual statewide family and community events focused on awareness, education, prevention and resources. Community donations help secure venues and allow those gatherings to grow.
In May, its Skating For Change events bring the mission to the rink. The owners of Christiana Skating Center and Dover Skating Center partner with the nonprofit to offer Delaware youth and families opportunities to skate while supporting its work.
October brings a different setting, with hayrides and bonfires at Milburn Orchards. The Friends of Delaware Hayride combines a familiar fall tradition with the organization’s efforts to unite people around healing and recovery.
Together, the activities reflect an approach that makes room for families and community members to participate through shared experiences.
Service is another central part of the organization’s work.
Firm Foundation Recovery reports carrying out three service projects annually in and around Delaware. Its service activities include improving housing, providing food and clothing to people experiencing homelessness, hosting speaker jams and creating supportive recovery environments.
These efforts connect recovery with practical ways to help others. They also give participants opportunities to contribute their experience and energy to needs within the wider community.
The nonprofit’s peer-driven initiatives reach children, families and people new to recovery. According to its website, lived experience helps those involved connect with others and respond to gaps in support.
“This ‘we’ concept of serving with our lived experience is life changing,” the website states.
Community partnerships help sustain the effort. Firm Foundation Recovery offers sponsorship and advertising opportunities for businesses and other supporters interested in contributing to its mission while building relationships within their communities.
For the organization, the larger goal is a Delaware where helping people affected by addiction becomes a shared commitment, and where those building lives in recovery have opportunities to serve others.
A skating rink, a service project or an evening beside a bonfire offers a different doorway into that work. Each creates space for people to gather, participate and support a mission built around healing.
Through those connections, Firm Foundation Recovery is working toward a future in which recovery has a place in everyday community life, one helping hand and one changed life at a time.
