name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A tale of two farmers: Ager, Balkcom compete for NC-11 seat
text:
Jamie Ager hosts a concert rally at Asheville Yards on Oct. 13, 2026. Ager is the Democrat running for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District against state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)ASHEVILLE — About 3,000 people gathered at Asheville Yards last week for a concert rally with Jamie Ager, who’s running against GOP state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to represent North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. The contest could play a pivotal role in the control of the U.S. House. 
Wearing trucker hats, shirts, or buttons in the campaign’s signature kelly green saying “Ager for U.S. Congress,” attendees encouraged each other to knock on doors and work the polls. Others waved signs claiming, “I’m a mountain Democrat and proud of it.”
The Cook Political Report rates the seat as “toss up,” and Democrats see Ager as their best chance to win in the district, which has been reliably red for most of the past 35 years.
“Jamie’s a great guy,” Patricia Derrough said. “He is honest, hardworking, and has good values. Just what Western North Carolina needs by working for all the people, not just the wealthy.”
Derrough says she’s known the Ager family her entire life. Her ancestors moved to Western North Carolina in the 1700s; Ager’s came later. His great-grandparents moved to Fairview in 1916, where the family has been ever since.
“They used to have square dances regularly. Everybody in town went,” Derrough said.
Ager’s grandfather, Jamie Clarke, represented NC-11 in Congress. His older brother Eric serves in the North Carolina House, in the same seat their father John once held.
Jamie Ager at Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
As a fourth-generation farmer, Ager and his wife sell grassfed beef, pastured pork, and fresh eggs to grocery stores, restaurants, and individual customers. They also host events at Hickory Nut Gap Farm — along with barn dances, there’s stargazing, meditation, and hayrides.
“My boys drive the tractors,” Ager said with a smile, referring to his sons Cyrus, Nolin, and Levi. “It’s a good job for them, to give a little hayride and give those people a little perspective on growing up here on the farm.”
But Ager’s rival also has deep roots in Western North Carolinian, where her family has lived for eight generations. Balkcom grew up on her family’s apple farm in Henderson County and is well known in her community, where she’s a mortgage loan officer. 
The campaign trail
NC-11 is geographically vast, spanning 16 counties and about 6,200 square miles. The mountain terrain means many routes contain switchbacks or tunnels, requiring slower speeds. 
President Donald Trump has handily won the district three times. It has elected only one Democrat, Heath Shuler, to Congress since 1991. Many thought this year would be no different. 
In August, incumbent GOP Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his bid for reelection, after reports of inappropriate conduct. The U.S. House voted to censure him in September. 
The North Carolina Republican Party selected Balkcom as his replacement, leaving her with roughly three months to campaign. 
Ager, on the other hand, launched his campaign about 18 months ago. Since then, he’s traveled extensively across Western North Carolina, speaking with voters about their priorities. He’s held events from Cherokee to Burnsville to Hendersonville. 
“I’ve met so many wonderful people that are too busy to worry about politics because they’re too worried about how to make payroll on Friday afternoon,” Ager said. “One thing I hear over and over again is that people in this country are sick and tired of partisan politics, and we need leaders in this country who are going to work hard for the people in our community.”
Goals for Washington
Ager said his top priority in Congress would be securing funding for Hurricane Helene relief. 
At Hickory Nut Gap, the storm knocked out the power and toppled trees. The farm typically earns more than half of its revenue during harvest season, and with local restaurants closed, it temporarily lost some of its biggest customers. 
“We were devastated, and all we knew to do was get chainsaws out, start sawing our way out, checking on neighbors, doing everything everybody did here in Western North Carolina at that time,” Ager said. “We came together to put ourselves back together and do everything we can, and I think we need some of that kind of spirit up in Washington, D.C.”
Like Ager, Balkcom has been active in Helene relief and recovery efforts. She helped secure funds at the state level and wants to do the same in Congress. 
A member of the state legislature since 2023, her primary accomplishment so far has been sponsoring a bill banning transgender athletes from competing in women’s and girls’ sports.
“I want to work hard for the people that live here, and that’s what we were voted in to do. I want to do that in Washington, just like I have in Raleigh,” Balkcom told Spectrum News. “I’ve been serving in the General Assembly, helping farmers for the last four years.”
She’s gotten funding from national Republican House leaders like Speaker Mike Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, and Majority Whip Tom Emmer, according to reports filed with the Federal Election Commission. Balkcom also received donations from most of the GOP members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation and some of her state House colleagues. 
But she’s still building name recognition across the sprawling district. Her campaign website reveals almost nothing about her policy priorities. 
And when Spectrum News asked Balkcom if she thought Edwards should resign from Congress, she took a lengthy pause before saying she wasn’t sure. She gave similar answers to other questions.
Balkcom declined to be interviewed for this story.
“It’s certainly not ideal,” political scientist David McLennan said. “She’s had some interviews that have shown a bit of inexperience. When you have a real short window of opportunity, it makes it difficult to campaign.”
Republican Reps. Jennifer Balkcom, front, and Erin Paré speak against allowing transgender athletes to compete against female students in sporting events at the NC General Assembly in April 2023. Balkcom is now running for NC’s 11th Congressional District. (Screenshot from livestream of committee hearing)
Homegrown candidates
Before Edwards, Republicans Madison Cawthorn and Mark Meadows held the seat. Each left office under a cloud. It’s left Western North Carolinians hungry for change, Democrats say. 
Ager tells voters he wants to lower the cost of living and remove corruption from politics by overturning Citizens United and banning members of Congress from trading stocks. 
“The whole place looks like a big old coin-operated machine. If you don’t have any money to put into that machine, you don’t get any favors out of that machine,” he said. “We need somebody who’s going to fight for the people here in Western North Carolina.”
Last month, both candidates debuted ads aiming to appeal to the same mountain community. 
Ager’s ad, titled “Barn Dance,” featured live music as he rallied his supporters at one of his events. 
“Nobody cares what politics you are when you’re in the middle of a square dance,” Ager told NC Newsline. 
Image from Balkcom’s “Mom” ad, one of two unique spots currently running in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. (Photo: YouTube)
Balkcom aired an ad, titled “Mom,” where she talks about her mother teaching her to be strong.
“When someone broke into her house, she shot them,” Balkcom said in the video.
The national political scene
Republicans are facing a tricky political climate amid rising costs across the board and declining approval ratings for President Donald Trump. 
Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper has consistently polled ahead of former Republican National Committee and NCGOP chair Michael Whatley in the contest for North Carolina’s open U.S. Senate seat. National fundraising groups have temporarily paused spending on campaign ads for the race, focusing on other states instead. 
NC Republicans Tillis, Moore prepare for GOP losses in upcoming election

Republicans currently hold a 218-212 majority in the U.S. House, with four vacancies and one independent caucusing with the GOP. 
The GOP has deployed Trump, Vice President JD Vance, and other Republicans to North Carolina to stump for candidates like Whatley and Balkcom. Vance is scheduled to hold a rally in Hendersonville Monday. 
Even so, despite the district’s newly competitive nature, not all residents have been following politics closely. Some don’t get to know the candidates until they head to the polls.  
“It’s really dependent in part on the Democratic wave, and whether it’ll be a ripple or a tsunami, it’s impossible to tell right now,” McLennan said. “The next few weeks and overall turnout are going to be very important.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado activists call for transparency measures as they attempt to track ICE flights out of Denver
text:
Dana Miller, Kristen Aldretti and Amy Farrar watch a plane scheduled to transport people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement out of the Signature Aviation terminal at the Denver International Airport on Sept. 13, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)On a Sunday morning in September, three Colorado women met at the cell phone lot near Denver International Airport and waited for a flight from Texas to arrive.
They watched a flight tracker as the plane flew closer to Denver, and prepared to meet it as it landed. But they did not go to the typical arrivals terminal, and they were not awaiting visiting family and friends. This was a plane scheduled to pick up people detained in Colorado by U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement and transport them to Mesa, Arizona.
Dana Miller, Kristen Aldretti and Amy Farrar drove to the Signature Aviation terminal immediately southeast of the main airport and waited behind a fence near the perimeter of the runway. An Air Wisconsin plane pulled into view, and the typical choreography of an ICE flight began: An unmarked bus pulled up, people began loading white bags of personal belongings onto the airplane and officers laid out silver shackles on the tarmac.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Typically, the women would watch people exit the bus, get shackled and then directed onto the airplane. They carried a handheld tally counter to track the number of detainees, and planned to count the pairs of feet they could see under the bus, since it blocked their line of sight to the plane stairs that day.
But then a security guard pulled up and asked the trio to leave, and they left the terminal, which is private property, without protest. It wasn’t the first time they were kicked out during their dozen or so outings to the airport. Once they got back into their car and pulled out onto the road, a private security vehicle trailed them for about a mile and then turned around.
“Regardless, we learned things,” Aldretti said, categorizing the outing as a success even though they did not witness people getting on the flight. “We learned that they are still parking the buses in front so we can’t see (the stairs). We learned that sometimes the pilots come out. Those are all things that need to be documented, and it goes into our learning for next time.”
Two days later, they were back, and saw 32 people led onto an ICE flight. On Sept. 29, it was 33.
“The general public, at this point, has a common view of what happens when people get picked up from ICE,” Miller said. But there’s still a gap in understanding what happens between someone’s initial detainment and their release or eventual deportation, she said.
“We want people to see what it really looks like,” she said of ICE flights. “It’s when the shackles are all laid out on the pavement, and the sun is shining on them, and then you see them getting put on people, and then people struggling to walk. People should know.”
Calls for cameras
Domestic ICE flights happen on a semi-regular basis out of the Denver airport. There were 118 flights between January and August this year, according to research from Human Rights First. They are part of the Trump administration’s program of mass deportations. Aldretti and Miller began heading to the airport to observe the flights in mid-July, and Aldretti posts about them on a dedicated Instagram account that has grown to almost 1,000 followers. Farrar joined more recently and lives the closest to the airport among the three.
“We have privilege, and if we’re not going to be the ones doing this important work and standing up for others who are vulnerable, who will be?” Aldretti said.
People in shackles are led off a plane flight-tracking databases show is operated by Arapahoe County, Colorado-based Key Lime Air at Alexandria International Airport, Louisiana, on Oct. 11, 2025. (Photo by Madelyn Murphy/Colorado Newsline)
Their goal is to physically witness and count the people being boarded onto these flights and feed it into a national network of volunteer ICE flight observers called Habeas Flight Watch. That website hosts a live dashboard of confirmed ICE flights and volunteers rely on it to track when a flight lands in their city. Other “birders” in the network are able to take clear photos of passengers in an effort to connect people with lawyers and family. The setup at Signature Aviation, with a nearly opaque fence and no clear sight line to the plane, makes that hard.
“If we could even get pictures of these passengers to share with their family members, to share with their lawyers … to make sure that their family knows where the hell they are (would be ideal),” Farrar said.
The group, as well as other immigrant advocacy organizations, have called on city and airport leadership to increase transparency and local surveillance around ICE flights. They see an example in King County, Washington, near Seattle, where county officials in 2023 ordered the airport to log every flight and maintain a livestream to show ICE flight operations. The county recently hired a flight monitoring and outreach coordinator to count passengers and flag safety violations. Activists pressured county officials for years over the issue.
“I hope (we get) the live camera feed, where the public and folks who are monitoring this from a legal perspective can identify (people) and just document this,” Denver City Council member Stacie Gilmore told Colorado Newsline. She said she has heard commitments from airport leadership that they are working on evaluating the feasibility of such a measure.
Signature Aviation did not reply to a request for comment.
The transparency concerns in Denver came to a head recently as council members debated whether to approve a lease for regional passenger service through a subsidiary of Key Lime Air at the airport. Key Lime Air is a Colorado-based company that has operated hundreds of ICE flights since last year, when Colorado Newsline first reported that it was flying for the agency.
An airport spokesperson wrote in an email that leadership has been in discussion with a “number of stakeholder groups to hear their concerns and ideas” over the issue.
“Obviously, it’s not nearly enough, but I think monitoring of these flights is a good first step to actually be able to see what’s happening, and bring a wider lens to the broader public,” said Brandon Gehrke Quintanilla, an organizer with Aurora Unidos CSO who met with airport leadership. He said the Key Lime lease coming before City Council was enough leverage to put pressure on the airport and city leaders about the ICE flights.
City Council delayed the lease approval vote, but then passed it 11-1 on Oct. 13 under the promise from airport officials to continue conversations about transparency measures with advocates like Miller. Gilmore was the lone “no” vote. No council member directly mentioned cameras or livestreams.
“The things I expect moving forward is that the collaboration continues with the community organizations — collaboration and partnership, not lip service,” council member Serena Gonzales-Gutierrez said during that meeting. “I also would like that we implement and maintain transparency measures, such as tracking ICE activity. I know other airports have done this. I want us to be creative and think about how we are doing this.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas Explained: How to vote early in the 2026 midterm election
text:
Signs direct voters inside the Lee County Courthouse in eastern Arkansas in February 2024. (Photo by Antoinette Grajeda/Arkansas Advocate)Early voting begins Monday in Arkansas and continues for two weeks leading up to the general election on Nov. 3. 
Arkansas voters can head to their local polling location to cast their ballots in the races for U.S. Senate, Arkansas governor and the state Legislature, among others. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
More than 1.85 million voters are registered to vote in Arkansas, according to the secretary of state’s office. Over 1.6 million are registered as “Party Optional,” meaning they have no party affiliation. 
Roughly 155,000 Arkansans are registered Republicans and 85,000 are registered Democrats. The state also has more than 755 Libertarians and 125 Green Party members. 
Here’s what to know about early voting in Arkansas:
How do I know if I’m eligible to vote?
To participate in the Nov. 3 election, you must have registered to vote in Arkansas by Oct. 5. 
Your local county clerk will send you a personalized voter registration card once your application is processed, and it could take several weeks. 
Arkansans should not assume they’re registered until they’ve received their voter registration card, according to the secretary of state’s office. 
You can check your voter registration status by calling your local county clerk or visiting www.voterview.ar-nova.org.  
What if I need to update my voter registration?
You can update your information at an early voting site if your name or address has changed, according to the secretary of state’s office.
When is early voting?
Early voting runs Oct. 19 through Nov. 2. Election Day is Nov. 3.
During early voting, polls are open from 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. Monday through Friday and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Saturday. Early voting ends at 5 p.m. on the Monday prior to the election. 
Where can I vote?
In most counties, early voting is conducted at the county clerk’s office, according to the secretary of state’s office. Local newspapers will publish designated sites in counties with polling locations other than the county clerk’s office. 
A 2025 law requires an early voting location in cities with more than 15,000 residents. The legislation was proposed in response to a 2024 legal battle over early voting in Crittenden County. 
You can find polling sites by calling your local county clerk or visiting www.voterview.ar-nova.org.
Do I need an ID to vote?
Yes. Arkansas voters are required to verify their voter registration with photo identification, such as a driver’s license or passport. 
If you don’t bring an ID with you to the polls, you can cast a provisional ballot. 
In order for the provisional ballot to count, a voter must present a document or photo ID to verify their registration to the county board of election commissioners or the county clerk by noon on the Monday following the election.
How do I know what races I can vote in?
To view sample ballots, call your local county clerk or visit www.voterview.ar-nova.org.
Information about candidates running for federal and statewide office, as well as the Arkansas House and Senate, is available on the Advocate’s 2026 Voter Guide.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New group seeks to help US small towns lead the clean energy transition
text:
Mayor Mondale Robinson, of Enfield, North Carolina, at the town’s aging substation (Photo: Elizabeth Ouzts/Canary Media)
As the mayor of tiny Enfield, North Carolina, Mondale Robinson has huge clean energy ambitions. Among them: building a solar farm to power the entire town of about 2,000, replacing the town’s decrepit substation to distribute those renewable electrons, and building a thermal energy network to provide heating and cooling and reduce exorbitant electric bills.


But Enfield is one of the poorest towns in the state, where the average household income hovers around the poverty line. As mayor, Robinson earns $500 a month. There are no sustainability officers, no grant writers, no policy teams to help him push this plan forward.


One way Robinson is trying to overcome these hurdles is by working with allies from the closest major metro area. Lawyers from Chapel Hill’s Southern Environmental Law Center, for instance, are negotiating the town utility’s next electricity contract so that it can produce its own solar energy. Researchers at Durham’s Duke University are helping design the geothermal project.


Yet too many doors remain closed to Robinson. The U.S. Conference of Mayors, which has galvanized city leadership on climate solutions, doesn’t extend full membership to leaders of towns as small as Enfield. And most foundations tend to overlook such communities.




Mayor Mondale Robinson and Canary Media contributing reporter Elizabeth Ouzts at a Climate Week NYC summit on rural America and the clean energy transition (Photo: Daniel Krieger/Canary Media)



So Robinson, a longtime political organizer, decided to do what he’s always done: Join together with his cohorts to fight for change. At a Canary Media summit on clean energy in rural America in September, he announced that he’s launching a new small-town coalition. If towns like his work together, he believes, they can help get new federal policies enacted, attract new donors, and have greater access to experts who can help them confront a host of challenges, from the climate crisis to housing and food insecurity.


“One small town can be ignored,” he said. “Thousands of organized small towns become a national constituency.”


Robinson’s National Conference of Small Cities and Rural Mayors is designed for officials of locales with fewer than 30,000 people. The figure is not arbitrary: the U.S. Conference of Mayors serves mayors of cities with populations above that benchmark.


“The national organization that speaks for mayors doesn’t even allow us to be full members,” he said. Yet census data shows that towns like Enfield make up 93% of all incorporated municipalities and house some 60 million people, he said. “America is a nation of small towns.”


At the same time, Robinson points out that 90% of philanthropy goes to urban areas. “If you consider rural people as a collective, we will be bigger than the largest populated state in this country,” he said, referring to California. “And yet, we are not being invested in in a way that makes sense.”


Robinson’s new coalition is still in the early stages. “Right now, we’re trying to recruit the first 100 founding mayors,” as well as anchor foundations, he said.
As economic damage from climate change grows, NC experts urge ‘pre-recovery’ planning 



Longer term, his goals for the group include training, peer-to-peer networks, regional collaboration, and a shared voice in federal advocacy. He also believes that small towns, with minimal footprints and more ability than big cities to be nimble, are the best places to test and refine new clean energy models, just as Enfield is aiming to do.


Already, the town has helped form a new nonprofit, Enfield Energy Futures, which has won a small seed grant to pursue the thermal energy network. Its utility could become the first to run such a project in the Southeast.


“What we’re doing here in Enfield,” Robinson said, “with no resources, or very little resources, is how we change the lives not just of the people in Enfield but everybody who is living in a small town across this country.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Opportunity Zones can help bring investment, development to Idaho areas that need it most
text:
An orange "detour ahead" sign alerts motorists of a new route around new housing construction in Boise in summer 2026.  (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho’s newly approved Opportunity Zones could help bring more housing, businesses and jobs to communities across the state. The attraction for investors is the potential tax savings.
This month, Idaho Commerce announced that the U.S. Treasury approved 25 zones, including areas in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls. The new Opportunity Zone designations take effect Jan. 1.
An Opportunity Zone is a designated area where the federal government offers tax benefits to encourage private investment. The idea is straightforward: give investors a financial reason to put money into communities that could benefit from more economic activity.
In Boise, the five areas identified by the city are Downtown, Shoreline, University District, South Boise Village and West Boise. These are general descriptions of the selected areas. The actual boundaries determine whether a particular property is included.
In North Idaho, the officially designated list includes parts of Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls, as well as areas around Blanchard and Kellogg, Smelterville and Wardner. Other designated communities include Caldwell, Garden City, Nampa, Pocatello and Twin Falls.
The state’s announcement provides the complete list and a link to look up the boundaries.
The program connects investors with projects that need money. An investor who sells stock, real estate or a business at a profit may face a tax bill on that gain. By investing an eligible gain through a special investment vehicle called a Qualified Opportunity Fund, the investor may receive tax benefits. The fund puts that money into qualifying property or businesses within a zone. The IRS explains the basic structure here.
Imagine a business owner who sells a company and wants to invest some of the profit. Across town, a developer wants to turn an underused property into apartments with shops on the ground floor. If the project is in an Opportunity Zone and meets the program’s requirements, an Opportunity Fund could connect that investor’s money with the development. The investor receives an ownership interest, and the project receives money to help move forward.
Under the new rules beginning in 2027, a qualifying investor generally can delay tax on the invested gain for five years and reduce the amount of that gain subject to tax. Holding the investment for at least 10 years may also allow the investor to avoid federal tax on qualifying growth in the investment’s value.
Coeur d’Alene also offers a potential partnership story. Idaho Capital Sun reported that Kootenai County and the Coeur d’Alene Tribe both sought designation for the local tract. The application summary identified vacant tribal land as an opportunity for investment involving the Tribe, local governments, and private developers. That possibility deserves attention, although the designation itself does not establish a finalized development partnership.
For investors, those benefits can make a long-term investment more attractive. For developers and business owners, the program can help attract money from people willing to wait for a project to mature. That could support a new apartment building, the redevelopment of an older commercial property, or the expansion of a qualifying business. Residents may benefit from additional homes, employment, and services.
Those outcomes are possibilities, not promises.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Attorney General touts success of Trump task force in Memphis
text:
Joined by U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn and U.S. Marshals Director Gady Serralta, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche visited Memphis, Tennessee on Oct. 17, 2026, to discussed the Memphis Safe Task. (Photo: U.S. Department of Justice)U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche joined federal and state leaders in Tennessee on Friday to tout the record of the Memphis Safe Task Force a little more than one year after President Donald Trump first established the multi-agency crime-fighting force. 
Overall crime in Memphis is now at a 25-year low, Blanche said, giving the task force credit for the reduction in violent crimes, robberies and vehicle thefts. Crime, local officials have noted, began trending downward in the city in the year before the task force was convened. 
Family demands answers after Memphis Task Force agent kills man at Burger King

Blanche gave no timetable for a potential end to  the enhanced law enforcement presence, saying the task force will remain in the city “as long as it takes.” 
“We haven’t won yet. It’s not over,” he said. Blanche did not define terms for a successful completion of the task force’s mission in Memphis.  
He also reiterated the Trump administration’s goal to replicate the model across the country, singling out Chicago as a goal. Like Memphis, the city is minority white, and majority Democrat.
“If you think about a place like Chicago, if Chicago called me and said, ‘we want to replicate Memphis in Chicago,’ we could transform an entire city, one of the most pivotal cities in this country, in the same way that we’ve transformed Memphis,” he said
Since September 2025, the task force has brought hundreds of federal law enforcement officers to the city and surrounding Shelby County to serve warrants, make arrests, detain immigrants, conduct traffic stops and recover missing children, often working in tandem with the Tennessee Highway Patrol and other state and local law enforcement officers.  Gov. Bill Lee deployed hundreds of soldiers with the Tennessee National Guard to support the effort. 
ACLU claims Memphis Safe Task Force harassing plaintiff

The task force has been welcomed by Republican leaders, including Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican nominee for governor, who praised the task force at Friday’s roundtable discussion in a Memphis warehouse alongside state Sen. Brent Taylor and Memphis Police Chief CJ Davis.
But it has faced pushback by many in the Democratic-leaning city as a form of over-policing of predominantly Black and brown communities — pushback that grew earlier this year after the fatal shootings of four Black men by task force members in four separate encounters earlier this year. 
Critics and community groups have also highlighted dangerous high speed chases and the heightened presence of officers conducting immigration enforcement in areas of Memphis with large immigrant populations. 
Several lawsuits filed by journalists, local leaders and community groups have alleged intimidation against bystanders attempting to monitor enforcement activity and the refusal by state agencies participating in the task force to provide public records.

title: Nine Arkansas legislative races to watch in midterm election
authors: Tess Vrbin, Antoinette Grajeda, Ainsley Platt
text:
The Arkansas State Capitol seen from the northeast on Nov. 11, 2025. (Photo by Sonny Albarado/Arkansas Advocate)Republicans are all but guaranteed to maintain their majority in both chambers of the Arkansas Legislature in 2027, with most sitting GOP House members and several of the party’s senators unopposed or not on the ballot.
To break the Republican supermajority of more than three-quarters needed in each chamber to pass most budget bills, Democrats would need to flip three Senate seats and six House seats. That’s a tall order in a state where Republicans have led the Legislature and held all statewide offices for over a decade.
Just over a third of the 117 legislative races on the midterm ballots are contested. Some seats are undefended and some are in competitive regions such as northwest Arkansas and the Little Rock suburbs. A few contests feature candidates who have run before and lost, and others include former lawmakers seeking reelection, some in different or redrawn districts.
Republican Rep. Karilyn Brown (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
One Senate race won’t be decided until Dec. 15, when voters in White County and parts of Faulkner and Cleburne counties will choose former Republican Sen. Jonathan Dismang’s successor in a special election.
Here’s a look at nine interesting legislative matchups:
 House District 67

Voters in parts of Jacksonville and Sherwood will see a rematch between six-term Republican Rep. Karilyn Brown and Democrat Andrew Cade Eberly.
Brown defeated Eberly by 559 votes in 2024. Her campaign website states that she supports lowering taxes and is “a champion for students and teachers.”
Andrew Cade Eberly (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Eberly, an Army veteran and cybersecurity professional, is vice chair of the Pulaski County Democratic Party. Among his priorities are “when someone in Jacksonville has a medical emergency, help is close enough to save their life,” according to his campaign website.
Jacksonville’s only hospital, Unity Health, closed its emergency room and medical-surgical unit in April, partly due to low insurance reimbursement rates, an issue leading hospitals statewide to downsize.
Cynthia Nations (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
 House District 55

Democrat Cynthia Nations is challenging two-term Republican Rep. Matt Brown in a rematch of their 2024 race.
House District 55 encompasses part of Faulkner County, including a portion of Conway, where both candidates live. Brown won this district in 2024 with nearly 59% of the vote.
Nations, a retired Conway Public Schools teacher, has the support of the Arkansas Education Association and is running on the idea that “public money should stay in our public schools.” 
Republican Rep. Matt Brown (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Brown was one of the 78 members of the House who voted for the LEARNS Act of 2023, which established Educational Freedom Accounts, Arkansas’ universal school voucher program.
Allison Grigsby Sweatman (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
 Senate District 13

Allison Grigsby Sweatman, a social worker and former president of the Young Democrats of Arkansas, is running a second time for the Senate seat covering North Little Rock, Sherwood, Maumelle and Jacksonville.
Sweatman faces two-term GOP Rep. Brandon Achor of Maumelle, a pharmacist who consistently champions policies to make prescription medication more affordable.
The two are running to replace term-limited Republican Sen. Jane English, who defeated Sweatman in the 2022 election.
Republican Rep. Brandon Achor (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Achor was among the dozens of GOP lawmakers who sponsored the LEARNS Act, and his campaign website reiterates his support for the school voucher program.
Sweatman has been a vocal opponent of school vouchers, and her website states that she supports accountability for the use of public money and an income cap on voucher recipients.
Achor has also supported ongoing efforts to phase out the state’s income tax. A banner at the top of his campaign site says, “Allison Sweatman opposed cutting your taxes!”
Cassandra Mayes (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
 House District 71

Democrat Cassandra Mayes and Republican Stephen Bright are running for the Maumelle House district seat currently held by Achor. 
Mayes is an educational consultant who worked for the Little Rock School District from 2016 to 2025. In June, she called for Maumelle schools to split from the Pulaski County Special School District, which was embroiled in a desegregation court case for decades.
Bright was in the House from 2003 to 2011 and is running to represent Maumelle again. He currently chairs the Arkansas Capitol Arts and Grounds Commission, part of the secretary of state’s office.
Stephen Bright (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Bright’s approach to education policy, according to his campaign website, includes bolstering trade schools and “teaching students and educators how to use AI responsibly and effectively.”
In September, Mayes alleged that Bright has not lived in Maumelle since 2008 despite maintaining Maumelle voter registration and consistently voting there.
Bright refuted Mayes’ allegations of voter fraud to KATV, saying that not changing his registration was “a simple oversight during a move” to Little Rock and that his registration became accurate again when he moved back to Maumelle.
Republican Rep. Aaron Pilkington (Photo courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)
 House District 45

Five-term Republican Rep. Aaron Pilkington faces former Rep. Debra Hobbs, an independent running to reclaim a spot in Arkansas’ Legislature.
Pilkington, of Knoxville, was first elected in 2016. He is a regular advocate of expanding Medicaid to cover mothers for 12 months postpartum, and is also a supporter of data center projects that have become controversial in the state. 
Pilkington’s support of data centers has been a target of criticism from Hobbs, who served in the House as a Republican representing a northwest Arkansas district.
Debra Hobbs (via Facebook)
Hobbs departed the House more than a decade ago due to term limits. She ran unsuccessfully for the GOP nomination for lieutenant governor in 2014 and tried to reclaim her old House seat in 2016. She later moved to Johnson County. 
Clarksville, which is located in the district, has pushed back against a $6.6 billion data center being built next door to its local hospital. Clarksville’s city council approved a measure to issue up to $55 billion in industrial revenue bonds to support the project earlier this year, despite objections from many in the community. 
Charlene Fite (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Hobbs led efforts to place the bonds on the ballot, and the matter is scheduled for a special election in December — likely marking the first time anything related to data centers appears on the ballot in Arkansas.
 House District 24

Charlene Fite, a former Republican House member from Van Buren, is looking to regain her seat after her predecessor, Republican Rep. Brad Hall, dropped out of the race after being accused of domestic violence by his wife. Democrat Ryan Intchauspe is running for a second time to represent the district, which includes portions of Crawford and Washington counties. 
Ryan Intchauspe (Photo courtesy of Arkansas secretary of state’s office)
Fite, a retired school psychology specialist, served six terms in the House before stepping down in 2025. During her time in the Legislature, she sponsored laws related to deaf individuals, human trafficking and child sex victims.
Intchauspe, a Navy veteran, is focused on “raising wages for working families, improving public education, expanding access to healthcare, supporting veterans, and holding government accountable to the people,” according to his campaign site.
Democratic Rep. Diana Gonzales Worthen (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
 House District 9

Democratic Rep. Diana Gonzales Worthen is seeking a second term in office representing the state’s only Hispanic-majority district. The longtime educator and granddaughter of Mexican immigrants flipped the east Springdale seat in 2024, and will be challenged in November by Republican Matt Goff.
Gonzales Worthen said she’s running for reelection because the community deserves a representative “who is focused on us, not extreme policies that hurt our schools, businesses, and families.”
Matt Goff (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Goff is an Army veteran who runs his own business and participates in disaster relief missions with various organizations, according to his campaign site. If elected, Goff said he would prioritize law enforcement and first responders, “quality education without indoctrination,” veteran support, affordable housing and small business success.
Republican Rep. Jack Ladyman (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
 House District 32

Rep. Jack Ladyman, a Republican from Jonesboro, is seeking a seventh term in House District 32, facing a challenge from Democrat Erika Askeland.
The district covers Jonesboro in Craighead County. Askeland ran against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in 2024 and came away with 39.1% of the vote. Ladyman, a mechanical engineer and former mayor of Elkins, won 58.6% of the vote in 2024, facing Democrat David McAvoy and Libertarian Eric I.B. McGee.
Erika Askeland (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Askeland, a public school teacher, is running on a platform of improving public schools, fighting hunger and “protecting our tax dollars,” according to her website.
Ladyman has been an advocate for the state’s human development centers, which serve people with severe disabilities, and has said he would introduce legislation next year to fund a long-dormant atomic coordinator position within the state government.
Democratic Rep. Jessie McGruder (Photo courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)
 Senate District 9

After serving one term in a House seat he won by 123 votes, Democratic Rep. Jessie McGruder is vying for the open Senate District 9 seat against Republican Kenny Phillips. Sen. Reginald Murdock, a term-limited Democrat, previously represented the east Arkansas district and is running for mayor of Marianna.   
McGruder, a West Memphis School District coach, sponsored a 2025 law that requires an early voting location in cities with more than 15,000 residents. He proposed the legislation in response to a legal battle over early voting in his district. McGruder promised to fight for policies that promote economic growth, education, supporting veterans and investing in community enrichment programs if elected. 
Kenny Phillips (Photo courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)
Phillips is a small business owner who serves as the Marion School District’s transportation director. Phillips said he would fight for election integrity, support local schools, back law enforcement and support expanding veteran benefits. The Republican candidate said he would also work to bring economic development and infrastructure improvements to the district.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: What do we need after Nov. 3? Political imagination.
text:
A protestor holding a sign with the Pledge of Allegiance at the Auburn No Kings protest on March 28, 2026, on Toomer's Corner, in Auburn, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 
 How to register to vote
Oct. 19 is the last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 election. If you haven’t registered to vote, you can do so here. And if you’re not sure of your registration status, you can double-check it here.


I try to avoid political predictions. But it’s safe to say that whatever happens on Nov. 3, most of us will end up disappointed.
Certainly, if our preferred candidates don’t win. But even if they prevail, the embers of excitement will cool. And by the summer, whatever our leaders have done or failed to do, we’ll be awaiting or dreading the next election.
It’s a pattern in American politics. Our patience for new politicians and regimes lasts about six to seven months. In Alabama, where we return most incumbents to a state government many of us claim to hate, we’re often disillusioned as soon as the results come in.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
For better or worse, this makes it difficult to build lasting, productive coalitions. That’s fine if Reps. Lex Luthor and The Joker are trying to get fellow lawmakers to vote for the Blow Up Gotham Act of 2026. But it means more civic-minded officials lack the space and the will to implement effective public policies.
Why do we keep repeating this cycle?
In Alabama, there are a few answers. Our state constitution is anti-democratic and centralizes power in Montgomery. Meaningful political competition is the exception, not the rule. Party primaries are more likely to determine leadership than general elections. Voters conclude and are sometimes encouraged to believe that their vote is meaningless. Voter participation plunges, and few Alabamians feel invested in their leaders. We’ve been taught to expect little from a government that protects power above everything else. 
Let me propose another reason for this disillusionment. It helps me think about why even governments with large mandates end up faltering.
If you’re a late Gen Xer like me, you’ve lived your life under a political consensus: Major problems must be addressed by the private sector, not the public one. In this view, a government cannot deliver the answers. It can only help the free market find them. 
You may reject this idea and for good reason. If you need a doctor in the United States, you know the private sector has turned this essential service into a baffling ordeal of codes, claims and hidden charges. Countries with greater public investment in healthcare tend to have better outcomes (and spend less).
But this business-first, government-bad attitude is the baseline in American politics. It frames political discussions and sets boundaries on the debate. Politicians across the political spectrum have to work within these limits, even if they reject the premise. And politicians generally give voters a sense of what’s possible.
So our political imagination has rotted. Alabama has serious problems with rural healthcare, maternal healthcare, poverty and gun violence. Yet the only public policy that seems to command broad agreement is “economic development,” which all too often means throwing tens of millions or hundreds of millions of dollars at a business that will employ tens or hundreds of people. That’s nice. But it’s not a solution. It’s a localized painkiller.
There are other examples. Don’t expect adequate money for public schools; send your kid to a private one. We’ve got workforce participation issues in Alabama due in part to a lack of transportation, but don’t tell us to invest in public transit; buy a car.
We turn away from governments with some degree of accountability and toward a small clergy of entrepreneurs with none. They tell us they commune with the fickle divinity of the free market and receive answers that, like the Delphic oracle, may or may not answer the questions.
So we expect less of our elected leaders. Politicians become little more than helpmeets for the priests of commerce. And they tend to shrink from bold solutions, if they have any in the first place. There might be some marginal changes. A tax incentive here; a rewritten law there.
But a systematic approach? We rarely see that. We have been told for so long that the private sector is superior that we get leaders who believe that, too. Who have no sense of the potential of the public sector. And who end up delivering inadequate answers.
So we lose heart and begin thinking about the next election. But we are trapped in this post-Keynesian consensus that no longer works. Healthcare, housing and education: We need something more than prayers to the great god of private enterprise to solve them. 
We need bigger ideas. But more importantly, we need a new political mindset. One that sees government as an active and creative space where popular will and new ideas can make something other than public assistance for stockholders. 
In short, we need political leadership that understands citizens have as much of a stake in public affairs as any Big Mule. That takes its responsibilities seriously. That takes responsibility and doesn’t shuffle off public concerns to private enterprise.
An administration that engages the public like this is likely to hold onto its mandate for a longer time. Because it will hold onto the public longer. And maybe address the things we care about.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: In Alabama’s 3rd Congressional District, a longtime GOP incumbent faces a newcomer
text:
Voters in Alabama's 3rd Congressional District will choose between incumbent U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Saks (left), and Democratic nominee Lee McInnis, a first-time candidate. (Photos of Rogers and McInnis are submitted; Graphic by Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector) 
 How to register to vote
Oct. 19 is the last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 election. If you haven’t registered to vote, you can do so here. And if you’re not sure of your registration status, you can double-check it here.


The race in Alabama’s 3rd Congressional District features a well-entrenched Republican incumbent and a Democratic newcomer.
The 3rd Congressional District in east Alabama, covering includes Calhoun, Chambers, Cherokee, Clay, Cleburne, Etowah, Lee, Randolph, St. Clair and Talladega counties, will feature U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Saks, against Democratic nominee Lee McInnis.
The contest is not expected to be competitive. Cook Political Report rates Alabama’s 3rd Congressional District as an R+23, “solid Republican” district. Rogers has a major edge in fundraising, and has about $2.5 million on hand to McInnis’ $9,462.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rogers, who has represented the 3rd Congressional District since 2003, chairs the powerful U.S. House Armed Services Committee. In response to emailed questions, Rogers sent a statement that he was focused on “lifting up our communities and advancing conservative policies.”
“I have been proud to champion President Trump’s peace through strength agenda in Congress, and the next two years must focus on completing what the Administration and Congressional Republicans have started,” the statement said.
McInnis, a military veteran who has worked as a teacher and in the defense industry, said he chose to run because “no one was stepping up.”
“After 30-plus years of serving the nation in the Army and the intelligence community, it just became clear to me my service had not ended like I thought it had,” he said.
McInnes said his chief goal is to improve the quality of life for residents. During an interview on Wednesday, he listed obstacles that people in the community face, including the long distances that people must travel to deliver a baby during pregnancy and the healthcare benefits they are losing as insurance companies scale back coverage.
“We talk about how everybody in this district should have an equal shot at having a healthy life, and that includes healthcare, that includes clean water, that includes universal lunches for school children.”
The Democratic nominee criticized Rogers for voting in 2025 for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which among other provisions cut Medicaid funding and requires states like Alabama to pay more for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). State officials have said that Alabama could be on the hook for $174 million if it does not reduce the error rate, a measurement of changing household circumstances for those on the program.
Rogers in a statement in July 2025 cited the bill’s increased spending on defense as a reason for his support.
McInnis says he would make healthcare a priority and improve the quality of jobs and pay.
“If two people in a household are each working 40 hours per week, you should be able to survive,” McInnis said. “You should have enough money to live.”
McInnis also said he would work to improve the quality of jobs, saying “what really need are jobs that pay better money, that pay a living wage.” He also said he would work to improve water and broadband infrastructure in the area.
Rogers has often cited his work to secure federal money for the district, including $10 million for Jacksonville State University from earmarked requests and $6.5 million for the Advanced Manufacturing Center for Workforce Development facility at Auburn University.
“We must enhance our national security, boost our economy, and protect unborn lives,” Rogers said in the statement.
McInnis said people should vote for him because he will work to improve the lives of people in the 3rd District.
“My entire adult life has been in service to this country, and in service to the people of this country, and this is a continuation of that service,” McInnis said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: State of the Race: Despite Barr’s favorite status in KY Senate race, Booker pushes forward
text:
Supporters of Republican Andy Barr and Democrat Charles Booker, both running for U.S. Senate, squared off at the annual Fancy Farm political picnic on Aug. 1, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)Despite what polls and political analysts say, Democrat Charles Booker says he’s ready to win the race for Kentucky’s open U.S. Senate seat next month. 
In an interview with the Kentucky Lantern, Booker said the race against Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Barr “feels like the perfect storm.” He said his previous Senate runs — in 2020 where he did not win the Democratic nomination and then in 2022 against U.S. Sen. Rand Paul — gave him “the chance to earn trust” and build support across Kentucky. 
Booker added that he sees a change in the political world. 
“The bottom has fallen out for so many people in ways they can’t unsee: the rising gas prices, rising grocery prices, this devastation with Iran, this trade war with Canada,” Booker said.  “They’re seeing the swamp get bigger and bigger and deeper, and then they’re seeing people like Mitch McConnell and Andy Barr essentially give them the middle finger, and they’re tired of it.”
Democrat Senate Candidate Charles Booker speaks on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony / Kentucky Lantern)
Yet, polls sponsored by Booker’s campaign show that the race has long been in Republicans’ favor. Independent race raters, like Sabato’s Crystal Ball and the Cook Political Report, have kept the Kentucky seat in solid red territory despite moving other races across the country in Democrats’ favor.  
Jonathan Miller, a former Democratic state treasurer, said Booker’s path forward is “very narrow and really relies on a tremendous blue wave” about three weeks from Election Day, Nov. 3. 
“The hope would be to really tie himself to that blue wave and hope that Trump continues to fall in favor in the state and potentially the Trump visit goes poorly,” Miller said. 
Barr, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump ahead of the primary in May, spoke at the president’s rally in Highland Heights on Saturday. Trump’s endorsement propelled Barr to victory in a fiery GOP primary. Trump himself criticized Booker by name, calling him “a communist lunatic.” 
Jake Cox, a Republican political strategist, said he had “zero doubt” Barr will get a title change after the election. 
“Kentucky’s still an exceedingly red state. This is not a purplish state,” Cox said. He added that Republicans have held a registration edge over Democrats for a few years. 
‘Big government socialist crazy’
Booker and Barr will have one televised debate Monday at 7 p.m. ET on WKYT and carried by other Gray Media stations in Kentucky. Booker told the Lantern he would look forward to debating Barr and have a chance to push back on Barr’s claims that he is a “socialist.” In other Senate races, like Michigan and Texas, GOP candidates also are attempting to tie their opponents to such labels. 
Booker added that the “only label I care about is the label on those grocery prices that have been rising” and has spent his time on the campaign trail talking with voters. 
“He’s been throwing these names around to try to scare people, and we’ve been disarming that,” Booker said of Barr’s socialism comments. “One because we have done so much work over the years to earn the trust of people, but we’re speaking to the issues, and instead of sowing division, fear and chaos, we’re lifting up common sense.”
Barr told reporters in a press conference ahead of the Trump rally that he planned to speak about “the distinctions between common sense versus big government socialist crazy,” and referred to Booker as the “Mamdani of Kentucky.” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who won election in 2025, has since become a democratic socialist boogeyman for Republicans. 
Republican Senate Candidate Andy Barr on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026, at the annual St. Jerome Picnic in Fancy Farm, Ky. (Austin Anthony / Kentucky Lantern)
“I know cost of living is the number one issue facing the American people, and we look forward to talking about the difference between the parties and the vision on who is best equipped to lower the cost of living, it certainly isn’t the socialists,” Barr said. “Government intervention, big government policies produce scarcity and higher costs, and especially when it comes to gas prices.”
Cox, the GOP strategist, said the message around socialism works “because it’s not just a buzzword intended to freak people out,” but is an economic issue.
“It’s something where our tax dollars will increase, the amount of taxes we pay will increase, the amount we spend will increase, and at the end of the day, the less money you have in your pocket, the more government services that are being provided,” Cox said, adding that such services are viewed often negatively “because we don’t have great experiences with government services all the time.”
However, Miller countered that “the socialist buzzword has been used to a level of ad nauseum across the country” and it dampened the impact it would have had in years past. 
“You see a lot of Democrats really pushing back against that and being successful,” Miller said, giving the example of Zach Dembo in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, which is Barr’s open seat. Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado. 
What’s next?
Barr and Booker are vying to succeed longtime U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell in office. The Republican said in early 2025 that he would not seek reelection this cycle. He was first elected in 1984. 
If Barr is elected to the Senate, as it likely seems, Cox said he would enter the chamber as a freshman but he will do so with experience in Washington. Barr was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012. 
“Andy Barr is well-prepped and well knowledgeable on what exactly goes into the legislative process and understanding the Washington machine, so when he gets in there, there won’t be a delay in him figuring out and understanding what does it take to put money in the coffer that comes home,” Cox said. 
Barr will also be the junior senator to U.S. Sen. Rand Paul, another Republican. Cox said they have a “great relationship” and would be able to work together for the state. 
Miller said Barr probably will not have the power McConnell had right out of the gate. The long-time senior senator stepped down as the Senate Republican leader in 2024 after becoming the longest serving Senate party leader in U.S. history. 
“I think should he win, particularly by a comfortable margin, he could have a long career in D.C. He’s young and he’s very bright and he’s respected by his colleagues up there,” Miller said of Barr, but there has been recent backlash to politicians like McConnell overstaying their welcome in office. 
“I think that is a trend that might continue, so we won’t see as many five-, six-, seven-term senators as we have in the past,” Miller added. 
While Cox said Booker is likely to “return to life again as a double-digit loser in this election,” Miller said he may still have a political future ahead, particularly in Louisville. Booker had some encouragement to run for Louisville mayor in the past, but he did not. Now, incumbent Mayor Craig Greenberg is seeking reelection and is being challenged by Councilwoman Shameka Parrish-Wright. 
“Craig Greenberg is term-limited, so I could see Charles as a potential candidate for mayor four years from now,” Miller said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: The predicted blue wave probably begins in Kentucky on Nov. 3
text:
Zach Dembo speaks to constituents at a campaign fundraiser on Sept. 11, 2026, in Paint Lick, Kentucky. (Photo by Arden Barnes for KY Lantern)This column was originally published in the Northern Kentucky Tribune.
LEXINGTON, Ky. – It’s been 30 years or more since Kentucky was a bellwether state in national politics, but it might be this year. Part of it, at least.
That part is the section of Kentucky that the nation may know best, the Bluegrass Region around Lexington. Most of it is in the 6th Congressional District, the closest thing the state has to a “purple” district. It has turned redder with the elections of Republican Rep. Andy Barr, Donald Trump’s takeover of the GOP, and the legislature’s removal of Democratic Franklin County from the district. But now Barr is running for the U.S. Senate seat being vacated by Mitch McConnell, and the seat he has held for 14 years is very much up for grabs.
Trump carried the district in 2024 by 15 points, but has become an albatross for Republicans in the 6th District for the same big reason he’s at his record low nationally: a war of choice that has been a disaster, resulting in high fuel prices on top of persistent inflation.
Some polls say Trump’s net approval has dropped more here in Kentucky than in any other state, to minus 12 points, so he is surely farther underwater in the 6th District, where party registration is virtually even and one in eight voters don’t belong to a major party.
Presidential approval is the biggest factor in midterm elections, and voting locations in the district will be among the first in the nation to close, so it is likely to be an early indicator of how large the blue wave in the Nov. 3 midterms will be.
At this point, I give Democratic nominee Zach Dembo a small edge over Republican Ralph Alvarado. Nonpartisan rating outfits say the race leans Republican, but those ratings have been moving Dembo’s way, perhaps correcting an early bias that depended too much on recent performances in the district by Trump and by Barr, who has had weak opponents.
Now Trump’s brand is bad, which the Alvarado campaign clearly illustrated weeks ago by removing from its website all mention of the president except one photo in a 15-picture gallery. Dembo avoids naming the president, perhaps to avoid stirring up Trump voters, but he cites “the corruption in Washington D.C. and this Administration’s abuse of the criminal justice system,” his stated reason for resigning as a federal prosecutor.
Alvarado, a physician, is the race’s bad-luck candidate. In 2019, he ran for lieutenant governor with Matt Bevin, who lost his bid for re-election and then issued several controversial pardons, and recently was jailed for contempt of court for failure to file financial data in his Louisville divorce case. Democrats are hanging Bevin around Alvarado’s neck; in one of their latest ads Dembo points at a cutout photo of Bevin and says “This is my opponent. OK, you got me. But Ralph Alvarado is basically the same guy.”
That’s unfair to Alvarado, who had no previous ties to Bevin, other than being a state senator, and who “kept silent” about the pardons, as the ad says. But Bevin’s more toxic than Trump, and the spot ends with the Bevin cutout being carried by Gov. Andy Beshear, likely the state’s most popular politician – and Dembo’s most recent employer. (Dembo’s wife is a prosecutor for Republican Russell Coleman, the state attorney general.)
Republicans are running a flood of spots claiming Dembo would raise taxes and protect illegal immigrants, but he has not responded in ads, indicating that he believes voters driven by those issues are unlikely to vote for him. He has name recognition and support from his victory in a busy primary over more liberal candidates, and Democrats in tight races in other states say similar influxes of Republican ad money have had little effect.
Amid the ad barrage on Lexington TV, the most telling ad may be one for Barr in the Senate race, in which a “loyal Democrat” says she’s for him. Turnout is crucial in midterms, and national polls and early-voting data in some states show Democrats are much more motivated to vote than Republicans. Many registered Democrats who don’t pay much attention to politics could turn out and vote for Barr’s opponent, Charles Booker, mainly or solely because he’s the Democratic nominee at a time when the Republican label has gone bad.
Barr’s ad appears aimed at turning out registered Democrats who have become accustomed to voting for Republicans but aren’t inclined to vote in midterms. Those are voters Alvarado needs to get, but it’s hard to tell how he might get them, or much else about him. He declined to debate Dembo on KET Monday night, and his campaign ignored my repeated requests for an interview and access to any campaign event. It looks and acts like a campaign that’s on the back foot.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Norfolk-backed firm invests millions elsewhere as city waits
text:
Hampton Roads Ventures, created by the Norfolk Redevelopment and Housing Authority, is headquartered in this office building in Norfolk. (Photo by Jim Morrison/For the Virginia Mercury)Hampton Roads Ventures backed a $12 million investment in a grocery store in rural Marion, $10 million for a farm equipment distribution center in Martinsville and $3 million for a supermarket in Louisiana in the past year.
And once again, none of its projects were in Norfolk.
More than four years ago, Norfolk’s City Council passed a resolution requiring the for-profit subsidiary of the Norfolk Redevelopment and Housing Authority to seek projects in the city. Year after year, the annual report required by that resolution shows no progress supporting a project in the city.
This year’s report, filed on Sept. 30, does not outline any efforts to invest in Norfolk or the region. 
City council members said they were disappointed but not surprised. Two members who co-chair the city’s commission on housing, said they will push for HRV, which usually earns more than  $1 million in profits annually, to help back an affordable housing program being set up by the city. 
Jennifer Donohue, HRV’s chief executive officer, did not respond to an email seeking comment.
The HRV investments follow a pattern similar to that of recent years, backing the kinds of projects needed in Norfolk, but in other localities. 
In Marion, Food City opened a 56,700-square-foot store in September, replacing the grocer’s existing location and creating 50 new area jobs. 
Rural King, a national brand specializing in farm equipment, home goods, and outdoor needs, is investing $42 million, including the HRV tax credits, in a distribution facility in Martinsville projected to create 150 new jobs. 
And Rouses is building a 47,694 square-foot facility in Chalmette, La., that the company says will transform a dormant commercial corridor when it opens in 2027.
Over the last 18 years, HRV  has invested everywhere but Norfolk, contrary to the practice of other community development entities that focus locally. 
Community development entities like HRV, which was created in 2003 with the approval of the city council, may be offshoots of banks, nonprofits, public agencies or other financial institutions. 
They apply for New Markets Tax Credits from the U.S. Treasury Department and, if they prevail in the highly competitive process, they match projects with investors who earn a 39% tax break over seven years. 
The Treasury Department says it spurs $8 in private investment for every dollar invested.
Norfolk is a prime market for that investment, with 16 severely distressed census tracts given the highest priority for new markets tax allocations. The poverty rate in those ranges from 31% to as high as 80%, and the unemployment rate tops out at 40%.
The city council resolution, passed more than four years ago, pushed for the subsidiary to invest in Norfolk projects and sought more oversight. It followed a Virginia Mercury investigation revealing that HRV had allocated only a fraction of its $360 million in tax credits to Norfolk’s distressed areas. 
Since those stories were published, the tax credits allocations to HRV have grown to $470 million. It has not done a project in Norfolk since 2008. 
The for-profit subsidiary of NRHA has backed investments in 17 states and the District of Columbia, according to Treasury Department data. Those projects include grocery stores, foodbanks, health centers and agricultural companies.
The most recent Treasury Department report on community development entities shows HRV does not have any tax credits available to invest. It last won allocations in 2023. The next round of allocations will be awarded in late 2027. HRV appears to be the only local development entity in the country created by a locality that has not focused on local projects.
 Profit transfers to NRHA and others

From January through September of this year, HRV had a net income of $1.77 million, according to the report. Its largest expenses for those nine months were $406,000 for payroll, $216,000 for accounting and $152,000 for consulting. HRV has three staff members. 
HRV transferred $850,000 of its profits to NRHA for youth workforce development, capital investment to improve broadband access in NRHA communities, including Young Terrace, Diggs Town and Grandy Village, and intergenerational programming to bring together youths and seniors. 
In the nearly five years since the Mercury series was published, HRV has transferred more than $5.2 million to NRHA. In the 18 preceding years, it had transferred $1.3 million.
In previously unreported donations, HRV gave Norfolk State University a total of $300,000 in 2025 to support the athletic department in the wake of the school hiring former National Football League star Michael Vick as head coach. 
City Attorney Adam Melita, who took office in recent months, said he did not feel comfortable offering an opinion about whether the requirements of the resolution were met by the report because he was not in place when it passed. 
After reviewing the 2022 resolution, Carlos Clanton, a city council member, said he wanted to know more about the distributions. 
“I believe there is a legitimate question about the scope of the reporting requirements and whether the information currently provided gives the City Council a comprehensive understanding of HRV’s financial activities,” he added. 
“Transparency and accountability are particularly important given HRV’s relationship with NRHA and its origins in serving communities facing significant economic challenges.”
The donation was not mentioned in that year’s report to the city. Nor were other donations to other organizations in years past. That does not comply with the resolution, which requires NRHA to provide ”an accounting of the use of earnings distributed for its past and current fiscal year.”
HRV’s lawyer has said its investment decisions are led by an advisory board scattered across the country. But it’s not clear when or whether the board meets. 
HRV has denied public records requests despite the company being a subsidiary of NRHA, a public body subject to records requests. Similar entities, like the nonprofit Chicago Development Fund (CDF), hold public meetings of their governing and advisory boards. 
Norfolk’s city council has no control over HRV, although it appoints NRHA commissioners, some of whom serve on the HRV board. HRV is wholly owned by the NRHA. 
The Community Development Financial Institutions Fund, the federal agency that oversees the tax credits program, wanted public officials to have oversight of the for-profit Hampton Roads Ventures. Norfolk City Council’s 2003 resolution authorizing HRV, a requirement of state law, noted it would be “managed by the commissioners of the Authority.”  
 Council members suggest profits benefit affordable housing

Mayor Kenneth Alexander did not respond to emails seeking comment. However, four council members expressed disappointment that HRV once again failed to invest in Norfolk or even explain how it had marketed itself locally. 
Clanton and Jeremy McGee, city council members who co-chair the mayor’s Housing Commission, said separately that they are looking for HRV to potentially help with the city’s affordable housing crisis. 
While community development entities have backed for-sale affordable home projects in dozens of other cities, HRV has not. Nor has it contacted a St. Louis firm, suggested by a former council member, that specializes in making the projects happen nationwide and assumes any risk. 
Creating owner-occupied housing is a key to building generational wealth and helping people out of poverty. The interim report the commission issued earlier this year said the city needed to create more pathways to homeownership.
”Other communities have successfully utilized this financing mechanism to help nonprofit and mission-driven developers create homeownership opportunities, rehabilitate vacant properties, and support mixed-use development,” Clanton said. “These are approaches worth evaluating for Norfolk.”
In the absence of HRV backing a Norfolk project, McGee suggested using the annual revenues for housing. 
”I think that there’s an opportunity to redirect those (HRV) profits to address the housing crisis that is staring us in the face, and to really put those dollars to work to create housing opportunities that are definitely needed in Norfolk,” he said.
Council member John “JP” Paige said he supported the payment to Norfolk State because Vick’’s hiring brought attention to Norfolk. But he also lamented the lack of Norfolk projects. 
”We need to do more. We need grocery stores here now,” he added. ”We’re in a housing crisis.”
Council member Courtney Doyle was succinct: “I continue to be disappointed that year after year they do not invest in Norfolk and they don’t demonstrate any interest in doing so.”
