name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan advocates work to ease election security anxieties as November 3 approaches
text:
A test ballot is submitted to a precinct tabulator in the Lansing Elections Office prior to the August primary. July 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. With just over two weeks until the November 3 general election, anxieties over federal interference on Election Day, as well as fears about the security of casting a ballot in the first place, are ever-present in conversations about election integrity in Michigan.
Advocates and nonprofits are working to assuage those concerns — as Wayne State University election law professor Michael Brady said in a call with Keep Our Republic on Wednesday, “This election is business as usual.”
Andrew Walchuk, the policy director and counsel for Common Cause, attributed this to what he described as President Donald Trump’s villainization of election officials and even individual voters and communities who he dislikes. 
“He has created this environment of people who are engaged in a way that they’ve never been engaged before,” Walchuk said. “We have seen outreach across the country and so many of our states, from partner organizations that never have been involved in elections, just small community groups that are wondering what can we do, and for me that really says that people care about our democratic system, people care about their right to vote, and they’re not going to take kindly to someone who is trying to tear it all down.”
Different groups are taking different approaches to convincing Michigan’s voters that the ballots they cast on or leading up to Nov. 3 will be counted securely and fairly. 
Lansing City Clerk Chris Swope said in an Oct. 13 press conference that the “sheer number of different municipalities” involved in Michigan’s largely decentralized election system provide an important check for election security. 
“The county clerk, the city and township clerks work together. The county programs the election, and then the clerks execute it. There’s a separation of duties that provides additional security,” he said. “Not only do we have over 1,600 clerks in Michigan, but we have thousands upon thousands of election workers that are your neighbors working in the polling places on Election Day, and those are identified by party. And there are certain duties that have to be done by a Democrat and a Republican.”
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Lansing City Clerk Chris Swope take questions from reporters on Feb. 21, 2024. | Kyle Davidson
Walchuk’s organization, Common Cause, is also part of a broader Election Protection Coalition that is maintaining a voter hotline to assist voters with casting their ballot and to report any concerns that they have on Election Day, which Walchuk described as having “first line responders on the ground for any issues that might be coming up for voters.”
“What we want to ensure, and what we believe will happen because of efforts like our organizations and so many allies in this space, we want to make sure that voters feel safe and secure, exercising their right to vote,” he said. “I think that we will be able to ensure that with the work of you know the thousands of volunteers who become part of this program during the election period.”
Two potential threats from the federal government are also front of mind for many voters experiencing election anxieties — the presence of federal agents, especially armed ones, at polling places, and the weaponization of the U.S. Postal Service by the Trump administration to limit the power of mail-in voting.



Quotation







The idea that some of these monitors, whether intentionally or unintentionally, will disregard the rules governing third-party observers in the state where they are, and will try to assert some level of authority that they do not legally have, that piece does worry me.


– Andrew Walchuk, the policy director and counsel for Common Cause


Walchuk distinguished between armed federal agents from agencies like ICE or the Department of Homeland Security, who are not allowed to be present at polling places, and standard election monitors, generally from the Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, which has existed since 1957. 
“What really worries me is the fact that the civil rights division has been decimated by this administration, and so what we are seeing is a massive number of folks who just do not have the experience and training,” Walchuk added. “The idea that some of these monitors, whether intentionally or unintentionally, will disregard the rules governing third-party observers in the state where they are, and will try to assert some level of authority that they do not legally have, that piece does worry me.”
Clinton Township Clerk Kim Meltzer and Kent County Clerk Lisa Lyons said in the press conference hosted by Keep Our Republic that they intend to rely on local law enforcement in the case of federal agents on the ground on Election Day, though Meltzer emphasized, “It’s not likely to happen.” 
“I am not law enforcement. It’s not my background. So I’m grateful that we do have a police department in some contract with the local, or the county sheriff. Clerks can rely upon local law enforcement in that capacity,” Meltzer said. “Workers want to make sure they’ve got all the tools necessary to service their constituency, and we provide that for them.”
Pictured clockwise: Clinton Township Clerk Kim Meltzer, Kamryn Hoadley, Michigan senior advisor with Keep Our Republic, Kent County Clerk Lisa Posthumus Lyons and Mike Brady, a member of Save Our Republic’s Michigan Advisory Council, participating in a Zoom press conference on Oct. 14, 2026. (Screenshot)
Walchuk also said that when talking to voters, he makes sure to highlight the court victories that have blocked Trump administration policies that would make mail-in voting harder.
“The U.S. Postal Service has been handling mail voting for decades, and this is a process that they know how to do, and they have already stated that they will once again, as they have in past years, take extraordinary measures to ensure that ballot mail is delivered on time. So that gives me confidence that is something that USPS has done in the past,” he said. “What I really blame is the Trump administration for introducing all of this confusion about mail voting and for creating a distraction as it tried to add a new duty on top of all of the other duties that the USPS has of delivering election mail, of deciding whose mail actually gets delivered, but that was blocked.”
Swope similarly said that he had been concerned about changing the role of the postal service to serve as the “gatekeeper of ballots,” but those policies were not enacted.
“I always say the United States postal system is a great institution, but they are not infallible. So we have occasional reports of ballots just not making it to the voter. What I try to do is keep in communication with the voter,” he said. “That communication is key as we get close to an election. I email folks a reminder just so that if they mailed it and they thought it came and it didn’t, that’s their flag. The communication is key, but by and large the post office does well. But there are just occasional mishaps.”
Kaitlyn Wilkins, the founder of the Screaming Eagle Creative Collective nonprofit running the In Michigan We Trust campaign, said that the key message that she is seeking to get across to voters in terms of trust in absentee voting is the fact that it is enshrined in the Michigan Constitution, with safeguards in place. 
“Your signature gets verified two times: once on your application, once from your return envelope against the vote your signature on file,” she said, echoing Swope. “There’s video monitored drop boxes, and you can track your ballot like a package and sign up for email alerts from the time you mail it to the time it gets counted.”
Volunteers handed out flyers with voting information at the No Kings: Vote Early demonstration in downtown Grand Rapids Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Emma J Nelson/Michigan Advance)
Other advocacy organizations are focused on specific portions of the elections process in their work to ensure to voters that the process is fair and secure.
One such group is the Michigan Election Observation Project, which launched an advisory board and began an effort to recruit hundreds of Michiganders to serve as election observers in 15 counties — Genesee, Macomb, Oakland, St. Joseph, Kalamazoo, Berrien, Ottawa, Kent, Washtenaw, Leelanau, Antrim, Marquette, Ingham, Wayne and Muskegon. 
“At a time when we have hotly contested elections days away, we’re pleased to have MEOP in our state to help provide even greater transparency and trust in our elections. The public benefits when credible, fact-based information is readily available,” said former Gov. John Engler in a press release announcing the election observation effort.
Looking past Election Day, the Election Truth Alliance is helping voters understand state laws around recounts and audits and providing information to candidates and voters about what can justify a recount request.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Data centers and AI: a rare and raw issue  in Virginia for this midterm election
text:
An aerial view shows a data center situated near single-family homes in Northern Virginia. The backlash against data centers has become a flashpoint in state and federal races across the country. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)If you’re alarmed about the proliferation of data centers — gargantuan, windowless megastructures that power social media, live-streaming, cloud storage, e-commerce, text messaging, cryptocurrency, online betting, artificial intelligence and near-universal security surveillance — you’re in good company this election year.
From sea to shining sea, Jane and John Q. Public have emerged from comfortable obscurity to pack marathon meetings of local zoning and governing boards, unified in full-throated opposition to locating data centers in their communities.
The dispute is alive and thriving in this midterm congressional election.
Americans are scared and angry, and nowhere is that truer than in Virginia, the holy land of data centers. Loudoun County, an exurb of Washington, D.C., is home to the planet’s densest concentration of them, and they’ve been springing up like toadstools elsewhere across the commonwealth.
Governmental deference to data centers and the uber-wealthy corporations behind them is faltering, however, as officeholders across the political spectrum — some of them once cheerleaders for the industry — feel firsthand the fresh, hot wrath of constituents defending the most important investments of their lives: their homes.
Funny how perspectives change when re-election is at stake.
Politically, data centers were barely a blip on the screen a year ago. Now, they are featured in candidate talking points and campaign ads, particularly those aired by or favoring Democrats. More on that later.
“This issue is not going away. It just continues to be amplified, and it is going to have an impact on elections here in Virginia and nationally,” said Mark Rozell, a political science professor at the Schar School of Policy and Government at George Mason University.
A statewide poll of 1,101 registered Virginia voters at the end of March by the Schar School and the Washington Post showed a collapse in public support for data centers. Only 35% of respondents were comfortable with a data center in their communities. In 2023, the same poll found 69% were OK with it.
“It’s a rare consensus issue right now for both parties because the public is decidedly on one side of this issue.” Rozell said, noting the potency the issue has in Virginia’s 1st and 7th Congressional Districts where data centers are a daily concern. “Whether it’s accurate or exaggerated fear, … politically there is a great deal of fear out there.”
Following the money for this election cycle, however, reveals Big Data has been kindest to Virginia Democrats.
Of the reported $372,000 given since Jan. 1, 2025, to 10 Virginia congressional and Senate candidates by the data processing and computer services sector, almost four of every five dollars went to Democrats, according to OpenSecrets.org, a nonprofit and nonpartisan tracker of American political spending and influence. Just two recipients — 1st District Rep. Rob Wittman and 2nd District Rep. Jen Kiggans — are Republicans.
It’s hard to overstate the grassroots activism the data center boom in Virginia has provoked since the start of this year, but the issue is not new. Opposition has galvanized residents into clear, effective and organized voices against data center encroachment for a decade or more, and with notable successes lately.
Elena Schlossberg of western Prince William County began battling data centers near her home in 2014. The former makeup artist and middle school counselor became a driving force in the Coalition to Protect Prince William County that recently prevailed over plans to develop the 2,000-acre Dulles Cloud South project that would have packed 4.3 million square feet of computer servers into a structure several stories tall. It would have been the largest such facility on earth.
Not that long ago, Big Tech leviathans like Google, Amazon or Meta could pick their sites almost at will as elected leaders of different localities competed for an edge in landing a data center for their communities. Now, Prince William, Fauquier, Loudoun and Carroll counties are among a growing number of localities denying, delaying or limiting data center construction.
“What’s changed is that community after community after community finally woke up,” said Schlossberg. “The strategy of the industry had been to simply ignore the concerns of the community — concerns we were highlighting about (electrical) grid stress and affordability, about elected leaders not listening to their constituents.”
They’re listening now. 
At the state level, this year’s legislative dispute over whether to end a sales tax exemption that saves data centers tens of millions of dollars on new equipment purchases brought the commonwealth closer than it has ever come to a government shutdown from missing the deadline to pass a new state budget.
That disagreement was between Democrats: the Senate majority versus the House of Delegates majority allied with Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger.
At the federal level, U.S. Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., has become a new convert for the data center resistance, Schlossberg said. Until recently, she said, he had kept his distance from her group, calling data centers “a local issue.” Now, the first ad of his campaign for a fourth term focuses on data centers and AI.
“We as a coalition begged Mark Warner to get engaged in the Digital Gateway (project) problem,” she said. “Now, suddenly, he’s concerned? He’s making a statement that ‘they (data centers) need to cover their own costs’ and ‘this is a problem.’ No kidding!”
Yet Republicans face a steeper climb as they struggle to retain their congressional majorities, and the reason is not new: a deeply unpopular Republican president allied with tech billionaires, and a GOP-run Congress that won’t stand up to him.
Republican incumbents saw the peril of risking Donald Trump’s wrath when he garroted the political career of Republican former 5th District Rep. Bob Good, once a loyal Trump footman, for briefly backing Trump’s 2024 primary rival, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. 
Should they need fresher reminders, look to Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky and GOP Sens. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana and John Cornyn of Texas, all of whom lost safe seats in bright-red states to Trump-anointed primary challengers.
So, when Trump took a stand in September supporting full-throttle development of artificial intelligence and the data centers that sustain it — even as top AI researchers warned it could kill humankind — most GOP candidates fell meekly in line, though a few oppose laissez faire AI growth.
Was last month’s presidential show of obeisance toward the world’s mightiest tech companies necessary? Was there any doubt about it after Trump’s second inauguration when Big Tech multibillionaires literally stood beside him as he was sworn in?
If not for fear of Trump, how many more Republicans in this election would publicly align themselves with ordinary voters against limitless wealth and influence from an industry poised to rule the planet?
I suspect there would be quite a few. They talk to people and they read polls. It would fit comfortably into their rhetoric championing working folk. Besides, who doesn’t love a good David vs. Goliath narrative? But it’s late in the game for such an epiphany now.
Issues like this rarely present themselves in politics. It’s real and raw, grounded in deep fear and tenuous hope. Trivialize it at your peril. And for candidates now talking the talk, Schlossberg had a warning.
“If you run and win on this issue but don’t produce the receipts,” she said, “you won’t win again.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Dominion’s energy roadmap keeps fossil fuels in the mix, expands solar
text:
Dominion's Scott Solar pilot battery project in Powhatan. (Courtesy of Dominion)Dominion Energy plans to add more than 39 gigawatts of new power generation over the next 20 years as electricity demand surges across Virginia, according to the company’s latest filing with the State Corporation Commission.
Over that period, Dominion plans to build more than 21 gigawatts of new solar energy, 3.5 gigawatts of battery storage, 9 gigawatts of natural gas, 3.3 gigawatts of wind, and 2 gigawatts of small modular reactors.
The filing is part of the annual update to Dominion’s integrated resource plan (IRP). It is not a concrete list of projects but a roadmap of how the company expects to meet energy demand. 
While this year’s update will not be litigated or subject to changes through final order, the filing outlines where the company expects demand to go and how it plans to meet it.
A key part of the plan is continued reliance on fossil fuels despite the Virginia Clean Economy Act’s mandate to retire carbon emitting energy sources – namely coal and natural gas. 
The company’s filing states green energy sources are not commercially viable or dispatchable enough to meet annual load growth of roughly 4%, or 500 to 700 megawatts, with power demand expected to double by 2045. 
Those figures do not include load growth for the cooperative utilities that also rely on Dominion for power and transmission.
“To meet the energy and capacity needs associated with the load forecast, and in the absence of a commercially viable carbon-free, dispatchable generation alternative, natural gas generation will remain a critical component of the (Dominion’s) strategy to reliably meet generation demand,” the filing stated.
Projections for increases in the average residential customer’s bill will vary depending on whether they use the company’s preferred calculation or the method directed by the SCC. Under the company’s calculation, a household using 1000 kilowatt-hours a month would see its monthly bill rise to an estimated $258.03 by 2036 and $283.65 in 2046. 
Under the SCC’s mandated calculation method, monthly bills are projected to reach $320.26 in 2036 and $458.22 in 2046. Dominion has continued to push back on the SCC’s methodology for calculating bills in later years. 
“(Dominion) believes that this methodology results in overstated bill projections because it does not reflect anticipated growth in sales over the period on which each portfolio is based,” the filing stated.
The company says bringing more energy generation projects online will reduce its reliance on power purchases from the regional grid operator,  PJM. Virginia is one of the largest importers of energy on the East Coast.
“Our preferred plan calls for more than 39 gigawatts of new power generation assets over the next 20 years – more than three-fourths of which is carbon-free solar, offshore wind, energy storage and advanced nuclear technology – and a decreasing reliance on more costly purchases from the PJM market,” Dominion spokesperson Jeremy Slayton said.
The SCC will review the filing and accept the plan if it is deemed sufficient. A full trial on the updated integrated resource plan is scheduled for fall of 2027.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: No-nonsense Ken Block ran for governor twice and lost. Will his 3rd time charm RI voters?
text:
Independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block shakes hands with spectators on Atwells Avenue in Providence during the annual Federal Hill Columbus Day Parade on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. (Courtesy of Block campaign)Ken Block’s campaign calculus rests squarely on the numbers. 
Battling against entrenched party politics as an independent candidate for governor with only modest name recognition and even less campaign cash, he looks to polling as proof he can beat Democratic rival Helena Buonanno Foulkes.
“Her favorability, beyond anything else, where her numbers are, is the reason I sleep well at night,” the 60-year-old software engineer said.
He need only look to two recent polls, from WPRI-TV 12 and the University of New Hampshire, each showing Block was the only gubernatorial candidate who more voters liked than disliked. The most recent, from WPRI on Oct. 13, put Block’s net favorability rating at 27. Foulkes had a net favorability rating of minus 1, while GOP nominee Aaron Guckian stood at minus 20. 
The same survey put Foulkes 9 points ahead of Block among likely voters — significant progress given the 27-point lead she held over him in an August survey.
But nearly 1 in 10 voters still don’t know enough about him to form an opinion, compared with just 2% who said the same for Foulkes.
That’s even though his name has lingered on the fringes of local political talk for the last 12 years, ever since his second gubernatorial campaign ended in a bruising defeat against Allan Fung in the 2014 Republican primary.  
Even after Block became a leading voice in the chorus of criticisms against Gov. Dan McKee after the abrupt 2024 closure of the Washington Bridge. He paid for two billboards over the replacement highway in 2024.
“If they had done their job, you would be home already,” read one.
Block insists he never contemplated a comeback until friends asked him if he might run again over dinner in March. 
“I think he sees a time right now where he can really make a difference,” Jen Block, his wife of 26 years, said in a recent interview. “Who am I to hold him back?”
Her husband’s ambitions carried him through a 2008 federal lawsuit and subsequent statewide signature collection campaign to start the Moderate Party, debuting as the party’s first gubernatorial candidate in 2010. Three years later, he was the public face of the successful movement to get rid of the master lever that allowed for straight-party voting in Rhode Island.
In 2020,the Trump campaign hired his firm to audit the 2020 elections for alleged voter fraud. He found none, documenting the evidence in a 2024 book, “Disproven.”
Few challenges compared, however, to running for office.
“What surprised me the most, was how much it reached into the deepest parts of my brain and engaged me in a way few activities I have done in my life have,” he said.
After two previous campaigns, independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block, shown at his home in Barrington, now sees the governor’s office within striking distance. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Answers for unsettled voters but no tax returns
Over the hum of landscapers outside his Barrington home one recent morning — Block said he normally mows his lawn but doesn’t have time this year — the software engineer lays out his strategy. 
“People are unsettled politically, and they’re looking for different answers,” Block, 61, said. “My job is to capitalize on that, and show voters across the spectrum that I have the answers they’re looking for.”
The Providence Journal described him as “wide-eyed and wonkish” during his first campaign in 2010. Now Block has the confidence and charisma of a seasoned politician, despite never having held or won elected office.
His beliefs haven’t changed from his last two campaigns. But he’s learned the art of delivery. Short face-to-camera video clips on his campaign website — a series titled “Ken I Be Honest?” — explain his positions on education, energy costs, and partisan politics.
He still doesn’t love walking into a restaurant, interrupting people’s meals to introduce himself, but he can get over the discomfort, shaking hands, kissing babies and waving in parades. The campaign has him on the go all the time. 
His afternoon schedule includes a phone interview with Reuters, a presentation to Rhode Island College student reporters and a “meet and greet” at a supporter’s home in Greenville.
“He is more understanding of how difficult day-to-day life is probably than ever before,” said Matt Schwiech, Block’s campaign manager, who also worked on his 2014 campaign. “That’s because he’s really out talking to voters, listening to their concerns.”



Quotation







People are unsettled politically, and they’re looking for different answers. My job is to capitalize on that, and show voters across the spectrum that I have the answers they’re looking for.


– Ken Block, independent candidate for governor


Block has a lot of ideas to ease the affordability crunch: getting rid of car inspections (and the $55 biannual cost), making state public transit free for a year and tackling “hidden” taxes on energy and cell phone bills.
He grew up in Connecticut in a household where both his parents worked, “scrimping and saving” in his words, to pay for college for him and his two siblings. His dad was a college professor and his mom an occupational therapist and nurse. 
Block graduated from Dartmouth College in New Hampshire with a computer science degree and student loan debt, which he paid off within four years of graduating thanks to his early career as a consultant for Brightstar Lottery — then GTech — in Providence.
“My ‘nice car’ is a 6-year-old Kia,” Block said.
The president of Simpatico Software Systems, which he founded in 2001, Block and his six-person team have consulted for international companies, defense contractors and government agencies, including the states of Texas and Rhode Island. He declined to share details of current customers, citing confidentiality.
Block also refused to provide a copy of his tax returns. 
Since launching his 2026 campaign, he has put more than $200,000 of his own money into his account, with more than $1.2 million in personal loans dating back to his first run in 2010, according to public campaign finance reports. He has just over $236,000 cash on hand as of Oct. 5.
His four-bedroom, 2.5-bath farmhouse in Barrington — one of the state’s wealthiest communities — was valued at nearly $1.9 million in fiscal 2026. The undeveloped land cost $275,000 when he and his wife bought it in 2004, according to property records.
Both his children graduated from The Wheeler School in Providence, where Jen Block provides academic support to middle school students. Annual tuition currently costs $54,000 for students in grades 9 to 12. Max Pearlstein, a school spokesperson, confirmed via email that employees’ children qualify for tuition discounts, but did not say how much is discounted.
Patrons outside an Atwells Avenue bar in Providence greet independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block during the annual Federal Hill Columbus Day Parade on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. (Courtesy of Block campaign)
Buses, housing and the bridge 
Block has ridden a Rhode Island Public Transit Authority bus just once — so long ago he can’t remember the exact when. But he can’t forget the agonizingly slow 90-minute  commute from his home to his Warwick office. 
“Never again,” he vowed. 
Low ridership is a pain point for the perpetually cash-strapped public bus agency. Block’s solution after talking to riders, RIPTA employees and transit advocates: make it fare-free for a year, increasing ridership and then make the popular routes more frequent while getting rid of the hardly used ones. 
His no-nonsense approach focuses on maximum efficiency and results, with pain points identified from personal experience.
He finds the state tax payment portal impossible to navigate. He pays his accountant to submit the quarterly corporate payments for him.
He was so frustrated with the required monthly paper filings for the state sales tax license on his book he stopped selling it at book fairs and speaking gigs, referring enthused readers to other retailers.
Rather than spending half a million dollars per unit to spur affordable housing development — the present cost of state housing development according to calculations from the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council — Block thinks the state should focus on identifying, acquiring and redeveloping open or unused space, with buy-in from municipalities. There’s no cost estimate for his plan, which Foulkes and Guckian have both criticized for lack of detail.
Time on the state’s lawsuit against 11 contractors accused of negligence in repair or inspection of Washington Bridge is probably better spent on reshaping the management and practices within the state transportation department, he concluded. And the nearly $1 million cost to restart the state truck trolling program? 
“Not happening” if he’s elected.
His tax and business ideas don’t sound too far off from what Republican Guckian has pitched, though Block insists the two couldn’t be more different.
Block loves the details, the numbers and the reports. He could talk for hours about the ways to fix the state’s troubled payroll system.
“This is where I eat and live,” he said. 
A promise to hold weekly pressers
Convincing a Democratic supermajority in the Rhode Island General Assembly to allocate money to clean house and eliminate the people in charge of the payroll debacle — on his to-do list for the first 100 days in office — won’t be so easy, he acknowledged.
Block said he would air disputes with the legislature via a weekly press conference.
“The way I’ve gotten things done that the General Assembly doesn’t want to have done, and I’ve done that a few times now, it’s through effective use of the bully pulpit,” Block said. 
Beneath the strong-willed, persuasive personality is a gentler Block, one who takes his employees out for lunch, prefers to listen to jazz music while driving and lets his 7-year-old Goldendoodle, Tilly, in and out of his backyard a half-dozen times with endless patience during a 90-minute interview. 
Politics wasn’t always his passion. He preferred computers, hooked since his uncle gifted him an Apple II in the 1980s, when Block was a high school student.
A saxophone player who toured briefly with a jazz band after college, Block was much more likely to wax poetic about music than policy or elections. Stephen Conlin, a close friend from college, recalled “epic” ping-pong battles with Block in the basement of their shared Boston rental.
“He’s a very competitive person, as am I,” Conlin said. “His accounting of the results always differed from mine.”
That same competitive spirit is why Block isn’t running as a third-party candidate this time.
“Because I want to win,” he said.
Rhode Island Current will have a profile of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes on Tuesday. Republican Aaron Guckian was unavailable for a sit-down interview despite multiple requests. The governor’s race has a total of five candidates. Also running are independents Jasjit “Jay” Gotra and C.D. Reynolds.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: No one filed to run in a special Isle of Wight election. What happens now?
text:
Voters in Isle of Wight County’s District 1 will choose a new school board member by write-in vote after no candidates qualified to appear on the special election ballot. (Photo by  Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)By Mechelle Hankerson / WHRO
When Isle of Wight voters scan their ballot this election season, they’ll notice something different: Instead of names next to bubbles, voters will find a space to write in a name for recently vacated school board seat.
Former school board member Brandi Perkins resigned from the board on July 31. By the time the county issued a writ of election to fill the seat, the deadline to file as a candidate passed.
Now, three of the residents whom the board considered for Perkins’ temporary replacement are hopeful that write-in campaigns can work: Former public schools finance official Jeff Ryder, civil engineer Greg Brown and nonprofit director Candy Hayes.
“It reflects the challenging intersection of deadlines,” said Jesse Richman, political science professor at Old Dominion University. “You’ve got a deadline for ballot preparation, and because the state starts voting so early now … those deadlines are pretty early.”
Isle of Wight voters might feel some deja vu: Last year, Jarad Ford won the District 3 school board seat via write-in. He said he found it best to take a personal, small-scale approach to campaigning.
“I want people to know that these local positions matter,” he said. “The responsibility to be civically engaged dictates the fabric of our community.”
In addition to getting their ideas to voters, candidates running write-in campaigns have to make sure voters have basic information, like what they’re running for and perhaps most importantly, how to spell their name.
Virginia election law and guidance says write-in votes that are variations of the same name should be accounted for together (like Johnathon Doe and John Doe), and if there is any confusion, the local electoral board decides what names should be counted together.
“I kind of had to add that as part of my campaigning,” Brown said. “Just educating people that, ‘Hey, you probably don’t know this, but there is a special election for school board that’s going to be on the ballot. And also, nobody’s name is on the ballot. It’s all write-in.’”


 Learn more about the candidates








Candidates running write-in campaigns for the Isle of Wight school board were considered for appointment to the board. Here are the application packets they submitted to the school board:
Greg Brown
Candy Hayes
Jeff Ryder



All three candidates campaigning for the District 1 school board seat are first-time candidates and were considered for appointment to the seat.
Ryder did not respond to a request for an interview. The resume he submitted to the Isle of Wight School Board for appointment shows he’s worked in school district finance since 2012. Ryder is retired now, and his last held position was Assistant Superintendent of Finance for the East Aurora school district in Illinois.
“Every financial decision ultimately affected classrooms, teachers, families, and the future of the community,” Ryder wrote to the board. “That perspective has shaped both my career and my appreciation for the important role that thoughtful school board governance plays in the success of a school division.”
Hayes runs a nonprofit called Daniel’s Blessing. She said it’s meant to expose kids to experiences they may not otherwise have. Each year, for example, she brings participants to the Virginia Opera.
Hayes has an adult child and moved to Isle of Wight five years ago.
“When people say, ‘You don’t have a kid in school, why do you want to do this?’ Because I have kids. … (They’re not) my biological kids, but they are my kids, and I care about them. I care about their future.”
Hayes has been on a number of community boards, including the Smithfield Schoolhouse Museum board and the Norfolk Botanical Gardens President’s Council on Diversity and Inclusion.
Hayes isn’t ready to say what she would like to work on as a school board member. Instead, she said, her focus will be to bring people together to begin work.
“Listening,” she said. “Listening to the kids, listening to parents, listening to the staff. “People feel like they’re not heard, so I just want to bring (them) together. … Maybe we can get more things done.”
Brown, however, has several ideas on what he would focus on as a school board member. His wife was a teacher and now works part-time in schools. He also has two children in Isle of Wight schools.
He said he would like to ensure there are better services for students who need them – specifically students in gifted education and young students who need special education resources.
Brown said his family struggled to make sure one of his children was being challenged enough, and wants to build on some recent programming the district has introduced for gifted students, such as a districtwide day focused on science, technology and art topics.
“If our kids aren’t necessarily getting seen, there’s probably a lot of other kids that aren’t either, and they need somebody willing to speak up for them,” Brown said.
He said he would like to focus on how long it takes to identify students who need accommodations, and would like to find a way to make that process faster.
School security and food services are also priorities for Brown.
“We have a widely varied economic population in Isle of Way County, and a lot of kids they’re not getting regularly fed unless they are coming to school,” he said. “We need to take care of the kids because if they’re hungry, they’re not learning.”
Freelance reporter Nash Phillips contributed to this report.

name: National
title: Bear killings skyrocket as garbage, birdfeeders draw them into conflict
text:
Bears rummage through garbage at a dumpster in Whitefish, Montana. Wildlife officials nationwide have received a record number of calls about human-bear conflicts this year. (Photo courtesy of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks)Bears are having a very bad year. 
Across much of the United States, a warm winter and persistent drought have decimated the natural foods that black and brown bears rely on. With nearly every station at the buffet in short supply, the adaptable eaters are turning to human food. 
From California to Connecticut, desperate bears have raided garbage cans, broken into homes and cars, torn through chicken coops and pulled down birdfeeders. Wildlife officers in many states have received a record number of calls, working overtime through the summer to deter bears, put out traps and euthanize animals who pose persistent problems. 
“I’ve had officers who have had to work three weeks in a row, working 18-hour days, day after day,” said John Livingston, public information officer with Colorado Parks and Wildlife. “We have been worried about the mental health of some of our officers who are dealing with these issues. Some of them are having to euthanize a lot of bears this year. Nobody gets into this line of work because they want to put down animals.”
In a typical year, Livingston said, Colorado will euthanize 60 to 90 bears that run afoul of the agency’s two-strike policy for bears that have caused property incidents and are deemed to pose a threat to communities. By the end of August this year, wildlife officers had already euthanized 294 bears. Many states are seeing similar increases.

State wildlife agencies say their officers are spread thin and have had to prioritize which human-bear conflicts to respond to. They have mostly focused on educating residents and removing attractants such as birdfeeders and unsecured garbage cans from populated areas. In some states, lawmakers and wildlife officials have stiffened penalties for humans who feed bears, intentionally or otherwise. 
Wildlife experts stress that humans are almost always the guilty party when conflicts arise. Residents fail to secure their garbage, leave barbecue grills unattended and hang birdfeeders in easy reach. 
Bears are naturally wary of humans. But when food sources are in short supply, they roam far and wide looking for sustenance. With a powerful sense of smell and massive caloric needs, they’re drawn to easy food sources like dumpsters. Once they’ve learned that human developments can be a source of food, they may climb over backyard fences and barge through screen doors. 
Food failures
Across much of the West, a warm, dry winter left the landscape parched this year. Amid the regional drought, warm conditions in many Rocky Mountain states caused the spring “greenup” to happen weeks earlier than normal — before most bears had emerged from their dens. 
After missing out on that critical early nutrition, bears were dealt a second blow when a late frost wiped out the wild berries in several Mountain West states. 
“It’s an exceptionally bad food year, and it’s pretty widespread,” said Chris Servheen, a former grizzly specialist with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service who now serves as co-chair of the North American Bears Expert Team with the Bear Specialist Group, a volunteer conservation organization. “They’re trying to find food and put on weight and they can’t. They’re spending time traveling looking for food, and they’re encountering people more frequently.”
While a handful of bear incidents have involved scratches or bites, wildlife experts said bears are not any more aggressive toward humans this year. Only a small fraction of encounters result in a physical conflict. Brown bears, also known as grizzlies, can pose a danger to humans. But black bears, which populate much more of the country, have killed humans only on extremely rare occasions — including one fatal attack in New Mexico this year.  
On average, bears of all types kill less than one person per year across the entirety of North America. 
Livingston, the Colorado official, said that wildlife officers spotted four tagged bears this year in the city of Durango. Those bears had been tagged in a study more than a decade ago and hadn’t been seen since, thriving deep in the backcountry. 
“In a year like this, they’ve been driven back toward town,” he said. “When you’ve got these big, mature 18- to 20-year-old bears that are having to come into town and resort to that kind of food, it shows us how intense the food failure has been.”
New Mexico is facing a similar crisis, Source NM reported. New Mexico wildlife managers have killed more black bears this year than any full year on record. Game officers or residents reported killing 307 bears that posed threats to public safety since April. 
While Eastern states have not been hit with the same drought conditions, many are still seeing increased conflicts, a result of growing bear populations and more humans moving into bear habitat. Tennessee has euthanized 61 bears so far this year, up from an average of 20 over the previous five years. 
In many places, valley bottoms offer reliable foraging when food sources at higher elevations are scant. But valley bottoms also have the highest concentration of human settlements. 
Count salmon. Get paid. Expect grizzlies.

“In a year like this where (bears) are all down in the low elevations where we are, it’s inevitable they’re going to stumble into the millions of garbage cans on the landscape,” said Jamie Jonkel, bear conflict specialist with Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks. “Starting in June, we were seeing desperation in our (bear) population, and through July it got quite crazy.”
Montana wildlife officials have taken thousands of citizen reports of human-bear conflicts this year. In a single day, eight bears came into Missoula to forage during the night and spent the daylight hours roosting in trees, waiting for traffic to clear. 
In many Western states, wildlife officials say that some sows — especially first-time mothers — have abandoned their cubs, unable to provide for them. That’s created more issues as starving young bears have wandered into neighborhoods, without a mother to guide them away from conflict.
In Utah, which has a smaller bear population than many other Western states, wildlife officers have euthanized 70 bears this year, up from the previous record of 24. 
“There just isn’t a heck of a lot for them to eat out on the landscape,” said Chad Wilson, game mammals coordinator with the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources. “Do you humanely euthanize the bear, or do you put it in a spot where it’s going to most likely starve to death or get in trouble with people again?”
In some cases, wildlife officers will trap and relocate bears. But officials in several states said that is often ineffective, as bears will return to populated areas once they’ve become habituated to human food. 
California has also seen an uptick in bear-related conflicts, said Alex Heeren, research scientist with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. Roughly half of the reported incidents in which bears caused property damage involved chicken coops, he said, which seems to be a “gateway” for increased conflict.
 States respond

Wildlife officials in many states say their officers are spread thin and are eager for bears to go into their winter torpor — a period of dormancy that is not true hibernation. 
For the most part, officials have focused their efforts on educating residents and removing attractants and food sources that could bring bears into developed areas. Nate Bowersock, black bear and furbearer biologist with the Missouri Department of Conservation, said that some officers advise the use of electric fences and paintball guns to deter bears from residential areas. 
Bowersock serves as national chairman of BearWise®, an education program of the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies. 
Jonkel, with the Montana wildlife agency, said staff there are “strung out and overwhelmed,” while residents grow impatient when officers are too busy to respond to their bear incident immediately. 
“The bears show us where the problems are,” he said. “They introduce us to the people that have chronic attractant issues. We’ll have a group of 10 houses and everyone’s doing everything right. Then one new person will move in and in the course of one summer retrain all of the local bears to start visiting their house, and then next thing you know all heck’s broken loose.” 
Trump administration says developers, loggers can kill endangered species

Some states are starting to take a firmer approach. Colorado legislators passed a law this session to enact stricter penalties for residents who leave out food that bears can access. It expands the statute to cover those who “knowingly” feed bears; the law previously addressed only “intentional” feeding. The law also increases the fines for such behavior, with a maximum of $5,000, and removes a requirement that first-time offenders receive only a warning. 
In North Carolina, the state Wildlife Resources Commission passed an emergency rule earlier this month to prohibit intentional and negligent feeding of bears in Buncombe County — where a large percentage of recent bear-related incidents have occurred. While such behavior is already banned under city and county ordinances, the state rule makes it a criminal, rather than civil, offense, and creates jurisdiction for state wildlife officers to conduct enforcement. 
According to the agency, the state has had 115 incidents where bears forced their way into buildings since 2023. Seventy-four of those have occurred in the past five months. 
Wildlife managers say stricter enforcement may help in some cases, but with so many people moving into bear habitat, they expect conflicts to continue. At the same time, climate change is making conditions hotter and drier across much of the country, causing droughts and intensifying wildfires. Such changes could increase the frequency of lean food years for bears. 
“The main takeaway is that nobody’s figured out what the perfect answer is,” said Livingston, with Colorado Parks and Wildlife. “Bears are really good at exposing where we’re weak.”
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Engling aims for quick jump from unknown staffer to statewide Indiana office
text:
Secretary of State candidate Max Engling speaks with a delegate at the Indiana Republican Convention in Fort Wayne on Saturday, June 20, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Max Engling was a twenty-something Republican staffer for an obscure congressional committee when Kevin McCarthy first encountered him more than a decade ago.
McCarthy soon hired Engling for his office while working his way through Republican leadership positions to become speaker of the House.


About Max Engling
Age: 39
Residence: Cicero
Education: Bachelor’s degree from Indiana University-Purdue University Indianapolis, master’s degree from the U.S. Naval War College
Occupation: Central Indiana regional director for U.S. Sen. Jim Banks
Previous: Republican staff of the U.S. House Committee on House Administration; aide to Rep. Kevin McCarthy, including as director of member services while McCarthy was House speaker in 2023
Family: Wife Kelcey and four children


McCarthy praises the work ethic of Engling, whom he promoted within a few years to a role overseeing funding for the 435 congressional offices and orientation programs for newly elected House members.
“I would get a lot of accolades based upon his reflection of how he managed and how he worked with people,” McCarthy told the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
Engling moved back to Indiana with his young family in 2023 after a dozen years in Washington with his eyes set on becoming a congressman himself, only to see his campaign fail to gain attention and fall short the following year.
He now has a huge chance for political redemption as he’s leading the Republican ballot as the party’s secretary of state candidate with the charge of keeping Beau Bayh — and Indiana’s best-known Democratic name — from winning a statewide office for his party for the first time since 2012.
Conservative drive and congressional ambitions
Engling spent most of his teenage years living with his family on a small farm near the rural Illinois town of Congerville, about a half hour drive from Peoria
He was mostly homeschooled there and was 19 when he moved in 2006 with his parents and seven siblings to the Hamilton County town of Cicero after his father, who worked in hospital administration, started a new job in Indianapolis.
Engling says he worked construction, restaurant and other jobs to pay his way through college, graduating from Indiana University-Purdue University Indianapolis in 2010. 
He became inspired by the tea party movement that developed in reaction to President Barack Obama’s administration and decided to move to Washington.
“I was very invested in that strong conservative policy and the folks who were going out to Washington to make real change at the federal level,” Engling said in an interview. “I told my boss at the time — he knew how I was wired — and I said, ‘I’ve really got to try and serve where all these conservative folks are going.’”
The first reply to his resume was for a job on the House Committee on Administration staff. Engling started there in 2011 and advanced over the next few years working for the committee that handles federal election legislation and oversees internal operations of the House.
He credits his time on the committee staff with giving him a background in election and voting policies, which are key functions of the secretary of state’s office.
McCarthy was the top congressional Republican as House minority leader when he brought Engling onto his office staff in 2019. The California congressman promoted Engling to member services director as he became House speaker in 2023.
Republican Max Engling speaks to reporters after a debate on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Engling, however, was soon planning a return to Indiana after Republican U.S. Rep. Victoria Spartz announced in February 2023 that she wasn’t going to seek reelection. 
That opened up the congressional district where Engling had lived and where he and his wife Kelcey were married at a Noblesville church in 2011.
McCarthy said he wanted Engling to stay on his staff but believed Engling could be a good House member.
“The one thing I did know is he was going to go back to Indiana, regardless,” McCarthy said. “That’s home for him. He’d been away, which I consider kind of serving his country by working in Congress, and he wanted to take his family back there. So, I was encouraging.”
Engling, his wife and four children moved to suburban Indianapolis in the summer of 2023 as a Republican rebellion was growing against McCarthy, which resulted in his ouster from the speakership that October.
Engling jumped into the congressional race, only to see his chances torpedoed when Spartz reentered the race in early 2024. He ended up finishing third in the Republican primary with about 10% of the vote.
Becoming a statewide candidate
After the congressional campaign, Engling worked several months for the Beck’s Hybrid agricultural company before landing back in the political world in early 2025 as central Indiana regional director for newly elected Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Banks.
The job had him representing Banks at community events and meeting with community leaders — and in contact with Republican activists.
Trouble was soon brewing with the prospects of current Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales winning reelection in the face of a Bayh campaign preparing to highlight numerous controversies over office spending, hiring and travel by Morales.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
Engling says some Republicans suggested he enter the race, but that he held off until Banks withdrew his endorsement of Morales about a month ahead of the state Republican convention where the nomination would be decided.
“He said to me, ‘Well, if you are prepared to go, we can’t do this anymore as far as the current secretary of state, and if you’re ready to go I’m fully behind you. Let’s go,’” Engling said.
Banks quickly endorsed Engling, calling him “a key member of my team” and “a strong conservative.”
Banks touted Engling at the state convention ahead of Engling’s victory over Morales. The senator has since then stayed in the background of Engling’s campaign and his Senate office and campaign staff haven’t responded to numerous phone and email messages from the Capital Chronicle seeking an interview with him about Engling.
Engling makes his pitch
Engling arrived by himself for an interview at a downtown Noblesville coffee shop, about a 15-minutes drive from the rural Cicero home he and his wife own.
He makes the argument that he would be more vigilant than Bayh in enforcing voting laws, seeking to tie Bayh to controversies elsewhere in the country.
“States run by Democrats end up in positions like Los Angeles, counting for weeks at a time after the election day is over, or New Jersey, where they have 6,600 people on the voting rolls that are not eligible to vote,” Engling said. “Pointing out directly something that’s happening now, and how we in Indiana continue to strengthen our election integrity and not go that direction is important.”
He points to his time in Washington as giving him the experience to navigate proposals through the General Assembly.
“Putting all of those things together, being able to build the coalition to get priorities accomplished is something that none of the other candidates can say,” Engling said. “They don’t have that experience.”
Bayh refutes arguments over his election integrity positions, emphasizing that he supports Indiana’s law requiring state-issued identification to vote.
Indiana Democrats hope Beau Bayh leads them from political wilderness

“If anyone knows about making our politics and making our government look more like California, it should be Max Engling,” Bayh said. “He worked for the people of California in Congress, working for Kevin McCarthy for several years. So it’s just pretty hypocritical coming from him trying to make this race about national issues when he’s been in charge, working for the people of California and representing their interests in Congress while I was in the United States Marine Corps.”
Bayh has aired television ads labeling Engling as someone who became a millionaire while working for Congress and trading tech stocks.
Those claims are based on Engling’s 2024 congressional candidate financial disclosure showing a net worth between $1.2 million and $2.7 million — including a Virginia home he and his wife sold last year for $1 million. 
Engling also reported owning stock in four individual companies, one of which was between $15,000 and $50,000 of shares in the artificial intelligence company Nvidia.
Engling calls claims against him of insider trading “unequivocally false,” saying “the four stocks I own are worth less than $50,000 total, and I have never sold them.”
“Appreciative of all of the opportunity”
Engling has traveled around Indiana in his attempt to go within a matter of months from being a little-known political staffer to a statewide office holder.
A recent poll showed that nearly half of likely voters had not heard of him, almost double the percentage who had not heard about Bayh.
Engling makes appeals on his conservative stances and cites his government experiences, such as working for Banks while often not mentioning McCarthy as a D.C. mentor.
“I’m very appreciative of all of the opportunity that he’s given me,” Engling said of McCarthy. “He knows that. I think it’s more of, you have a pretty limited window to say to folks here what you did and how you did it and how it makes sense in the secretary of state’s role as far as what you’ve done.”
McCarthy, for his part, said he didn’t mind Engling not bringing up his name.
“Why would he? He’s running for office,” McCarthy said. “His last job was working for Senator Banks. In Indiana, who is someone going to have more ability to know or interact with: Senator Jim Banks. Why wouldn’t you do that?”



Minor fame for making “Most Beautiful” list
Max Engling gained a bit of attention soon after starting work in Washington when he landed on The Hill news outlet’s 2012 list of the “50 Most Beautiful People.”
The article cited the then-25-year-old’s time with a side gig modeling for print-ad campaigns for Kohl’s, Carson Pirie Scott, Sears and American Crew before he moved to D.C.
Engling seemed sheepish about the designation when asked about it by the Capital Chronicle.
“I think it was an interesting story,” he said. “If you would ask 2012 Max if that would be a good repeat, I think it would probably be better just to stick in my lane of working on policy and keep your head down and work hard.
“I did work in restaurants, I was working construction,” he said. “There was, I think, two semesters where I was working between 60 and 70 hours a week, while pulling 15 credit hours at IUPUI.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A Providence elementary school principal is reaching for another star. It’s within her grasp.
text:
Leviton Dual Language School Principal Jennifer Walker interacts with a third-grade student in the cafeteria of the Providence school on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)As far back as grade school, Jennifer Walker was sure she’d become a teacher. Then, her experiences at Providence’s Classical High School super-charged her ambition with a passion to become a two-way bilingual teacher.
Many of her Classical classmates spoke Spanish at home but got zero support for their native tongue at school. In 1989, when Walker graduated, educators were nearly frantic to teach immigrant kids strong English to help prepare them for life and careers in America. But young Walker was incensed that the school system stripped her friends of a valuable asset and made them take a “foreign” language to boot. Why not teach a few regular academic classes in Spanish? She would have taken one.
After college, grad school, and a Peace Corps stint in the Dominican Republic that deepened her own Spanish, Walker returned home to take a job in Providence. Fast forward: She is now the principal of Leviton Elementary Dual Language School, a K-5 two-way, Spanish/English bilingual school in the heart of South Providence. It’s the only school in the capital city where every classroom is dual language.
Journalist researcher Chad Aldeman called out Leviton as a “Bright Spot” in his search for schools that helped kids “beat the odds” in student reading performance. Publishing his results in The 74, he scoured the nation’s achievement and demographic data looking for such schools in all 50 states. When I piled on more local data to verify his results, Leviton jumped out of the pack with its two-way bilingual strategy. 
Bilingual education uses the same curriculum to teach all subjects but switches from one language to the other — say, Spanish in the morning; English in the afternoon, and then flipping the order of languages each week. 
Each grade level has two classes, half dominant in each language. Two teachers, also dominant in each language, trade classes, seamlessly continuing the curriculum’s instruction. Teachers pair each kid with a classmate at a similar academic level, but rooted in the different languages, providing academic buddies who can support each other throughout the day. 
Research shows bilingual education generally produces moderate to major academic gains, but also bestows significant other brain-related benefits. Socially, students cultivate genuine empathy and curiosity for each other’s culture. It’s a win/win strategy that should be made far more available.
Leviton has a second big asset: the consistency of its leadership. 
In 2011, Walker was teaching first grade in a small bilingual program within a larger school that was moved to the Leviton building for a whole-school approach. The new principal was Javier Montañez.
Montañez grew up in Puerto Rico, then immigrated here. After a hard-knock youth, he got his G.E.D. and worked hard to pursue a career in education. While at Leviton, he was appointed to be the superintendent of the Providence Schools. 
“Both students and staff adore him,” Walker said of Montañez. She said she most admired “his unwavering commitment to putting students first in all of his thoughts, actions, decisions, and policies.”
Montañez calls Walker “one of the pioneers of the dual language program” who “always went above and beyond to support the work we were doing.”
During his watch, Leviton’s school rating rose from a one- to three-star school in Rhode Island’s one-to-five-star system. Impressively, Leviton’s absenteeism rate (12.4%) is far lower than the state’s (19.7%) and Providence’s (25.3%) 
Montañez launched a terrific school that Walker has since maintained and enhanced.
Jennifer Walker, principal of Leviton Elementary Dual Language School in South Providence, stands before a mural in the school painted by Providence artist AGONZA. Walker says a dedicated staff is key to improving student performance. About 70% of Leviton’s educators are Hispanic, compared with 16.2% districtwide. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Still, other schools have excellent academic strategies and consistent leadership, so what else might be the secret sauce in Leviton’s success?
“My staff,” Walker answered immediately. 
Yes, of course, I replied. Every principal first mentions the staff when asked. 
She pushed back firmly: “No, it’s the staff.”
Only 5.1% of the state’s educators are Hispanic, according to the Department of Education’s report cards. The Providence district has 16.2%. Walker did a quick count of her current staff and concluded 70% of Leviton’s educators are Hispanic. 
And many of her teachers grew up in South Providence or neighborhoods like it. Most came up through the city’s school system. Those backgrounds do make the staff an unusual asset.
“The teachers here know that education brought them out of that low-income world,” she said. “They know what the kids are up against. They’re committed to the kids because they were once them. Our community is special.”
Historically, Leviton’s classes have never been strictly 50/50, with half of each class dominant in one or the other language. Leviton has a lot of what Walker calls “newbies,” recent arrivals. Many other kids speak Spanish at home and in their communities, but grew up here, adequately steeped in English to qualify as “English-dominant” by the district’s Registration Center.
At last, this year’s incoming kindergarten is for-real 50/50. White families have been moving into the neighborhood because they like its diversity, because rents are cheaper than elsewhere in the city, and because Leviton is an increasingly known, desirable option, a district-based school of choice. The quality of the school is desegregating it naturally.
Mind you, Walker’s commitment notwithstanding, two-way bilingual is not magic. Leviton’s program has challenges. The Providence Public School Department chose to have reading and phonics programs consistent across the district, a smart decision but one that poses problems for two-way. For example, Walker bemoans that the phonics program doesn’t frontload vowel sounds in phonics for each language since they’re different. 
When she retires, Walker said she will go to work on just such curriculum problems. Her dedication to bilingual education will be lifelong.
But for now, she’s going to help Leviton be the first Rhode Island urban school to get that fourth star. If you saw her determination, you’d put money on it. She’s a bright spot all on her own.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Victims’ attorneys ask New Hampshire Supreme Court to roll back YDC Settlement Fund changes
text:
Assistant Attorney General Mary Triick argues to state Supreme Court justices that the state does not have a contractual obligation to stay true to the exact parameters of the YDC Settlement Fund system it set up in 2022, on Oct. 14, 2026, in the Frank R. Kenison Supreme Court Building. Watching on are Justices Bryan Gould and Patrick Donovan (background) and attorney Daniel Deane (foreground). (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)A group of people who say they were abused as children under the state’s care argue that New Hampshire officials have pulled the rug out from under them. Now, they want the state Supreme Court to intervene and make New Hampshire stay true to a promise they say was made to them.
New Hampshire’s juvenile justice system has in recent years been rocked by allegations of sexual, physical and emotional abuse spanning decades. At the heart of the scandal is the Sununu Youth Services Center, a state facility formerly known as the Youth Development Center or YDC, where hundreds say they were raped, beaten and emotionally tortured by staff. 
As a deluge of lawsuits hit the state, lawmakers in 2022 created the YDC Settlement Fund and a process in which victims can avoid a lengthy court battle in favor of mediation. They tasked an independent administrator with overseeing the process. The fund has already paid out millions to victims, though much less than if all those victims had gone through superior court and won. 
However, in 2025, after Gov. Kelly Ayotte took office, she and the Legislature made changes to the process. Instead of an independent administrator overseeing the fund and mediation, the administrator would be appointed by the governor — who can fire the administrator as she sees fit — and the attorney general would now have veto power over any settlement awards. The changes were slipped into the omnibus budget legislation enacted that summer. John Broderick, the former administrator who says he was forced out by the changes, has repeatedly accused the state of cheating victims and breaking promises it made to them when it created the fund in an effort to save the state money.
The victims’ attorneys agree. Last week, they asked the New Hampshire Supreme Court to block those changes. They argued the state entered into a binding contract with the victims, who elected to participate in the settlement fund process before the changes were made. The court heard oral arguments in the class-action lawsuit on Wednesday.
“The state made an offer,” Daniel Deane, an attorney with Nixon Peabody representing the victims, said. “More than 1,900 child abuse victims accepted that offer by filing a claim, staying thier lawsuits and suspending their place in line. One day after the final deadline (to elect to participate in the settlement process), the state changed a core part of the bargain.”
Deane argued that when the victims accepted the deal, the administrator’s decision was final, an element he referred to as “the finality of the awards.” By giving the attorney general a veto after the administrator’s decision, the state has violated a “binding contract” with the victims.
Assistant Attorney General Mary Triick, on behalf of the state, rejected the premise that the state had a binding contract, pointing to the fact that the victims had the ability to pull out in the middle of the process. She called it an “illusory contract,” a legal term that refers to a deal that is unenforceable because both sides haven’t made a commitment.
“It’s not a contract,” she said. “Because if one party can walk away at any time, then you don’t have a contract.”
Triick argued that if the Legislature wants to “do something extraordinary” and bind future lawmakers to their past decision, it must use language that makes that “unmistakably” clear. She said it did not.
Deane countered that “that was the bargain that was struck. The state offered an asymmetrical arbitration process.” He said victims participated in the process with the promise of that asymmetrical deal.
Justice Bryan Gould expressed skepticism.
“Isn’t that true of any illusory contract?” Gould asked. “That there’s a deal that’s been struck, but if one side isn’t obligated, neither side is obligated.”
Deane disagreed.
“I don’t think that’s illusory,” he said. “I think that’s the state reneging on what they originally promised.”
While the victims’ attorneys also disapproved of the decision to change the administrator from an independent position to a political appointee under the governor’s office, that was not at question in court Wednesday.
“We’re not conceding that moving the administrator under the executive branch and making them terminatable at-will of the governor is also a breach,” Deane said. “But the finality of the awards is the most fundamental term.”
The Supreme Court is expected to rule on the case soon. Merrimack County Superior Court Judge Dan St. Hilaire previously dismissed the suit. The victims hope the Supreme Court will override the lower court.
Meanwhile, Gerard Boyle, a retired circuit court judge appointed by Ayotte to succeed Broderick as YDC Fund administrator, has restarted mediation after a pause in work. As of January, the fund doled out 425 settlements for an average of (including interest) about $560,000, according to state reports. There were 1,689 pending claims at the time. Boyle asked lawmakers earlier this year to add $55 million into the fund, which has been depleted over the years, to pay out more victims. Lawmakers gave him $20 million. It will likely cost the state much more than $55 million to compensate every victim.
Daniel Deane argues that the state violated a binding contract when it made changes to the YDC Settlement Fund in 2025, in front of the New Hampshire Supreme Court on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s sexual violence reporting system for colleges has gaps. Lawmakers want answers.
text:
LSU students walk in and out of the Student Union on Monday, March 20, 2023, on Highland Road in Baton Rouge. (Matthew Perschall for Louisiana Illuminator)Six years after a national sexual assault scandal roiled the state’s flagship university, Louisiana lawmakers question if the reporting system implemented in its wake provides enough information. 
In 2020, LSU became engulfed in controversy following a USA Today investigative report that revealed how the university mishandled sexual misconduct complaints against student-athletes. A subsequent probe revealed a number of institutional problems regarding Title IX, the federal law that covers sex-based discrimination in the realm of education. 
The next year, Louisiana lawmakers strengthened state laws around campus sexual misconduct, creating a new category called power-based violence that includes Title IX offenses and other related abuse. A statewide reporting system was also implemented to inform lawmakers, students and families about how often abuse happens and how state colleges and universities respond to it. 
Students and campus employees can report suspected power-based violence and Title IX incidents to their schools, but a relatively small amount of information about these reports is made public. Schools only have to provide basic information, including the type of incident that led to the formal complaint, the investigation status, the gender of the people involved and what discipline, if any, was issued.  
The first of Louisiana’s power-based violence reports was made public in January 2023, reflecting data collected the prior fall. But they only give a partial picture of what survivor advocates say is a much bigger sexual violence problem on Louisiana campuses. 
“This is not acceptable for me. And just because this is how it’s been done, this is how it’s written, doesn’t mean that it’s right,” state Sen. Regina Barrow, D-Baton Rouge, said of the state’s power-based violence processes. “The president of every university should be carrying the torch for Title IX to be recognized on the campus.”
