name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: New Ohio bill proposes task force to address childcare, early childhood education
text:
(File photo by Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).New legislation coming at the tail end of the current Ohio General Assembly seeks to study early childhood education regulation in the state.
Ohio House Bill 1023, sponsored by Republican state Rep. Josh Williams of Sylvania, would establish an “early childhood education governance and outcomes task force,” according to the language of the bill.
“The Task Force’s work should seek to answer the fundamental policy question of whether Ohio’s existing early childhood investments, governance structure, and programs are effectively preparing children to enter kindergarten ready to learn and providing the foundation necessary for long-term academic success,” the bill states.
The task force would “evaluate whether Ohio’s regulatory structures governing early childhood education optimally support” everything from kindergarten and school readiness to the use of state and federal funding.
The state has received federal funding for Head Start, funded a Publicly Funded Child Care program for low-income households, created vouchers to assist with child care costs, as well as overseeing a star-rating system for childcare and early education facilities.
“Some children are set up to struggle long before they ever walk into a kindergarten classroom,” Williams said in a statement. “We need to understand what is working, where the gaps are, and how to give every child a stronger start.”
Under H.B. 1023, the task force would be made up of three members each of the Ohio House and Senate, all appointed by the leaders of the chambers. At least one appointee from each chamber has to be from the minority party.
Other task force appointees would include a member of the Ohio departments of Children and Youth, Education and Workforce, Medicaid, Health, and Developmental Disabilities. Outside of state departments, the task force would have a representative from the Children and Youth Advisory Council “with expertise in early childhood education and care,” an expert in early childhood education and kindergarten readiness, an educator licensed in pre-kindergarten through eighth grade, an early childhood education provider, experts in child development and education data, and a parent or guardian of a child in or recently out of early childhood education.
The group would be tasked with making recommendations about the administration of early childhood education programs within state government, and “whether the existing governance structure in Ohio provides sufficient coordination, accountability, and educational focus across early childhood programs,” according to the bill.
One thing that won’t be under the purview of the task force is a review of childcare licensing, health and safety regulations, or the daily operations of childcare providers “except to the extent that such matters directly affect educational quality, kindergarten readiness, program participation, or educational continuity.”
A final report will be due by Dec. 1, 2027, including an inventory of programs and funding sources, enrollment and eligibility information, and identification of “gaps or unnecessary duplication,” along with recommendations on improving the system as a whole.
Many child advocacy groups are still reviewing the legislation before it goes to committee hearings, where testimony will be heard from those for and against the measure. Tami Lunan, organizing director for the CEO Project, a program within the Ohio Organizing Collaborative focused on the childcare system, said she appreciates lawmakers working to improve the early childhood education system and coordinate among agencies, but no study or coordination will bring childcare out of its funding shortage.
“Underinvestment has reduced childcare capacity, leaving parents unable to work and businesses without the workforce they need,” Lunan told the Capital Journal. “If Ohio wants better outcomes for children and working families, meaningful investment must be part of the solution.”
The national group First Five Years Fund found Ohio had a 13% gap in the supply of childcare services for the more than 800,000 children in Ohio aged five and under, and the 67% of households with children whose parents or guardians are all in the workforce.
Child care is a top issue in the upcoming November election, with the affordability concerns being raised as candidates for governor and the legislature face the voters.
This is not Williams’ first foray into legislation related to early childhood education and childcare. His previous measure had to do with enforcement of fraud regulations related to childcare facilities, with Ohio House Bill 649 looking to use the power of the Ohio Auditor of State’s Office and the Ohio Attorney General’s Office, if needed, to prosecute any potential claims that funding from the Publicly Funded Child Care program were being used inappropriately.
While he said he does not allege there is “widespread fraud in Ohio,” in arguing in support of that bill, he said the Ohio Department of Children & Youth “is not doing a good job of investigating it.”
The Ohio legislature has pushed different legislation in an attempt to address concerns about the lack of access and cost challenges related to childcare. Childcare vouchers were included in the last budget, and the Publicly Funded Child Care program was also funded, though lawmakers didn’t increase the funding, as childcare experts had urged them to do.
Lawmakers also approved a pilot program that would allow employers who apply to be a part of the program to share the cost of childcare. Participating employers would split the cost between them, the state, and the eligible employee.
The newest legislation will have to have a quick turnaround to be implemented, since the current General Assembly’s current term ends Dec. 31. If it isn’t approved before then, the bill will need to be reintroduced at the start of the new General Assembly in 2027.

title: 9 years ago, gun violence took my father. Today, Ohio political silence is costing more lives
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by David DeWitt/Ohio Capital Journal)Oct. 12 marked nine years since my father was murdered.
Nine years. Nearly a decade of birthdays, holidays, milestones, and ordinary moments marked by the absence of someone who should still be here.
People often talk about grief as something that fades with time. What I’ve learned is that grief never ends. It evolves, but it never leaves.
It shows up in empty chairs at family dinners. It lingers in the silence during holidays. It appears during life’s happiest moments, reminding you of the person who should have been there to celebrate with you.
Since my father’s life was taken, our country has endured an unprecedented era of gun violence. Families across Ohio and throughout the nation have joined a club that no one ever wants to become a member of.
Children have buried parents. Parents have buried children. Communities have been rattled by bullets and forever changed by violence. Local economies have felt the tremendous cost that gun violence imposes.
Hospitals, victim service providers, mental health professionals, schools, law enforcement agencies, and community organizations have stretched resources to meet growing needs.
Behind every statistic is a family.
Behind every number is a name.
And behind every act of violence is grief that never truly ends.
Some families are experiencing that grief for the first time today.
At this very moment, someone in Ohio may be receiving a phone call that will divide their life into a “before” and an “after.” They are planning a funeral they never imagined having to arrange.
They are answering impossible questions from children. They are helping parents navigate a loss no parent should ever experience. They are trying to understand what life looks like without someone they love.
Many of these tragedies are preventable.
While America has recently seen encouraging declines in homicides, early data suggests some of the largest decreases on record. Yet another crisis continues to grow in the shadows. Suicide rates remain at all time highs and continue to claim lives, often erasing much of the progress made elsewhere.
Since the beginning of 2017, the year my father was murdered, an estimated 409,640 Americans have died from firearm-related causes and another 321,721 have been injured.
The United States has experienced 4,973 mass shootings and more than 17,000 unintentional shootings. Most troubling of all, at least 47,725 children and teens have been shot or killed. Behind every one of those numbers is a family, a community, and a future forever changed.
Those aren’t just statistics. One of those numbers is my dad. They are our neighbors, classmates, teammates, friends, sons, daughters, mothers, and fathers. They are empty chairs at dinner tables, missed birthdays, unfinished dreams, and families forced to navigate a lifetime of grief.
That reality forces us to ask an important question:
What can we do when someone is experiencing the darkest moment of their life?
How do we intervene before a tragedy occurs?
How do we protect a person from themselves while also protecting those around them?
One answer is the adoption of common-sense policies such as Extreme Risk Protection Orders.
This is not about taking away constitutional rights. It is about creating a legal, temporary intervention during a crisis. It is about giving families and communities another tool to save a life.
The same is true for secure firearm storage laws. We have witnessed far too many tragedies involving children who gained access to loaded, unsecured firearms. In a matter of seconds, lives are forever altered.
Responsible gun ownership includes responsible gun storage.
That should not be controversial.
In fact, it should be a conversation we have more often.
And yet, as we enter another election season, I cannot help but notice the silence.
Candidates are asking for votes. Campaign signs are appearing in our neighborhoods. Speeches are being given. Promises are being made.
But where are the conversations about firearm deaths?
Where are the discussions about protecting children from their leading cause of death?
Where are the proposed solutions for reducing suicides, preventing accidental shootings, supporting families impacted, and saving lives?
Too many candidates seem afraid to engage in these conversations because they are difficult. Some fear being labeled “anti-gun.” Others avoid the topic altogether because it is politically uncomfortable.
But difficult conversations should not make us silent.
They should challenge us to think creatively.
They should encourage us to ask hard questions.
They should inspire current and future leaders to seek solutions.
Most importantly, they should help us save lives.
Gun violence has been the leading cause of death for children and teens in America for years. It surpasses car crashes and many diseases that once dominated those discussions. This is a uniquely American crisis, and it demands uniquely American leadership.
The conversation should not be about choosing between the Second Amendment and public safety.
We can support both.
The Second Amendment is a constitutional right. But with every right comes responsibility.
Responsible gun ownership means storing firearms securely and away from children. It means recognizing that guns are not toys. It means understanding the consequences when firearms fall into the wrong hands.
It means having honest conversations about risk, accountability, and prevention. And it means coming to terms with that guns are dangerous and should be viewed that way by both gun owners and non-gun owners alike.
These discussions are not attacks on responsible gun owners.
They are opportunities to define what responsible ownership looks like.
For nine years, I have carried the pain of losing my father. Other families have carried that burden for decades. Some are carrying it for the very first time today.
That is why I am asking every candidate running for local office, state office, governor, or any position of public trust a simple question:
What will you do to save lives?
What policies will you support to protect children?
How will you encourage responsible gun ownership?
How will you address suicide prevention?
How will you handle the mental health crisis in our state and country?
How will you support survivors and victims’ families?
What difficult conversations are you willing to have?
The answers matter.
Because leadership is not measured by the conversations we avoid. Leadership is measured by the challenges we are willing to confront.
Ohio stands at a crossroads. We can choose action. We can choose prevention. We can choose policies that save lives and support families.
Or we can choose silence. And silence is not a political strategy.
Silence is not leadership, it’s complacency.
Silence is surrendering our responsibility to protect our children and accepting preventable tragedies as inevitable.
Silence is accepting that another family will receive the phone call that changes everything and failing those who can no longer speak for themselves.
Silence is avoiding the difficult conversations because they are politically uncomfortable and refusing to confront a problem that continues to devastate families across Ohio and our nation.
Silence is the absence of courage when courage is needed most.
And silence will not save a single life.
Nine years after losing my father, I know silence has never healed a wound, prevented a tragedy, or saved a life and one thing that I know for certain: every life saved means another family won’t have to experience the grief that mine lives with every day.
That alone makes these conversations worth having.
When the next family receives the phone call that changes everything, will we be able to say we did everything we could to prevent it?
Because the question before us is no longer whether we can afford to have these conversations. The question is whether we can afford another life lost because we refused to.
After nine years without my father, and after more than 738,184 Americans shot, killed, or injured by firearms since his murder, I already know the answer.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Skill games saga ends with outlawed gambling machines removed … for now
text:
State Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) speaks at a rally Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, where business owners and volunteer organizations urged lawmakers to pass legislation to legalize and tax skill games. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital Star) Pennsylvania’s skill game industry grew for more than a decade in a legal gray area where courts said the commonwealth’s gambling laws couldn’t touch them. 
That changed earlier this year, when the state Supreme Court said the estimated 70,000 skill game machines in small businesses and private clubs across the state were, in fact, unlicensed slot machines and therefore illegal.
Now, those machines sit unplugged and dark, awaiting transfer to storage and an uncertain fate, after state lawmakers were unable to reach a compromise to tax and regulate the industry before the high court’s ruling took effect Oct. 14.
The General Assembly’s inaction, with only five days left in the current session, means a multi-billion dollar revenue stream for thousands of businesses and organizations, such as volunteer fire companies, will disappear, at least temporarily.
While some lawmakers and members of the public held negative sentiments about skill games, citing the expansion of gambling and the associated societal ills, most people favored legalization, according to the Franklin and Marshall College Poll in June. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More than seven out of 10 people who responded said they were in favor of regulating and taxing skill games, up from 60 percent in February 2024.
“There was generally public support for this idea of fixing this problem,” Berwood A. Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at F&M, said. 
He added that even if the notion of legalizing skill games had been unpopular, lawmakers had cover from the Supreme Court. In its opinion, the justices noted the General Assembly “has spoken clearly,” by amending the state Gaming Act in 2017 to make clear that skill games are legally indistinguishable from slot machines.
“If interested parties find the application of the General Assembly’s laws to be undesirable, the proper remedy lies with the same legislative body that wrote those laws,” Justice David Wecht wrote for the court.
Those interested parties showed up at the Capitol by thousands, loudly stating what was at stake for skill game operators and their communities. 
At an Oct. 6 rally on the Capitol steps, Delaware County tavern owner Joe McGee said the skill games in his bars have helped him improve his business and support the local volunteer fire companies and youth baseball programs while keeping the price of a Miller Lite at $3 or $4.
Supreme Court denies request to extend deadline for skill games

“All we want is sensible regulation, and we need it now. We can’t wait. We can’t wait till next year,” McGee said, flanked by hundreds of fellow business owners and lawmakers.
So why hasn’t the legislature been able to pass legislation on skill games?
“I don’t think anyone can explain why certain things get done and others don’t in the legislature,” Yost said, adding that the seemingly straightforward task masked layers of ideological complexity even within the same caucus.
He noted Republicans, who control the Senate, are generally loath to increase the size of government by creating new revenue streams, but at the same time are pro-small business and might balk at anything that would harm them.
“Our divided government has kind of led to policy moderation and that means some things that have a lot of support don’t happen because it runs up against something that one of the parties is opposed to,” Yost said. He noted broadly popular initiatives such as privatizing liquor sales and school choice have failed because of partisan ideology. 
State Sen. Camera Bartolotta (R-Washington) said that while she sees the value of skill games to businesses and community organizations, she opposed Gov. Josh Shapiro’s plan to direct much of the revenue from a proposed tax to mass transit, which more heavily benefits large urban areas than her rural district. 
“I’m not going to look my constituents in the eye when they don’t have public transportation and say, ‘We’re going to ship it all to this place where it doesn’t help you,’” said Bartolotta, who was one of the Republican incumbents targeted by skill game interests in this year’s primary.
Spokespeople for Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) and House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery) did not return messages from the Capital-Star requesting interviews. 
Yost added that the skill game issue is unique because of the way the industry grew upon shaky legal footings.
“I can’t remember anything analogous to this,” he said. 
Skill games in a Virginia corner store. (Ned Oliver/Virginia Mercury)
The history of skill games in Pennsylvania
 The company that would become the predominant force behind skill gaming sought to legitimize gambling in spaces where illicit video poker operations had lurked for decades.  
In 2013, Georgia-based Pace-O-Matic (POM) arranged for Pennsylvania State Police to seize one of the earliest skill game machines at the American Italian Club in Aliquippa, Beaver County, according to the company’s website.
After examining the machine, Beaver County Common Pleas Judge Harry Knafelc ruled in 2014 that winning a series of puzzles and memory games was based predominantly on skill. For that reason, the judge ruled, the machine was distinct from a slot machine and “a gambling device per se.”
Neither county prosecutors nor the state attorney general’s office, then led by Attorney General Kathleen Kane, challenged the ruling, and a legal path for skill games was blazed.
Since the 2014 ruling, POM has won five rulings in favor of the machines’ legality, including the 2023 Commonwealth Court ruling that the Supreme Court overturned this year.
Pennsylvania’s casinos launched following the 2004 passage of the Horse Racing Development and Gaming Act. State lawmakers spent years debating how to regulate and tax it to support horse racing and tax relief.



Quotation







“This is one of those situations that I view as the pursuit of the perfect at the expense of the good. A good spot for most Pennsylvanians is a compromise on regulation and taxation that lets businesses keep some of the revenue. That shouldn’t be an unattainable goal.


– Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick


While one owner surrendered his license after being charged with lying to regulators about his ties to a Scranton organized crime family, the casino business grew over two decades into a $7 billion industry with nearly every flavor of gambling in 17 casinos, truck stops and online.
Skill gaming grew too, and while there are no official numbers on its size, Gov. Josh Shapiro’s proposal to tax the industry put the potential new revenue at $2 billion with a 52% levy on gross revenue, allowing an inference that the industry generates in excess of $4 billion annually.
As skill games became increasingly popular with players and business owners, who shared in the revenue, others in the legal gaming business took notice and pushed back. In addition to casinos, which lobbied heavily against plans to legalize skill games, the Pennsylvania Lottery claimed in 2019 that skill games cost it $138 million in sales. 
Lawmakers were divided over the situation. Former state Sen. Tommy Tomlinson introduced a bill that year that would make “a criminal offense for anyone to knowingly make, assemble, maintain, lease or sell Games of Skill.” It was the first of several bills to simply outlaw the devices.
Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) introduced his first legislation to regulate and tax skill games in 2023, with a proposal to require annual licensing fees of $1 million for distributors, $25,000 for operators and $250 for individual establishments. It was estimated to bring in about $300 million in tax revenue.
Yaw’s district includes Miele Manufacturing, which makes the physical machines. He did not respond to a request for comment.
Yaw and other lawmakers have since floated legislation to tax skill games at different rates. 
Senate leaders endorsed a plan to tax skill games at 35%. Sen. Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming), whose district includes skill game maker Miele Manufacturing, sponsored competing legislation to tax the machines at 16%. Yaw and Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) also introduced a bill to impose a monthly fee of $500 per machine.
Miele Group, based in Muncy Township, Lycoming County, manufactures Pennsylvania Skill Games, which have been the subject of legislative efforts to regulate and tax the slot machine-like devices. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Casino slot machines and video gaming terminals are taxed between 34% and 54% depending on the category of casino. While lawmakers broadly agreed that they needed to act before the Oct 14 deadline, no action was taken. 
Four lawmakers, Yaw and Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) and Reps. Danilo Burgos (D-Philadelphia) and Jonathan Fritz (R-Wayne) filed an emergency petition asking the court to extend the deadline to give the legislature more time to work
The petition was later withdrawn and subsequently refiled without Burgos’ name. That was a result of pressure from Bradford, who said support for Burgos’ legislative proposal by rank and file lawmakers undermined the leadership, SpotlightPA reported.
Ultimately, the court rejected the request without comment and the deadline passed without action.
Jonathan Caulkins, professor of operations research and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University, said he wouldn’t view the inaction as a failure on the part of the legislature.
He noted in a commentary for The Conversation that was published by the Capital-Star earlier this month that the focus on taxing skill games overlooks the bigger picture of whether gambling should be freely and widely available.
“One could argue that the error was in the earlier legislation that left it ambiguous as to whether skill games were actually gambling devices, or that the courts took so long to clarify that they are,” Caulkins said in an email.  
Even if the legislature’s inaction resulting in skill games being removed from their places around the commonwealth represents a policy decision, Lehigh University political science professor Chris Borick said, simply letting the deadline pass is neither orderly nor decisive.
“I guess if you don’t want these things in the state, I guess you won, but they can come back,” he said. “There’s a lot of opportunity cost for the state and there’s a lot of things that could have been resolved in a more efficient way and that to me suggests that a different policy could have been more productive.”
While the situation appears complex, Borick said the question before the legislature is simple. 
“This is one of those situations that I view as the pursuit of the perfect at the expense of the good,” he said. “A good spot for most Pennsylvanians is a compromise on regulation and taxation that lets businesses keep some of the revenue. That shouldn’t be an unattainable goal.”

 Catching Our Eye

• The overtly partisan Ohio Supreme Court. The Columbus Dispatch’s Laura A. Bischoff reports, “Democrat Jennifer Brunner loses federal lawsuit over partisan election labels.”
With less than three weeks left before Election Day, a federal court upheld a state law requiring partisan labels for candidates running for appellate and supreme court seats in Ohio.
Ohio Supreme Court Justice Jennifer Brunner, the only Democrat currently holding statewide elected office, filed a lawsuit over the law, saying it violated her First and Fifth Amendment rights. She argued that forcing candidates to carry a party label conflicts with judicial ethics rules.
In July 2021, Gov. Mike DeWine signed into law a measure requiring party labels in general elections for some judges. Since then, Democrats have lost every race for Ohio Supreme Court.
• Jim Jordan’s plans. CNN reports, “House Republicans face a potential clash over who will be GOP leader if they lose the midterms.”
When House Speaker Mike Johnson decided in September to send lawmakers home early to their districts ahead of the midterm elections, House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan quietly made clear that he would have handled the situation differently, according to a source close to Jordan.
In a private conversation with one Republican lawmaker, Jordan said he would have kept lawmakers in Washington longer to hold more votes that would be politically challenging for Democrats. He also expressed interest in holding more votes on President Donald Trump’s elections overhaul bill that has been blocked in the Republican-led Senate, arguing that would help House Republicans on the campaign trail even if the bill won’t be signed into law.
• Bernie Moreno’s plans. Bloomberg reports, “Senator Expects ‘Last Supper’ Budget Bill if GOP Loses Power.”
Sen. Bernie Moreno wants senators to stay in session from the election through the end of the year without a break to pass a party-line budget bill with all their priorities if Republicans lose in the midterms next month.
• Ohio Womens’ Monument. The Toledo Blade’s Danny Eldredge reports, “State leaders unveil Ohio Women’s Monument.”
A new landmark honoring generations of women who fought for suffrage and equality is now established on the grounds of the Ohio Statehouse.
The Ohio Women’s Monument was unveiled Wednesday after more than six years of work by the Ohio Women’s Suffrage Centennial Commission, Capitol Square Foundation, Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board, and Ohio Arts Council.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: The story Florida’s new driver licenses tell ain’t necessarily so
text:
The new design for Florida driver licenses via DHSMV.Listen up: Florida is back.
WAY back.
Not that we were ever not the free-est, greatest, top-est state in the USA, it’s that we just got even more awesome.
Our governor is presenting us with a brand-new driver’s license design, and it is HAWT.
The old one was, like, so mid, as the kids say, so vanilla.
On the front, there’s a piece of the state seal kind of tangled up in big letters reading “FL,” and on the back, there’s another “FL” and a little Florida outline (in case you forget where you live) with American flag stripes kind of flopping around.
Totally “Ohio,” as the kids also say, or did last month, at least: It can be hard to keep up, even for us hip folk.
But, thanks to the artistes at the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicle the new driver’s license is FIRE.
On the front, it says, “Florida,” like you’d expect, but the “O” is an orange!”
So cute.
Then you got your state seal, some palm trees, and a sweet little gator wrapped around that gold star that shows you’re not an illegal or a terrorist or, as our vice-president likes to point out, some non-European weirdo trying to destroy American culture.
That’s not all, either.
It’s hard to see exactly, but there seems to be a partial map of the Gulf of America coastline and a manatee.
Don’t we love our manatees!
 Something less foreign
Over to the left of the card, there’s a misty image of the Castillo de San Marcos in St. Augustine.
For those of you who don’t know history (and, let’s face it, that’s almost every single person in Florida! No shame! We come here to pretend the past never happened!), the castle was built by the Spanish in 1672 to keep the British and the French from horning in on their empire.
How about this for cool? San Marcos is made of coquina, which is a limestone formed by the tiny squished up bodies of shellfish from millions of years ago, who would, I’m sure, be gratified by their Florida legacy.
It’s located on the western shore of Matanzas Bay, which is named for that time in 1565 when the Spanish killed a bunch of Huguenots. The French had stolen the land from the Spanish, who had stolen it first from the Timucua people.
“Matanzas” means massacre.
Come to think of it, we should probably change those names to something less foreign.
Castle St. Mark. Mass Murder Bay.
And what about that last hurricane? “Isaías?” Seriously?
Please. As U.S. Rep. Jimmy Patronis says, storms in the Gulf of America should be given “American names people can pronounce.”
OK, 4.8 million Spanish-speaking Floridians and every meteorologist in the state could pronounce “Isaías,” but if a congressman can’t say it, and our governor, who calls it “weird” and “not normal,” can’t say it, either, we have a problem.
Our governor, who knows Jesus spoke English, chose to call the hurricane Isaiah, which is obviously a fine American Bible name.
But let us return to the Big Beautiful Driver’s License, specifically its fabulous back side.
There’s the space shuttle Discovery, which is the one that didn’t blow up.
Discovery may have been entirely built in the Woke Paradise of California, but it was launched from Florida’s own Kennedy Space Center, thank you very much.
The new design for Florida driver licenses via DHSMV.
 Circle of Life
There’s a nice barcode containing all your personal info, including whether you’re a sex offender, and the date Florida became a state (1845).
More oranges, too, lots of oranges — a whole pile of oranges!
No doubt the boo birds, nay-sayers, and whiners will point out Florida’s pretty thin on actual oranges these days.
It’s not our fault. Three decades ago, the orange industry sold 225 million boxes a year but, what with the greening disease, population growth, and California eating our breakfast in the juice market, today it’s more like 12 million boxes, a drop of 95%.
OK, that’s not ideal, but look at it this way: The oranges gave their lives and their groves to make way for Central Florida’s great real estate market.
The new license honors the Ghosts of Citrus Past.
Same with the manatee.
Debbie Downers complain the Feds won’t put manatees on the Endangered Species List, and say stuff like, “Jeez, Florida only has around 8,000 manatees total and as of October this year we’ve lost 500, some dying of natural causes, many dying because dudes like to run over them with their jet skis and power boats.”
It’s the Circle of Life!
But the best part is Florida’s return to our original state motto, “Let Us Alone,” in big letters, emblazoned across those oranges.
“Let Us Alone” originally appeared on a flag presented to our first statehood governor, William Dunn Moseley, at his inauguration in June 1845.
Moseley was a job-creator, owner of a fully staffed plantation in Jefferson County where at least 80 Africans learned valuable skills such as cotton-picking.
The flag was a demand that the federal government butt out of Florida’s highly profitable economic system woke types call “slavery.”
 Freedom!

The motto is an unapologetic assertion of states’ rights to treat certain people as badly as we want. It had a wide-ranging influence on the most important events in American history.
In his inaugural address as president of the Confederate States of America, Jefferson Davis, said, “All we ask is to be let alone.”
The libs in Washington didn’t let us alone, so we were forced to fire on Fort Sumter.
Four years ago, our governor revived another beloved symbol: the Gadsden Flag, the one with the coiled rattler warning, “Don’t Tread On Me.”
Great patriots still cherish the snake and his warning: They waved the flag when the America-hating Barack Obama became president, then they waved it again on Jan. 6, 2021, when True Americans rallied on a Day of Love at the Capitol, trying to stop the communists, the feminists, the gays, the immigrants, and the ungrateful minorities from stealing the election from our rightful liege lord, Donald J. Trump.
You can now get that handsome venom-shooter on a Florida license tag.
The governor exulted: “This is how we feel about our great country that is right now being systematically destroyed by the radical Left.”
The Jan. 6 Heritage American activists expressed their belief in white America by beating up Capitol cops and threatening civil rights.
Now you can drive your nativism.
Screw that patriotic pit viper on the back of your loaded F-150 and experience the extra special glow that comes from being on the wrong side of history.
And think of the pride you’ll feel when you whip that driver’s license out at the Publix Lotto counter or in the bar or when some minority cop pulls you over merely because you had six or seven Coors and might be drifting over into other people’s lanes.
That’s freedom!
Tell the Law to let you alone. You are a rocket-rocking, orange-squeezing, manatee sandwich-eating, gator-kissing real Floridian, and anybody who hates our freedoms can go live in Canada or Iceland or some other stupid place.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT can opt to help students through a new federal tax program
text:
It seems everyone is talking about Nicole Hannah-Jones’ recent New York Times piece describing the educational experiences of her daughter, Najya, in the New York City public schools. If you haven’t read it, suffice to say that those experiences were less than ideal.
In recent days there have been dozens, if not hundreds, of commentaries on Hannah-Jones’ piece, and each one seems to have a different take on who is the villain in the story. Writing in the NY Post, Daniel di Martino insists that it is teacher’s unions. In the Free Press, Coleman Hughes suggests that an unwillingness to discipline disruptive children is a large part of the problem. In Slate, Jill Filipovic identifies no clear villain, but notes we need to make sure we are, ”not lowering the bar just because some students have a harder time clearing it.”
What all the commentators can agree on is that many, many schools in the United States are deeply dysfunctional. And, for this reason, many, many U.S. school children are receiving (as Hughes puts it in the Free Press), “[not just] a subpar education; they get no education, period.”
Fortunately, help is on the way. In 2025 the federal government created a provision that could put over $270 billion dollars every year into our educational system. The money would come from an optional tax credit (the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit) which, starting January 1, allows each U.S. citizen who owes at least $1,700 in taxes to (instead of paying tax) donate up to that amount to a scholarship granting organization (SGO) of his or her choice. Unlike a tax deduction, the credit means the donation is completely cost-free to the taxpayer.
The SGOs would take the money raised and use it to pay for educational expenses for children in their respective states.  The term SGO is a misnomer, since the money disbursed need not be a scholarship in a traditional sense.  It could be used for any “qualified elementary or secondary education expense” and could be given to both public and private school students.  The law specifically allows expenses as diverse as books, technology, tutoring, extended day programs and special needs services.
Hannah-Jones’ article points out that disadvantaged school districts typically have less money available to them even though their student bodies have higher needs.  This is primarily because public schools in the U.S. are mostly funded from local property tax receipts. Raising taxes is clearly not possible in poorer areas where citizens are already struggling to make ends meet. The new tax credit breaks down the correlation between local property tax revenues and resources available to schools, providing a new mechanism for monies to flow to under-resourced schools.
What is the catch, you ask? Only one. Any taxpayer is eligible to donate (again, at no cost to him or herself) to a qualified SGO. However, if you want your gift to go to help students in your state, your governor has to opt in to the program. If not, you can only donate to a scholarship granting organization in a state whose governor has opted in.
You would think it would be a no-brainer for states to opt-in. However, the IRS reports that as of October 13, 31 have done so and Connecticut is not one of them.  SGOs need time to plan to handle the new donations that will be coming in. 
Given the potential benefit to their neediest students, my only question is, “What is Connecticut waiting for?”
Christopher Rhoads is an associate professor in the Neag School of Education at the University of Connecticut.  The views expressed here are his own and do not represent those of his institution.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Turek campaigns with former U.S. Sen. Tom Harkin in final stretch before election
text:
Democrat Josh Turek, running for U.S. Senate, spoke with a driver as he and former Iowa U.S. Sen. Tom Harkin knocked doors in Ottumwa Oct. 18, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)OTTUMWA — Democrat Josh Turek said Sunday he believed President Donald Trump “accurately identified the problem” Iowans face as they struggle with issues like rising costs — but he argued Trump and Republicans’ failure to lower prices since taking power will drive voters to support his campaign for U.S. Senate.
Turek was joined Sunday in Ottumwa by former U.S. Sen. Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat who served in the U.S. Senate for 30 years, for a door knocking and ‘get out the vote’ effort in the final days leading up to the Nov. 3, 2026 election. As Harkin and Turek rallied with Wapello County Democrats before heading out to knock doors around the city, Harkin told a crowd that he believed Turek has “real grit,” referencing the movie “True Grit” with John Wayne.
“I’ve got to tell you, Josh Turek has a real grit,” Harkin said. “He’ll outwork you. He’ll outwork any candidate. He’ll out-campaign you. And all of the time, keeping his sense of who he is and what he believes in and what he supports. You couldn’t ask — at this point in time in our country and what needs to be done in Washington to stop some of this madness, to get us back on a kind of an even keel, not one that’s way to the right or way to the left, but an even keel — you couldn’t ask for a better person to support than Josh Turek.”
Democrat Josh Turek, running for U.S. Senate, knocked doors in Ottumwa with former U.S. Sen. Tom Harkin Oct. 18, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Turek, a state representative from Council Bluffs, is facing U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, a Republican currently representing Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, in the election. On the campaign trail, Turek has highlighted his own moderate positions and willingness to work across the aisle. In recent campaign ads, the candidate has spoken about his support for strengthening border security and improving the U.S. immigration system, saying, “I’ll work with anyone to fix it, including President Trump.”
Trump won Iowa in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections, and Republicans have seen major victories in the state in recent election cycles, including an all-Republican federal delegation. But polls and political forecasters believe Democrats have an opportunity in Iowa this election to pick up the U.S. Senate seat, as well as other congressional and statewide offices.
When Harkin was in the U.S. Senate from 1985 to 2015, the Democrat served alongside longtime U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley, a Republican. Speaking with reporters, Harkin said he believed Iowa’s shift from a relatively “purple” state to strongly supporting Republicans in recent elections was less of a reflection of Iowans becoming more conservative and more about voters’ frustration with traditional politics.
“I just think that a lot of Iowans felt — rightfully so — that people in maybe in both parties were not really paying attention to their basic needs,” Harkin said. “They then sort of said, ‘Well, we’ll try something new and maybe flashy, like Trump.’ I mean, he is an engaging personality and so they kind of went that way, but I don’t believe it was anything permanent.
“I think Iowans decided that maybe we needed a change, but now their lives haven’t gotten any better. They’ve gotten worse, and that’s why I think this year Iowans once again are going to say, ‘Wait a minute. We need to have a new change because what we thought we were getting in the past, which would make our lives better, has not happened.’ And so I think now Iowans are looking for new types of representation,” Harkin said. “People have a new kind of an approach, a way of working in government to really make their lives better. So that’s why I think there’s going to be some big changes in this election.”
Turek agreed, saying he believed Trump’s message on the campaign trail in past cycles spoke to Iowans’ concerns.
“I think that Trump accurately identified the problem,” Turek said. “I mean, he was out there saying, ‘I’m going to drive down your grocery bill, your gas bill, your electric bill. I’m going to keep us out of forever wars.’ But it’s been exactly the opposite of what people have ended up getting. And so now I think that Iowans are really waking up.”
The Democratic candidate said Iowa is “uniquely hurting” because of Trump and Republicans’ policies, pointing to rural healthcare closures spurred in part by Medicaid cuts made in the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act, as well as the negative impacts of tariffs and the U.S. Iran war on Iowa’s agriculture economy.
Turek also argued Iowa is not a red state.
“We’re a common-sense state that has masqueraded red,” he said. “Thirty years, they send Senator Harkin up there along with Grassley. Trump’s last midterm, we win three of the four congressional races. … I think that Iowans, more than almost any other state, they vote for the person, not just the party. And I think that in me, they see one of them, a true Iowan, someone that’s gone through a lot of economic struggle, a lot of healthcare struggle, and someone that’s going to go up there, not to enrich myself, not to look out for the haves, the billionaires, large corporations, but someone’s going to go up there and actually fight for the people.”

title: Michigan Democrats rally for union support as 2026 get-out-the-vote effort begins
text:
Democratic Michigan gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson speaks at a rally hosted by the Michigan Democratic Party and the Northern Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026 in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — With just two weeks to go until the Nov. 3 general election, Michigan’s Democratic nominees rallied with union workers in an attempt to energize supporters in a wide get-out-the-vote effort.
The rally, hosted by the Michigan Democratic Party and the Northern Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters, was held Sunday at the Detroit Union Carpenters and Millwrights Skilled Training Center in Detroit.
U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial candidate and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson headlined the rally, which also featured Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist, the Democratic nominee for secretary of state; Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, the Democratic attorney general nominee; and state Rep. Donavan McKinney (D-Detroit), the Democratic nominee in the 13th Congressional District. House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) and Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield also spoke at the rally.
Each candidate and nominee boasted about their union support in their respective races and touched on the stakes of the election — especially as they try to capitalize on the favorable environment for their party in the upcoming contest.
Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a rally hosted by the Michigan Democratic Party and the Northern Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026 in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Benson said she was bullish on the party’s chances.
“Are you guys ready to shock the nation and elect Democrats up and down the ballot in 16 days?” Benson said to a fired-up crowd of workers. “Are you ready to build more things in Michigan and create more well-paid union jobs for the people of this state? Are you ready to fight for democracy? Well, I am too.”
Benson said she understands the needs of working people because her parents were special education teachers. She pledged to continue fighting for workers’ rights if elected governor. Benson faces the Republican nominee, U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township).
“I know tariffs and the war in Iran are cutting jobs and raising prices on gas and groceries and just about everything we buy. And that’s why, as governor, I’m going to go to the mat for you and use every tool in my toolbox to ensure we’re protecting our jobs and lowering our prices,” Benson said. “I know that that is what Michiganders deserve, and I know our opponents have no plan to do any of that. We will ensure that Michigan’s workers are the centerpiece of everything we do for our economy.”
Members of the Northern Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters listen to Michigan’s 2026 Democratic candidates at a rally on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026 in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
El-Sayed, who has positioned himself as the pro-union candidate in his race with former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-White Lake), said that he would aim to create an environment for workers that allows for union organizing in every sector of American life.
“We’re going to stand with working people against the corporations who, for too long, have been able to dictate terms so that they can make a second $1 billion, while our folks struggle to make their first $100,000,” El-Sayed said. “And while we’re at it … we’re going to make sure that corporations can’t continue to buy and sell politicians in the same way that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump have been bought and sold their entire career.”
Vance calls Michigan’s U.S. Senate race a ‘test’ of gratitude versus grievance in rally for Rogers

El-Sayed also noted that despite the opposition he’s received en masse from Republican leaders including President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, he’s been focused on talking about issues that affect working people instead of making this race about him and his story. Vance recently delivered remarks in Michigan that focused heavily on El-Sayed, his platform and his comments on his Muslim faith.
“They don’t know Michiganders,” El-Sayed said. “We’re open-minded and we’re big-hearted. We’re earnest and we’re gritty. We just don’t want to be taken advantage of by a billionaire from New York or a millionaire from Florida. … We’re not going to back down for the next 16 days, or the next six years after that, because it’s our union movement, it is our state of Michigan, and we aim to stand up for it and protect it.”
Detroit will be a major battleground for the candidates. Rogers, in particular, is seeking to chip away at El-Sayed’s support there, where U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) performed strongest against him in the primary. While Detroit, a majority-Black city, has consistently backed Democratic candidates, Rogers has been exploiting division within the party by courting Black voters who preferred Stevens in August and those who have reservations about El-Sayed. That outreach includes members of the Jewish community in Detroit and its surrounding suburbs.
Rogers opened a Detroit field office this weekend to further those goals.
Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield speaks at a rally hosted by the Northern Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026 in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Sheffield urged Detroiters to turn out for the party in light of those attempts to chip into the Democratic base.
“Electing them is going to take all of us. We cannot take anything for granted,” Sheffield said. “We can’t stand on the sidelines when so much we know is at stake. Our voices have power. Our votes have power. And when we vote, we help decide what comes next. What comes next for our families and for our communities and for our state.”

name: VTDigger
title: Then Again: Hoff overcame opponent and power of incumbency to make history
text:
The Times Argus newspaper of Nov. 7, 1962 announces Phil Hoff’s stunning victory. Via Newspapers.com
History is not destiny. That said, historically speaking, if you want to get elected governor of Vermont, it helps to already be governor of Vermont. Incumbency has historically offered a tremendous electoral advantage. In fact, it has been 64 years since an incumbent governor has lost an election. That’s 23 times in a row that an incumbent governor has stood for re-election and won. 
That streak makes Vermont an outlier nationally. (Incumbents in Connecticut have streaks dating further back, but they have needed to stand for re-election less often because their terms run four years, not two as in Vermont.) Indeed, the election of 1962 marks the only time in the past 173 years that an incumbent Vermont governor has lost a general election.
Those statistics, however, don’t show what was going on behind the scenes to make that streak possible. Vermont was essentially a Republican-run state from 1854, when the party was founded, until 1962. Vermonters initially embraced the GOP for its opposition to slavery and stuck with it for a variety of reasons, including its fiscal conservatism, social policies, such as temperance and support for public schools over religious ones, and party loyalty. During those years, the real action was in the GOP primary — whoever won the primary was a lock to win the general election. But “action” is probably too strong a word. Republican party leaders devised an orderly succession within state government. Politicians were expected to work their way up a ladder, from speaker of the Vermont House to lieutenant governor to governor. In addition, party leaders worked to quell any regional rivalries by ensuring that politicians from the east and west sides of the Green Mountains alternated who held each office. The GOP’s succession system, dubbed “the Mountain Rule,” functioned smoothly for more than a century.
The only hiccup came in 1946, when Gov. Mortimer Proctor, the fourth member of his family to serve as governor, lost in the Republican primary to Ernest Gibson, Jr., a charismatic World War II veteran and former U.S. Senator who broke ranks by challenging a sitting governor. Although Gibson’s subsequent victory in the general election was yet another win for Republicans, his campaign represented a threat to the party leaders’ authority.
If the 1946 Republican primary showed that the establishment was starting to lose control of the GOP, the general election in 1962 demonstrated that the party itself had lost its grip on the state.
The first signs of weakness appeared in 1958 when Democrat William Meyer won the election to the U.S. House from Vermont. It was the Democrats’ first statewide victory in 105 years and the first statewide defeat for a Vermont Republican ever. In Vermont, Meyer benefited from a divided Republican party, a weak Republican challenger, and strong candidates at the top of the state’s Democratic ticket who brought supporters out to vote. 
Nearly as alarming for GOP leaders was that year’s gubernatorial election, which saw Democratic challenger Bernard Leddy lose by only 781 votes to Robert Stafford. The barely triumphant Stafford blamed Republicans’ lackluster performance on a lack of “effective party discipline.”
Meanwhile, even after newly elected Democratic Congressman Meyer’s startling victory, the Democrats failed to gain momentum immediately. In the 1960 election, all of the party’s statewide candidates, including incumbent Meyer, lost. Stafford, sensing Meyer’s weakness, had challenged and defeated the Democrat instead of running for re-election as governor. 
If you take the long view in politics, however, sometimes you can win by losing. The result in the 1960 gubernatorial race, won by Republican House Speaker F. Ray Keyser, ended up creating the circumstances that would make Democrats a statewide force for the first time since before the Civil War.
Keyser had not been most Vermont Republicans’ first choice for governor. In the primary, Keyser was set to face Lt. Gov. Robert Babcock and Vermont House member W. Arthur Simpson. Party insiders thought Babcock would make the strongest candidate. The situation became more complicated, however, when Babcock inadvertently turned the primary into a four-man race. Brattleboro attorney A. Luke Crispe hadn’t planned to run for governor that year—until Babcock tried to talk him out of it. 
In Sam Hand’s history of the Vermont Republican Party, “The Star That Set,” Crispe recalled:
“We were having a drink and discussing it, and Bob said, ‘Luke, you can’t win. You know what happened to you two years ago, and the people won’t forgive you’—these were not his exact words but the gist of it—‘for becoming intoxicated or drunk on two or three occasions.’ And I said, ‘Bob, I couldn’t make up my mind but I just made it up. Now I’m going to run and prove to you that I can stay sober in a campaign,’ and had I stayed out of it, Bob would have been Governor.”  
Instead, Keyser won the primary with just 29.6% of the vote, finishing 729 votes ahead of Babcock. Crispe finished a respectable third.
With a pronounced receding hairline, Keyser looked perhaps a decade older than his true age. He was in fact just 33 years old, the youngest governor ever elected in Vermont. At the time, he was also the nation’s youngest governor and, as Hand noted, “quickly settled in as its most beleaguered.”
Despite overwhelming Republican majorities in Vermont’s House and Senate, Keyser never held sway over the state Legislature, where factionalism made the body nearly ungovernable. The 1961 legislative session dragged on for nearly seven months, the longest in history at that point, the press reported. 

As a handsome and charismatic Navy veteran, Phil Hoff reminded many people of the recently elected President John F. Kennedy. Wikimedia Commons

The session was also noteworthy for the emergence of a bipartisan coalition of first-term legislators, dubbed the Young Turks, who cooperated to pass liberal reforms. Although they weren’t always successful, the Young Turks drew favorable press coverage that brought them to public attention. 
Though only 37 and in his first term in office, one of the Young Turks, Democrat Rep. Phil Hoff of Burlington, decided to challenge Keyser in the next election. Keyser had done little to make himself popular with members of his own party. Republican Young Turk Rep. Richard Mallary complained that the governor “for reasons best known to himself…has worked harder and longer” on a bill that would benefit power companies by repealing an electricity tax “than on any other single piece of legislation.” 
Keyser also locked horns with Sen. Asa Bloomer of Rutland over how to implement a court-ordered reapportionment of the state Senate. Over Bloomer’s objections, Keyser successfully pushed for Rutland County to lose a Senate seat that was given to Chittenden County. Democrats hoped Republican dissatisfaction with Keyser would result in some GOP voters crossing over to support Hoff.
In Hoff, the Democrats had a candidate who reminded many people of recently elected President John F. Kennedy; both were young, handsome, and charismatic Navy veterans. Unlike Kennedy, however, Hoff was a Protestant, so he would avoid the anti-Catholic bias that existed in some rural areas.
Vermont had such a long history as a Republican bastion that Democrats knew defeating even an unpopular governor would be a stiff challenge. As part of their strategy, Democrats wanted to ensure that the most popular Vermont Republican of the day, U.S. Sen. George Aiken, didn’t feel threatened in his re-election bid. The last thing Democrats needed was an energized Aiken to mount an aggressive campaign that would draw large numbers of Republicans out to vote. 
Seeing Aiken as unbeatable, Democrat leaders put forward W. Robert Johnson, who called himself a “political neophyte.” Aiken felt so confident of his imminent victory that just days before the election, he magnanimously commented, “Bob Johnson is a good neighbor, and a good member of the business community. If you vote for him Tuesday, you’ll be voting for a good man.” 
The gambit seemed to work. With Aiken not actively campaigning, and it being a midterm election, many Republican voters stayed home. Republican turnout dropped 35 percent compared to the election of 1960. Democrat turnout also fell, but by only about half as much. 
Late on election night, Tuesday, Nov. 6, 1962, the Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS) declared that Keyser had been re-elected. But shortly after midnight Winooski, the last of Vermont’s 246 communities reporting votes, announced that Hoff had won an overwhelming victory in that city, taking roughly 90 percent of the vote. Winooski’s tally put Hoff over the top. According to newspaper reports the next morning, Hoff had won the state by a mere 759 votes. The count was close enough that Keyser demanded a recount, but the resulting count only increased Hoff’s winning margin. Still, it had been a very tight election; Hoff prevailed by only about 1%.
Some observers, including some Vermont Republicans, viewed Hoff’s election as a chance to redefine Vermont. Former Gov. Gibson sent his well wishes: “(Y)our election is a good thing for Vermont, and I think a breath of fresh air into the musty tombs of our state administration will re-invigorate and put life into our state — perhaps I should say cause a reincarnation.” 
Phillip H. Hoff for Governor poster, from the Vermont Historical Society Museum, Montpelier Vermont
With Hoff’s victory, Republicans’ complete dominance in statewide elections ended. In fact, in the following election in 1964 Democrats took most of the statewide offices; Hoff won reelection, while fellow Democrats won the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, treasurer, and auditor of accounts races. 
That is not to say that Republicans disappeared from the political scene. Far from it. It’s just that since Hoff was elected, power has been shared more equally between the two major parties. For example, since 1962 Democrats have held the governor’s office for roughly 33 years and the Republicans for about 30. Meanwhile, Progressives and Independents have also won statewide office. 
Vermont’s political history is nuanced, ever-changing, and deeply human. Like financial advisers warning their clients, the only certainty is that “past performance is not indicative of future results.”   
While history tells us that incumbency has represented a definite advantage in Vermont, there are no guarantees in politics. History cannot predict the future, much like financial advisors who warn that “past performance is not indicative of future results.”

title: After Iowan’s death, assisted living company fires regional administrator
text:
Lawton Senior Living, an assisted living center in Woodbury County. (Photo via Google Earth)  An assisted-living company recently fired one of its top administrators after a resident death in Iowa resulted in a care facility being cited for numerous violations and its license being downgraded to conditional status.
State records indicate Natasha Kanealy, 39, began working for Jaybird Senior Living, also known as JSL Workforce Solutions, in July 2017, most recently as the company’s full-time regional director of clinical operations.
In 2025, the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing inspectors visited one of the company’s facilities, the Parker Place Retirement Community, which is an assisted living center in Parkersburg. DIAL ordered Parker Place to stop accepting new patients, while also placing the facility’s license on conditional status. Parker Place was one of the businesses over which Kanealy had oversight responsibilities, according to state workforce records.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In August 2026, DIAL inspectors investigated another of the company’s businesses, Lawton Senior Living, an assisted living center in Woodbury County, and issued a report citing the facility for 31 regulatory violations.
Inspectors said the Lawton home’s “management company failed to provide adequate oversight and operational direction to maintain a safe, healthy environment and ensure consistent service delivery to tenants at Lawton Senior Living.” The inspectors described what they called “systemic breakdowns” in operations, resulting in unsanitary living conditions, a lack of completed background checks on staff, a failure to respond to “significant” medical events, and also noted “chronic staffing shortages” that had left the home’s memory care unit understaffed.
Caregiver of resident who died was 16 years old  
The inspectors reported that an 88-year-old female resident of the home was taken to a hospital emergency room by ambulance on April 6, 2026, and was diagnosed with multiple wounds, including bruises and skin tears on her arms, legs and face, as well as multiple fractured ribs and a broken hip. The woman died two weeks later, with medical records showing evidence of blunt force trauma with head and neck contusions.
A subsequent investigation indicated that a 16-year-old universal worker at the home had been working alone in the dementia-care unit with woman and nine other residents, during an evening shift when the woman’s injuries were most likely sustained. The teenager allegedly told inspectors he saw the woman fall to the floor and that although she was not making sounds or speaking after the incident, he had put her to bed without informing a nurse or documenting the alleged fall.
According to the DIAL inspectors, some of the staff later concluded the injuries most likely were caused not by a fall but by an employee of the home. Inspectors say the state medical examiner said he could not determine the cause of death but that the injuries to the woman’s left side suggested they were not the result of her falling on her right side as had been reported.
According to state inspection reports, the 16-year-old employee was fired the day the injured woman was taken to the hospital. The youth allegedly told inspectors he had completed all his training at the home on a computer, was given no hands-on training, and had not worked with a nurse on his skills. He also alleged he had been given no specific training on emergency situations, the individual residents, or the residents’ care plans.
In addition, inspectors reported, records showed the youth and two other employees had administered medications to residents without having completed the required, DIAL-approved course on medication management.
As a 16-year-old employee, inspectors reported, the youth was not “old enough to pass medication,” regardless of training. In Iowa, individuals as young as 16 can work in health-care settings such as assisted living centers and can also become certified nursing assistants.
According to state records, one employee of the Lawton home told inspectors the 16-year-old universal worker had been tasked with training him to work in the memory care unit, but that the teenager then told him he didn’t like training his co-workers and did not like people.
Previous deaths at Jaybird-managed homes
State inspectors said they reviewed 15 employee files and found that in five of the 15 cases, the home had not completed the mandatory background checks on those individuals before putting them to work in the home.
After citing Lawton Senior Living for 31 regulatory violations, DIAL fined the facility $13,500. Because Jaybird Senior Living didn’t appeal the fine, DIAL then reduced the penalty 35% to $8,775.
State workforce records indicate that on Aug. 17, 2026, Jaybird Senior Living fired Kanealy for allegedly failing to meet the “essential leadership, clinical oversight, regulatory compliance, and accountability responsibilities” of the job. Kanealy then applied for unemployment benefits, which led to a Sept. 29, 2026, hearing before Administrative Law Judge Daniel Zeno.
In a recent decision, Zeno ruled that Kanealy was entitled to collect unemployment benefits, finding that she had “attempted to perform the job to the best of her ability.” Kanealy’s inability to meet her employer’s work expectations did not establish the sort of job-related misconduct that would disqualify her from collecting benefits, Zeno stated in his ruling.
“The employer did what was in its best interest and ended Ms. Kanealy’s employment, but the employer has not established disqualifying, job-related misconduct,” Zeno ruled.
Jaybird Senior Living is headquartered in Cedar Rapids and manages 17 care facilities in Iowa, as well as 28 facilities in 10 other states. Jaybird manages Bondurant’s Courtyard Estates at Hawthorne Crossing, the assisted living facility where 77-year-old Lynne Stewart froze to death in January 2022. Jaybird is also the former manager of Keelson Harbour Senior Living, an assisted living center in Spirit Lake where 95-year-old Elaine Creasey froze to death in December 2021.
No criminal charges were filed in the Keelson Harbour death, but in the Courtyard Estates case, a caregiver was charged with second-degree murder before prosecutors agreed to a plea deal that resulted in the murder charge being downgraded to misdemeanor dependent adult abuse.
Jaybird is a for-profit company headed by CEO Kevin Russell, a former lawyer and investment banker from Rancho Santa Fe, California.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Kanealy, Russell or the two Jaybird executives who testified at Kanealy’s unemployment hearing.

title: Vermont colleges should recruit closer to home
text:
Dear Editor,
If Vermont schools hadn’t overlooked the current pool of stateside kids looking for a quality Vermont college, enrollment at those places wouldn’t have collapsed as it has. Until college administrators get smart, they’ll have a parade of international students using Vermont as an entryway to America and not for higher learning. 

READ MORE

Why weren’t students from northern New England, where I lived for 42 years, and other stateside locations tapped for Vermont’s schools? Why does it seem that Vermont was chasing the elusive — frankly, nonexistent — international students well-versed in English who wanted to stay in Vermont after graduation? In my opinion, that pool doesn’t exist. 
Meanwhile, Vermont offers fewer and fewer choices for colleges. 
Betty LaChausseeBoca Raton, Fla.
